66186276B48953429733047.name: Idaho
66186276B48953429733047.summary:
A trans visitor to Idaho stands under the United States federal framework in every respect concerning documents and entry. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', and that an applicant declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening that matches one's presentation.

Within Idaho, facility use is criminalised. House Bill 752, signed by the governor and effective 1 July 2026, makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room that does not match their birth sex in government buildings and in any private business open to the public, including gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues and hospitals. The first offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to one year in jail; a repeat offence within five years carries a felony of up to five years.

Contested status is the practical reality rather than settled law. On 30 April 2026 the ACLU of Idaho filed suit arguing that HB 752 violates due process, equal protection and privacy and targets no actual criminal conduct; six transgender Idahoans brought the challenge before the law's 1 July 2026 effect. The ACLU describes the measure as the only state law extending bathroom criminalisation to private businesses and as carrying steeper penalties than other states' bans. National wire reporting on the legislature's passage of the ban and the jail threats it carries states that the lawsuit has partially blocked it.

A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.

66186276B48953429733047.tangentialFactors:
Idaho's facility law sits inside a wider pattern. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban.

Enforcement has already produced an arrest. In April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Identity documents are the other fast-moving restriction. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, with rights groups describing the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.
66186276B48953429733047.localsOnly:
Four successive legislative rounds ran in Idaho from 2023 to 2026, culminating in HB 752; the law reaches residents and visitors alike, since liability turns on birth sex rather than on documents presented or residency status.

Facility liability attaches in settings residents use routinely: government buildings and public-facing private businesses, with the enumerations covering gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues and hospitals. A second qualifying offence within five years is charged as a felony carrying up to five years, so a resident's exposure escalates on repetition rather than on the seriousness of any underlying conduct, which the ACLU's filing states the law does not address.

The constitutional challenge was brought by six transgender Idahoans alongside the ACLU's 30 April 2026 filing, and rests on due-process, equal-protection and privacy grounds.

66186276B41335105066757.name: Louisiana
66186276B41335105066757.summary:
Louisiana stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, effective January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted. Passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until they expire, but trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The American Civil Liberties Union has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on documentation and on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports. A trans visitor entering Louisiana can therefore expect documents that do not match their presentation.

Visa exposure is a separate matter. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code SWS25. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. Airport screening carries a further disclosure risk: the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to Transportation Security Administration officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Violence risk in Louisiana is measured independently of its legal position. Louisiana records the highest per-capita killing rate of trans women of any state: 24.7 per 100,000 trans women per year on a reported basis, with 19 recorded cases, against 23.5 for the state that ranks highest on legal-safety measures. The figures rest on a base of 428 United States victims across 2008 to 2025, and every figure is an undercount floor rather than a total. The analysis reporting the rate cautions that legal-risk rankings do not sort physical safety, and notes that the states holding the worst legal positions hold the highest measured killing rates.

The attack on a trans couple in August 2026 shows how that risk interacts with local procedure. Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders were beaten by a mob at Cypress Black Bayou Park in Benton over restroom use. Sanders, who has a pre-existing spinal injury, and Rush, who sustained a concussion and blood pooling, were both charged with disturbing the peace while no attacker was arrested. Rush was denied hospital care, was jailed in a men's facility and was searched by a male guard despite a 'female' marker on her driver's licence. The plea deal offered to the couple had not been signed. The municipality simultaneously voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances, and the Sheriff's Office confirmed that no one else was arrested that day.

Custody exposure for trans residents of Louisiana is documented and deadly. Yella (Robert) Clark Jr., a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence at Angola prison, was killed in a fight with several inmates on 2 April 2024. Her death was at least the 16th killing of a trans or gender-expansive person recorded by the Human Rights Campaign that year and the fifth that April alone. Deaths of trans and gender-expansive people in custody are systematically under- or mis-reported, so the recorded count understates the pattern.

The conduct of custody authorities is a documented risk for trans residents. Deaths of trans and gender-expansive people in custody are systematically under- or mis-reported, so official counts understate the pattern.

Charging decisions can fall on victims rather than attackers. Rush and Sanders were charged with disturbing the peace while no attacker was arrested, and the Sheriff's Office confirmed that no one else was arrested that day. Civil-rights attorneys who reviewed the case noted that the plea deal offered had not been signed.

Entry and screening add two further exposures. 66186276B52324970173776.name: Tennessee
66186276B52324970173776.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to the United States. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted; passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Identity-document rules are the fastest-moving area of restriction at state level. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, with rights groups describing the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the documents a visitor is asked to produce are read against the rules of the state they are standing in.

Facility use is regulated in a substantial number of states. Bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement is not theoretical: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Within that national picture, Tennessee's Adult Entertainment Act (2023, SB 3/HB 9) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment', a definition that explicitly includes 'male or female impersonators', on public property or anywhere a child could see it. A first offence is a Class A misdemeanour carrying up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine; a second violation is a Class E felony carrying 1 to 6 years and fines to $3,000. The reach of the definition means gender-expression itself, not the content of a performance, is what the statute penalises, so public visibility carries criminal exposure rather than only venue-level licensing consequences.

The statute is enforceable and current. It survived federal challenge on procedural grounds, the appeals-court ruling upholding it stands after the Supreme Court refused to hear the challenges in February 2025, and a separate suit brought by performers remains ongoing.

A further Tennessee measure narrows access to shelter. Under the 2026 'Riley Gaines Women's Safety and Protection Act', trans women are barred from women's shelters, which removes a common emergency resource for a trans visitor in distress.

Advocate: the Supreme Court refused to hear challenges to Tennessee's drag ban, leaving the appeals-court ruling upholding the 2023 Adult Entertainment Act in place; a separate suit remains ongoing, with performers saying they refuse to be silenced.

The Needle national analysis (July 2026, TGEU/Williams data): Tennessee's killing rate of trans women runs at 7.8 per 100k per year (10 recorded deaths, 2008–2025, an undercount floor), and the state is graded in the 'Worst Laws Passed' tier.

66186276B64014601259366.name: Kansas
66186276B64014601259366.summary:
Visitors stand under the United States federal framework in every state. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passport applications are issued only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted, while passports already bearing an X remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

Facility use is regulated across a substantial part of the country. Bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans by gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Kansas sits at the restrictive end of that pattern. SB 244, signed in February 2026, confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in government buildings and creates new civil and criminal penalties, including a private right of action under which an individual may sue a person suspected of a violation for roughly $1,000. The law bars updating driver's licences and state IDs and invalidates existing licences whose gender marker is inconsistent with sex assigned at birth. The Department of Revenue has been mailing written notice, and many holders have already been told their licence is now invalid.

Kansas is one of four states designated do-not-travel for trans people. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the most recent addition, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends. An advisory assessment dated 20 February 2026 moved Kansas from 'Worst Laws' to 'Do Not Travel', the first such addition in a year, following the bathroom-bounty provision that lets private individuals sue trans people encountered in wrong-sex facilities.

Litigation is already running. Within days of SB 244's enactment in late February 2026, two trans men filed Doe v. State of Kansas in Douglas County District Court, represented by the ACLU and Ballard Spahr, citing fear of violence under the bathroom-restriction and ID-invalidation law.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country, advisories that followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

66186276B69138566591314.name: Mississippi
66186276B69138566591314.summary:
Mississippi lies within the United States national framework on travel documents and entry, and that framework is the first exposure a trans visitor faces. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, so new passports are issued only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, while passports already issued with an X marker stay valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment.

Entry and screening add two further exposures under the same national rules. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 provide that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', and that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. At the checkpoint, secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, according to the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide.

Mississippi's own law is among the most restrictive. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records that Mississippi enacted bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity in 2024 and 2025, and that the state defines sex by birth in statute. The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update places Mississippi in its 'Worst Laws Passed' category, among states the assessment describes as having legislatively erased transgender people; that grading derives from a five-year legislation-tracking methodology with a scoring rubric.

Judicial treatment of gender transition is settled against the petitioner. On 17 April 2025 the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a transgender teen undergoing gender transition cannot change his name, denying a petition filed nearly two years earlier by a then-16-year-old whose parents both consented. The majority opinion by Justice James D. Maxwell II referred to the trans boy as a 'minor female' and cited the 2023 REAP Act, which bans both surgical and non-surgical treatments for transgender minors, as Mississippi's express public policy against children receiving gender-transition assistance; a chancellor may grant a minor's name change only where clearly in the child's best interest.

Violence risk is documented at a rate above the national comparison line. A state-by-state analysis of killings of trans women published on 16 July 2026, covering 2008 to 2025 and adjusted for undercounting, records 6.6 such killings per 100,000 trans women per year for Mississippi, against a US general-population homicide rate of 6.0 per 100,000 printed as the comparison. One federal prosecution cuts the other way: the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Mississippi reported that Joshua Brandon Vallum was sentenced to 49 years in federal prison for the bias-motivated murder of a transgender woman in Lucedale.

66186276B83300161667341.summary:
Visitors stand under the national framework in every state. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until they expire. Travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. A civil-liberties union has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement refusing visas to trans athletes seeking to enter to compete in women's sporting events, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Oklahoma restricts facility use by statute. The Movement Advancement Project's national tracker lists Oklahoma under K-12 school-facility bans, with enactments in 2022 and again in 2025, grouping it with the states that bar transgender people from bathrooms and facilities matching their gender identity. Nationally, such bans are in force in nine states and one territory, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances.

Birth certificates are the live document question in Oklahoma. House Bill 1225, which would require a male or female designation on Oklahoma birth certificates and prohibit changes with very little exception, passed its most recent vote 70-17 and headed to Governor Kevin Stitt's desk as of 6 May 2026. Its authors say it is designed to strengthen the existing law being challenged in federal court by transgender plaintiffs including Tulsa resident Rowan Fowler, and the state Attorney General's office confirmed the bill clarifies that Oklahoma never permitted gender birth-certificate changes; critics called it further discrimination.

The July 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map assigns Oklahoma its per-state grade and lists the state among the worst for legislation targeting transgender adults. That edition added a fourth 'Do Not Travel' state and tracked changes to the 'Worst Laws Passed' tier.

66186276B98021244841737.name: Alabama
66186276B98021244841737.summary:
Alabama stands under the United States national framework, which applies in every state. Travel documents are the sharpest exposure: since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents. Passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

Identity documents are the fastest-moving area of restriction at state level. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers; rights groups describe the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the rules a visitor encounters depend heavily on the state involved.

Facility use is regulated in a substantial number of states. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement is documented: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Alabama's own facility bans, enacted in 2022 and 2024, are in force. The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update records that Alabama's 'Don't Say Gay' bill carries a bathroom ban extending to college campuses, placing the state in the assessment's worst-law grouping of legislatively-eroding jurisdictions. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map tabulates these state bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity.

Foreign governments have responded publicly. Following the federal document and data rules, multiple countries issued advisories warning their trans citizens about travelling to the United States. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Internal risk assessments are equally stark. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.

Recorded killings of trans women in Alabama stand at 3.8 per 100,000 per year, an undercount floor, on the 428-victim base covering 2008 to 2025, according to The Needle's July 2026 national analysis using TGEU and Williams data. That analysis grades Alabama in the worst-law group.

66186276B82803899326534.summary:
Visitors to Indiana stand under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and now issues passports only as M or F from supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the department to proceed with its changed treatment. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged under the code 'SWS25' and an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth potentially treated as fraud and barred permanently. Airport screening carries a separate exposure: secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can disclose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers.

Indiana's identity documents are the sharpest state-level constraint. The Bureau of Motor Vehicles' ban on gender-marker changes to driver's licences and identification cards took effect on 1 February 2026, ending the long-standing route by which a resident could obtain such a change through a court-ordered gender change or a physician statement. 66186276B31593004124297.name: Utah
66186276B31593004124297.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor to Utah. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted. Passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad; the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Within Utah, facility use is the operative state rule. HB 257, 'Sex-based Designations for Privacy, Anti-bullying, and Women's Opportunities', was introduced on 11 January 2024 and signed by Governor Spencer Cox on 30 January 2024, requiring people to use bathrooms and locker rooms in public schools and government-owned buildings that match their sex assigned at birth. Trans people can defend themselves against complaints under the legislation by showing documentation of gender-affirming care, and new government buildings must include single-occupant bathrooms. The ACLU of Utah opposed the bill, warning that it risked discriminatory enforcement.

Utah also operates a reporting channel under HB 257: a form through which residents can report transgender people in 'privacy spaces' such as changing rooms and restrooms, with complainants able to choose whether their names are included while the state investigates each reported violation. Reporting describes the statute as barring trans Utahns from using bathrooms or competing in a sport that matches their gender identity.

66186276B38006515706420.name: South Dakota
66186276B38006515706420.summary:
South Dakota stands under the United States national framework, and that framework is the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted; passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Within that national frame, South Dakota's own restriction is a facility ban. Governor Larry Rhoden's office announced on Friday 21 March 2025 that he had signed House Bill 1259 the previous day, restricting trans people from using bathrooms matching their gender identity in public schools and state-owned buildings. The measure took effect on 1 July 2025 and marks the first time in state history that a comparable anti-trans bathroom bill has been placed on the books.

The bill's reach is institutional and specific. House Bill 1259 passed the state House by a 49-21 vote and limits restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas in state-run facilities to the same 'biological sex', primarily targeting K-12 schools and state colleges including off-campus activities. Its 'reasonable accommodation' clause and the floor debate raised the prospect that incarcerated trans people would be placed in solitary confinement in order to comply.

A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 lists South Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults, drawing on five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric for the worst bills, and records that federal policies continue to create legal difficulties for transgender people nationwide. The same assessment identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated.

sources.title: Governor signs bathroom bills mandating who can use which facilities | News Letter Journal (Wyoming News Exchange)
sources.summary: Wyoming News Exchange reported that on Monday, March 3, 2025, Gov. Mark Gordon signed two facility measures into law. House Bill 72, the 'Protecting privacy in public spaces act,' covers sex-designated restrooms, showers, sleeping quarters and locker rooms at public facilities. Senate File 62, 'Sex-designated facilities and public schools,' requires public school children from pre-kindergarten up, including charter school students, to use restrooms aligned with sex assigned at birth. SF 62 requires districts to provide a 'reasonable accommodation' to any student who does not wish to use a multiple-occupancy restroom or locker room matching the gender at that student's birth.

66186276B10933057601622.blindSummary:
Travel documents are the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor to this state/province, because it stands under the national framework of the parent nation. Since January 2025 a national executive order has required national identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the national passport authority stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are issued only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted. Passports already issued with a X remain valid until expiry, but trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. a national civil-liberties organisation is suing the passport authority on behalf of seven plaintiffs, a legal-aid organisation maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with national records, and the national supreme court recently allowed the passport authority to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. a national executive order of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a passport authority announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the parent nation to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'an internal marking'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure: a national transgender equality organisation's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to screening officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

Facility use is the sharpest state-level exposure here. On 3 March 2025 the governor signed House Bill 72, the 'Protecting Privacy in Public Spaces Act', which covers sex-designated restrooms, showers, sleeping quarters and locker rooms at public facilities. a trans visitor using any public restroom, shower, changing area or sleeping quarter in the state therefore acts against a statutory sex-designation rule rather than a matter of local custom. a national equality-mapping project carries the per-state/province list of bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, with the year each was enacted, and records these facility bans as signed in March 2025.

Schools are covered by the companion measure signed the same day. Senate File 62, 'Sex-Designated Facilities and Public Schools', requires public school children from pre-kindergarten up, including charter school students, to use restrooms aligned with sex assigned at birth, and requires districts to provide a 'reasonable accommodation' to any student who does not wish to use a multiple-occupancy restroom or locker room matching the gender at that student's birth. The provision governs residents and their children rather than visitors directly, but it fixes the same sex-designation principle across the state's education estate.

Independent assessments place this state/province at the restrictive end of the national picture. a legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 lists it among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults; the assessment is built from five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric identifying the worst bills, and it records that national policies keep creating legal difficulties for transgender people across the parent nation. The same assessment identified the latest state/province flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the national document and data rules. At least eight foreign countries adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the parent nation, advisories that followed detentions of foreign citizens over visa issues.

66186276B10933057601622.tangentialFactors:
Wyoming's facility statutes belong to a wider pattern rather than standing alone. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map documents bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity across multiple states, each with its enactment year, so a visitor crossing state lines encounters materially different rules within a single country. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban.

Enforcement of such statutes is no longer hypothetical anywhere in the country. In April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

The July 2026 risk assessment is a compiled judgement rather than a single statute: it draws on five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric for the worst bills, and was republished on 27 August 2026 by a regional LGBTQ outlet. Its authors record that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends, and that federal policies keep creating legal difficulties for trans people across the country.

Identity-document rules also vary sharply between states. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, which rights groups describe as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions.

66186276B64762166704956.name: West Virginia
66186276B64762166704956.summary:
Every visitor to West Virginia stands first under the federal travel-document regime. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required United States identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department stopped processing the X marker, and new passports are issued only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted. A trans or nonbinary visitor can therefore arrive holding papers that do not match their presentation, with airport screening and visa decisions following the same national rules, including the February 2025 State Department policy refusing visas to trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events.

West Virginia's own restriction is statutory and recently enacted. Governor Patrick Morrisey signed Senate Bill 456, the 'Riley Gaines Act', on 12 March 2025, after the state Senate passed it on 3 March and the House of Delegates on 6 March. The law defines 'woman' as an adult human of the female sex and 'man' as an adult human of the male sex, and frames its purpose as preserving women's single-sex spaces on that biological basis.

The facilities covered reach considerably further than restrooms. The statute names locker rooms, bathrooms, rape crisis centers, dormitories, prisons and domestic-violence shelters, which places a trans visitor inside its scope in university accommodation, correctional settings and victim-support services as well as in washrooms and changing areas. At the signing the governor stated that bathrooms, locker rooms, domestic violence shelters and rape crisis centers should be kept private for women only, an official statement of intent that shapes how the provisions are likely to be applied.

A national legal risk assessment dated July 2026 places West Virginia in its 'Worst States' group, a tier covering fifteen states and one step below the four states designated do-not-travel: Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas. The same assessment records Idaho as the most recently promoted do-not-travel state, the fourth so designated, following a felony bathroom ban carrying up to five years imprisonment that is partially blocked by courts but remains in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists. The assessment's national frame is one of worst policies in effect, with the 2026 legislative season continuing to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures.

66186276B86295910312663.summary:
Arkansas stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Act 619 became law on 11 April 2023, making Arkansas the fourth state to confine trans students to bathrooms matching their birth sex in K-12 schools, and the provision was amended and extended in 2025. Because the statute is directed at schools, a visitor's direct exposure to it is narrower than in states whose bans reach adult facilities in government buildings and other public places.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. 66186276B63937528568220.name: Iowa
66186276B63937528568220.summary:
A trans visitor to Iowa stands under the United States federal framework on travel documents and screening. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department stopped processing the X marker, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports. Visa decisions follow the same framework: Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes entering to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code SWS25, and an applicant declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening carries a separate exposure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guidance describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening matching one's presentation.

Iowa's public-facility-use rule is the sharpest state-specific exposure for a visitor. Senate File 482, signed by Governor Kim Reynolds on 22 March 2023 and effective immediately, requires anyone in an Iowa school, including students, staff, parents and visitors, to use only multiperson restrooms and changing areas that correspond with the biological sex listed on their birth certificate; the restriction reaches multiperson restrooms and locker rooms at public and private elementary and secondary schools. Single-person facilities are available to trans students who obtain written consent from a legal guardian. Des Moines news reporting at the time recorded Iowa school districts scrambling to comply as the restriction took effect.

Senate File 538, also signed on 22 March 2023, bars doctors from administering gender-affirming care to anyone under 18, covering puberty blockers, hormone therapy and transition-related surgery.

Iowa's adult coverage position is narrower than its minor-care ban. On 8 March 2019 the Iowa Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Good v. Iowa Department of Human Services that the state discriminated against two transgender women by denying their Medicaid claims for transition-related surgery, holding that excluding Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming surgery violates the Iowa Civil Rights Act. The ACLU of Iowa litigation timeline records the path from the lawsuit filed on behalf of Mika Covington and Aiden Vasquez over Iowa Medicaid's refusal to cover medically necessary gender-affirming surgery through that March 2019 ruling and the litigation that followed, which kept Medicaid surgery coverage available to transgender adults in Iowa.

Assessments of legal risk place Iowa near the top of the restricted tier. Erin In The Morning's Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map of July 2026, published by Stonewall News on 27 August 2026, grades every state under a national frame of worst policies in effect; Iowa sits in 'The Worst States' group, comprising Alabama, Arkansas, Iowa, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi, Ohio, Oklahoma, North Dakota, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, West Virginia and Wyoming. That tier is one below the 'Do Not Travel' designation held by Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas, where Idaho's top-tier status rests on a felony bathroom ban carrying up to five years, partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists, and Kansas on its bounty-hunter civil-suit regime.

The Movement Advancement Project's equality map catalogues state bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to gender identity, and is cited for Iowa's enacted facility ban and for an 18-state group defining sex as biological sex; Iowa is not listed among states defining sex by birth in statute.

66186276B79689460185872.name: South Carolina
66186276B79689460185872.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor to the United States. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, so new passport applications are issued only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

South Carolina's facility ban, enacted in 2024, now reaches campuses. Governor Henry McMaster signed House Bill 4756 into law on 15 May 2026, requiring transgender students in South Carolina public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth. The Senate amended the bill before passage, and the ACLU of South Carolina issued a response on 18 May 2026 framing the measure as discrimination against trans students in K-12 and higher education.

Restriction also reaches people in state custody. Reporting by Metro Weekly of 11 July 2026, drawing on the Transitics tracker, records South Carolina as one of four states, alongside Tennessee, Arkansas and Utah, holding 'freeze-frame' policies that restrict the treatments transgender inmates may receive while incarcerated. That documentation establishes an in-prison treatment restriction. The article records no South Carolina case or ruling on cell placement, special units, or solitary or segregation for trans prisoners.

66186276B65591139260314.name: Florida
66186276B65591139260314.summary:
Florida stands under the United States national framework, which sets the sharpest risks for a trans visitor. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the department to proceed with its changed treatment. Entry adds a second exposure: Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', and an applicant declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. Checkpoint screening carries a third, involuntary disclosure risk: secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers.

Florida's own 2023 facilities law (Fla. Stat. 553.865) makes remaining in a sex-segregated restroom or changing facility that does not match sex assigned at birth a criminal trespass once a government employee orders departure, punishable as a second-degree misdemeanour with up to 60 days in jail. The statute reaches every building owned or leased by state or local government, including state offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons and jails, local immigration detention, state parks and toll-road plazas, and it purports to cover all schools, public and private. Only private businesses fall outside its scope, and the ACLU advises fact-specific judgment and legal counsel rather than a general rule of safety.

Enforcement has moved from theory to arrest. Marcy Rheintgen, a 20-year-old trans college student, was charged on 19 March 2025 after police, alerted in advance, arrested her washing her hands in a women's restroom at the statehouse, following her declaration 'I am here to break the law' — believed to be the first arrest under Florida's transgender bathroom restrictions. On 20 June 2025 Leon County Judge Lashawn Riggans threw the trespass case out: as a defendant charged under the Safety in Private Spaces Act she had no standing to argue the law itself was illegitimate, so the statute was never substantively tested and its scope remains untested by a court.

66186276B73402293045483.name: Nebraska
66186276B73402293045483.summary:
Nebraska lies within the United States national framework, and that framework sets the first layer of exposure for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until they expire. The ACLU is litigating on behalf of seven plaintiffs and the Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment.

Entry and screening follow national rules rather than Nebraska law. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement refusing visas to trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events, with applicants flagged internally under the code SWS25 and a declared gender other than sex assigned at birth treated as fraud capable of permanent bar. At the checkpoint, secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can disclose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, and the National Center for Transgender Equality sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

At state level, Executive Order No. 23-16, signed by Governor Jim Pillen on 30 August 2023 and styled a Women's Bill of Rights, defines sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, declares a person's biological sex fixed at birth, and ends state recognition of transgender people. The order asserts biological differences in athletic ability and safety that warrant sex-based segregation in some athletic, social and educational spaces, and it backs single-sex access to bathrooms and changing rooms. A visitor using facilities in state buildings therefore encounters a regime that does not recognise a gender marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth.

Detention carries documented harm. Nebraska houses trans prisoners by sex assigned at birth in men's facilities, and on 10 August 2022 U.S. District Judge Brian C. Buescher ruled for prison officials in a suit brought by a transgender inmate identified only as Jane Doe, who was diagnosed with gender dysphoria and transitioning while held among male prisoners. She had been placed in a cell with a convicted male sex offender who assaulted her; the judge dismissed the failure-to-protect claim, the failure-to-treat and surgery-denial claims, writing that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could find the providers deliberately indifferent to her serious medical need and that she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. He also found no basis to infer a substantial risk from the cellmate's sexual-offence conviction coupled with her vulnerability as a transgender inmate transitioning in a men's prison.

66186276B22971435435932.name: Kentucky
66186276B22971435435932.summary:
Visitors to Kentucky stand under the United States federal framework on travel documents and screening. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passports are issued only as M or F, so a trans visitor's papers may not match their presentation. Airport screening, visa discretion and the refusal of visas to trans athletes seeking entry for women's sporting events are likewise national rules that apply on arrival in Kentucky as anywhere else in the country.

Kentucky has legislated against transgender facility use in its public schools. Senate Bill 150 was enacted on 29 March 2023 when the Kentucky legislature overrode Governor Andy Beshear's veto; the statute restricts which bathrooms transgender students may use in public schools and is the single 2023 Kentucky law carrying the K-12 facility restriction. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map, which catalogs such bans state by state, lists Kentucky's 2023 K-12 facility ban among its entries.

Direct exposure for a visitor is confined by the law's setting. The restriction governs restrooms in public schools rather than commercial premises, transport hubs or hotels, so an adult trans traveller is unlikely to encounter it outside a school building. The statute nonetheless places Kentucky among the states that have enacted facility restrictions against transgender people.

Implementation runs through local school districts. In April 2023 the Kentucky Department of Education issued guidance to districts on carrying out the 2023 rules, advising them to remove sex education from the fifth-grade curriculum and to tread cautiously with the bathroom-ban provisions. A visitor accompanying a child, or entering a school site, therefore encounters a restriction administered at district level under state guidance.

66186276B80192890672447.summary:
A trans visitor to Montana stands under the United States national travel-document regime. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth; new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. Travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports. A visitor's documents may therefore mismatch presentation or identity.

Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Montana has enacted state restrictions that would ordinarily rank it among the country's worst jurisdictions, including a facility-use ban and a public-buildings bathroom ban, but Montana's courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined those laws under the state constitution. Adult restrictions that were passed have not taken full effect. The practical position a visitor encounters in Montana therefore differs sharply from what the statutory book alone would suggest.

That court record makes Montana the single exception in the 2026 anti-trans legal-risk assessments: the only state whose grade improved, moving from 'worst laws' to 'high risk' in the February 2026 cycle as injunctions accumulated. The July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment ranks states by expert reading of bills covering adult and youth restrictions, and the same pattern of judicial blocking lifts Montana's standing in that assessment as well.

66186276B13694661525286.name: Missouri
66186276B13694661525286.summary:
A visitor to Missouri stands under the national framework of the United States in every setting. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passports are issued only as M or F, so a trans visitor's documents may not match their presentation. Airport screening and visa decisions follow the same national rules, including the State Department's February 2025 announcement that trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', with a declaration of a gender other than sex assigned at birth capable of being treated as fraud and a permanent bar.

Missouri prohibits gender-affirming medical care for minors. The Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, Senate Bill 49, took effect on 28 August 2023 after a judge denied a preliminary injunction sought by the ACLU of Missouri, Lambda Legal and other counsel; the statute bars hormones and puberty blockers for under-18s unless the patient was already in treatment, and prohibits all transition-related surgery for minors.

The litigation has moved against the plaintiffs at every stage. Suit was filed on 25 July 2023 in Cole County Circuit Court by three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA. A Missouri judge upheld Senate Bill 49 on 25 November 2024, and on 13 January 2026 the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously upheld the ban on transition surgeries, cross-sex hormones and other gender-affirming care for minors, quoting the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that upheld Tennessee's similar law. Counsel have said they would appeal, and the case continues toward trial on the merits.

Correctional settings are separately restricted. An appropriations law signed by Governor Mike Kehoe and effective 2 July 2026 bars any state funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery for transgender people in Missouri prisons, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. Missouri thereby became the seventh state, and the second in 2026 after Oklahoma, to ban such care for inmates; Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical statutes, while comparable measures in Idaho and Georgia were blocked by federal courts.

The SAFE Act also bars Missouri Medicaid from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, which reaches adults as well as minors, and exposes violating providers to licence revocation. The statute sunsets in 2027; lawmakers have signalled they want it made permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative seeks to ban such care indefinitely.

a visitor to the state stands under the national framework in every setting. an executive order of January 2025 requires national identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passports are issued only as M or F, so a trans visitor's documents may not match their presentation. Airport screening and visa decisions follow the same national rules, including the State Department's February 2025 announcement that trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'an internal marking', with a declaration of a gender other than sex assigned at birth capable of being treated as fraud and a permanent bar.

The state prohibits gender-affirming medical care for minors. The Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, Senate Bill 49, took effect on 28 August 2023 after a judge denied a preliminary injunction sought by the state ACLU affiliate, Lambda Legal and other counsel; the statute bars hormones and puberty blockers for under-18s unless the patient was already in treatment, and prohibits all transition-related surgery for minors.

The litigation has moved against the plaintiffs at every stage. Suit was filed on 25 July 2023 in a county circuit court by three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA. A state/province judge upheld Senate Bill 49 on 25 November 2024, and on 13 January 2026 the state supreme court unanimously upheld the ban on transition surgeries, cross-sex hormones and other gender-affirming care for minors, quoting the 2025 national supreme court ruling that upheld a comparable law in another state/province. Counsel have said they would appeal, and the case continues toward trial on the merits.

Correctional settings are separately restricted. an appropriations law signed by the governor and effective 2 July 2026 bars any state/province funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery for transgender people in state/province prisons, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. The state thereby became the seventh state/province, and the second in 2026 after one other state/province, to ban such care for inmates; three states have near-identical statutes, while comparable measures in two other states were blocked by national courts.

The SAFE Act also bars the state Medicaid programme from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, which reaches adults as well as minors, and exposes violating providers to licence revocation. The statute sunsets in 2027; lawmakers have signalled they want it made permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative seeks to ban such care indefinitely.

Missouri's restrictions sit inside a national pattern rather than standing alone. The federal document rules, the visa policy for trans athletes and TSA screening procedures apply to a visitor in Missouri exactly as they apply in every other state, and the National Center for Transgender Equality's guidance describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers.

Facility use is regulated in a substantial number of states: bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with some jurisdictions treating trans bathroom use as a criminal offence in certain circumstances, while twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred, with a trans student arrested and handcuffed at the Florida state capitol in April 2025 in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Identity documents vary sharply by state. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, described by rights groups as a template other legislatures are following; the Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes and on what conditions.

Foreign governments have responded to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens after detentions of European citizens over visa issues, and a national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four.

On the map's comparative scoring Missouri sits slightly below the national score of 0.36.
