66186276B62688952876525.name: Alaska
66186276B62688952876525.summary:
Alaska stands within the United States national framework, so the federal document rules bind every traveller arriving in Juneau, Anchorage or anywhere else in the state. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, and passports already issued with an X remain valid only until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the Department to proceed with its changed treatment. A visitor's passport can therefore mismatch their presentation and be lawfully refused a matching marker.

Entry screening carries two further national exposures. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', and that an applicant declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. At checkpoints, the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose trans status to TSA officers and other passengers.

Alaska's own record is graded Moderate in Erin In The Morning's national legal-risk assessment of July 2026, grouped with Kentucky and North Carolina: states that have passed one or two laws aimed at transgender adults, enacted multiple laws targeting transgender youth, or are advancing negative laws quickly. That places Alaska above the worst-law and do-not-travel tiers and below the protective groupings, slightly below the national score of 0.36. Idaho was flagged do-not-travel on 13 July 2026, bringing the total of so-designated states to four; Alaska is not among them.

Restriction in Alaska has arrived through appointed regulatory boards rather than the legislature. The Alaska State Medical Board, whose members are appointed by Gov. Mike Dunleavy, voted unanimously on 22 August 2025 to recommend restricting medical care for transgender youth and approved a draft regulation classifying gender-transition care for anyone under 18 as 'unprofessional conduct' subject to disciplinary action. That draft must still be vetted by the Alaska Department of Law and then pass through a 30-day public comment period, so it is not yet in force. No adult-care ban accompanies it.

Facility rules in Alaska are local rather than statewide. The Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District board voted 5-1 on 19 October 2022 to permanently require transgender students to use bathrooms matching their sex at birth or a private option such as the nurse's office, overturning guidelines that had stood for more than seven years; AP described the policy as an apparent first for Alaska. It binds a school district, not adult access to public facilities, and no adult facility ban is recorded for the state. Nine states and one territory do have school and government-building bathroom bans, and in April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed at the Florida state capitol in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Gov. Dunleavy's earlier bid to limit transgender students' access to single-sex facilities failed, while a board he appointed limited transgender girls' participation in girls' sports teams. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no facility ban at all, and the Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates, so the document rules a visitor encounters after entry depend on the state involved. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, advisories that followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

66186276B75419826371250.name: Georgia
66186276B75419826371250.summary:
Georgia stands under the national framework that governs every state. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F from supporting documents, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports. A visitor whose documents no longer match their presentation should expect that mismatch to surface at federal checkpoints.

Entry and screening follow national rules rather than Georgia law. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code SWS25, and that declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and a permanent bar. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose trans status to officers and other passengers.

At state level, the rules a visitor encounters vary sharply. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth, which rights groups describe as a template other legislatures are following; the Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes and on what conditions. Facility use is regulated in a substantial number of states: bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and enforcement has begun. In April 2025 a trans student who announced she was there to break the law and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, identified by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights.

Foreign governments have responded to the federal document rules with public advisories. At least eight countries abroad, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens, advisories that followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Within Georgia, a July 2026 national data analysis places the recorded killing rate for trans women at 4.8 per 100,000 per year, among the highest in the country. The figure is an acknowledged floor drawn from an undercounted monitoring project, and it sits at or near the state's general homicide baseline, which is itself elevated against the national average. Calibrated that way it indicates an elevated version of an existing, non-trans-specific violence risk rather than an organised anti-trans campaign, while remaining serious.

The documented street violence is concentrated in Atlanta. In April 2023 the Atlanta Police Department said it was actively investigating three violent crimes against transgender women in the city that year, after two Black transgender women were fatally shot a week apart; a January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition also remained open. The department acknowledged the epidemic-level violence that Black and Brown transgender women face.

Georgia restricts gender-affirming care for minors. Governor Brian Kemp signed Senate Bill 140 on 23 March 2023, barring licensed medical professionals from providing hormone therapy or surgery related to gender transition to patients under 18, with licence revocation as a possible penalty; minors who began hormone replacement therapy before 1 July 2023 may continue. The ban took effect on 1 July 2023, and the ACLU of Georgia said it would sue.

Coverage for adults and state employees moved in the opposite direction. In October 2023 plaintiffs announced a settlement with Georgia's State Health Benefit Plan in federal court in Atlanta, requiring the plan to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for employees, spouses and dependents, after a December 2022 lawsuit argued the plan discriminated by refusing to pay. The public-employee health plan's coverage of gender-affirming care therefore continued by settlement despite the 2023 care ban.

Care access has nonetheless contracted on the ground under federal funding pressure. Visitors to New Hampshire stand under the United States national framework in every respect that touches identity documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department no longer processes the X marker, and passports are issued only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted. Entry rules add a separate exposure. Within that national regime, New Hampshire carries an unusually high recorded incident load. GLAAD's 2025 national census documents 72 anti-LGBTQ incidents in New Hampshire during 2025, the second-highest count of any state after California's 198, and ahead of Texas at 66, Ohio at 50 and Washington at 50. The figure exceeds counts recorded in states with several times New Hampshire's population, which is the strongest single indicator in the sourced material of what a trans visitor may encounter on the ground.

Checkpoint and screening exposure follows national procedure: the National Center for Transgender Equality describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can disclose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department no longer processes the X marker, and passports already issued with it remain valid only until expiry. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 places Virginia in its Low-Risk States group, alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, defined as states that largely refrain from targeting transgender adults. The same assessment names Virginia with Arizona as a state that has enacted anti-trans policies affecting transgender youth which, on the assessment author's reading of state-specific factors, appear unlikely to be extended to adults. The practical exposure for an adult visitor therefore sits with the federal document, screening and visa rules rather than with any Virginia statute aimed at adults.

66186276B94082813086253.name: District of Columbia
66186276B94082813086253.summary:
The District of Columbia stands under the United States national framework: travel documents are the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F from supporting documents, and passports already carrying X remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports. Entry adds a second exposure: Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 refuse visas to trans athletes seeking to enter to compete in women's sporting events, flag applicants under the code 'SWS25', and treat a declared gender other than sex assigned at birth as potential fraud with permanent bar. Checkpoint screening can disclose status involuntarily, through secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs, as the National Center for Transgender Equality's guide describes.

As a national district, the District of Columbia is reached directly by the national legislature and the national executive, which is the structural reason its standing has changed. The national legislature attached a bathroom ban for the District of Columbia, and transgender-rights activists arrested while protesting that ban at the Capitol are covered in a report of 5 December 2024. The District's own protective local code remains on the books and the District itself has no facility ban as of the September 2026 confirmation, but the local layer is overridable from above; the direction of travel is mixed, and the jurisdiction no longer holds its former most-protective placement.

The July 2026 national legal risk assessment places the District of Columbia on its Low-Risk list alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Wisconsin, while stating that the District may no longer be considered most protective because it can come under attack from Congress and from executive actions. The same assessment designates Idaho the fourth state flagged do-not-travel for trans people and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.

66186276B78821008370123.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to the United States. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

The state-level picture a visitor enters differs sharply by jurisdiction. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, which rights groups describe as a template other legislatures are following. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances; twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred: in April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed after using a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Foreign governments have responded publicly. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Maine sits in the Low-Risk States group of a national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026. The same assessment separately flags that Maine has increased in risk because of capitulation over sports bans in the University of Maine system, and it identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated while recording that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.

The Maine risk signal traces to 21 March 2025, when the University of Maine System announced compliance with federal restrictions on trans sports participation after the US Department of Agriculture suspended federal funding for research and programs while investigating possible sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programmes. The system affirmed compliance with the new national rules once that funding was suspended, rather than defending its trans students and athletes. sources.title: Inmate at women's prison files suit over housing of transgender prisoner (Sun Journal, Maine)
sources.summary: Sun Journal (3 Apr 2026, Mark LaFlamme) reports that Maine Corrections houses Andrea Balcer, a 27-year-old transgender woman and convicted double murderer, in the women's facility at the Maine Correctional Center in Windham, where she has been held for at least a year as of April 2026, meaning placement by current gender identity rather than birth sex. On 3 Apr 2026 inmate Katie Mountain (41) filed a 30-page complaint against MDOC Commissioner Randall Liberty, Warden Ben Beal and Balcer, alleging chronic harassment and assault by the trans prisoner; attorney Cynthia Dill filed it. No ruling has been reported. The harassment and assault claims are allegations, while the placement of a trans woman in the women's prison is documented.

66186276B78821008370123.blindSummary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to the parent nation. Since January 2025, a national executive order requires national identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The national foreign ministry stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted; passports already issued with a X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. a national civil-liberties organisation has sued the foreign ministry on behalf of seven plaintiffs, a national legal-advocacy group maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with national records, and the highest court recently allowed the foreign ministry to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. an executive order of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a foreign ministry announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the parent nation to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'an internal marking'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. a national trans rights organisation's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to transport security officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

The state-level picture a visitor enters differs sharply by jurisdiction. One state/province has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, which rights groups describe as a template other legislatures are following. a national identity-document mapping project sets out state/province by state/province which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions. state/province bathroom bans applying to trans people in schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one state/province, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances; twenty-nine states, four state/province and the national capital district have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred: in April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed after using a women's restroom at one state/province capitol, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state/province bathroom-restriction law.

Foreign governments have responded publicly. At least eight foreign countries adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the parent nation, and those advisories followed detentions of foreign citizens over visa issues.

This state/province sits in the low-risk group of a national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026. The same assessment separately flags that this state/province has increased in risk because of capitulation over sports bans in the state university system, and it identifies one further state/province as the latest flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated while recording that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the national measures driving nationwide trends.

The state's risk signal traces to 21 March 2025, when the state university system announced compliance with national restrictions on trans sports participation after the national agriculture department suspended its funding for research and programs while investigating possible sex-based discrimination in nationally funded education programmes. The system affirmed compliance with the new national rules once that funding was suspended, rather than defending its trans students and athletes. The state's standing is therefore better than the parent nation overall, with an upward risk direction.

66186276B31549545599635.name: Delaware
66186276B31549545599635.summary:
Visitors to Delaware stand under the United States federal framework in every respect that governs entry and travel documents. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU is litigating on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 refuse visas to trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events, flag applicants internally under the code 'SWS25', and permit an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth to be treated as fraud and barred permanently. Checkpoint screening carries its own exposure: secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can disclose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers.

Delaware itself does not add a state-level layer of restriction. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 places Delaware in its Low-Risk States group, alongside Arizona, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, defined as jurisdictions that largely refrain from targeting transgender adults without specialising in their protection. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records no ban on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity for Delaware, and no Delaware statute of that kind appears in the inventory.

sources.title: Transgender legal history in the United States (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal policy on housing transgender prisoners has shifted repeatedly. A January 2015 ICE memo directed housing transgender immigration detainees according to gender identity, and in 2016 the US Department of Justice released guidelines forbidding corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units solely on birth anatomy. In 2018 the Federal Bureau of Prisons revised its Transgender Offender Manual in the opposite direction, deleting the sentence that the Transgender Executive Council 'will recommend housing by gender identity when appropriate' and making placement 'a case-by-case basis' in which 'biological sex' is 'the initial determination', with gender identity used only 'in rare cases'. No Delaware-specific placement policy is documented.

66186276B6628180846672.name: Pennsylvania
66186276B6628180846672.summary:
Visitors to Pennsylvania stand under the United States federal framework. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker and will issue passports only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, and passports already carrying X remain valid until expiry. The ACLU is suing the State Department over the changed treatment of trans passports, and the Supreme Court has allowed the Department to proceed. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 separately bar visas for trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events, with applicants flagged under the internal code SWS25, and a declared gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud carrying a permanent bar.

Checkpoint screening carries a separate risk of involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

A national anti-trans legal-risk assessment in its July 2026 update places Pennsylvania in its low-risk tier, covering states that largely refrain from targeting transgender adults without specially protecting them, while recording that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights nationally alongside the federal measures driving that trend.

The legislative pressure in Pennsylvania is concentrated on youth school sports rather than on transgender adults or on facility access. The state Senate passed Senate Bill 1293, the Save Women's Sports Act, on 22 April 2026; the measure would bar transgender female athletes from girls' and women's teams in the commonwealth. Governor Josh Shapiro called supportive lawmakers extremists, and it was unclear whether the House of Representatives would take the bill up. The Senate had already approved an earlier version, Senate Bill 9, on 6 May 2025, reserving teams designated for women to biological females in K-12 and collegiate sport and sending it to the House, with sponsors including Senators Judy Ward and Kristin Phillips-Hill.

Governor Tom Wolf vetoed comparable legislation on 11 July 2022. That bill would have required public K-12 schools and colleges to designate sports as male, female or coed, with athletes in female-designated sports required to have been assigned female at birth; it had passed the Republican-led legislature largely on party-line votes.

A national equality tracker records no public-facility-use ban for Pennsylvania, so the restroom exposure a visitor faces in the state is set by federal and airport rules rather than by any state restriction on facility use.

66186276B91272823970344.name: Wisconsin
66186276B91272823970344.summary:
Visitors to Wisconsin stand under the national framework of the United States. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted, and passports already holding an X marker stay valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, and the Supreme Court has allowed the department to proceed with its changed treatment.

Entry and screening add separate exposures. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 provide for refusal of visas to trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events, with applicants flagged under the code SWS25, and a declaration of a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud carrying a permanent bar. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers.

An independent national legal-risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 places Wisconsin in its Low-Risk States group, alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia and the District of Columbia. Those are states described as having largely refrained from targeting transgender adults while not taking extraordinary steps to protect them, a comparatively favourable position inside a country whose rating for trans visitors fell after the 2025 federal rollbacks.

No anti-trans measure has been enacted at the Wisconsin state level in the areas the assessment grades. Governor Tony Evers vetoed Assembly Bill 465 on 6 December 2023, blocking a restriction on health care for transgender youth, and vetoed a bill on 2 April 2024 that would have limited high school athletes to teams matching sex assigned at birth, a veto he had promised since the bill's introduction and which the bill's sponsor called disgusting. Democrats lacked the votes to stop the bill's passage in the Legislature, so the measure reached the governor's desk and died there.

Restrictions on care for minors in Wisconsin originate in federal funding pressure rather than state law. On 13 January 2026 UW Health and Children's Wisconsin each announced a pause on gender-affirming pharmacologic care for patients under 18 after the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services said it would deny Medicaid and Medicare payments to hospitals providing such care; mental and behavioural health services continued. Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul had joined a coalition of states seeking to block the HHS declaration.

66186276B37442548568489.name: Michigan
66186276B37442548568489.summary:
Michigan stands under the national framework of the United States. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and now issues new passports only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted. Passports already holding an X remain valid until expiry, but trans and nonbinary travellers report confiscation or blocked applications, some stranded abroad, the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the department's changed treatment to proceed.

Entry carries a second exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement refusing visas to trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'; an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. At checkpoints, secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can disclose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers.

Michigan's own civil-rights statute expressly covers gender identity. Governor Gretchen Whitmer signed the first major expansion of the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act on 8 March 2023, codifying sexual-orientation and gender-identity protections that had already been unlawful conduct since a Michigan Supreme Court ruling in July 2022. The legislature also banned the gay and trans panic defense in 2024, which bears on how assaults against trans people are defended in Michigan courts.

A national anti-trans legal risk assessment dated July 2026 places Michigan in its low-risk tier, crediting the state with fairly robust non-discrimination policies while identifying shortfalls in healthcare equity and in protections for incarcerated transgender people. The same assessment designates the United States 'Do Not Travel' for transgender people overall, so the favourable state rating does not neutralise the national picture a visitor enters under.

sources.summary: The July 2026 anti-trans legal risk assessment map places Michigan in the 'Low-Risk States' tier and states that Michigan (with Nevada) has 'enacted fairly robust non-discrimination policies but fall short in ensuring healthcare equity and providing protections for incarcerated transgender individuals'. The same map designates the United States 'Do Not Travel' for transgender people overall.

A federal judge denied civil-rights advocates' request to halt a neighbouring state's ban on gender-affirming medical care for minors. Hormones and puberty blockers are barred after 28 August, transition surgeries for minors are prohibited, and the law sunsets in 2027. The case indicates how regional courts have treated such care bans and is not evidence about Michigan law.

66186276B98615608994420.summary:
Travellers entering Nevada are subject to the United States federal document regime. Executive Order 14168 of 20 January 2025 recognises only two sexes and directs federal agencies to a binary definition; the State Department suspended applications for passport gender-marker changes and ended the self-identified 'X' passport option on 22 January 2025. Passports issued before January 2025 carrying a marker other than sex assigned at birth remain valid until expiry, but new applications are processed only as M or F.

Entry rules add a separate exposure. Under Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025, trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events are refused visas, with applicants flagged under the code 'SWS25', and an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and permanently barred.

Nevada issues state identity documents on far more permissive terms than federal policy now allows. Since 2016 Nevada Vital Records has issued a corrected-gender birth certificate on two affidavits alone, without sex reassignment surgery, and equivalent changes are available for driver's licences and state IDs. A 2019 measure added an 'X' third-gender designation to licences, birth certificates and state IDs with no medical documentation required. A visitor holding a Nevada identification bearing an X marker nevertheless travels on a passport governed by the federal binary rule, so the two documents can disagree.

66186276B21291522594454.name: Maryland
66186276B21291522594454.summary:
Maryland sits inside the United States federal document regime, which is the sharpest document risk for any trans visitor to the country. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, so new passports are issued as M or F on the supporting documents submitted; passports already carrying an X marker remain valid to expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU is in litigation with the State Department, and the Supreme Court has allowed the department's changed treatment of trans passports to proceed. A visitor's passport can therefore mismatch the traveller's presentation, and there is no state override available inside Maryland.

Entry adds a second exposure that applies at the border rather than inside the state. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code SWS25. The same announcement states that declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. Airport screening carries a related involuntary-disclosure risk: the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guidance describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening type matching one's presentation.

Against that federal backdrop, Maryland is among the more protective states for trans residents. The state's Trans Health Equity Act, sponsored in the Maryland House of Delegates by Del. Anne Kaiser, D-Montgomery, extends Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming treatment; its legislative passage in 2024 is tracked in firm commentary as the measure moved through the Senate. Coverage of gender-affirming care is one of the substantive protective features a trans visitor encounters in Maryland, and Maryland's document rules and its treatment of trans health care stand apart from the restriction wave visible in other states.

Facility access is where the national picture diverges sharply by state. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with some jurisdictions criminalising trans bathroom use in certain circumstances, while twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia carry no such ban. Maryland is not among the jurisdictions identified in that reporting as enforcing a facility restriction. Enforcement elsewhere is not theoretical: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, identified by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. Visitors entering states with such bans, including through transit, face a different regime.

Protective law in Maryland has not prevented violence against trans residents. On 11 September 2026 a 27-year-old Black trans woman, Sophie Lee, was found shot in Baltimore's Charles Village and died, the second Black trans woman shot to death in Baltimore within ten weeks. A July 2026 analysis plotting recorded anti-trans incidents against each state's law score places Maryland in the 'Safest States' band, at a law score of 23.5 with 11.1 recorded incidents, and notes that Louisiana records both the worst law score, 24.7, and the highest recorded incident count, 11.6, a comparison the analysis uses to argue that protective law floors do not by themselves determine incident counts.

Monitoring and external guidance point the same way. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving national trends; Maryland is not identified in that assessment among the flagged states. Multiple foreign governments have issued their own advisories: at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, those advisories following detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Detention carries its own exposure. Federal policy on housing transgender detainees and prisoners moved sharply between 2015 and 2018: a January 2015 ICE memo directed that transgender immigration detainees be housed according to gender identity, and 2016 Department of Justice guidelines forbade corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units on birth anatomy alone. The Federal Bureau of Prisons revised its Transgender Offender Manual in 2018, deleting the sentence that the Transgender Executive Council 'will recommend housing by gender identity when appropriate' and replacing it with case-by-case placement in which biological sex is the initial determination and gender identity is used only in rare cases.

A 2021 California study found that 69% of surveyed trans women prisoners reported being made to perform unwanted sexual acts, 58.5% reported violent sexual assault, and 88% reported a 'marriage-like relationship'. 66186276B35012827062242.name: Colorado
66186276B35012827062242.summary:
Colorado stands under the United States federal framework, which sets the baseline a trans visitor carries into the state: since January 2025 federal identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth, the X marker is no longer issued, airport screening follows national procedures that can disclose a traveller's trans status, and visa discretion over transgender athletes seeking entry for women's sporting events applies at any port of entry including Denver. State law here runs against that current rather than with it.

The Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act expressly covers gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing and public accommodations, and the legislature expanded that coverage again in 2025. Public-accommodation coverage is the provision a visitor would rely on directly, in hotels, restaurants, shops and venues.

Colorado's highest court has enforced that protection against federal pressure. On 18 May 2026 the Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5-2 that Children's Hospital Colorado violated state anti-discrimination law when it suspended gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, and ordered a lower court to issue an injunction requiring the hospital to resume puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Justice William Hood wrote that continuing treatment for cisgender children while stopping it for transgender youth meant the decision denied the petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity; two justices dissented on the ground that federal threats could shut the hospital system.

The limits of that protection are visible in funding. From 13 October 2026 Colorado suspends Medicaid coverage of hormone therapy, puberty blockers and other gender-affirming care for transgender youth because a federal rule finalised in August 2026 blocks federal funds for such care under age 18, and under 19 in the CHP+ child programme; the state Medicaid agency says resuming coverage will require legislative action. State protections here are therefore operative but exposed to national defunding.

Detention risk should be assessed on the same terms. Colorado has no identity-based housing statute for prisons. Transgender women were historically held in men's facilities in the state system, and the relief achieved came through litigation rather than a baseline rule: a 2019 class action alleging sexual and physical violence and denial of care produced a court-approved 2024 consent decree, Raven v. Polis, in Denver District Court requiring expanded health care, voluntary specialised housing and payments of about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admission of liability. An earlier 2019 settlement paid Lindsay Saunders-Velez $170,000 over the safety of a transgender inmate held in a men's prison.

66186276B10610315112087.tangentialFactors:
Identity-document rules vary sharply across the United States, so a visitor's exposure changes at the state line. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions; Kansas has gone the opposite way, enacting a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, a statute rights groups describe as a template other legislatures are following.

Facility use is regulated in a substantial number of states. Bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances; twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, identified by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

66186276B73434888205604.name: New Jersey
66186276B73434888205604.summary:
A trans visitor to New Jersey is bound first by United States federal rules, which apply identically in every state. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passport applications are decided only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted. Passports already issued with an X marker stay valid until expiry, but travellers whose papers no longer match their presentation can expect questions at issuance and at the border. The ACLU's lawsuit on behalf of seven plaintiffs and Lambda Legal's documentation guidance are the outstanding points of challenge, and the Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to continue its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, followed by the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025, requires refusal of visas to trans athletes seeking to enter to compete in women's sporting events, with applicants flagged internally under the code SWS25. The same announcement treats a declaration of a gender other than sex assigned at birth as potential fraud, carrying a permanent bar. A visitor travelling for sport should assume the rule is applied mechanically.

Checkpoint procedures risk involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as steps that can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Inside New Jersey the measured legal environment is among the most protective in the country. The July 2026 national legal-risk assessment, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, places New Jersey in a fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier whose laws have, in the assessment's words, gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights. On the separate state-by-state dataset of killings of trans women covering 2008 to 2025, New Jersey records 3.4 per 100,000 per year, four recorded deaths in total, and is labelled 'Safest States'.

sources.summary: State-by-state dataset of killings of trans women 2008-2025 (TGEU Trans Murder Monitoring / Williams Institute): New Jersey = 3.4 per 100k per year (4 recorded deaths), labelled 'Safest States', against 428 US trans women confirmed killed since 2008. Central finding: state anti-trans law hostility does not correlate with where trans women are killed (trendline nearly flat over the 26-state comparison) - law predicts government treatment (ID, healthcare, bathroom access), not private violence.

July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills (youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate/driver-license restrictions, end of legal recognition): New Jersey sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier (CA, CO, CT, HI, IL, MA, MD, MN, NJ, NM, NY, OR, RI, VT, WA), whose laws have 'gone above and beyond in safeguarding' trans rights. Contrast tier: worst-law states carry up to 5-year prison terms (Idaho) or arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use (Florida).

Nationally the map counts 16 states and the District of Columbia holding shields, covering 38 percent of trans people aged 13 and over, while 32 states and five territories, covering 56 percent, hold none.

Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, some stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

A separate entry exposure applies to trans athletes. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'; an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening can disclose status involuntarily. Hawaii's own standing is at the protective end of the national range. A national legal-risk assessment dated 13 July 2026, built from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills including youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition, places Hawaii in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier, whose laws are described as having gone beyond minimum safeguards for trans rights.

66186276B15934532614691.name: Massachusetts
66186276B15934532614691.summary:
Travellers to Massachusetts stand under the United States federal framework for travel documents, visa decisions and airport screening. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, and new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents submitted; passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 that followed it, mean trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events face visa refusal, and that declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth at application may be treated as fraud with permanent bar. These rules apply in Massachusetts as they do in every other state.

The State Department document regime is not uniform in its consequences at state level. A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment, compiled from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition, places Massachusetts in its fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington. The same assessment records that the least protective states carry up to five-year prison terms for trans people, as in Idaho, and arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use, as in Florida.

Healthcare is the clearest area of state-level protection relevant to a visitor. The Movement Advancement Project's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, with data as of 27 September 2026, lists Massachusetts among states holding a shield law or executive order from 2022. Such a shield law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care delivered in Massachusetts was banned in the patient's home state, which is directly relevant to a visitor travelling from a jurisdiction with a youth-care ban.

National equality-map research records Massachusetts as having shield and non-discrimination provisions covering gender identity that are enforceable against out-of-state actions arising from other states' restrictions. Against that, the Movement Advancement Project records that 32 states and 5 territories, 56 per cent of the figure tracked, hold no shield protection of any kind, so a visitor's exposure to restrictive law elsewhere does not stop at a state line in either direction.

66186276B2592965416524.name: New Mexico
66186276B2592965416524.summary:
New Mexico stands under the national framework of the United States, and that framework is the first exposure a trans visitor faces. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry and screening follow national rules regardless of which state the visitor lands in. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'; the same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. At checkpoints, secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, according to the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide, which sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

Facility use and identity documents are regulated state by state, so the rules encountered inside New Mexico differ from those in states that restrict them. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances in some jurisdictions, while twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred: in April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed after using a women's restroom at a state capitol, identified by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, described by rights groups as a template other legislatures are following. Multiple foreign governments, at least eight European countries including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for their trans and nonbinary citizens after the federal document and data rules, and a national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies four states now designated do-not-travel for trans people.

Within that national picture, New Mexico sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier of the July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington. The ranking is built from a rubric applied over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition, and it records that the laws of the protective-tier states have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

New Mexico also operates a shield or refuge law, listed by the Movement Advancement Project's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map as 'State has shield law or executive order 2023'. The law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal in New Mexico has been banned in the home state of the person travelling for it. That protection is directly relevant to a visitor arriving from a state with a care ban, and it applies alongside, not instead of, the federal document and entry rules.

66186276B97229519707655.name: Oregon
66186276B97229519707655.summary:
Visitors to Oregon stand first under the United States federal framework, which applies in every state. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted. Passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers have reported passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The American Civil Liberties Union is litigating against the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on documentation and on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

A second, separate exposure arises at the visa stage. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking entry to the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code SWS25. The same announcement states that an applicant declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. A trans visitor may also face checkpoint screening that involuntarily discloses status: the National Center for Transgender Equality describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers.

At state level Oregon sits at the protective end of the national spectrum. The July 2026 national legal-risk assessment, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the removal of legal recognition, places Oregon in a fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington. The assessment describes the laws of these states as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

Healthcare is the strongest documented Oregon-specific protection for a visitor. The Movement Advancement Project's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, with data as of 27 September 2026, lists Oregon as a state with a shield law or executive order from 2023. The shield provision protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal in Oregon has been banned in the patient's home state, which makes Oregon directly relevant to visitors travelling from states with youth-care bans. Nationally the map records that 16 states and the District of Columbia, holding 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, have shields, while 32 states and five territories, holding 56%, have none; youth-care bans tracked on the page include some that have been permanently blocked.

The contrast with the restrictive states is marked. In the same July 2026 assessment, the worst-law states carry prison terms of up to five years in Idaho, and Florida operates an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use. Facility restriction is not theoretical elsewhere: state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, and in April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed for using a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, identified by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban.

Foreign governments have responded to the federal document and data rules by advising their own trans citizens. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.

66186276B98073251815399.name: Rhode Island
66186276B98073251815399.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to Rhode Island, because they are issued under national rules rather than state ones. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, new passport applications are processed only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, and passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry and screening follow the same national layer. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'; the same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. Airport screening carries a separate exposure: the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can reveal a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Against that background, Rhode Island is listed among the 'Most Protective' states in the anti-trans legal risk assessment published on 13 July 2026, in the gender-identity non-discrimination tier, and the assessment also places Rhode Island among jurisdictions whose shield protections are enforceable against out-of-state action. The same assessment reports erosion at the federal layer and concludes that the top tier can no longer be considered most protective nationwide, so a visitor's protection at the state level coexists with the document, visa and screening rules described above. No Rhode Island-specific restriction on identity documents, facility use or care appears in the source inventory.

66186276B17406925856308.name: Vermont
66186276B17406925856308.summary:
A trans visitor to Vermont remains subject in full to the United States federal travel framework. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted; passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on documentation and how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Within that national layer, Vermont is listed as of July 2026 among the most protective states on gender-identity nondiscrimination. The same assessment records that the federal layer is under attack through the House bathroom ban, so that tier on its own can no longer be considered most protective. Vermont also has shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches that are enforceable against out-of-state action, and it appears in the nationwide directory of such jurisdictions.

Identity documents remain the fastest-moving area of restriction elsewhere in the country. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers; rights groups describe the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the rules encountered outside Vermont depend heavily on the state involved.

Facility use is regulated in a substantial number of states. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity; in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement is documented: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends. Vermont is not among the designated states.

66186276B98555229882405.name: Washington
66186276B98555229882405.summary:
Visitors to Washington stand under the federal framework that applies in every state. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passports are issued only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted. Passports already bearing an X marker remain valid until expiry, but trans and nonbinary travellers report confiscation or blocking of documents at application. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and a State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 bar visas for trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events, flag applicants under the code SWS25, and allow an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth to be treated as fraud and permanently barred.

Checkpoint screening carries a separate exposure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guidance describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can reveal a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

Washington itself sits at the protective end of state law. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 names Washington among the federation's fifteen Most Protective states, and specifically among states including Colorado, Hawaii and Maryland with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial hair removal and an expanded range of gender-affirming procedures, together with refuge protections for people fleeing restrictive states. The same assessment flags two Washington ballot initiatives, I-001 and I-638, as targeting transgender residents.

Washington also appears in nationwide shield-law tracking. Mapresearch.org's equality map lists the state among jurisdictions with shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches that are enforceable against out-of-state action, and includes it in the full all-states directory.

Placement and care in custody are governed by court order. In October 2023 Washington state prisons were legally required, under court order and rulings, to provide gender-affirming healthcare and, where indicated, sexual-reassignment surgery to inmates. In July 2024 a trans woman prisoner was transferred from a women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate of the women's prison, documenting birth-sex housing used as a sanction.
