64170238B96397749018979.name: Monaco
64170238B96397749018979.summary:
Monaco's legal framework on sexual orientation has deep roots: homosexuality has been legal since the 18th century, and hate crimes and hate speech motivated by sexual orientation are penalised. Reported discrimination is described as rare. The sources disagree on the broader point: Outright International states that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned, while Queer In The World describes prohibitions on SOGI discrimination as existing only in certain contexts.

A trans visitor faces no documented legal exposure in Monaco. There are no bathroom or facility restrictions on record, no reported anti-trans incidents, and no border friction: entry is normally made across the short land frontier with France under the common border-free travel zone. The principality is roughly 200 hectares in extent, heavily policed, and a low-crime luxury destination where street violence of any kind is unusual.

The US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report found no significant changes in Monaco and recorded no torture, arbitrary detention or similar abuses; the only significant issues it identified were the criminal libel and lèse-majesté provisions, which it reports are not enforced. The human-rights machinery applicable to a visitor is therefore benign in practice rather than protective in design.

The assessment rests on that gap. Practical safety is very high and anti-trans hostility is not documented, but the principality offers little explicit trans protection: no functioning legal gender recognition process is described anywhere in the source material, and couple- and family-level recognition for same-sex partners stops short of equality. Visitors are advised to check current local law and customs before travelling.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (last updated 12 March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections — hate crimes and hate speech on sexual orientation are penalised, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned (reported discrimination is described as rare); same-sex couples have no marriage or adoption, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is limited.

French gay travel guide Monaco page: no gay Pride is held anywhere in Monaco (visitors are sent to France or Italy for one); the ~200-hectare state is pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Nice-Matin via Monaco Haut Commissariat (March 2025, French): homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly 10 people dare to be openly out; Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo: "C’est le triste bilan de Monaco".

Queer In The World Monaco guide (updated 3 December 2023): homosexuality legal and SOGI discrimination illegal only in certain contexts — limited protections with room for improvement; advises visitors to stay current with local laws and customs.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Hate-speech protection rests on Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression, which bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016 (technological crime law), punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2–5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months–3 years. In July 2010 a Monegasque court jailed a man for 5 days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 added 'sexual orientation' to Civil Code articles 238-1 (6 months–1 year for violent acts not causing total incapacity), 239 (10 years for attacking a partner or co-resident) and 421 (5 years' probation for unprovoked attacks on a person or group). Monaco does not recognize same-sex marriage, and ILGA-Europe's 2019 ranking (45th of 49 European countries) notes that transgender people cannot alter their legal gender. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a cohabitation agreement (contrat de vie commune), introduced in Parliament on 16 April 2018, unanimously approved by the National Council on 4 December 2019 and in force six months after publication in the Journal de Monaco; it is signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax, not like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and parents/children. Same-sex couples have no right to adopt children. The LGBT community supports some gay-friendly establishments inside Monaco, but there are no official gay bars, clubs or events in the country, unlike nearby French cities Marseille, Nice and Lyon. Monaco is not an EU member, so EU LGBT-rights protections do not bind it, though it has strong cultural and economic ties with France. Monaco has no armed forces, only a National Guard; France handles defence and allows openly gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people to serve. The age of consent is 15 for both same-sex and opposite-sex relationships. The 2011 anti-discrimination bill's article 44 would have required a school programme every year of primary and secondary cycles to sensitise against racism and all article 1 discriminations (including sexual orientation), but the Council of Government did not approve the bill and its 18 December 2012 replacement dropped the sexual-orientation provisions. Same-sex couples' inability to adopt children directly affects family formation for youth, and most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral.

64170238B96397749018979.tangentialFactors:
LGBT visibility in Monaco is exceptionally low. No gay Pride is held anywhere in the principality, and travel guides direct visitors to events across the border in France or Italy. There is no discernible local scene, and a local newspaper account reports that roughly 10 people are willing to be openly out.

A Council of Europe rapporteur, Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo, summarised the principality's standing as "C'est le triste bilan de Monaco", and Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings despite the long history of decriminalisation. International guidance for visitors recommends staying current with local laws and customs.

Adjacent legal risk for any traveller, not specific to trans people, comes from the criminal libel and lèse-majesté provisions, which the State Department describes as on the books but unenforced. The territory also markets itself with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory, which speaks to visitor hospitality rather than to legal status.
64170238B96397749018979.localsOnly:
Same-sex couples have no access to marriage or joint adoption in Monaco. The Nice-Matin account carried by the Haut Commissariat adds that there is no equal inheritance or succession rights, no survivor pension, and no parental leave for same-sex partners.

Residents live with very limited visibility: about 10 people are reported to be openly out, no Pride event exists locally, and there is no established community scene to congregate in. Outright International characterises LGBTIQ visibility in the principality as limited and reports discrimination as rare, though it records no legal ban on discrimination by ground of sexual orientation or gender identity.
64170238B96397749018979.outOfScopeNotes:
The two accessible sources conflict on whether SOGI discrimination is prohibited. Outright International's country overview, last updated 12 March 2026, says it is not banned; Queer In The World, updated 3 December 2023, says it is illegal only in certain contexts. The conflict is unresolved here and the stricter reading should not be relied on without checking current Monegasque statute text.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, sex-and-gender marker changes on identity documents, or what happens to a trans visitor's passport at the frontier. The absence of a documented process should be treated as not sourced rather than as confirmed absence.

The enforcement record behind the hate-crime and hate-speech provisions for sexual orientation is likewise not documented in the inventory, and no source applies those provisions to gender identity specifically.

Unverified dimensions (no source found in the 2026-10 review): D4, D5, D8.

SYN-ABW.name: Aruba
SYN-ABW.summary:
Aruba stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

On 8 September 2016 the Staten of Aruba passed a civil-code amendment opening registered unions to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5, with four abstentions. The amendment extends the marriage articles of the civil code to those registered unions and grants spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights. Aruba's own news service reported the vote as making the island the first in the Caribbean to act.

Marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognised throughout the Kingdom, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route. The Associated Press reported that religious and cultural opposition to the measure was strong, and that neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed such unions at the time.

GlobalGayz records that the Aruban government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until it was challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands.

sources.summary: Official Aruba tourism board page marketing the island as an established LGBT destination: positions feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering, and quotes a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. Self-description by the destination's own marketer, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

Aruba's own news site (Sep 9, 2016): parliament passed the civil-law amendment granting civil partnerships to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5 on Sep 8, 2016, making Aruba the first island in the Caribbean; the campaign ran 2.5 years, with openly-gay MP Desiree de Sousa-Croes as sponsor and an Igualdad Aruba petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

GlobalGayz cultural report (edited Jan 2017): Aruba described as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curacao; notes the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands, and that same-sex adoption is legal; Catholic influence noted as the main brake.

Associated Press (Sep 9, 2016): parliament voted 11-5 with four abstentions to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered same-sex unions, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights; marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognized kingdom-wide, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route; religious and cultural opposition was strong, and neither Sint Maarten nor Curacao allowed unions at the time.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
Same-sex sexual activity is legal in Aruba for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. This is the only youth-specific legal threshold given; the text contains no findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation. The Aruba Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds including 'heterosexual or homosexual orientation'. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed. On 12 July 2024 the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation, in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba.

Aruba is frequently called one of the Caribbean's most LGBT-friendly islands. Several specific gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as 'LGBT-friendly'. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba. The last is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.' Openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes publicly introduced the registered partnership bill in August 2016.

Harassment has nonetheless occurred. Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge (2004–2007), which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognize same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition to LGBT rights.

SYN-AIA.name: Anguilla
SYN-AIA.summary:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory whose law is local law: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the island, and they can be applied there only by Order in Council.

Sex between men in private is legal, but the repeal was imposed from London rather than enacted by Anguilla's own legislature. On 5 January 2001 the Privy Council ordered decriminalisation of private consensual same-sex conduct in five Caribbean territories — Anguilla, the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands — acting unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. Anguilla had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories. A first-person account published in June 2023 dates the change to 2000 rather than January 2001.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguilla law. A commercial destination-wedding service states that plainly while marketing the island's venues to same-sex couples, which means a ceremony performed there carries symbolic status only.

Public LGBT life on the island is close to invisible: no community organisations, no venues, no Pride, and only a handful of hotels marketed to gay travellers. Anguilla's roughly 15,000 residents and 35 square miles are given as reasons the scene stays small, and the muted, not 'out and proud' atmosphere is attributed to the imposed colonial legacy rather than to local choice. A queer family visiting in June 2023 described the trip as uneventful.

sources.summary: GlobalGayz country report on Anguilla (2012): profile of a 35-square-mile island about 100 miles east of the British Virgin Islands, framing gay life against dependent-territory law — Britain holds ultimate legal authority and decriminalisation came by British order rather than local repeal, with local religious protest against the change; Anguilla never had the exact prohibition law itself in the same form.

Commercial destination-wedding page for Anguilla: states plainly that 'Same-sex marriage is not currently recognized under the law in Anguilla', while marketing the island's venues for ceremonies — useful as a practical marker that only symbolic ceremonies are possible for same-sex couples there.

Associated Press via SodomyLaws (Jan 5, 2001): Britain's Privy Council ordered decriminalisation of private consensual same-sex conduct in five Caribbean territories — Anguilla, Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and Turks and Caicos — acting unilaterally after local legislatures refused to repeal, drawing protests from religious leaders.

AFAR first-person travel piece (Jun 2023): a queer family's visit finds gay sex legal in Anguilla through the British decriminalisation order (article says 2000) but a muted, not 'out and proud' scene rooted in that imposed colonial legacy rather than local choice; notes roughly 15,000 residents as one reason the gay scene stays small.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: LGBT expression in Anguilla is constrained by a 'subdued and subtle climate of homophobia' that has pushed local LGBT people toward secrecy. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in The Valley marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia. There are no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs, which the source attributes to the island's small population, and no community infrastructure, though non-legal ceremonies of same-sex couples have taken place. Anguillian law provides no legislative protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity: the Constitution outlaws discrimination only on grounds of 'race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex or place of origin'. The age of consent is higher for homosexuals (18) than for heterosexuals (16). The Marriage Act defines marriage as 'the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife'; same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Anguilla is one of the British overseas territories that has not legislated for civil partnerships. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 2001, following an order of the United Kingdom Privy Council that also affected four other UK overseas territories. Comparatively, Anguilla sits at the end of a spectrum in which decriminalisation is settled but relationship recognition is absent, and where the absence of any organised local LGBT presence means visitors encounter neither hostility campaigns nor visible support infrastructure.

SYN-BES.name: Bonaire Sint Eustatius and Saba
SYN-BES.summary:
Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba) consists of three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Dutch national law governs civil status, marriage and anti-discrimination, and the same statutory framework that applies in the European Netherlands operates on the islands.

Same-sex unions have been registrable in the islands since 2012. On 4 December 2012 the Census Office in Saba registered the first such union in the Caribbean Netherlands, between Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, an Aruban national aged 26, and Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, a Venezuelan national aged 27. Both were visiting residents rather than local inhabitants, establishing that the registry performs civil ceremonies for persons without island residency.

Practical arrangements for a civil ceremony are documented on Saba. Saba Tourism identifies the Court Room in the Administrative Building as the most straightforward venue for an efficient civil ceremony, and records registrar Julieta Woods as flexible in accommodating couples' requests. The island maintains a functioning destination-wedding infrastructure, including caterers, florists and accommodation providers.

For this record: travel-facing evidence that the island markets itself as equality-friendly with statutory protection behind it.

Dutch Caribbean Legal Portal (5 Dec 2012): the Census Office in Saba registered the Caribbean Netherlands' first same-sex union — Aruban Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez (26) wed Venezuelan Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto (27) on 4 Dec 2012, two visiting residents. Saba Tourism official weddings page: the simplest venue for an efficient civil ceremony is the Court Room in the Administrative Building; registrar Julieta Woods is documented as flexible with couples' wishes; full destination-wedding infrastructure (caterers, flowers, accommodations). For this record: practical logistics for a couple — civil ceremonies on Saba run routinely through the island registry.

SYN-BLM.name: Saint Barthélemy
SYN-BLM.summary:
Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France proper.

No provision of that framework restricts a trans or same-sex visitor. Same-sex marriage has been available since 2013, the statute covering discrimination on grounds of gender identity is in force, legal gender-marker change requires neither surgery nor sterilisation, and the French ban on conversion practices adopted in 2023 applies. Gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery have been available under French law since 1975.

Two limits sit alongside that coverage. Non-binary identity is not recognised in French law, so a visitor whose documents record a non-binary status has no legal counterpart on arrival. Gender-affirming care is provided on a small island with very limited specialist capacity, which affects continuity of treatment rather than its legality.

Detention is the clearest downside risk. Saint Barthélemy falls within the French prison administration, where policy recognises only biological sex for placement. Reporting by the controller-general of detention places finds that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women assigned to men's facilities under birth-sex placement, suffer the most serious harm in the system; a 2011 case in Nantes sent a trans woman to a men's prison. The controller-general's opinion of 25 May 2021, drawing on some 40 referrals since 2010, concluded that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of deprivation of liberty. A trans visitor detained here would enter that same placement regime.

Visitor-facing accounts describe a discreet luxury culture rather than an organised scene. Guides report full legal equality on roughly 8 square miles with about 10,000 residents, a yacht-based economy long accustomed to gay couples, and same-sex couples drawing no attention; a luxury operator records no LGBTQ venues and no Pride-specific events, but also no hostility, with staff trained for diverse guests. An aggregate rights assessment scores the territory 7.7 out of 10, with nine positive indicators and one red flag covering limited healthcare access, and notes that no government issues LGBT+ travel advice for Saint Barthélemy while the UK Foreign Office shows no warnings.

sources.summary: French prison-system reporting: the controller-general of detention places finds trans detainees — overwhelmingly women held under birth-sex placement — suffer the most in prison; administration policy recognises only biological sex (a 2011 Nantes case placed a trans woman in a men's prison). BLM detainees fall under this French system.

France's Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty draws on about 40 referrals since 2010. It finds serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations applicable also to intersex and non-binary persons.

The French framework applies in Saint Barthélemy: legal gender-marker change without surgery or sterilisation, hormone therapy and surgery available since 1975, anti-discrimination coverage; non-binary recognition limited.

Aggregate rating 7.7/10, with 9 positive rights and 1 red flag: legal gender change without surgery, anti-discrimination law in place but limited healthcare access. No government LGBT+ travel advice exists; FCDO shows no warnings. No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted.

Low crime, an open and accepting culture, no Pride-specific events, and staff trained for diverse guests. Visitors are high-end and discreet; there are no LGBTQ venues or scene, and no hostility is noted.

SYN-BLM.tangentialFactors:
The territory's legal position is a direct extension of the French metropolitan framework rather than an autonomous local code, so any change in French law on identity documents, anti-discrimination coverage or detention policy reaches Saint Barthélemy without a local legislative step.

Detention policy is where the French framework reads worst, and the controller-general's 2021 opinion frames the problem as system-wide rather than confined to any single facility, which is why the same placement rules are a live consideration here.

Social reception and legal status diverge from several regional neighbours: the guidance found describes no visible scene and no hostility, and the discretion noted by operators reflects the territory's small, high-end tourist economy rather than any pressure to conceal.

The one red flag in the aggregate assessment concerns healthcare capacity, an infrastructure constraint that also limits what the anti-discrimination protections can deliver in practice.
SYN-BLM.localsOnly:
Residents change their legal gender marker under the French procedure, which since the 2016 reform requires no surgery and no sterilisation; the resulting document is a French identity document valid for travel.

Hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery have been available under French social security arrangements since 1975, but the resident population of roughly 10,000 supports only limited local specialist care, and treatment often depends on mainland France.

The anti-discrimination statute covers gender identity in employment and services, and the 2023 national ban on conversion practices applies to residents as well as visitors.

Residents in custody are held under the same French detention administration described above: placement follows birth sex, and the controller-general's findings on the treatment of trans detainees apply to the system that holds them.

SYN-BMU.name: Bermuda
SYN-BMU.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Bermuda; local legislation governs, and the United Kingdom measures could be applied only by Order in Council.

Bermuda decriminalised consensual sex between adult men in 1994, when the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to strike two sections of the Criminal Code. In July 2013 the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and, in the same instrument, on grounds of age; same-sex marriage was not permitted at that time.

Same-sex couples married in Bermuda in 2017 lost that route the following year. The Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act in February 2018, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships available to same-sex and opposite-sex couples alike, which made Bermuda the first jurisdiction anywhere to revoke marriage equality. In March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld that restoration of the opposite-sex definition of marriage, so a partnership rather than a marriage is the status available to same-sex couples.

For a transgender visitor the decisive fact is the protection gap. Bermuda has no legal recognition of transgender people and no gender-recognition framework, so there is no route to amend a gender marker on local documents and no recognition machinery a visitor could rely on at the border or in dealings with local authorities. The 2013 amendment's protected ground as enacted is sexual orientation; the inventory does not record gender identity as a protected ground, and no hate-crime provision covering gender identity is sourced here.

sources.summary: Bernews (Feb 2018): Bermuda's Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples - the reversal that made Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality.

Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, July 12) as 'incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre', an instance of organised religious hostility toward visible same-sex couples.

LGBTQ Nation/AP (July 2013): Bermuda's Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation (also banning age discrimination); same-sex marriage not then permitted.

Royal Gazette (14 May 1994): the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, removing two Criminal Code sections. The debate split the island, with religious leaders divided and the Christian Coalition staging marches against it.

SYN-BMU.tangentialFactors:
Organised religious hostility shapes the social climate for visible same-sex couples. In July the AME church and other congregations protested a Norwegian Dawn cruise sailing to Bermuda as incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre, and the Christian Coalition staged marches against the 1994 decriminalisation vote, with religious leaders publicly divided over the debate.

Bermuda sits in a small group of jurisdictions that have withdrawn a marriage right after granting it, and the 2022 Privy Council ruling confirms that the withdrawal is settled rather than provisional. Visitors should expect partnership-based rights, not marital ones, in any interaction that turns on relationship status.

Marriage remains restricted to opposite-sex couples under the definition upheld by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in March 2022.

The Human Rights Amendment Act of 2013 gives residents a discrimination remedy on the grounds of sexual orientation and age. Transgender residents have no statutory route to legal recognition of their gender identity, and the sourced record does not establish gender identity as a protected ground or a hate-crime category.

Whether gender identity functions as a protected ground under Bermuda's human-rights legislation, whether any local gender-recognition statute exists, and whether hate-crime provisions reach conduct motivated by gender identity are all unresolved on the present inventory; none of these points is sourced here.

The enforcement record of the 2013 discrimination protections, including complaint volumes and outcomes, is not sourced. Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 or its 2025 single-sex-services code has ever been proposed for extension to Bermuda by Order in Council is likewise unresolved.

SYN-COK.name: Cook Islands
SYN-COK.summary:
New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to the Cook Islands, while local criminal law governs conduct on the islands.

Sections 154 and 155 of the Cook Islands Crimes Act 1969 criminalised sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male, carrying maximum terms of seven years and five years respectively, with consent explicitly not a defence. Later coverage of the repeal cited a maximum of ten years for indecent acts between males. The penalty figures reported for the 1969 provisions differ across the sources, but all agree the offences were never enforced in living memory.

Parliament voted on Friday 14 April 2023 to strike the provisions from the Crimes Act through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023. A note attached to the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands, and the same bill added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. The repeal removed a colonial-era provision still on the statute books rather than an active prosecution threat.

Decriminalisation was stalled for years before 2023. A draft Crimes Bill, written with assistance from New Zealand, would have deleted sections 154 and 155, and a 2017 select committee recommended their removal; MPs subsequently backtracked on that recommendation. In 2020 parliament again deferred the bill's report by three months.

Same-sex marriage remains prohibited in the Cook Islands under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000. The islands' only LGBTI community organisation, the Te Tiare Association, campaigned for repeal across the whole period, and its members described the 1969 provisions as homophobia brought by colonisation into a society whose pre-contact history accepted same-sex relationships. The Cook Islands population was about 21,000 when the bill was drafted in 2017.

sources.summary: PinkNews (14 Apr 2023): Cook Islands parliament voted on Friday to remove the never-enforced 'indecent acts between males' law — exposure of up to 10 years under the 1969 Crimes Act — through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023; a note in the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBTQ+ people, and the bill also adds protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.

PinkNews (1 Oct 2020): decriminalisation stalled again — MPs deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months. Traces the full path: colonial-era 1969 sections 154/155 (up to 7 years for sex between men) criminalise; a 2017 select committee recommended removing them and 'indecent acts between men'/sodomy were struck from the draft, but MPs later backtracked and the kick-down-the-road continued; notes colonisation introduced the taboo into a historically accepting society.

PinkNews (3 Aug 2017): draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand help, would remove sections 154/155 of the 1969 Crimes Act — up to 7 years for gay sex and 5 years for 'any indecent act with or upon any other male', with consent explicitly not a defence. Population 21,000; the country's only LGBTI community group, Te Tiare Association, welcomed the move (member Valentino Wichman quoted on the law's homophobia).

RNZ Pacific (10 Aug 2017): public submissions opened in parliament on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed a submission from the Te Tiare Association representing the country's LGBTI community was already before the select committee; at least three lawyers expected to speak on penalties and sentencing.

SYN-CUW.name: Curaçao
SYN-CUW.summary:
Curaçao stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here. It is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, holding full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights without delay, and a package of rights requests was delivered to ministers in The Hague. Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly endorsed equal rights for everyone.

That endorsement ran against organised opposition from within her own party. Winifred Raveneau's fierce resistance had already forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel after a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement, and parliamentary opposition to equal-rights measures continued even as the island's own government publicly backed the community.

Community infrastructure exists but is small. An LGBT centre, the Pink House, opened in Curaçao in 2010, and reporting from GlobalGayz (updated January 2017) treats Curaçao, Aruba and Bonaire as quietly gay-friendly places within the Kingdom while crediting Curaçao, with Sint Maarten and Aruba, as a driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites an IGLTA award naming the island the most gay-welcoming in the region.

For a trans visitor the composite reads as low legal risk with thin trans-specific infrastructure: no documented state hostility toward trans people, an active but negotiating community, and no sourced local gender-recognition pathway or trans-specific care capacity.

Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites Curaçao's IGLTA award as 'most gay welcoming in the region'; a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.

SYN-CUW.tangentialFactors:

Regional travel-culture surveys place the ABC islands — Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao — in a quiet, tolerant mainstream, a framing that describes general gay-friendliness rather than any trans-specific guarantee.

The record shows a persistent gap between Kingdom-level intent and island-level practice: an equal-rights agreement signed by all Kingdom governments in 2015 sits alongside a 2013 Pride permit issued on such short notice and under such strict conditions that the event had to move venue. Because Curaçao governs its own internal affairs, the permitting authority a visitor's event would face is local.
SYN-CUW.localsOnly:

Domestic politics is split on the question. Commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly backed equal rights for everyone in 2015, while her party colleague Winifred Raveneau mounted fierce opposition and used the permit process to obstruct the 2013 Gay Pride. Residents therefore live with official support and organised parliamentary resistance at the same time.

Advocacy has been routed through the Kingdom's central government: a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague after the 2015 agreement among Kingdom governments' representatives.

Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag points to an IGLTA award naming the island the most gay-welcoming in the region as evidence of its standing.

Entry, visa and border-screening practices that could expose a visitor's trans status are not sourced, nor are document or marker rules for passports and identity papers issued in Curaçao or by the Netherlands.

Hate-crime or hate-speech protection covering gender identity, and any enforcement record under it, is not sourced. Nor is trans-specific healthcare capacity, its availability to visitors, or any exclusion of trans-related care.

Whether the Pride permit friction documented in 2013 recurred after that year, and whether the 2015 Kingdom equal-rights agreement has been implemented in Curaçao legislation, both remain unresolved on this inventory.

No sub-national variation within Curaçao is sourced; the island is treated as a single unit throughout.

SYN-CYM.name: Cayman Islands
SYN-CYM.summary:
Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in the Cayman Islands in 2001 by an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature declined to act, and the reform left an unequal age of consent in its wake.

London–local friction over the scope of protections is documented from 2009, when the United Kingdom's Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the draft Cayman Islands constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission deplorable and warning that the drafting could leave the territory's courts affording less protection than Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the draft's list of discrimination grounds was open-ended.

The judiciary outran the legislature on relationship status. In March 2019 Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the prohibition on same-sex marriage; the Court of Appeal reversed that ruling in August 2019, so no same-sex marriages can be performed locally. In December 2020 the immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had married in Ireland, with the Court of Appeal holding that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. The practical position for a visitor is therefore recognition of an existing foreign marriage for immigration effects, without any locally conferred marital status.

Public visibility carries official backing. The territory's first Pride parade, held on 7 August 2021 and organised by the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation, drew around 600 participants including the premier, the governor, ministers and members of the Legislative Assembly. Participants were asked by organisers to refrain from excessive displays of affection, a condition reflecting sensitivities about public space rather than a legal prohibition.

sources.summary: PinkNews (11 Aug 2009): UK MPs on the Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the Cayman Islands' draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission 'deplorable' and warning the drafting could leave Cayman courts affording citizens less protection than the European Convention on Human Rights Art 14 requires; the FCO countered that the discrimination-grounds list was open-ended. Early-dated evidence of London–local friction over LGBT protections that frames the later recognition rulings.

Cayman News Service (29 Jul 2021): around 600 people — including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs — joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade (Sat 7 Aug 2021 debut), an historic turnout with broad official participation; participants were asked to refrain from excessive displays of affection (organisers' condition amid public-space sensitivities). Evidence of high official tolerance in the tourist-facing environment.

Washington Blade (30 Dec 2020): immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who wed in Ireland. The Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie had struck down the same-sex marriage ban in March 2019; that ruling was overturned on appeal in Aug 2019, while the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived.

SYN-CYM.tangentialFactors:
The Cayman Islands presents a pattern in which official tolerance and judicial protection run ahead of the legislature. Public events enjoy visible participation by the territory's most senior officeholders, while the statutory position on marriage remains restrictive and the age of consent has not been equalised.

The recognition ruling establishes a distinction that shapes visitor expectations: a valid foreign marriage can be given legal effect in immigration matters even though the same union cannot be contracted locally. Refusing that effect was held to be unequal treatment on sexual-orientation grounds.

The 2009 exchange with the United Kingdom's Foreign Affairs Committee shows that disputes over how far anti-discrimination protection extends have been conducted between London and the territory's own framers, with the local argument resting on the open-ended character of the listed discrimination grounds.
SYN-CYM.localsOnly:
Residents cannot marry a same-sex partner locally, since the March 2019 Grand Court ruling that struck down the marriage prohibition was overturned on appeal in August 2019. A resident who marries abroad may find that marriage recognised for Cayman Islands immigration purposes following the December 2020 Court of Appeal decision, but that recognition does not by itself confer marital status within the territory.

The unequal age of consent introduced alongside the 2001 decriminalisation remains the operative statutory position on the evidence available, and continues to expose residents to differential treatment under the criminal law.

Officials participate openly in LGBTQ community events: the premier, the governor, ministers and Legislative Assembly members joined the roughly 600 attendees at the first Pride parade on 7 August 2021. Organisers' request that participants avoid excessive displays of affection was a condition set by the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation for the public-space event.

The constitutional text is defended on the basis that its list of discrimination grounds is open-ended rather than exhaustive, an argument the Foreign and Commonwealth Office advanced against the Foreign Affairs Committee's criticism in 2009.
SYN-CYM.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the unequal age of consent identified after the 2001 decriminalisation has since been amended by the Legislative Assembly is unresolved in the available sources; no later legislative text is provided.

The scope of the December 2020 recognition beyond immigration effects is unresolved. Whether a foreign same-sex marriage is given general legal effect in the Cayman Islands, for purposes such as property, succession or next-of-kin status, is not sourced here.

No source in the inventory addresses whether the territory has enacted a civil partnership, domestic partnership or equivalent status scheme, or whether any such bill is pending.

Nothing in the inventory covers hate-crime provisions, their wording or their enforcement, or recorded incidents of violence against trans people in the Cayman Islands. Those questions remain unsourced rather than answered negatively.

Whether the Court of Appeal's equality reasoning in the recognition case has been applied to other areas of law, and whether any further appeal or legislative response followed, is not established by the available material.

SYN-ESH.name: Western Sahara
SYN-ESH.summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory under military administration by Morocco, and the territory stands under Morocco's penal code wherever its security services operate. Same-sex intimacy is criminalised, carrying six months to three years of imprisonment, and the broad discretion police hold in applying morality provisions is the instrument turned on visibly trans people.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, a partially recognised state and African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara and separately records homosexuality as illegal for men and women, and illegal there for decades. A July 2017 global legality roundup lists it as a criminalising jurisdiction, so both claimed frameworks record criminalisation.

Rights reviews document involuntary outing of trans people, discrepancies in expression at checkpoints and in registry records, an absence of gender-affirming healthcare, and no legal gender recognition; a 2021 route to recognition covers intersex people only. Morocco's religious establishment has publicly condemned transition.

Enforcement stacks on top of the occupation. Morocco charged 170 people in a single year, an organised outing campaign ran in 2020, and rights defenders are prosecuted at the territory's own courts. Human Rights Watch reported on 9 December 2005 the trial of seven Sahrawi human-rights defenders charged with fomenting illegal protests, calling the charges dubious and demanding a fair trial. A 2018 legal study recorded LGBTI Sahrawis exposed to violations by state and non-state actors alike.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch dispatch (9 Dec 2005): trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests; HRW called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. Documents Moroccan state authority exercised over the territory (security services, courts) and detention of Sahrawi activists - the legal framework a visitor to the territory stands under.

PinkNews global legality roundup (Jul 2017): lists the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women, and states that it has been illegal there for decades. The partially-recognised state, an African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara. The status recorded for July 2017 is criminalised.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: A 2009 USCRI report found that Sahrawi government officials running refugee camps in Algeria said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges even while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) states there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence. Multiple sources (Council for Global Equality, Equaldex, ILGA) describe same-sex sexual activity as illegal in the SADR for both males and females, punishable by up to three years in prison. In 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said the Constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it', and CEAR concludes this leaves no legal protection for LGBTQ people against discrimination or violence. Same-sex activity is also illegal in Morocco, which occupies most of the territory the SADR claims. Most residents of the country are Muslim and same-sex relationships are seen as a foreign phenomenon. The region was under Spanish colonial rule until 1976, and homosexuality was not decriminalized in Spain until 1979, shaping the legal and social inheritance of the territory.

SYN-ESH.tangentialFactors:
Two claimed governments over the same ground both record criminalisation: Morocco's penal code applies on the ground, while the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic lists homosexuality as illegal for men and women and has done so for decades. A visitor processed by either authority faces the same underlying status.

The 2005 trial shows the territory's courts are used against dissent as such, not only against gender non-conformity. Human Rights Watch judged the charges against the seven defenders dubious, which indicates that proceedings originating in these courts offer little protection to someone whose case attracts official disapproval.

Partial recognition complicates protection. The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic's African Union membership since 2016 does not settle consular responsibility for a foreign visitor detained in the territory, and the sources do not identify which authority would handle such a case.

The 2018 legal study attributes violations to state and non-state actors alike, so the exposure recorded for LGBTI Sahrawis is not confined to official conduct and does not end at a police station door.
SYN-ESH.localsOnly:
Sahrawis living under Moroccan administration face the same penal exposure recorded for Morocco, where 170 people were charged in one year, and an organised outing campaign documented in 2020 reached residents of the territory.

Gender-affirming healthcare is unavailable, and no legal gender recognition exists; the 2021 route to recognition applies to intersex people only. Expression discrepancies at checkpoints and in registry records expose trans residents during routine movement and paperwork.

The religious establishment in Morocco has condemned transition publicly, which shapes the environment for residents seeking care or documentation. The 2018 legal study records LGBTI Sahrawis exposed to violations by both state and non-state actors.
SYN-ESH.outOfScopeNotes:
Which penal code applies in the parts of Western Sahara administered by the Polisario Front rather than Morocco is unresolved in the sources; the inventory records Moroccan law for areas under Moroccan control and the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic's own criminalisation listing, without mapping the boundary of application.

No sourced material covers entry or visa rules for the territory, passport or gender-marker rules for foreign documents, hate-crime protection, or recognition of partners. These are not sourced rather than absent.

The figure of seven defendants in the 2005 trial comes from the Human Rights Watch dispatch alone and is not corroborated by a second source in the inventory. The 170-charged figure and the 2020 outing campaign are recorded for Morocco; their incidence inside Western Sahara is not separately quantified.

SYN-FLK.name: Falkland Islands (Malvinas)
SYN-FLK.summary:
The Falkland Islands, a British Overseas Territory with its own Legislative Assembly, legislate locally. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1989 and the age of consent has been equal since 2005. Same-sex marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017; the bill passed the Legislative Assembly in March 2017 by 7 votes to 1, and the registrar general subsequently confirmed that it is law. Civil partnerships are open to opposite-sex couples as well as same-sex couples.

The Constitution Order 2008 bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation at Article 16. The provision covers sexual orientation only; the sources do not identify a gender-identity ground in the Constitution.

UK frameworks do not reach the Islands. The UK Equality Act 2010 and the Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Falkland Islands, and the territory's own ordinances govern instead. These include the Crimes Ordinance 2014, which makes sexual-orientation hate-stirring an offence; the Crime and Public Order (Equality) Ordinance 2014, which provides sexual orientation as an aggravating factor in sentencing and recognises acquired gender under a UK Gender Recognition Certificate; and the Prisons Ordinance 2017.

The Crime and Public Order (Equality) Ordinance 2014 has permitted legal gender change since 2014. Gender recognition is not available on a self-identification basis, and no non-binary status is recognised.

The registrar general also confirmed that same-sex marriage is not legal in the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands, a separate dependency for which the UK is responsible; the equality reform applies to the Falkland Islands themselves.

sources.summary: PinkNews (12 Apr 2017): the Legislative Assembly passed same-sex marriage (7-1) plus civil partnerships open to same-sex AND opposite-sex couples, after a public consultation showing 90% support for same-sex marriage and 94% for civil partnerships in the ~3,000-resident territory — the operative equality reform.

Rob Salerno blog (22 Jun 2017): the Falklands registrar general confirmed by reply that the same-sex marriage and civil partnership bill passed in March is law, resolving the outstanding question of its assent; the same registrar confirmed that same-sex marriage is not legal in the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands dependency.

Mirror summary of the Wikipedia LGBTQ rights page (wiki-derived): legal since 1989, equal age of consent since 2005; same-sex marriage and civil partnerships since 29 April 2017; stepchild and joint adoption since 2017; constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination; UK responsible for defence; attitudes largely positive (90% consultation support).

The United Kingdom remains responsible for defence of the territory, while the Legislative Assembly handles domestic legislation, including criminal and equality law.

SYN-FRO.name: Faroe Islands
SYN-FRO.summary:
Faroe Islands stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

The Faroe Islands are a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Domestic equality and family law are set locally, beneath a Danish human-rights framework. Same-sex marriage arrived only in 2017, late for the Nordics, after friction between church and state.

In 2006 LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000, demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics. The territory had neither at that date. Surveys of the period found violence and discrimination against openly gay people not uncommon and legally unaddressed.

Religiously motivated opposition sits openly in Faroese politics. On 7 September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic prime minister Johanna Sigurdardóttir and her partner, citing his religion. The refusal concerned the presence of an openly gay head of government at an official table.

Opposition to public visibility continued. In July 2015, when av Rana demanded that Pride be banned from its position two days before the national holiday, singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him. His party remains formally opposed to homosexuality.

For a trans visitor the recorded hostility is political and rhetorical rather than physical. The named targets are openly gay public figures and a Pride event, and the actions on record are a refusal to sit at a banquet and a call for a ban. Violence risk appears low on the sourced material.

PinkNews (7 Sep 2010): Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic PM Johanna Sigurdardottir and her partner, citing his religion — signals the prominence of religiously motivated opposition to openly gay public figures in Faroese politics.

Gay Iceland (Jul 2015): when Faroese MP Jenis av Rana demanded Pride be banned (held two days before the national holiday), singer Eivor Palsdottir publicly urged people to ignore him; his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality — documents anti-Pride pressure and organised public pushback.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was legalized across the Kingdom of Denmark; the age of consent was then set at 18 for male same-sex relations, and the Faroe Islands did not follow Denmark's 1977 move to a gender-neutral age of 15 until 1988. The only criminal penalties touching LGBTQ people in the text are under the anti-discrimination law: anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. That provision took effect on 1 January 2007, making the Faroe Islands the last Northern European country to ban discrimination and harassment based on sexual orientation. Wikipedia country coverage: Expression has been a recurring flashpoint: the first gay pride march in 2005 provoked much controversy, and in June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter to the editor, 'Hvar eru vit á veg?', attacking national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the centre. Public petitioning also figures: a petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures, while an internet petition after the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen collected 20,000 signatures and eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2006 openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out, and he and his family then received threatening telephone calls; police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, became mentally ill and died by suicide in 2012. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn — nowhere else had the group been attacked. The 2007 law criminalises public threats, insults or degrading statements against LGBT people with a fine or up to two years' imprisonment.

SYN-FRO.tangentialFactors:
The Faroes followed the rest of the Nordics rather than leading them: the 2006 petition was explicitly framed as bringing the territory into line with its neighbours on registered partnership, and equal marriage came only in 2017.

Scale shapes how opposition reads. With a population of roughly 47,000 at the time of the petition, 20,000 signatures represented a very large share of the electorate, and a single MP refusing a banquet draws national attention in a polity of that size.

Pride is scheduled two days before the national holiday, which supplies opponents a framing beyond homosexuality itself. Organised pushback came from a nationally prominent singer rather than from an institution.

The sources bear on sexual orientation. No gender-identity claim appears among them.

Equality and family law for residents is made in the Faroe Islands, under a Danish human-rights framework; the 2006 signature drive was the instrument used to demand it, at a point when neither anti-discrimination protection nor a registered-partnership law existed locally.

The Centre Party of Jenis av Rana remains formally opposed to homosexuality, and its leader's refusal of a 2010 state banquet was made on religious grounds. Residents have organised counter-mobilisation: Eivor Pálsdóttir's 2015 public call to ignore a Pride ban demand shows domestic cultural pushback from public figures.

Same-sex marriage has been available since 2017, following church-state friction over the change.

SYN-GGY.name: Guernsey
SYN-GGY.summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

On 10 December 2015 the States approved same-sex marriage by 37 votes to 7. Two alternatives were put and rejected as insufficient: a civil-partnership-only scheme, and a single secular status called Union Civile that would have applied to all couples alike. The enabling legislation was left to a separate bill, which commenced in 2018.

Family recognition moved earlier the same year. A review of the Adoption Law recorded at page 1170 of the States of Guernsey Billet d'État of 24 June 2015 ended a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples adopting. The States agreed that same-sex couples may adopt, that civil partnerships are recognised for that purpose, and that both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

No source establishes legal gender recognition or trans-specific protection in force in Guernsey.

sources.summary: States of Guernsey Billet d'État of 24 June 2015 records the review of Adoption Law at p.1170, which led to adoption rights for same-sex couples.

BBC (10 Dec 2015): States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage 37-7, rejecting both civil-partnership-only and single 'Union Civile' alternatives; implementing legislation separate and not expected before 2017. Charity Liberate: 'historic day'; debate described as 'extremely positive'.

BBC (24 Jun 2015): Guernsey repealed its 50-year Adoption Law's ban on unmarried couples adopting — States agreed same-sex couples may adopt, with civil partnerships recognised and equal parental responsibility for both partners (Jersey had approved the same change two days earlier).

BBC (23 Sep 2011): Guernsey adopted the UK's relaxed blood-donor rules — gay/bisexual men eligible after 12-month deferral, targeted ~7 Nov 2011 to match the UK change, ending the local 1980s HIV-era ban; other donation restrictions unchanged.

sources.title: Guernsey Prison - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Guernsey's only prison, Les Nicolles, opened in 1989 and holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages; it has 11 wings, capacity 139, is operated by the States of Guernsey, and held about 99 prisoners in November 2024. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
Same-sex sexual activity is legal in Guernsey for both men and women. It was criminalised until decriminalisation prior to 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the UK; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences in its criminal law, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for private-life conduct that is lawful elsewhere.

Transgender people have been able to legally change their gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law only allows a new birth certificate to be issued and does not amend or remove records from existing birth certificates, so prior gender markers remain on the original record. Guernsey is also the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted civil partnership legislation, though UK civil partnerships were recognised for succession purposes from 2 April 2012.

A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 banned discrimination based on gender identity. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had specifically outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States of Guernsey passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously (33-0) explicitly including sexual orientation, rejecting all amendments proposing exemptions for small businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations; it takes effect from 1 October 2023.

SYN-GGY.tangentialFactors:
Guernsey's reforms of the 2010s track the United Kingdom closely rather than running ahead of it. On 23 September 2011 the island adopted the United Kingdom's relaxed blood-donor rules, with the local change targeted for about 7 November 2011 to match the United Kingdom's own timetable. Gay and bisexual men became eligible after a twelve-month deferral, ending a local ban dating from the 1980s HIV era; other donation restrictions were left unchanged.

The adoption reform belonged to a small regional pattern. Jersey's assembly approved the same change two days before Guernsey's, and the two jurisdictions moved in the same session of work rather than one following the other.

Organised opposition at the marriage debate was thin. The charity Liberate called it a historic day, and the States debate was described as extremely positive before the 37-7 result.
SYN-GGY.localsOnly:
Residents adopting in Guernsey are assessed under the amended Adoption Law, which recognises civil partnerships and assigns equal parental responsibility to both partners of a couple.

Local blood services apply a twelve-month deferral to gay and bisexual donors alongside the standard donor restrictions. The 1980s-era exclusion is no longer in force.

Les Nicolles, opened in 1989, is Guernsey's only prison. It is operated by the States of Guernsey, has 11 wings and a capacity of 139, and accommodates male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages. The population stood at about 99 in November 2024.
SYN-GGY.outOfScopeNotes:

The material reviewed on Les Nicolles contains no rule for housing trans prisoners by birth sex or identified gender, no trans-specific unit, and no stated solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners. Nothing on the prison-housing axis can be verified from it.

No Order in Council extending the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 to Guernsey appears in the sources reviewed, so the Act and its 2025 single-sex-services code are treated as not applying. Confirming the absence of such an order is a research task still outstanding.

SYN-GIB.name: Gibraltar
SYN-GIB.summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing territory whose own legislature and Supreme Court govern its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council. No such extension is on record in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap for a trans visitor is gender recognition. No route exists in Gibraltar to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore expects to travel on a document whose gender marker cannot be altered by any local process, and to be read in public under that marker.

Discrimination protection covering sexual orientation and gender reassignment has been in force since 2007. The sourced material does not set out what that protection covers in practice: whether it reaches service counters, single-sex facilities, health care, or employment in the visitor's own terms is not stated.

Same-sex activity has been legal since 1993, with an equal age of consent since 2012. Civil partnerships have existed since 2014, and same-sex marriage was passed unanimously in December 2016. A Supreme Court ruling in 2013 established a right of adoption by same-sex partners.

The 2016 marriage bill followed a public consultation opened in December 2015, which returned 3,490 replies from an electorate of 24,117. Reporting at the time described the population as divided over the change, while noting that an inter-ministerial committee chaired by a government minister had weighed the arguments and that the main parties supported the amendment; a draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act was placed before Parliament in August 2016.

Official language on hostility has been directed at anti-gay abuse rather than at transgender persons. In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse. That statement evidences an enforcement intent against homophobic abuse; it does not establish trans-specific protection.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Gibraltar's Parliament passed a bill on 19 September 2013, given royal assent on 25 September and in force on 10 October, amending the Crimes Act 2011 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation as a hate crime. In July 2021 the Justice Ministry began investigating a further proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence, prompted by what Chief Minister Fabian Picardo called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' on social media during Pride month. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for 'transgender identity'. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, de jure legalising LGBT adoption, after a long-term lesbian couple denied adoption for lack of legal recognition of their relationship challenged the law; the government amended the law through the 2014 civil partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024 and explicitly allows same-sex couples to adopt children without discrimination. In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy. The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender was equalised at 16. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 8 April 2011 that the higher age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set an equal age of consent of 16 that took effect on 23 November 2012. Before that, gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009. The Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 enquiry into overseas territories recommended making discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status illegal in all overseas territories.

SYN-GLP.name: Guadeloupe
SYN-GLP.summary:
Guadeloupe stands under France's national framework: French criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules on identity documents apply here as they do in the metropole. Same-sex marriage is available, gender-identity discrimination is prohibited, and legal gender recognition follows the simplified French procedure. No legal penalty attaches to trans existence.

Custodial settings are the documented risk area. A BuzzFeed News report of January 2018 found that in French prisons, whose rules govern detention in Guadeloupe, the placement of trans women follows the legal gender recorded on the incarceration papers, which may not correspond to the person's presentation; in practice, assignment is said to weigh the individual's best interests, with individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings used where possible. The national preventive mechanism, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, reporting serious violations of fundamental rights across French detention facilities and drawing on some forty referrals received since 2010.

Support infrastructure has expanded. Guadeloupe's first dedicated LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, offering reception, support and guidance for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities; it was driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations. During the opening, the minister responsible for family affairs and diversity, Aurore Bergé, announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted to overseas territories.

Community organisation is visible and growing. A September 2023 interview with organisers of Secret's Out described community members increasingly reconciling their lives with their orientation, with activism advancing after Martinique, alongside the work of Amalgame Humani's. In 2025, Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe. A 2023 local mapping of anti-LGBT violence exists, and organisers describe a gap between legal protection and lived experience.
