sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: French law applicable in Guadeloupe decriminalised same-sex relations in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained this in the 1810 Code, while public morality laws continued to be used against LGBTQ people; in Alsace and Lorraine, annexed in 1940, men were interned in Nazi camps and persecuted under Vichy despite the absence of a sodomy law. Vichy's article 334 of 6 August 1942 (later 331) set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. The Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity (art. 330, 2nd alinea), repealed in 1980. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980; the Senate has yet to vote. A conversion therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and/or €30,000. The law of December 2004, passed 31 December 2004, made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders called it a serious infringement of free speech. It created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste, an MP from the ruling UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Pride has been held in Paris since 4 April 1981 (Place Maubert, about 10,000 people), reaching 500,000 participants in 2019, with events in dozens of other cities. Transgender people have changed legal gender without surgery or medical diagnosis since 1 January 2017 (law signed 18 November 2016), but must still appear before a court to change the gender marker; a first name change can be done at the registry office. Self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were both dropped from the final bill. Until 2015 France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens, leaving many in legal limbo; the Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father, the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised, and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be considered the mother of the child she conceived before her sex change, while a 2017 legal bid for 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation. In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness, removing gender identity disorder by decree, though French trans rights organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems in gender-affirming healthcare: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent, self-determination model. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned the Little Mermaid Observatory, a group opposed to all gender transition for minors, to report on youth gender care, which called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'; a bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, with no update since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Blood donation deferrals for gay and bi men were cut to four months in April 2020 and abolished entirely on 16 March 2022. The French Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access, though this did not change actual practice. In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic violence as 'unworthy of France' after a rise in attacks, and a report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, France's interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away. In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos announced a policy fighting all forms of discrimination including homophobia in schools as one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline for students and staff, and requiring all French schools to give guidance on LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms; in February 2019 the use of 'parent 1' and 'parent 2' on school enrolment forms caused widespread conservative outrage. Legislation to ban medical transition for under-18s passed the Senate in May 2024, prompting large-scale protests, making trans minors a direct legislative target.

SYN-GUF.name: French Guiana
SYN-GUF.summary:
French Guiana stands under France's national framework as an overseas department: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France.

Legal gender recognition has been available on a simplified administrative basis since 2017, by declaration, with no requirement of surgery, sterilisation or psychiatric diagnosis. Anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity has been in force since 2012, and hate-crime sentence enhancement provisions were added in 2017. Nothing in French law criminalises trans status or gender expression.

Same-sex relations and same-sex marriage are legal under French law. Pride events are held, the scene is small and anchored in Cayenne, and a travel guide rates the territory "Very Safe for LGBTQ+".

The sharpest documented state machinery is custodial. Trans women incarcerated in France on the basis of their legal gender occupy a legal gray area, and that practice reaches French Guiana as a jurisdiction applying French prison law. The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism, reported on 25 May 2021 that serious violations in the treatment of transgender persons persist across French places of deprivation of liberty; its findings apply to detention facilities here.

The friction a trans visitor meets is practical rather than legal. Specialised gender-affirming healthcare is thin, remoteness pushes residents into metropolitan France for care, and local reporting describes transphobia and cultural taboos that discourage visibility and reporting of incidents.

SYN-IMN.name: Isle of Man
SYN-IMN.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the Isle of Man. Local law governs, with United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency whose parliament, Tynwald, frames these questions through its own bills. The Legislative Council's proceedings of 26 April 2016 record the Third Reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 alongside consideration of the Equality Bill 2016, which is the primary legislative record of the island's marriage-equality debate.

Employment protection preceded that debate by a decade. On 30 November 2005 the House of Keys adopted an amendment to the Employment Bill, tabled by Onchan MHK Peter Karran, barring dismissal of gay and lesbian employees on sexual-orientation grounds and aligning the island's employment law with United Kingdom human-rights law.

Political commitment at the top of the Manx government followed. On 9 June 2015 Chief Minister Allan Bell publicly backed same-sex marriage and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition.

The Marriage and Civil Partnership Act received Royal Assent and same-sex marriage took effect on the island in July 2016. The first conversion of a civil partnership to a marriage was completed within days of entry into force. Civil partnerships have been legal on the island since 2011 and are convertible to marriage without a second ceremony, and the registration process has run as a routine administrative matter.

SYN-MSR.name: Montserrat
SYN-MSR.summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal in Montserrat. In January 2001 the British government scrapped the anti-gay statutes applying to Montserrat and four other Caribbean territories, stating that the laws violated signed international human rights agreements. The reform reached the island as an Order in Council from London, overriding the objections of local politicians and religious leaders rather than following their consent.

A trans visitor should expect a very small, widely dispersed population with almost no visible public LGBT life. Reporting from 2012 describes the local social scene as decimated, capturing the mood with the observation that gay people 'are everywhere but hardly here'.

That scarcity has physical causes. Hurricane Hugo in 1989 and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption wastelanded the south of the 104 km2 island and displaced more than half the population northward, scattering an already thin community across a reduced habitable area.

The 2001 reform was met by religious leaders who called it totally unacceptable, and the territory's politics at the time read as a cultural rift with London. Nothing in the available sources documents organised opposition, community organising, or visible hostility since.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia: Montserrat's gay scene is very limited, with no gay bars, nightclubs or other venues on the island, though several hotels welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies. Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code ban discrimination based on sexual orientation, defining 'discriminatory' as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status. As a British Overseas Territory, Montserrat must also comply with international human rights instruments, including adherence to the European Convention on Human Rights and its non-discrimination and equality obligations. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, stating that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family. The age of consent is higher for homosexual activity (18) than for heterosexual activity (16). Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been legal since 2001, decriminalised retrospectively by an Order in Council under Sections 3(1) and 3(7) of the Caribbean Territories (Criminal Law) Order, 2000. Lesbian activity was never illegal, while group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences.

SYN-MSR.tangentialFactors:
Montserrat sits in a regional pattern in which several nearby jurisdictions retained colonial-era prohibitions; Britain's January 2001 action covered Montserrat alongside Turks & Caicos and three other Caribbean territories, which suggests the island's decriminalisation was an administrative consequence of its status as a British Overseas Territory rather than a locally driven reform.

Disaster history bears on what a visitor will find. The 1989 hurricane and the 1995 eruption cut the habitable surface of the island, concentrated the remaining population in the north, and hollowed out the social networks through which any minority community would otherwise be found. Recovery has been described as only partial more than a decade after the eruption.

The gap between formal legality and lived environment is unusually wide here: the law changed in 2001, while the sources describing social conditions date from 2012 and depict a scene with little visible presence in either direction.
SYN-MSR.localsOnly:
Local politicians and religious leaders opposed the 2001 decriminalisation, with clerics publicly denouncing the change as totally unacceptable. The reform was framed by opponents as an imposition from London and a cultural rift, and the territory appeared resigned to following the order rather than implementing it on its own initiative.

Residents live with a population that was halved and redistributed by two disasters in seventeen years. The remaining community is described as scattered and private, and the gay social scene as decimated, with no indication in the sources of an organised local LGBT organisation, venue, or public event.

SYN-MTQ.name: Martinique
SYN-MTQ.summary:
Martinique stands under France's national framework. Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department in full, so identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime operate here as in the metropole. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1815, the 2013 marriage-equality law applies, and gender-marker change is available through the simplified judicial route introduced by the state's 2016-17 reforms.

Discrimination protection rests on several instruments that reach the island directly. Goods and services have been covered since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2), employment since Labour Code article L1132-1 in 2008, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, where the wording 'sexual identity' was replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. Nothing in the criminal law criminalises being trans.

Detention is the sharp exception. Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code requires that detainees be placed in facilities matching the gender marker on their identity documents, so placement follows the marker rather than anatomy. In practice most trans women are therefore held in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them; a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records detainees telling trans women 'we don't want any women here'. The French prison framework governs Martinique's establishments as French law, and this pattern of placement and threat reaches them.

The CGLPL, France's detention-places watchdog, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed, and it makes recommendations on placement, isolation, safety and staff training. Because the opinion addresses French establishments as a category, its findings bind the department's prisons too.

Community infrastructure on the island is real but small. JM Concept 972 is a Martinique lesbian, gay, bi and trans network providing information, meetings and services, and running private parties and garden parties supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters, with dated events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September 2025.

The French prison framework applies to the department's establishments as French law.

Also lists local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: French law governs Martinique, and the following national provisions apply in the department. Homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic public comments were made illegal by a National Assembly amendment approved 31 December 2004, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; the same law amended the 1881 Law on the Freedom of the Press to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence, and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. Christian Vanneste, an MP in Chirac's UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though the conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Since 1 January 2017 transgender people can change their legal gender without surgery or a medical diagnosis, but must still go before a court to change the gender marker, while a first name change can be done at the registry office. The bill was signed 18 November 2016 after passing the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly, with the Constitutional Council ruling it constitutional on 17 November 2016 and dropping the original self-certification provision; before that, legal gender change had been banned for decades until the 1992 European Court of Human Rights case B. v. France. A report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose by 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims, up from about 1,380 in 2018. Penalties increase where physical assault or murder is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, and since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating cause for all crimes punishable by prison. Conversion therapy was banned by a bill published 1 February 2022. Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state cover for women under 43, and the MSM blood donation deferral was removed on 16 March 2022. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems with gender-affirming healthcare, including extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, with treatment covered by Sécurité Sociale under ALD 31. In March 2024 centre-right Republican senators commissioned The Little Mermaid Observatory to report on youth gender care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government with no update since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access. Earlier state hostility includes the 1960 Mirguet amendment treating homosexuality as a 'national scourge' alongside alcoholism and the Vichy age-of-consent law of 6 August 1942 setting 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign against anti-LGBTQ bullying, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day, and in March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms. LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM.

The CGLPL opinion is a national finding drawn from sites in France itself; it establishes the standard of treatment French establishments are held to, and it is the most substantial official admission of harm to trans detainees in the French system.

Comparison with the surrounding legal picture is unhelpful for visitors worried about criminal liability: the conduct at issue has not been an offence on the island for two centuries, and the contemporary dispute concerns the adequacy of protection and custodial treatment rather than legality.

Local support is anchored by JM Concept 972, a lesbian, gay, bi and trans network running information, meetings and services alongside private and garden parties, with a 2025 calendar that includes 4 July, 15 August and 5 September. SYN-MYT.name: Mayotte
SYN-MYT.summary:
Mayotte stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

No law criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage has been available on the island since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975, and the National Assembly's vote simplifying legal gender change for trans people extends to the department.

Placement in custody follows the gender marker carried on the identity document under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code. Trans women are therefore typically held in all-male facilities, where other detainees threaten them; anatomy does not determine where a person is placed.

The national detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty. Its opinion rests on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people, and on inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. Those findings bind Mayotte's establishments as French establishments.

Formal rights and lived experience diverge. A 2023 account of Bruno Agar, a teacher at the university centre of Mayotte, and his Malagasy partner describes a long and complicated path before the two married at Sada Town Hall, on a predominantly Muslim island where same-sex marriage remains a rarity in Africa and the Islamic world.

Legal representation on the island is thin. A gay-friendly lawyer directory returns no referenced practitioner for Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada and other towns, while Maître Isabelle Zribi, a lawyer at the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation based in Paris, is listed as available to take instructions.

SYN-NCL.name: New Caledonia
SYN-NCL.summary:
New Caledonia is a French collectivity in which France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system, while the territory legislates locally on many domestic matters. The result is a mixed record: the protections that visitors would rely on are national French provisions that apply here, and no source in this inventory records any local ordinance narrowing them.

Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality statute, which applies as French law; France's first wedding under that statute was reported on 29 May 2013, and the bill had been announced for introduction in Parliament in October 2012 as a campaign commitment. Nothing in the inventory criminalises trans people or same-sex relations.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual identity became prosecutable under the French Penal Code through the 2012 sexual-harassment legislation, and that provision was reworded to read gender identity in 2016. As a penal provision it extends to New Caledonia, so discriminatory conduct and transphobic motivation can be pursued as discrimination rather than as a distinct offence.

Detention is the sharpest documented risk. Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code places prisoners according to their legal gender marker, so trans women are ordinarily held in all-male facilities where assault by other detainees is reported, placement following the identity document rather than anatomy. The French detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on-site inspections at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. The French prison framework governs establishments in this collectivity, so the placement rule and the recorded pattern of violations apply here.

The overall assessment is therefore one of formal protection under an inherited national framework combined with a documented, unresolved vulnerability in custody. This record is evidence-thin on local conditions: it establishes what the law says and what the national machinery has found, and does not establish how those provisions are experienced on the ground in a small, close-knit society.

SYN-PCN.name: Pitcairn Islands
SYN-PCN.summary:
The Pitcairn Islands stand under the United Kingdom's framework: defence and external affairs are reserved to the United Kingdom, and United Kingdom domestic measures such as the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not apply here of their own force. Local law governs, and those measures could reach Pitcairn only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and that guarantee has been in force since 2010.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, and it recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn.

Adoption has been available to same-sex couples since 2015 and is open to married, unmarried and single people alike.

No source in this inventory addresses trans-specific law: legal gender recognition, sex markers on identity documents and entry screening are undocumented for Pitcairn, so a trans visitor has no sourced basis for expecting either a protection or an obstacle on those points.

SYN-PYF.name: French Polynesia
SYN-PYF.summary:
French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France, and French law governs it in matters of justice and civil status. Trans visitors therefore enter a legal regime in which gender recognition, detention policy and the rights framework are set by Paris, while much of daily life is regulated by the territorial institutions in Papeete.

France's national treatment of trans detainees reaches French Polynesia. Detention follows the gender marked on an identity document, and Article D248 of the French Code of criminal procedure requires separate men's and women's establishments; a trans woman holding a male marker is consequently held with men. BuzzFeed News, reporting on the situation in France in January 2018, treated this as a legal grey area rather than a settled outcome.

The national preventive-mechanism for places of deprivation of liberty, the CGLPL, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that France's Law 2016-1547 removed the requirement for medical transition or surgery when changing the gender on civil status, but that no norms were ever added governing how detainees should be housed in line with that change. Serious violations were documented across French detention, and the CGLPL's framework applies to French Polynesia's prisons. A trans visitor who is detained in the territory is therefore exposed to housing arrangements that national regulators themselves have found incompatible with the country's own gender-recognition law.

Gender-diverse healthcare in French Polynesia is limited by the small number of specialists available locally. Some trans residents, including rae-rae, face rejection from their families and leave for mainland France to obtain specialised services that the territory cannot provide. The gap between the law on paper and the care actually reachable in the archipelago is the most concrete material constraint for a trans person staying any length of time.

A reform effort to narrow that gap failed. Under Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua, the territorial government tabled a social-security bill that would have fully reimbursed hormonal treatment with progesterone and testosterone, matching mainland France. After heated debate in the Territorial Assembly the bill did not obtain sufficient support and lapsed.

The cultural setting is unusually documented. The mahu role, a traditional Polynesian recognition of gender diversity in which individuals embody both male and female qualities and hold recognised standing, predates colonisation, and mahu and rae-rae are visible across the islands in daily life. The territory hosted its first international LGBTQIA+ rights colloquium in 2023, bringing territorial government and church representatives together with the University of French Polynesia. Reporting from OutTraveler in July 2025 described this openness as ingrained in the culture rather than secured by law, noting that a visiting gay couple checked online whether the destination was safe before travelling and found mainstream inclusivity and acceptance operating without pride flags or organised protest. The 118-island territory has no Pride movement to speak of, which visitors read either as reassurance or as evidence that visibility is tolerated rather than defended.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: French national law, drawn from Wikipedia country coverage, with no stated bearing on French Polynesia: sodomy provisions were repealed by the Penal Code of 1791 and the Penal Code of 1810 retained that silence; an indecent-exposure clause (article 330, 2nd alinea) inserted in 1960 by the Mirguet amendment doubled penalties where the act was homosexual and was repealed in 1980, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under it, with the Senate yet to vote. A Vichy law of 6 August 1942 set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 in 1982; LGBTQ people in Alsace and Lorraine were interned in Nazi camps after 1940. The law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, punishable by up to €45,000 and/or 12 months' imprisonment, criticised by Reporters Without Borders and defended by the Chirac government; Christian Vanneste was convicted under it in January 2006 and that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Sexual orientation became a protected ground in employment and services in 1985, 'sexual identity' was added in July 2012, and on 18 November 2016 'gender identity' replaced it in article 225-1 of the Penal Code, with the Labour Code covering sexual orientation and gender identity in recruitment and training. Assaults motivated by the victim's sexual orientation attract heavier penalties, and in 2017 transphobia became an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison. A report of 16 May 2020 recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against roughly 1,380 in 2018. The conversion-therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and took effect on 1 February 2022; Le Refuge estimated 3-4% of its helpline calls concerned conversion therapy. The Académie Nationale de Médecine described the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem'; a March 2024 report commissioned from The Little Mermaid Observatory called gender-affirming care a 'health scandal' and youth transness a 'social contagion', and a bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 without National Assembly action since 23 July 2024. Late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommend puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) date from 1999; same-sex marriage passed the National Assembly 329-229 on 12 February 2013 and was signed on 18 May 2013, with joint adoption rare thereafter and assisted reproduction extended to lesbian couples from September 2021. Schools observe 17 May under the 2019 Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign, enrolment forms use 'parent 1' and 'parent 2', and since March 2019 higher education institutions should use trans students' preferred names. Mayotte reports frequent family rejection and discrimination, and in 2014 only about 20% of overseas residents viewed homosexuality as a sexuality like any other, against 77% in metropolitan France.

SYN-PYF.tangentialFactors:
The protection available to a trans visitor in French Polynesia rests on a national equality and anti-discrimination regime that France applies to the territory, while the everyday indicators a traveller can observe are cultural rather than institutional. The absence of visible protest or organised community signalling should not be read as absence of risk management; acceptance described by travellers is diffuse and social, and the underlying legal remedies run through French courts and national bodies rather than through territorial institutions.

Detention is where the mismatch between the national recognition framework and its application is sharpest. France has reformed who qualifies for a legal gender change without disturbing the rules that determine where a person is locked up, and the national preventive mechanism has recorded the resulting violations. A trans visitor whose documents carry a marker inconsistent with their presentation is the person most exposed to this, both at arrest and at any later stage of the process.

Healthcare capacity is a structural difference from mainland France, not a temporary shortage. Hormonal treatment available through reimbursement in Paris is not equally obtainable in Papeete, and the failed territorial bill confirms that the shortfall is recognised politically and left unresolved. Visitors who rely on continuity of treatment should plan around what is locally prescribed and compounded rather than around what the French social-security system covers on the continent.
SYN-PYF.localsOnly:
Residents are bound by the same French civil-status machinery that governs trans visitors: the gender on the civil registry determines identity documents, and the requirement for medical or surgical intervention was removed by Law 2016-1547. The CGLPL's finding that implementing norms for detention were never written applies to territorial prisons as much as to metropolitan facilities.

Reimbursement of progesterone and testosterone through the territorial social-security system was proposed and rejected after debate in the Territorial Assembly, so residents currently bear the cost of hormonal treatment that mainland France covers. Specialist services are concentrated abroad, and family rejection is recorded as a reason trans residents, including rae-rae, relocate to France.

The mahu role carries cultural standing within Polynesian society, and territorial institutions have engaged publicly with LGBTQIA+ questions through the 2023 colloquium involving the Vice-President, the territorial government, churches and the University of French Polynesia. That engagement concerns reflection and education rather than new territorial legislation.
SYN-PYF.outOfScopeNotes:
It is unresolved whether Article D248 and the gender-marker detention rule described in the 2018 BuzzFeed News report have been revised since that reporting; the inventory sources the position as it stood then and through the CGLPL's 2021 opinion, and does not document a later change.

The inventory does not state whether French Polynesia has any territory-specific anti-discrimination statute of its own, nor how the national protections are actually invoked in the territory. Travel-writer accounts of mainstream inclusivity are single-perspective and describe visitor experience rather than measured incidence; the absence of reported incidents in the sources is not evidence that none occur.

SYN-REU.name: Réunion
SYN-REU.summary:
Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France proper.

Same-sex marriage reached Réunion with the metropolitan statute adopted in 2013, following the bill announced by Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault in October 2012 for passage through the National Assembly and the Senate.

Discrimination on the ground of 'identité sexuelle' has been prosecutable in France since the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 in July 2012, which made transphobic harassment a criminal matter. The provision is in force in Réunion.

Legal gender change rests on the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282, adopted by the National Assembly on 19 May 2016 after being tabled by roughly forty Socialist deputies. Three government sub-amendments tabled alongside it could narrow its scope, and the sources do not establish the final wording.

Detention is the sharpest documented exposure. Under article D248 of the criminal procedure code, prisoners are placed according to the sex recorded on their identity documents, which leaves transgender women held in male prisons in a legal grey area. BuzzFeed News reported on 12 January 2018 that such women are punished for considerably more than their alleged crimes, following cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid threats from other inmates.

The French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL) issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding the persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities. Its findings rest on referrals received since 2010 covering some forty transgender people, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site and documentary inspections, and it issued recommendations to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. The opinion addresses the national custody framework that covers Réunion.

No local violence series, enforcement pattern or institutional hostility programme appears in the sources, and equally no documented local support infrastructure; a small, discreet community should be assumed but is not evidenced.

French framework applying to Réunion as a department.

The detention findings are national in scope and issued by an independent supervisory body, not a local authority: the CGLPL opinion and the BuzzFeed reporting describe a systemic placement problem rather than a Réunion-specific programme.

Legislative scope was contested at the point of adoption in both 2012 and 2016, in the first case over adoption and in the second over government sub-amendments capable of limiting legal gender change.

SYN-REU.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any of the CGLPL referrals received since 2010 concerned a facility in Réunion is not sourced; the opinion covers French custody facilities as a whole and does not break its roughly forty cases down by territory.

The final text and practical scope of the 2016 legal gender change section, after the government's three sub-amendments, remain unresolved in the sources.

No sourced data exists on local support organisations, incidents of violence against trans people, or enforcement outcomes under article L225-1 in Réunion specifically.

Whether a corrected identity document changes actual prison placement under article D248 in practice is unresolved; the reporting describes a legal grey area rather than a settled rule.

SYN-SHN.name: Saint Helena
SYN-SHN.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha; local law governs, and the United Kingdom measures can be applied only by Order in Council.

Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful in the territory since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across all three island groups. The 2009 constitutional order imposed by the United Kingdom bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation territory-wide, and those protections have been in force since 2009.

Same-sex marriage was legislated island by island. The Ascension Island Council approved the marriage ordinance on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0, it was signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016, and it commenced on 1 January 2017. Tristan da Cunha followed on 4 August 2017 and Saint Helena on 20 December 2017. Adoption by same-sex couples became lawful the same year.

The sources in this inventory are aggregator and index pages covering LGBT rights generally; none addresses gender recognition, identity documents, entry screening, or healthcare access for trans visitors.

SYN-TCA.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
SYN-TCA.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the Turks and Caicos Islands. Local law governs the territory, and the United Kingdom measures reach it only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 2001, decriminalised through the United Kingdom-led Caribbean reform programme, and the constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

The Court of Appeal ordered the Director of Immigration to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the same-sex spouse of Richard Sankar. Reading "spouse" in the Immigration Ordinance to include a same-sex spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, the court held that a refusal on sexual-orientation grounds contravened the equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees, while leaving the constitution's male-female marriage definition untouched and treating it as controlling. Residence recognition is therefore available to same-sex partners of residents and visitors.

United Kingdom HM Passport Office operational guidance, current as of 2025, states that transgender citizens are recognised in the Turks and Caicos Islands and covers nationality, legitimacy, adoption, gender recognition, civil partnerships and marriage, and documents for the territory. Gender-recognised travel documents for this jurisdiction are handled by the United Kingdom passport authority.

A resident account from May 2009 describes a social environment with no visible scene, where privacy is the norm and little information about gay life circulates publicly. About two-thirds of residents are not originally from the islands.

SYN-VAT.name: Holy See
SYN-VAT.summary:
Vatican City presents essentially no criminal-law exposure to a trans visitor. Consensual homosexual conduct has not been subject to criminal prosecution in the territory in modern times, and decriminalisation has nineteenth-century roots; no documented criminal-law persecution of consensual same-sex conduct exists in Vatican City itself. Nothing about being trans is criminalised. There are no bathroom inspections, no morality police, and the gendarmerie and Swiss Guards do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of visitors of every presentation pass through each year without incident, and entry is made through the neighbouring city of Rome with no border formality or gender-related screening.

No legal recognition of gender exists in Vatican City, and no anti-discrimination protection, facilities rule, or document-amendment mechanism covers a visitor or a resident. The absence cuts both ways: there is no machinery that could confirm a trans person's status, and equally no statutory protection to invoke if a dispute arises.

The doctrinal climate is openly hostile. The Congregation for Catholic Education's 2019 document "Male and Female He Created Them" opposes what it calls gender theory, stating that it "denies the difference and reciprocity in nature of a man and a woman" and "eliminates the anthropological basis of the family." The 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity. These are statements of institutional position issued by Vatican dicasteries; they are not enforced against tourists and carry no visitor-facing penalty.

The realistic worst case for a visitor is a dress-code refusal at the basilica or the Vatican Museums, where shoulders and knees must be covered. That is a garment rule applied to everyone regardless of gender identity, and it is resolved by covering up. There is no scenario in the sourced record in which a trans visitor is detained, screened, or turned back on the basis of gender expression.

Vatican City operates no prison system. It holds only a few cells for pre-trial detention, and anyone sentenced to imprisonment serves the term in an Italian prison with the costs borne by Vatican City. Because no domestic custodial system exists, there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, no designated custody facility, and no documented case of trans prisoner placement in this jurisdiction.

SYN-VGB.name: British Virgin Islands
SYN-VGB.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the British Virgin Islands since January 2001, when the United Kingdom's Privy Council ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws in the British Virgin Islands and four other remaining British Caribbean territories after the local legislature declined to act. Local legislator Orlando Smith accepted the outcome publicly, stating that "there is nothing we can do."

The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, including its 2025 single-sex-services code, does not automatically apply in the British Virgin Islands. Local law governs, and measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to the territory only when brought into force by Order in Council. A trans visitor should not assume the Equality Act's discrimination and service-access protections are available there by default.

Family status remains contested rather than settled. In 2022 the Court of Appeal of the British Virgin Islands refused the BVI Christian Council's application for permission to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack in proceedings testing whether the same-sex marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome, celebrated in the United Kingdom, is valid under British Virgin Islands law. The appellate court found the proposed appeal had no realistic prospect of success. The trial court's finding had been in favour of the two women, and the litigation was also testing a declaration that the territorial prohibition on same-sex marriage is unconstitutional.

Opposition to same-sex marriage is organised locally through the BVI Christian Council, which pursued the appeal bid after losing in the court below. A trans visitor who is married, or who has a spouse, should expect the British Virgin Islands legislature and its courts to be the venues where recognition is decided, rather than the United Kingdom's Parliament, and should treat marriage recognition as unresolved rather than guaranteed.

Local legislator Orlando Smith conceded, 'there is nothing we can do.'
GlobalGayz (Aug 2012/2017) rates the BVI among the more gay-welcoming islands in the Caribbean, while describing native homophobia as 'silent and invisible' and gay life there as lived in secret.

SYN-VGB.tangentialFactors:

A visitor crossing between Caribbean jurisdictions should not read that ruling as a regional norm; the legal position of each territory governs separately.

The available social evidence is thin and points in two directions. GlobalGayz, writing in August 2012 and 2017, rated the British Virgin Islands among the more gay-welcoming islands in the Caribbean, while describing native homophobia there as "silent and invisible" and gay life as lived in secret. The gap between a favourable external rating and undisclosed local hostility is itself the risk signal: conduct that appears tolerated may carry consequences that are not visible to a visitor.

The same-sex marriage litigation indicates sustained local religious and civic mobilisation against recognition, pursued through the courts after failure in the legislature and the trial court. Any assessment of hostility should weigh that organised institutional opposition alongside the absence of the criminal law.

Local residents carry the burden of the recognition fight in the territory's own courts. Residents seeking protections against discrimination or equal access to services must rely on local legislation, since the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code do not apply automatically in the British Virgin Islands.

SYN-WLF.name: Wallis and Futuna Islands
SYN-WLF.summary:
Wallis and Futuna is a territorial collectivity of the French Republic and stands under the French national framework: the civil and criminal codes of France apply locally unless a local measure overrides them. No law in force criminalises trans people or same-sex relations, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity has been prohibited since the 2012 statutory extension covering employment, housing and access to services.

Legal gender-marker change is available on the basis of the 2016-17 French reforms, which removed the requirement for surgery or a psychiatric diagnosis. A trans visitor whose documents already reflect their lived gender can therefore present them without undergoing a separate local procedure. Non-binary recognition does not exist in French law, so a third-gender or X marker cannot be obtained. Nothing in the sources indicates trans-specific screening or questioning at the border; entry follows ordinary French procedure.

Practical exposure is shaped less by statute than by scale and social convention. The territory's roughly eleven thousand residents live in village settings where Catholic and Polynesian norms govern visibility and where anonymity is close to zero. A traditional third-gender role, fakafafine, is present in the community, but it coexists with stigma and concealment rather than open acceptance. There are no resident gender specialists, and residents travel outside the territory for any transition-related care; a visitor should assume no local capacity for routine or emergency gender-related healthcare.

No hostile state action toward trans visitors is documented. The one state-level adverse mechanism in evidence is the detention framework inherited from France. BuzzFeed News reported in January 2018 that trans women whose legal gender is marked male, largely those without sex-reassignment surgery, are held in all-male establishments in a documented legal grey area, citing the case of a trans woman transferred to a men's facility in Lille in 2014. The French national preventive mechanism, the CGLPL, concluded in its opinion of 25 May 2021 that serious violations of the fundamental rights of transgender persons persist in places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals concerning around forty transgender detainees since 2010 and on interviews with associations and experts; that opinion extended its earlier opinion of 30 June 2010 on trans prisoners. As a French collectivity, Wallis and Futuna stands under that detention framework.

The 2018 press account and the 2021 oversight opinion are consistent with each other rather than contradictory, and the Lille transfer shows the issue arising in metropolitan France, not only in outlying territories.

The presence of a customary third-gender role distinguishes the territory from jurisdictions where gender diversity is purely a legal question, but the sources treat fakafafine as coexisting with concealment rather than conferring protection. Comparison with mainland French practice is limited by the absence of any local enforcement data.

Village life leaves little privacy. Catholic and Polynesian social norms shape what is discussable in public, and the small population means that a person's legal status and medical history are difficult to keep separate from community knowledge.

Residents held in custody fall under the French detention framework described by the CGLPL, where placement decisions for trans detainees have been found to violate fundamental rights; the sources do not record how that finding has been applied in the territory's own facilities.

72843720B863019116732.name: Centro
72843720B863019116732.summary:
Visitors in Centro stand under Italy's national framework. Outright International records same-sex relations as legal throughout Italy for men and women, and that legal baseline has not prevented recurring violence against LGBT people, in particular against transgender people. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Annual Review documents that homophobic and transphobic violence continued in 2025, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes in which groups lure victims and then assault or rob them. Progetto Gionata characterises transphobia as the most severe and most widespread discrimination confronting transgender people in Italy.

The most serious traveller-specific findings in the national record concern physical violence. ANSA reports that convictions for the sexual assault of young transgender tourists in Campania were upheld on appeal in April 2026, confirming both that the assault occurred and that the victims were targeted while in Italy. On 5 July 2024 tgcom24 reported that a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to ten months in prison for stopping and beating a transgender woman with batons, which shows that transgender people face the risk of violence from the officers who stop them even where such conduct reaches criminal sanction. Organised entrapment schemes of the kind ILGA-Europe records present a comparable risk surface for transgender visitors who use dating and hookup applications, where victims are deliberately isolated before being attacked.

Within Centro, the region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence maintained by Progetto Gionata and covering 2012 to 2025 places Lazio and Toscana among the six Italian regions with the highest victim counts. The other four highest-victim regions lie outside Centro, in the north-west, the south and the islands' neighbouring areas, so elevated recorded violence is a national distribution rather than a feature of this region alone, but two of the six worst-affected regions are here.

The strongest judicial response to transphobic violence recorded anywhere in Italy arose in this region. On 24 January 2025 the news agency Dire reported that a first-instance court in Bologna recognised a "transphobic motive" in the punitive rape of a trans sex worker, sentenced the perpetrator, awarded damages to the victim and to the association that supports trans sex workers, and for the first time admitted the Movimento Identita Trans as civil party.

Anti-trans public messaging has also been restricted in the region's largest city. On 30 August 2025 Rome's municipal administration announced that the Consiglio di Stato had upheld the city's 2022 removal of Pro Vita & Famiglia posters attacking 'gender' ideology in schools. The court found the images discriminatory, one depicting a boy being given a red hairbow, and held that public spaces may not be used for messages that generate alarmism, fear or serious disturbance, particularly concerning minors; the campaign behind the posters had collected 105,000 online signatures.

One high-profile case involving a transgender defendant ended in the defendant's favour. On 5 March 2026 the Court of Cassation confirmed the appeal-court acquittal of trans woman Pinheiro Reis Duarte Hudson, known as 'Patrizia', over the death of Samuele De Paoli in Perugia on 27 April 2021. The court found that the death was caused by cardiac arrhythmia following accidental compression during a scuffle De Paoli started, making the homicide acquittal final in a case that had become a national anti-trans media flashpoint.

sources.summary: On 24 January 2025 a Bologna first-instance court recognised a transphobic motive in the punitive rape of a trans sex worker, sentenced the perpetrator, awarded damages to the victim and to the trans-movement association that helps sex workers, and for the first time admitted the Movimento Identita Trans (MIT) as civil party. This is the strongest judicial recognition of transphobic aggravation recorded in Italy.

Progetto Gionata's region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence, covering 2012 to 2025, names the Italian regions with the highest victim counts, six regions ranking at the top. Lazio and Toscana, both in Centro, are two of the six highest-victim regions, alongside Lombardia, Piemonte (Nord-Ovest), Campania and Puglia (Sud). The study supplies the per-region distribution of violence.

72843720B863019116732.tangentialFactors:
The political and institutional climate in Italy is openly hostile. ILGA-Europe reports that the Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from its Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second consecutive year, and that a cardinal described homosexual acts as a mortal sin. Human Rights Watch's 2025 World Report chapter on Italy records sustained hostile political rhetoric about LGBT people as contributing to a hostile environment, within a wider account of rule-of-law and civil-society constraints. Progetto Gionata's assessment of transphobia as the most pervasive discrimination facing trans people is consistent with this official climate.

Transgender people detained in Italy are held in an institutional environment that monitor reports describe as lacking consistent gender-affirming provision. The Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report of July 2025 sets out the legal and policy framework governing LGBTIQ detainees, the pathways available for gender affirmation in custody and the treatment of same-sex relationships in prison. A 2026 study in Frontiers in Psychiatry, drawing on a thematic analysis of transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons, records systemic gaps and institutional challenges in the care provided to incarcerated trans people.

One judicial development points against the pattern of hostility. In March 2025 the Civil Court of Asti recognised, for the first time in that court, the physical and psychological harm caused by homophobic mistreatment. The recognition concerns the setting the case arose from, and its reach beyond that court is not established by the source.

For comparison, the six highest-victim regions in Progetto Gionata's 2012-2025 study are Lazio, Toscana, Lombardia, Piemonte, Campania and Puglia, so four of the six lie outside Centro and the concentration of recorded anti-LGBT violence spans the north-west and the south as well as this region.

One judicial development points the other way: in March 2025 the Civil Court of Asti recognised, for the first time in that court, the physical and psychological harm caused by homophobic mistreatment, with its reach beyond that court not established by the source.

Against that national backdrop, Nord-Ovest hosts the country's first two practical civic gender-recognition schemes. Milan inaugurated Italy's first gender registry, the registro di genere, which lets transgender people use their chosen name on civic and municipal documents, public-transport subscriptions and staff badges; LifeGate presents it as a milestone for transgender rights in the country, and the scheme is tied to a 2022 council motion brought by the country's first elected transgender councillor. Turin runs the analogous Identita Alias practice at the municipality and the public libraries. For a gender-nonconforming visitor these determine whether a ticket window or municipal desk becomes an argument.

Progetto Gionata's breakdown of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence by region and city covering 2012-2025 shows that two constituent regions of Nord-Ovest rank among Italy's six highest-victim regions for that violence.

Detention is the sharpest documented exposure. Italy announced in January 2010 plans for one of the world's first dedicated transgender prisons at Pozzale, near Florence, converting a nearly empty medium-security women's prison into a specially equipped centre for about 30 of Italy's roughly 60 transgender prisoners, then mostly convicted of drug or prostitution offences. La Repubblica reported in 2013 that the Pozzale project was abandoned.

Progetto Gionata's breakdown of aggressions by region and city, 2012-2025, shows that the region's two constituent regions rank among the country's six highest-victim regions for anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence.

sources.title: Italy 'to open first prison for transgender inmates' | BBC News
sources.summary: BBC News (12 Jan 2010): Italy announced plans for one of the world's first dedicated transgender prisons at Pozzale, near Florence - converting a nearly empty medium-security women's prison into a specially equipped detention centre for about 30 of Italy's roughly 60 transgender prisoners (mostly convicted of drug or prostitution offences); gay-rights groups welcomed the dedicated space and its psychological support. The report states that until then transgender prisoners had been located in women's prisons 'where they are often segregated for their own safety' - the documented 2010 baseline for placement practice in Italy. Repubblica (2013) later reported the Pozzale project was abandoned.

sources.title: La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere | La Repubblica (Inchieste)
sources.summary: La Repubblica investigative report 'La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere' (28 Aug 2013): at that date the prison administration counted 69 transsexual prisoners spread across ten Italian facilities, with placement tracking legal sex - female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners who 'according to their identity card, count as men,' trans women were held in men's sections, and those who had already undergone sex-change surgery were 'destined for the women's sections.' Segregation practice: in some prisons trans prisoners were put in isolation when cells were lacking - described as the most inhumane way to preserve their safety - and protected sections such as the G8 section at Rebibbia (Rome) and the protected section at Poggioreale (Naples) imposed limitations, including on partner visits. Documented ruling: the 2011 Terni case in which the Spoleto surveillance magistrate ordered the local health authority to pay for the prisoner's hormone therapy 'to guarantee psychophysical integrity'; the ruling was appealed and followed by a July 2012 appellate decision. The dedicated Pozzale transgender prison project (2008-2010), which would have drawn trans women from the special wing of Sollicciano (Florence), was shelved.

72843720B59566147937015.name: Nord-Est
72843720B59566147937015.summary:
Visitors in Nord-Est stand under the national framework of Italy. Outright International records same-sex relations as legal throughout Italy for men and women, and the national civil-law provisions on identity documents, marriage and anti-discrimination protection apply in the region. That legal baseline has not prevented recurring violence against LGBT people, and in particular against transgender people.

ILGA-Europe's 2026 Annual Review documents that homophobic and transphobic violence continued in Italy in 2025, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes in which groups lure victims and then assault or rob them. Victims are deliberately isolated before being attacked, which makes dating and hookup applications a comparable risk surface for transgender visitors. Progetto Gionata characterises transphobia as the most severe and most widespread discrimination confronting transgender people in Italy, a finding consistent with the pattern of violence recorded by monitors rather than with isolated incidents.

The region's dominant constituent authority carries a documented record of official acts of hostility toward trans people. Deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014, published in the official Veneto regional government bulletin, approved a council motion committing the regional government to a mandatory "Natural Family Day" observance on the last school day before the Christmas holidays and rejecting the aims and content of the WHO Regional Office's Standards for Sexuality Education in Europe, with a pledge to deploy every available instrument against their adoption in the region's schools.

On 3 July 2018 the Veneto regional council passed motion n.340 at its 178th public session in Venice, pledging support for those who fight in defence of the natural family and for natalist policies. The two deliberations place the regional government on record as an active opponent of gender-awareness education, which is the institutional climate a transgender visitor or family enters when dealing with regional authorities and schools.

Transgender people detained in Italy are held in an institutional environment that monitors describe as lacking consistent gender-affirming provision. La Repubblica's investigative report of 28 August 2013 recorded that the prison administration counted 69 transsexual prisoners across ten Italian facilities, and that placement tracked legal sex: trans women were held in men's sections, prisoners who had undergone sex-change surgery were sent to the women's sections, and female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners who, according to their identity card, counted as men. Where cells were lacking, trans prisoners were put in isolation, described in the report as the most inhumane way to preserve their safety.

Protected sections carried their own restrictions. The G8 section at Rebibbia in Rome and the protected section at Poggioreale in Naples imposed limitations that included limits on partner visits. In the 2011 Terni case a surveillance magistrate ordered the local health authority to pay for a prisoner's hormone therapy to guarantee psychophysical integrity; the ruling was appealed and a July 2012 appellate decision followed, though the terms of that decision are not set out in the source.

Italy announced in January 2010 one of the world's first dedicated transgender prisons, converting a nearly empty medium-security women's prison at Pozzale, near Florence, into a specially equipped detention centre for about 30 of Italy's roughly 60 transgender prisoners, most convicted of drug or prostitution offences. Gay-rights groups welcomed the dedicated space and its psychological support. Before then transgender prisoners had been held in women's prisons, where they were often segregated for their own safety. La Repubblica reported in 2013 that the Pozzale project was abandoned.

The political and institutional climate is openly hostile. ILGA-Europe reports that Italy's Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from its Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second consecutive year, and that a cardinal described homosexual acts as a mortal sin. Human Rights Watch's 2025 World Report chapter on Italy records sustained hostile political rhetoric about LGBT people as contributing to a hostile environment, within a wider account of rule-of-law and civil-society constraints in the country.

72843720B81376294924159.name: Isole
72843720B81376294924159.summary:
Isole stands under the national framework of Italy. Outright International records same-sex relations as legal throughout Italy for men and women, and that legal baseline has not prevented recurring violence against LGBT people and in particular against transgender people. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Annual Review documents that homophobic and transphobic violence continued in 2025, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes in which groups lure victims and then assault or rob them. Progetto Gionata characterises transphobia as the most severe and most widespread discrimination confronting transgender people in Italy, which matches the pattern of violence recorded by monitors rather than isolated incidents.

The most serious traveller-specific finding is the sexual assault of young transgender tourists in Campania. ANSA reports that the convictions for that assault were upheld on appeal in April 2026, an outcome that affirms accountability for violence against trans visitors while confirming that the assault took place and that the victims were targeted while in Italy. Organised entrapment schemes of the kind ILGA-Europe records for gay men present a comparable risk surface for transgender visitors who use dating and hookup applications, where victims are deliberately isolated before being attacked.

Police violence against transgender people is documented and has been prosecuted. On 5 July 2024 tgcom24 reported that a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to ten months in prison for stopping and then beating a transgender woman with batons. The conviction shows that such conduct reaches criminal sanction, and it also shows that transgender people in Italy face the risk of physical violence from the officers who stop them.

Transgender people who are detained in Italy are held in an institutional environment that monitor reports describe as lacking consistent gender-affirming provision. The Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report of July 2025 sets out the legal and policy framework governing LGBTIQ detainees in Italy, the pathways available for gender affirmation in custody, and the treatment of same-sex relationships in prison. A 2026 study in Frontiers in Psychiatry, drawing on a thematic analysis of transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons, records systemic gaps and institutional challenges in the care provided to incarcerated trans people.

Within Isole the violence pattern is documented both as a single prosecuted incident and as a continuing regional catalogue. At roughly 5 a.m. on 26 April 2025 three young men were beaten in a fast-food restaurant in Catania solely because they were gay; the Procura etnea reconstructed a sequence of insults and threats preceding the physical assault, the victims were hospitalised, and video of the attack circulated publicly. A 5 June 2026 Catania-based outlet published a follow-up cataloguing continuing assaults and suicide cases across Sicilian towns, indicating that the 2025 pattern of attacks has not stopped.

Detention in Isole follows the same national pattern. la Repubblica's 2013 investigation into trans women in Italian prisons documents that detainees are held in men's sections because their identity documents still list them as male, that female hormones cannot be prescribed to detainees whose documents say male, that decisions bounce between prison directors and doctors with no national guideline, and that some facilities allow hormone treatment only if the detainee pays for it. Placement therefore follows registered legal sex rather than gender identity. A plan announced in January 2010 to convert an almost empty medium-security prison at Pozzale, near Florence, into one of the world's first facilities dedicated to transgender inmates was never realised, so no dedicated trans facility exists and trans prisoners continue to be held in ordinary facilities.

The political and institutional climate is openly hostile. ILGA-Europe reports that Italy's Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from its Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second consecutive year, and that a cardinal described homosexual acts as a mortal sin. Human Rights Watch's 2025 World Report chapter on Italy records sustained hostile political rhetoric about LGBT people as contributing to a hostile environment, within a wider account of rule-of-law and civil-society constraints in the country.

One judicial development points the other way. In March 2025 the Civil Court of Asti recognised, for the first time in that court, the physical and psychological harm caused by homophobic mistreatment. The recognition concerns the mistreatment of LGBT people in the setting the case arose from, and its reach beyond that court is not established by the source.

82249235B5553315981608.name: Alberta
82249235B5553315981608.summary:
Alberta is a province within Canada and stands under the national framework: gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16 in 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, no Canadian jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, and Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers. Entry carries no trans-specific friction, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker.

Alberta's own statutes run against that framework. In December 2024 the legislature passed a package of three measures affecting transgender people as a class: the Education Amendment Act 2024, which requires parental opt-in for classroom instruction and sets rules on student pronouns and school sports; a health-statutes act barring puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors; and related vital-statistics amendments. Egale Canada and the Skipping Stone Foundation announced constitutional litigation at the time, calling the package discriminatory.

The care prohibition is the element with direct bearing on a visitor. It is a statutory bar in Alberta's health statutes on puberty blockers and hormone therapy for anyone under 18, so gender-affirming medical care for a trans minor cannot be obtained in the province while it stands.

Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the same sitting and invoked the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield all three laws from judicial remedy for years. Egale Canada, the Skipping Stone Foundation and five families state that their court challenge to the underlying statutes continues regardless. The laws are in force and constitutional litigation is pending.

Trans people held in federal custody inside Alberta fall under Correctional Service of Canada policy in force since 2018, which accommodates offenders on the basis of gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth. Gender-diverse offenders may request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex or gender marker on identity documents, and a request is refused only where the Correctional Service finds unresolvable overriding health or safety concerns. As of 2025 the service reported 90 self-identified transgender women in federal institutions, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's.

The Office of the Correctional Investigator called the 2022 gender-diversity policy an important change but flagged two gaps: no clear parameters for what counts as an overriding health or safety concern, and no dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse.

Alberta's statutory package deliberately stops short of custody and shared facilities. Premier Danielle Smith's 12 February 2024 announcement covered the care ban, parental-consent rules for school pronouns and sexuality instruction, and a ban on trans women in women's sports, and stated that the measures would not include women's shelters, women's prisons or changing rooms. No provincial rule placing trans prisoners by birth sex was enacted, and no Alberta-specific trans-prisoner placement, special unit or segregation case is documented.

82249235B71336988791422.name: Saskatchewan
82249235B71336988791422.summary:
Saskatchewan stands under the Canadian national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code as amended by Bill C-16, passed by the Senate 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No Canadian jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities. Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, most provinces permit a change of the gender marker on official documents by declaration, federal identity documents can carry an X marker, and Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.

Provincial politics in Saskatchewan run against that current. Saskatchewan and Alberta are the two provinces that have enacted policy rollbacks affecting trans people living there, including school-facing measures on names, pronouns and notification of parents. These rules govern residents rather than visitors. Hate-crime pressure is national: police-reported incidents reached 4,882 in 2024 and have risen for six consecutive years, up 169% since 2018, with offences motivated by gender identity and gender expression among the fastest-growing categories, and Egale Canada documents an increasingly organised anti-trans movement.

The Saskatchewan school pronoun-notice policy announced on 22 August 2023 requires schools to seek parent or guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronoun of a student under 16. The province's senior trial court struck the rule down as unconstitutional in 2023; the government responded by legislating the consent rule into the Education Act and invoking the notwithstanding clause to immunise it from Charter review. On 11 August 2025 the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan, in Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74, set aside that 2023 chambers decision, holding that courts lack jurisdiction to test sections 1 and 15 Charter breaches of the policy where section 33 has been invoked, so the policy stands. The same ruling granted the government's appeal in part while holding that a judge retains jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, allowing UR Pride's litigation to continue in the Court of King's Bench.

The constitutionality of the shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court. On 6 November 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it would hear the appeals from the Court of Appeal decision, brought by both the province and UR Pride, which asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. No merits ruling has changed the policy, and students have lived under it since 2023.

Detention is the weakest part of the framework for someone held in custody. Since 2018 the Correctional Service of Canada accommodates federal offenders based on gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth and permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement in a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression regardless of anatomy or the sex or gender marker on identity documents, refusing a request only individually where overriding health or safety concerns cannot be resolved. As of 2025, of 90 self-identified transgender women in federal custody, 73 were housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. The Office of the Correctional Investigator's 2022-23 report welcomed the 2022 gender-diversity policy but flagged unclear override parameters and the absence of a dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse.
