82249235B4167839012994.name: New Brunswick
82249235B4167839012994.summary:
Visitors in New Brunswick stand under the Canadian national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker, and Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.

Provincial education policy is the layer where New Brunswick differs from the rest of Canada. Policy 713 (Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity) of the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development took effect on 17 August 2020, was revised on 1 July and 23 August 2023, and was revised again effective 1 January 2025. Under the current text, students of any age may choose the names and pronouns used for them informally in school, with parental consent encouraged but not required; formal use of a chosen name in official records for a student under 16 still requires parental consent. The revision was made by the Holt government and goes beyond the recommendations of child advocate Kelly Lamrock.

The application clause of Policy 713 covers the school environment as a whole and names the people it binds: all students, school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors. A non-resident present in a New Brunswick classroom, whether as a visiting professional, student teacher or volunteer, is therefore subject to the same name, pronoun and privacy rules as a pupil.

The 2023 revisions remain the reference point for what the province is capable of imposing. Changes taking effect on 1 July 2023 barred teachers from using the preferred names and pronouns of students under 16 without parental consent and dropped explicit wording permitting students to take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, in accordance with their gender identity. The Progressive Conservative government of Premier Blaine Higgs made the change without a legislative vote, citing complaints from parents and teachers; two ministers resigned in protest and two others were removed, eight party members including six cabinet ministers boycotted question period over the handling of the file, and dissidents called for a leadership review. The Holt government's 1 January 2025 revision undoes the 2023 consent rule, which had drawn protests outside the legislature and a constitutional challenge by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association.

Facilities are addressed by Policy 713 as originally written: the 2020 policy requires schools to provide gender-neutral bathrooms. Whether that requirement survives verbatim in the text revised on 1 January 2025 is not established by the sources.

In federal custody, the Correctional Service of Canada permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution matching their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex marker on their identification documents. Requests are assessed individually and may be refused where an unresolved overriding health or safety concern exists under the service's 2022 gender-diversity policy. As of 2025 the service recorded 90 self-identified transgender women in federal custody, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's; between fiscal years 2017-18 and 2024-25 it received 129 requests from people assigned male at birth for placement in women's institutions, with 35 approved, 72 denied and 22 withdrawn. The Correctional Investigator has criticised the unclear health-or-safety override and the absence of a dedicated abuse-reporting mechanism. This federal policy is the framework a trans person in federal custody in New Brunswick stands under.

New Brunswick is the clearest Canadian case of a provincial government reversing course on trans rights inside a single election cycle, and reversing it back. The 2020 policy protected 2SLGBTQIA+ student privacy and inclusion, the 2023 amendments restricted it, and the December 2024 decision restored it effective 1 January 2025. 14339913B23556801435424.name: Scotland
14339913B23556801435424.summary:
The United Kingdom's post-April 2025 Supreme Court regime operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. The code is the daily, nationwide consequence of the ruling: trans visitors use facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how to lawfully enforce that division.

Prison placement has been litigated to the same end. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, ruled the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory custody guidance unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis; the guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in prisons matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The preceding hearing had been told by the challengers that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard. Any visitor arrested in the United Kingdom should therefore expect placement by sex at birth, with contested suicide-risk arguments surrounding that outcome.

Searching and strip-searching follow the same rule. British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, with trans women searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; the prior policy had permitted a trans woman staff member to conduct an intimate search of a woman holding a Gender Recognition Certificate. Police Scotland's interim guidance of 25 June 2025 states that in custody and stop-and-search, any search involving removal beyond a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear is conducted on the basis of biological sex, though where a person's lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

The direction of travel is a court- and watchdog-led rollback rather than executive hostility, and it is contested at international level: on 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.

Scotland's prosecution system names anti-trans crime as its own charging category. The Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021 created a dedicated transgender-identity aggravation, and the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service reported 104 charges carrying it in 2025-26, up 21% from 86 the previous year and the highest level recorded since the Act took effect. Across all categories the Crown Office recorded 7,115 hate-crime charges in 2025-26, a rise of 17% on 2024-25 and the highest total since 2003-04. For a visitor who is assaulted or harassed, the machinery exists to see the offence counted and charged by name.

sources.summary: COPFS 'Hate crime in Scotland, 2025-26' (30 Jun 2026): 7,115 hate-crime charges in total, up 17% on 2024-25 and the highest since 2003-04. Sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category. Transgender-identity aggravation accounted for 104 charges, up 21% from 86, the highest level since the 2021 Act took effect.

Scottish Government 'Hate crimes recorded by the police in Scotland, 2024-25' (pub. 17 Feb 2026): police recorded 8,538 hate crimes, with the highest rates per 10,000 residents in Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh (about 32.25 each); 62% carried a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator — first annual report under the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021.

31927357B79016588373767.name: Distrito Federal
31927357B79016588373767.summary:
The Distrito Federal stands under the national framework of Mexican equality law, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition, that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, and that the states without such procedures should adopt them. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Lethal violence against trans people is documented at national scale. The annual report published in May 2025 by a Mexican LGBT+ news collective recorded 115 violent incidents against LGBT+ people across Mexico in 2024, of which 59 were killings. Transgender Europe's monitoring counts 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months, and AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.

Within that national pattern the Distrito Federal is a single data point, and in 2024 it was the largest one. For the first time Mexico City topped the national count with 17 LGBT+ homicides, 11 of them trans women, ahead of Nuevo León's 5. Part of the elevated count reflects the capital's superior reporting infrastructure rather than proportionally higher danger, but the raw figures remain a negative signal for a visitor.

The institutional response is the strongest of any Mexican state. Mexico City's congress approved transfeminicidio as a distinct crime in the local penal code on 19 July 2024, making the capital the second state to create the offence. The reform is known as the Ley Paola Buenrostro, after a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety. Article 148-Ter, added to the local code on 23 August 2024, typifies the killing of a trans woman or feminine-spectrum person by reason of her gender identity or expression.

Investigation practice has been reorganised around that offence. A dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit was created in December 2024 to cover all violent deaths of trans women, and its investigators may no longer demand legal name or gender change or medical documentation from trans people, removing a documented route to outing and delay when a crime is reported. The prosecutor's instrument FGJCDMX/04/2025 sets initial-response protocol rules for transfeminicide alongside feminicide investigations, and on 25 August 2025 the mayor of Mexico City launched a new Gender Police with 30 patrol units to handle cases of violence against women and girls in the capital.

Enforcement remains the open question. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions explicitly that the analysis must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

31927357B30741484985331.name: Nuevo Leon
31927357B30741484985331.summary:
Three trans women murdered in less than a week in July 2024 (one disappeared and found dead days later; one killed while sex work); four transfeminicides recorded in July 2024 alone and five for the year in the national NGO yearbook — second only to Mexico City. Activists reported six trans women killed in a short period and accused three levels of government of rights omissions. Nuevo León's penal code contains no transfeminicide offence, and its 2019 hate-crime provision covers sexual orientation but not gender identity — meaning a visitor assaulted in Monterrey faces a legal framework with no specific protective category. The state has an anti-conversion-practices law carrying 2-5 years, and the national observatory's verdict on such statutes is that transfeminicide 'advances in law but not in sentences.'

Legislative response has been refusal: an initiative filed by Colectivo Casa Trans was 'ignored and finally lapsed,' prompting a 50+-day protest encampment outside the state congress still ongoing in January 2026 (activists report harassment and lack of basic facilities at the camp). A PT deputy in 2026 could only ask the congress to 'unfreeze' the bill. There is no investigative unit, no protocol, and no named offence to invoke. The gap between nominal coverage and protection is documented in the observatory review 'transfeminicide advances in law but not in sentences.'

Context for comparison: Mexico City pairs a similar lethality record with a dedicated transfeminicide investigation unit (Dec 2024), mandatory-response protocols and a gender police force (Aug 2025); Nayarit was first in the country to typify the crime (March 2024). Nuevo León's explicit legislative refusal is the opposite signal.

31927357B49073316106075.name: Michoacan de Ocampo
31927357B49073316106075.summary:
Michoacán has not typified the killing of LGBT people as a hate crime under state law, an absence acknowledged by the state's own welfare officials and by civil-society monitors. Attacks against the community concentrate geographically in Tierra Caliente, the zone of armed-group influence, so risk inside the state is uneven rather than uniform: Morelia, the state capital, records the largest absolute number of LGBT homicides, but enforcement of any protective framework is weak throughout.

Homicide against LGBT people in Michoacán is sustained and documented. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes contra Personas LGBT, presented by Raúl Martínez of Colectivo Michoacán es Diversidad, counted 46 LGBT homicides in the state between 2015 and 2024, distributed across Morelia (11), Lázaro Cárdenas (6), Apatzingán and Uruapan (5 each) and Zamora (4). The deadliest year was 2015, with 10 victims. Trans women accounted for 27 of the 46 homicides, and the 25 to 39 age bracket was the most affected. Thirteen disappearances of LGBT people were reported between 2022 and 2024, a figure whose investigation status the civil-society data does not resolve.

The pattern continued into 2026. Six homicide cases against LGBT people were identified in the state in the first four and a half months of that year, three in Morelia and one each in Uruapan, Ocampo and Maravatío. One of them was 'Daniela', a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia on 2 April 2026; a suspect was arrested, an outcome that stands out against the surrounding pattern of inaction. At least 56 aggressions against the community have been registered in Michoacán since 2014.

Impunity is the decisive variable for a visitor assessing protection. Of the 46 hate-crime cases recorded by civil society in the state since 2015, only one was moving toward judicial proceedings: the murder of Meredith Escarlet, a trans woman killed in Tarímbaro. The state prosecutor's office keeps no disaggregated data on these cases, and the victims commission, the state human rights commission and the state council against discrimination lack the capacity or budget to act. No public prevention policy for LGBT violence exists in the state.

31927357B5337219705256.name: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
31927357B5337219705256.summary:
Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many Mexican states now operate administrative recognition procedures while others lack them entirely, and that implementation differs sharply from one state to another.

Veracruz was among the last states to legislate. Only in 2025 did its Congress reform the Civil Code to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, with no age requirement. The Human Rights Watch material for Veracruz concerns civil registry and identity documents only.

The state's practical-safety record is the worst in the national data. Letra S's report "Muertes violentas de personas LGBT+ en México — Informe 2021" found that Veracruz led the national count of violent deaths of LGBT+ people for the fourth consecutive year, with 10 recorded cases in 2021, ahead of Guanajuato with 9, Estado de México with 7 and Chihuahua with 6, while 19 of 32 states recorded any victims at all.

Those counts are floors rather than totals. The same Letra S report found that no name was published in a third of 2021 cases, and that in 43 percent of cases the recorded sex was male without any attention to gender identity.

Veracruz closed 2025 with 15 recorded hate crimes against the LGBT community, according to Diario de Xalapa. The Letra S Excela annual impunity report of 7 May 2026 counted 60 LGBT+ people murdered nationwide in 2025, of whom 35 (58.3 percent) were trans women, a national trans-women homicide rate of 23.7 per 100,000; on the state ranking Puebla recorded 7 killings and Veracruz and Guanajuato 6 each. The Veracruz figure includes the motel killing in Oluta in November 2025, the stabbing of a 27-year-old trans woman on 19 November, which came after the state observatory had already counted nine hate crimes that year, three of them against trans women. Danger inside the state is concentrated in the metro area and the Coatzacoalcos-Oluta corridor rather than spread evenly across it.

Prosecution is the weak point. Activist Leonardo Ruiz of Orgullo Xalapa told Jornada Veracruz that the state prosecutor's office (FGE) holds several open LGBT-murder files, including that of Edhibaldo Presa Parra, a Universidad Veracruzana professor found dead on 7 January. Activists say suspicion of a hate crime rests on motive patterns and the victim's orientation, and they blame impunity within the FGE; data from 'Soy Humano' put 2024 below the national average.

31927357B6525686063804.name: Oaxaca
31927357B6525686063804.summary:
As a state of Mexico, Oaxaca stands under the national framework in which legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state mapping (11 and 31 March 2025) records administrative name and gender-marker changes on birth certificates in 21 of Mexico's 32 states, guided by a 2019 Supreme Court ruling that set recognition standards and was extended to adolescents and children in March 2022. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Oaxaca is among the states that have built the procedure. A 2019 reform of the state civil code created an administrative route to legal gender recognition, a 2021 decree extended it to people aged 12 and over, and a June 2023 Supreme Court ruling reopened access for children under 12. The resulting law is confined to identity documents; it does not determine where trans inmates are held.

The exclusionary signal a visitor may encounter is documented from the festival floor. On 25 May 2024 the organising brotherhood of the Vela San Vicente Ferrer Goola 'Lado Sur' festival in Juchitán circulated a written invitation stating that men dressed as women would not be admitted. Muxe activists, among them defender Felina Santiago, whose advocacy spans three decades, filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body. Three velas proceeded on 26 May, with muxes affirming their place in local society and culture.

Violence forms the sharpest part of the risk picture. Trendencias reported in April 2025 that Oaxaca is Mexico's fastest-growing tourist destination and at the same time its most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community, with violent incidents under investigation in municipalities where armed groups operate and with possible municipal-police involvement. The murdered include muxe Cristian Hernandez Cutino, aged 31, and stylist Zulma Hernandez Mendoza, aged 43. The state response described in that reporting is stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform.

The ombudsman's own caseload shows the persistence of the pattern. Oaxaca's Defensoría del Pueblo opened 34 investigations into attacks on LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022, and violence against muxes continues: muxe teacher Marimar 'Estrellita' Santiago was killed in 2022 on the road to Huilotepec in the Istmo de Tehuantepec, prompting community demands for justice.

Formal rights and their delivery diverge across Mexico. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) finds that the country's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions explicitly that the analysis must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

31927357B1137737933275.name: Puebla
31927357B1137737933275.summary:
Puebla stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many Mexican states operate administrative procedures for recognition while warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, and called on the states that lack such procedures to adopt them. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Puebla's own regime rests on a 2021 reform of the state civil code passed by the Puebla State Congress, together with a corresponding implementing decree, recognising the right to legal gender recognition. The regime carries an 18-year minimum age that the Supreme Court voided in March 2022. No conforming amendment to the statutory text appears in the sources, so a visitor whose documents must match their presentation should expect the age floor to remain written into state law even though it no longer binds.

Puebla recorded the highest count of any state in 2025, with 7 LGBT+ people killed. Nationally that year 60 LGBT+ people were murdered, of whom 35 were trans women, 58.3% of the total, with victims across at least 17 states. A visitor weighing physical risk in Puebla is therefore measuring the country's leading state-level tally against whatever protection the recognition statute supplies.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and states explicitly that the work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals; trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018 and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity, but same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available. Since 2024, replacement of the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Tripura shows the country's clearest documented pattern of border-checkpoint profiling of gender-nonconforming presentation. In August 2024 Tripura police reported apprehending 15 Bangladeshi nationals, including 7 transgender individuals, in separate incidents within 24 hours. A bus search at the Panisagar checkpoint in North Tripura district, on the highway between Assam and Agartala, found detainees carrying fake Aadhaar and PAN cards and travelling to Mumbai via Guwahati. The state shares an 856-km porous international border with Bangladesh, which sustains the checkpoint geography.

Reporting of the same August 2024 incident by North East Today on 2 August 2024 records 7 Bangladeshi nationals detained at the Panisagar check post, of whom 2 were transgender individuals and 5 others were described by police as disguised as third-gender, travelling by bus to Mumbai. The official description frames trans presentation as a cover for infiltration rather than as identity, and it is applied to people stopped at a highway checkpoint on ordinary intercity travel.

A coordinated joint operation on 9 November 2024 detained 12 Bangladeshi nationals including minors and transgender people in 24 hours. The first group of 6, holding 3 transgender persons, was held after midnight destined for Mumbai; the second group of 6, including 3 children from Khulna, was held at Udaipur Railway Station, and a local helper, Md Hafizur, was arrested for facilitating movement.

For a trans visitor, exposure concentrates at land and rail checkpoints rather than in statute alone. Document verification at highway check posts and railway stations is the point at which gender presentation is read by police, and the published operations show transgender people being counted and described as a distinct category of suspect. This sits alongside the March 2026 narrowing of legal recognition and the 2024 removal of sexual-violence safeguards nationally, and against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people, including the Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police.

1811400B57209440839078.tangentialFactors:
Checkpoint friction against trans travellers is documented across India, not only in Tripura: a trans woman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender at a Kolkata railway station; transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024; CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024 although she presented a PAN card; and passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination, with the Allahabad High Court granting relief in February 2026.

The Tripura operations differ from those incidents in their stated rationale. Elsewhere the friction is described as routine verification or security screening; in Tripura the police account explicitly presents gender-nonconforming presentation as deception, using the phrase disguised as third-gender, which converts a checkpoint stop into an inference of bad faith.

The 856-km border with Bangladesh and the volume of fraudulent identity documents in circulation give Tripura police a stated operational reason for intensive document checks on buses and trains, so a trans visitor's stop is likely to be embedded in a wider immigration sweep rather than isolated.

The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people in India, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, which sits uneasily beside the published counts from Tripura's August and November 2024 operations.

1811400B32673734874058.name: West Bengal
1811400B32673734874058.summary:
West Bengal stands under India's national framework. Parliament's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill of March 2026 replaced the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals, so trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018 and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, read to cover gender identity, but same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available.

Criminal-law protection weakened nationally in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

The land border is a documented exposure point. South Dinajpur police arrested a Bangladeshi transgender person from Sirajganj district, named in reporting as Ali Mondal aka Bijli Mondal, together with the e-rickshaw driver who brought her across the border, on allegations of infiltrating India. Trans presentation operated as the basis for an illegal-entry charge rather than as identity, and the encounter was driven by state actors, which is the mechanism a foreign visitor transiting the border would meet.

Gender-checking conduct by security personnel is recorded in the provincial capital. On 18 August 2024 a group of trans women heading to RG Kar Medical College filed an FIR alleging that a Railway Protection Force constable at Rabindra Sadan metro station groped one of them to check her gender and made inappropriate remarks. Metro Railway and the Railway Protection Force denied the allegations and counter-filed an FIR against the group, while footage showed the trans woman in tears.

Crime recorded against trans people in West Bengal is detectable rather than absent. Of the seven Transgender Persons Act cases registered nationally in 2021, three were registered in West Bengal, the highest count that year alongside Assam and Kerala. National totals remain very small, 20 cases across 2019 to 2023, which the reporting attributes to police-registration bias rather than to low incidence, and a 2025 survey put prevalence at 27.2% physical violence and 22.3% sexual violence.

sources.title: The Reality of Transgender Welfare Boards in India: An RTI Investigation
sources.summary: The Quint (5 November 2024) publishes an RTI investigation into transgender welfare boards: West Bengal is one of the 12 states/UTs that notified a board, but the majority of boards have held fewer than one meeting per year since their creation, and the 17 existing boards 'are mostly running rudderless without a policy framework, compliance mechanism, or any power', with several functioning as non-transparent bodies that diffuse demands instead of serving trans people. West Bengal's constituted welfare board operates without a functioning policy framework.

1811400B91946361694107.name: Punjab
1811400B91946361694107.summary:
Punjab has no statute of its own targeting transgender people. The framework a trans visitor to Punjab stands under is India's national law, and within Punjab the documented signal is institutional rather than criminal: Pride Amritsar cancelled the parade scheduled for 27 April 2025 at the Rose Garden after mounting resistance from Sikh religious organisations, including the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht, with organisers citing religious-group opposition as the reason. The Washington Blade reported the cancellation on 23 April 2025. No state intervention to preserve the event is recorded in the audited sources, so organised religious opposition has compelled the disappearance of Punjab's annual public trans assembly.

The national statute governing transgender people in Punjab is the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019), passed by the Lok Sabha on 5 August 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on 26 November 2019, receiving presidential assent on 5 December 2019 and in force since 10 January 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA judgment recognising a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender, the Act grants transgender people the right to declare a self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people. Criticism of the Act holds that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. On 27 January 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Criminal-law protection weakened nationally in 2024. A five-judge bench of the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India on 6 September 2018, striking down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts, holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution and preserving the provision for non-consensual acts. In July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omits Section 377 entirely; the replacement removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters is documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people. In Punjab specifically, no criminal exposure is recorded, but public trans visibility carries a documented precedent of organised religious opposition that succeeded in stopping the 2025 Amritsar parade.

Union of India, striking down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts, holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution, and preserving the provision for non-consensual acts. No state intervention to preserve the event is recorded in the audited sources, so organised religious opposition has compelled the disappearance of the state/province annual public trans assembly.

The national statute governing transgender people here is the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019), passed by the lower house on 5 August 2019 and the upper house on 26 November 2019, receiving presidential assent on 5 December 2019 and in force since 10 January 2020. Following the supreme court's 2014 judgment recognising a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender, the Act grants transgender people the right to declare a self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination, creates a national council for transgender persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people. Criticism of the Act holds that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. On 27 January 2020 the supreme court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality.

The national parliament passed an amendment bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. The parent nation has an estimated two million transgender people.

Criminal-law protection weakened nationally in 2024. a five-judge bench of the supreme court ruled unanimously on 6 September 2018, striking down the provision of the former penal code that criminalised consensual same-sex acts, holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the constitution and preserving the provision for non-consensual acts. In July 2024 the former penal code was replaced by a new national penal code which omits that provision entirely; the replacement removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. a trans woman at a railway station alleged that a constable of the national rail protection force groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. At an international airport terminal in November 2024, security personnel stopped an openly transgender law student although she presented an identity card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; a high court granted relief in February 2026.

1811400B21167269026319.name: Tamil Nādu
1811400B21167269026319.summary:
Tamil Nadu operates within a national framework that narrowed in March 2026, when India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill and replaced the 2019 law's self-identification route with recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist; the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

Tamil Nadu is the most protective sub-national layer a trans visitor will encounter in India. It was the first state to introduce a transgender welfare policy, in 1995, maintains a dedicated Transgender Welfare Board, and adopted a comprehensive State Policy for Transgender Persons in 2025. On 4 August 2025 the Madras High Court, in WP 7284 of 2021, recorded that the state had brought that policy into effect and called it "a victory for transgender and intersex persons after their long struggle", expressly commending the government. Active judicial confirmation of executive protection of this kind is rare and gives a visitor a concrete institutional recourse in this state.

The state's official transgender-welfare portal publishes the gender-change application kit, comprising an affidavit form, a certificate of identity for change of gender, membership ID relaxation and user manuals, and documents the wider regime: free sex-reassignment surgery in government hospitals, access to housing and citizenship schemes, and the thirunangai and thirunambi administrative categories embedded in governance.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery nationally. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

Tamil Nadu's courts are also demonstrably being used. Crime-data analysis published on 30 January 2026 records the state as the only one with a Transgender Persons Act case in 2020, one of one nationally, and again in 2022, with 7 of the 11 national cases in 2023. The same analysis cautions that registration figures understate actual incidence.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters is documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people and a state government with an unusually deep welfare and recognition apparatus.

1811400B70654311394581.name: Chhattīsgarh
1811400B70654311394581.summary:
Chhattisgarh stands under India's national framework. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

Within Chhattisgarh, the recorded lethal violence against a trans person is a contract killing. On 22 November 2024 the Times of India reported that Kajal, alias "Coca Cola", a transgender woman, was lured out, stabbed and dumped in an abandoned quarry at village Dhabadih in Baloda Bazar district. The killing was ordered by a rival, Tapasya, for Rs 12 lakh to block Kajal's ascent to the Jora Math community head seat, the guru gaddi. Five suspects were arrested and Rs 10.5 lakh seized.

Festival entry in Bastar district has been screened on religious grounds. The Times of India reported on 23 September 2025 that the VHP and Bajrang Dal objected to non-Hindu sponsors of Navratri garba events and claimed the events had become platforms of obscenity and vulgarity, with participants admitted only if a tilak was applied. Non-Hindu participation in public cultural events is contested by Hindu nationalist groups, and the resulting conditions are imposed on whoever presents at the gate.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints, in police contact and at gated public events rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters is documented in 2024 and 2026, and a trans woman was murdered in Chhattisgarh in November 2024, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.

Non-Hindu participation in public cultural events is contested by Hindu nationalist groups.

Times of India, Raipur (22 Nov 2024): transgender woman Kajal, alias "Coca Cola", was lured out, stabbed and dumped in an abandoned quarry at village Dhabadih (Baloda Bazar) in a Rs 12 lakh contract killing orchestrated by a rival, Tapasya, to block her ascent to the Jora Math community head seat ("guru gaddi"); five suspects were arrested and Rs 10.5 lakh seized.

14911670B7632012573600.name: Ceara
14911670B7632012573600.summary:
Ceará stands under Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people: the Constitution, the Penal Code and federal anti-discrimination provisions apply uniformly in the state, and there is no state-level legal distinction governing gender identity or expression. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and an expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's documents and family status are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry.

After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. Courts have applied those provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing. The protective text does not describe routine experience: Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions.

The operative risk for a trans visitor to Ceará is sustained lethal exposure. The state recorded 11 killings of trans and travesti people in 2024, the highest total in its region and third highest nationally, and 8 killings in 2025, tied with Minas Gerais for the highest state total of that year. Two consecutive years at the top of the national ranking indicate an entrenched pattern rather than an isolated count.

The national victim profile sharpens that exposure for a visibly trans traveller: 97% of victims are travestis and trans women, more than half are aged 18 to 29, 70% of those with a recorded race are Black, and 97% are killed in public spaces, with most incidents outside state capitals. In 2025, 70% of the 57 victims with race data were Black, against an average of 77% across 2017 to 2025.

Detention carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region, and documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units. The study treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights, and notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, alongside national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

sources.summary: G1/Globo report (28 Jan 2025), citing the ANTRA dossier: Ceará was the Northeast state with the most killings of trans people in 2024, with 11 killings, third highest nationally.

Igbá Agência (26 Jan 2026): per the 9th ANTRA dossier, Ceará was among the states with most trans killings in 2025 with 8 cases; Brazil totalled 80 (18th year as world's highest). Among 57 victims with race data, 70% were Black (avg 77% over 2017-2025).

SBT News (26 Jan 2026): ANTRA 9th dossier — Ceará and Minas Gerais topped the 2025 state ranking with 8 killings each; Brazil's 80 total down 34% vs 2024, still 1st worldwide; 1,261 killings 2017-2025 (avg 140/yr).

sources.title: LGBTQ people in prison
sources.summary: Wikipedia's general overview article (28 Sep 2026) reports no codified Brazil-specific trans-prisoner housing policy. Its Brazil paragraph states only that traumatic social vulnerability and stigma facing travestis and transgender people shape rehabilitation. For comparison, the article sets out international placement norms: Scotland's 2022 inspection standards admit trans and intersex prisoners to facilities matching their lived or experienced gender, and Canada places prisoners by gender identity.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Brazil

The statement is footnoted (ref. 253) to a Mix Brasil (UOL) article, 'Vivemos uma inercia no congresso...', archived 18 Jan 2012.

14911670B91095571793858.name: Rio Granda do Norte
14911670B91095571793858.summary:
Rio Grande do Norte stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that marriage recognition, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate across the country, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled like anyone else's at entry and in family matters. No state-level statutory restriction or unique legal finding applies in Rio Grande do Norte.

The dominant visitor-facing signal is lethal violence against trans people. ANTRA's dossier for 2024 recorded 122 trans and travesti killings nationally, 16 per cent below the 145 recorded in 2023 and close to the 125-per-year average for 2008 to 2024; five of the victims were human-rights defenders and 95.9 per cent were travestis or trans women. The same dossier documents systematic under-counting because official bodies do not record LGBTQIA+ victims properly, which is the basis on which Rio Grande do Norte appeared with zero recorded killings in 2024.

The ninth ANTRA dossier, covering 2025, records 80 trans killings nationwide, Brazil's eighteenth consecutive year at the top of the global tally. In the state ranking Ceará and Minas Gerais lead with eight each, while Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte appear with four each. Against a population of roughly 3.5 million, four cases yield about 1.14 killings per million per year, the highest per-capita rate among all 27 units in 2025 and around three times the national figure of roughly 0.38 per million. The jump from zero in 2024 makes Rio Grande do Norte the sharpest deterioration in the dataset, and the dataset itself cautions against reading a single-year zero as evidence of safety.

Lethal violence against trans women in the state continued after both counted years. In the early hours of 4 May 2026, Emanuelle Samira Fernandes Neta, a 27-year-old transgender woman, was shot dead inside her rented home in the Dom Jaime Câmara neighbourhood of Mossoró after five men broke in and killed her while she slept; military police found the body on a routine patrol and one suspect was arrested with a pistol and booked for illegal firearms discharge and armed criminal association. In late February 2026 a transgender woman known as Naomi was found dead in her own home in Praia da Pipa, in the Tibau do Sul municipality, killed by stab wounds, with the Civil Police opening an investigation.

Detention, if it arises, is governed by national rather than state rules. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, requires that a person held as LGBTI be recognised by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing, and that placement be fixed by a reasoned judicial decision after the person has been consulted about their preference. Trans, travesti and intersex people must be asked whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell; LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited. No Rio Grande do Norte placement policy is documented in the sources held, and practice elsewhere in the country has been found to diverge sharply from this framework.

14911670B97385369352280.name: Paraiba
14911670B97385369352280.summary:
Paraíba stands under Brazil's national framework: same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and after the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that gender-marker rules and spousal-visa equality operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry.

The protective text does not describe what people encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite those provisions. The ANTRA 2025 dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, recorded 4 killings of trans and travesti people in Paraíba in 2025, tied with Paraná, Rio Grande do Norte and São Paulo, against a national total of 80. CNN Brasil's 2024 dossier recorded 5 killings in Paraíba in 2024, where Rio Grande do Norte, Acre and Roraima recorded zero and Bahia, Mato Grosso and Pernambuco recorded 8 each.

The dossier's consistent victim profile concentrates risk on people who present visibly in public: young, Black and poor, 97% of those killed travestis and trans women, most killings in public spaces at night and outside state capitals, and frequently mis-recorded by authorities.

Detention is governed nationally. The Secretaria de Direitos Humanos da Presidência da República published a federal portaria on 17 April 2014 setting where LGBT prisoners are housed across Brazil's prison system, which applies in Paraíba's state prison system: transsexual men and women must be forwarded to female prison units, gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons must be offered specific conviviality spaces, and LGBT inmates may use their social name, which must appear in the admission record, and choose male or female clothing. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, additionally requires a judge to fix the place of deprivation of liberty in a reasoned decision after consulting the person, recording the declared preference, and prohibits using LGBTI-specific living spaces as disciplinary isolation.

No jurisdiction-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement policy affecting trans people was found in the audited sources, and the sources document no Paraíba-specific implementation, wing, segregation practice or case under the federal portaria.

The ANTRA 2024 dossier, published 27 January 2025, ranks Minas Gerais 2nd nationally with 12 trans and travesti people killed during 2024, behind São Paulo with 16 and ahead of Ceará with 11; the state's cumulative count for 2017 to 2024 stands at 100. 14911670B2612452665424.name: Pernambuco
14911670B2612452665424.summary:
Pernambuco recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the second-highest count of any Brazilian state in the ANTRA dossier released on 26 January 2026, behind only Ceará and Minas Gerais at 8 each, against a national total of 80. The state's annual figures have fallen from 13 in 2022 to 9 in 2023 and 8 in 2024, so 2025 is the lowest count since 2022, but it remains among the highest in the country.

The danger is concentrated away from Recife. Roughly two-thirds of such killings occur in interior municipalities rather than the state capital, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policy are weaker, and the recorded victim profile is young (a majority aged 18–29) and overwhelmingly Black (70% of those recorded), travestis and trans women. A trans woman was shot dead inside her home in Belo Jardim, in the Agreste, on 2 October 2025; the Civil Police opened an inquiry to identify the author and motive and no arrests were reported at publication. Fabiana da Silva Lucas, a 30-year-old Black trans woman, was found dead of multiple knife wounds along highway PE-160 in Santa Cruz do Capibaribe on 7 July 2021, the third such killing in Pernambuco that month; the Civil Police told press that a 22-year-old suspect was lynched by locals at the scene.

Over a longer window the same dossier records 83 violent deaths of trans people in Pernambuco across six years, the sixth-highest total nationally for that period, within 349 killings recorded across the Northeast between 2017 and 2025.

No Pernambuco-specific legal restriction or ordinance was identified in the audited sources; the Brazilian national framework applies. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and after the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

Arrest carries a defined placement regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, allows a person to be recognised as LGBTI by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; the judge must fix placement in a reasoned decision after consulting the person, set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units, and record the declared preference, with later change possible and transfers prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited. National rules also give LGBTQ prisoners a separate place in prisons, the right to be addressed by social name, placement in women's prisons and the choice of male or female clothing.

14911670B19428866735507.name: Bahia
14911670B19428866735507.summary:
Bahia, in Brazil's north-east, records trans and travesti killings at a rate that places it among the country's highest-burden states. The ANTRA 2025 dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, counts 7 trans people killed in Bahia during 2025, behind only a handful of states; on the same reckoning Bahia ranks third nationally across 2017 to 2025 with 97 killings, after São Paulo (151) and Ceará (107). Valor Internacional reported the same state-level counts on 27 January 2026, and the figure appears in consecutive annual dossiers rather than in a single outlier year: the ANTRA dossier for 2022 ranked Bahia seventh among the states, with 7 killings of travestis recorded in the state that year.

The victim profile is consistent. The overwhelming majority of those killed are travestis and trans women, most aged 18 to 29, around 70% Black among cases in which race was identified, and most killings take place outside the state capital. The burden falls on Black trans women and on young people in interior municipalities, not on visitors to Salvador's tourist districts as a matter of statistical fact.

A specific case in December 2025 illustrates both the killing pattern and the response. G1 Bahia reported on 9 December 2025 that police were investigating the death of Rhianna, an 18-year-old trans woman, as a feminicide: she was strangled in Luís Eduardo Magalhães in the interior of Bahia on the weekend of 6–7 December. The suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove her body to the police station himself and was released after confessing and claiming self-defence; the Civil Police confirmed the feminicide classification notwithstanding the suspect's initial release.

Bahia-specific statutory restriction was not identified in the sources reviewed. The national framework governs: Brazil's Supreme Federal Tribunal ruled in 2019 that discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds are criminal, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism, and same-sex couples' marriage and spousal-visa rights have operated nationwide since 2013. Nothing in the audited sources indicates a Bahia ordinance narrowing or widening those national rules.

Rio de Janeiro state stands under Brazil's national framework. Lethal violence against trans people in Rio de Janeiro is low relative to the country as a whole. Three trans and travesti people were killed in the state in 2025, roughly 0.18 per million against a population near 17 million. Nationally the toll was 80 in the same year, so a visitor's exposure to fatal anti-trans violence here sits well below the Brazilian average, and below the country's first-place position in world rankings.

14911670B6484683145874.name: Goias
14911670B6484683145874.summary:
Goiás stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, federal anti-discrimination provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, and since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling transphobia is punishable on the same footing as racism. Same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationally, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

Goiás recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, out of the 80 recorded nationally in ANTRA's ninth annual dossier. Against a population of roughly 7.2 million that is a rate of about 0.69 per million per year, close to 1.8 times the national rate derived from the same year's 80 national killings. The national total fell about 34% year-on-year, and Brazil remained first in world rankings for killings of trans people; the victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence.

For a trans visitor the operative risk factor is geographic. The national dossier finds most such killings occur in interior cities outside the capitals, where monitoring, reporting and access to public policy are weaker, and a visitor travelling beyond Goiânia shares that interior exposure.

Detention stands under the national regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, requires a judge to consult an arrested person about placement among available male, female and LGBTI-specific units, records the declared preference, permits later change of placement, bars the use of LGBTI-specific living spaces as disciplinary isolation and prohibits compulsory transfer as punishment. On paper Brazilian rules also grant trans prisoners the use of a social name, forwarding to women's prisons and the choice of male or female clothing, with separate custody for LGBTQ prisoners.

No Goiás-specific ordinance, legal restriction or protection measure was identified in the audited sources. The risk profile therefore rests on the above-national per-capita killing count and the interior-concentration pattern rather than on any local legal hostility.

14911670B48776179681147.name: Para
14911670B48776179681147.summary:
Pará stands under Brazil's national framework: same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and federal anti-discrimination provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds. After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on those grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

No Pará-specific statute, ordinance or policy affecting trans people was found in the audited sources. The national framework applies uniformly in the state, and there is no documented local legal hostility or local protection to weigh against it.

The operative risk is violence. ANTRA's 9th annual dossier records 80 trans and travesti people killed across Brazil in 2025, with Brazil first in global rankings and the victims overwhelmingly travestis and trans women killed with extreme violence. Pará recorded 5 of those 80 killings, placing it in the middle band of the national distribution for the year.

The geographic pattern matters more than the state total. Roughly two-thirds to 68% of such killings nationally occur in non-capital cities, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policy are weaker, and the victims are overwhelmingly young Black travestis and trans women killed in public places. A trans visitor travelling beyond Pará's main metropolitan area lands precisely where the recorded killings sit.

Nightlife carries a documented targeting pattern. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions.

Arrest triggers a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

14911670B9724590061217.name: Alagoas
14911670B9724590061217.summary:
Brazil pairs a broad legal framework for LGBTI people with persistent violence against them in practice. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds. After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. The annual dossiers of the national trans movement put numbers on that gap: CNN Brasil reported on 27 January 2025 that 122 trans and travesti people were killed in Brazil in 2024, a figure 16% below 2023, and SBT News reported on 26 January 2026 that ANTRA's 9th annual dossier counted 80 killings in 2025, a fall of roughly 34% year-on-year. Alagoas accounted for 6 of the 122 killings in 2024 and 2 of the 80 in 2025.

Brazil ranked first in the world for the killing of trans people for a 16th consecutive year in the 2024 dossier and remained at the top of world rankings in the 2025 count. The victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence; in 2024 they were mostly young Black women, many from the Northeast, the region Alagoas belongs to.

Alagoas's own totals are small in absolute terms, so a few cases move the state's position sharply between consecutive annual counts, and the national totals themselves fell by about a third across the same two dossiers while Brazil kept the leading world ranking. For a visibly trans visitor, the hazard documented here is lethal violence directed at travestis and trans women, most of them young and Black, carried out with extreme force.

14911670B2082355341666.name: Mato Grosso
14911670B2082355341666.summary:
Mato Grosso stands under the national framework of Brazil, where same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and the 2019 ruling places transphobia on the same footing as racism under constitutional and federal criminal provisions. Entry, visa and gender-marker rules operate on the same footing for trans visitors as for anyone else. The National Council of Justice's Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where arrested or imprisoned LGBTI people are housed: recognition rests on self-declaration before a judge, placement is fixed by a reasoned judicial decision after the person has been consulted about their preference, LGBTI-specific spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Violence risk is the dominant finding for Mato Grosso. ANTRA's 9th annual dossier, released on 26 January 2026, records 3 killings of trans and travesti people in the state during 2025, against a national total of 80. That national figure is 34% below 2024, with at least 75 attempted homicides recorded in the same year and crimes marked by excessive violence. Brazil has led the global ranking of such killings since 2008, with 1,261 murders over 2017-2025, an average of 140 a year; 97% of victims were travestis or trans women, more than half aged 18-29, and 70% Black among racially identified cases.

Two features of that national pattern bear directly on a visitor's itinerary. First, 67.5% of killings occurred in interior cities rather than capitals, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policies are harder, which raises exposure for travel beyond Cuiabá and Campo Grande. Second, Mato Grosso's 3 cases place it 12th among Brazilian states for 2025, and the state has recorded 43 killings of travestis, trans women, trans men, transmasculine and non-binary people since 2017. Three cases on a small population is a statistically fragile reading, but the interior-city concentration is the more durable signal.

Two state-level measures cut the other way.
