14911670B84195346134564.name: Distrito Federal
14911670B84195346134564.summary:
Brazil pairs a broad legal framework for LGBTI people with persistent violence against them in practice. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds. After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. Courts have applied those provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing.

The Distrito Federal recorded 2 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, drawn from ANTRA's 9th annual dossier, which counted at least 80 trans and travesti people killed in Brazil over the year. The national total fell by about 34% year-on-year, yet Brazil remains first in world rankings for such killings, and ANTRA's data indicate that the victims are overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence. The Distrito Federal's 2 of 80 is a low absolute count for a major metropolitan area and produces a rate of roughly 0.67 per million on a resident population near 3 million, a figure that sits above the national rate implied by 80 killings across roughly 203 million residents. Both numbers are small-sample statistics, and a difference of a single case moves the territory's rate materially.

Brasília is the seat of the Supreme Federal Tribunal, the national protective apparatus, and the offices of human-rights bodies. ANTRA's own dossier is compiled and reported from Distrito Federal desks, and the capital hosts international diplomatic missions and NGO infrastructure that raise the visibility and institutional cost of anti-trans violence. This concentration of courts, prosecutors and monitoring organisations is the main reason a modest positive deviation of about 0.02 above the national 0.71 is defensible. Set against São Paulo (0.71, no deviation), which also leads in institutional capacity but recorded 4 killings in 2025 and 16 in 2024, the Distrito Federal's lower absolute numbers and concentration of protective infrastructure make it marginally safer for a visitor, though the margin is thin and rests on very small counts.

Detention carries a specific and contested regime that applies to visitors as well as residents. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

10402087B89016843004490.name: Sachsen
10402087B89016843004490.summary:
Sachsen is a Land within Germany and stands under the national framework: federal constitutional and equality protections apply nationwide, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and no Land can remove the federal floor.

Two documented 2025 features bear on visitor risk around queer visibility in Sachsen. On 31 May 2025 thousands marched through Dresden for CSD while neo-Nazis mounted a counter-protest aimed at disrupting the march; the march proceeded. Separately, Sachsen, Sachsen-Anhalt and Thuringia jointly launched a Länder initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act after the Fall Liebich abuse case, with the stated aim of blocking misuse of self-ID. Sachsen is therefore a co-sponsor of an organised multi-state push to roll back trans self-determination law, a documented legislative threat to trans people in the state.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor in Germany. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several states have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all.

How the exception is applied in practice remains unsettled. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025; authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, and critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law.

DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, a finding illustrated by the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted. The Berlin prison service maintains an official page in German with information and contacts for trans, inter and non-binary persons held across the city's facilities.

Screening is a documented flashpoint at German entry points. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity; she characterised the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and gave Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a debate about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic. Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reported on how Berlin saunas and similar venues now treat trans women, after months of public argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Reporting and support machinery exists for hostility encountered in country. The STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation in northern Germany, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

25490228B14384488423733.name: Comunitat Valenciana
25490228B14384488423733.summary:
Visitors in the Comunitat Valenciana stand under two layers of law. The national layer is Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, which guarantees real and effective equality for trans persons and LGTBI rights: under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16. With administrative self-declaration, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules. A visitor whose documents reflect a self-declared gender is treated on that basis in public facilities throughout the community.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Courts are applying the aggravation in practice: in Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300.

The Comunitat Valenciana holds a dedicated integral law on the right to gender identity and expression and a general LGTBI-equality statute, one of only a small number of communities to legislate in both categories. Ley 8/2017, de 7 de abril, integral del reconocimiento del derecho a la identidad y a la expresión de género (BOE-A-2017-5118) makes its purpose the guarantee of an adequate normative framework for gender self-determination for people whose felt gender identity differs from that assigned at birth, and requires public bodies of the Comunitat Valenciana to treat people according to their felt gender identity. Ley 23/2018, de 29 de noviembre, de igualdad de las personas LGTBI (BOE-A-2019-281) covers non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, with access and admission rights at Article 56.

Enforcement evidence in the community is documented. The Audiencia Provincial de Valencia, Section 5, handled a case arising from a June 2022 incident in a Valencia park in the Patraix district, where an 18-year-old with several minors insulted, chased, recorded and mocked a trans woman solely because of her gender identity. The adult accepted six months' prison, suspended on condition of committing no offence for two years, plus a EUR 720 fine and a EUR 1,000 moral-damages indemnity to the victim; two minors had already been sentenced to supervision measures, and the case was handled by the fiscal coordinadora de delitos de odio. The same pattern of a gender-identity-motivated offence investigated, charged and resulting in a court sentence also appears in the national picture, where a juvenile gang in Valencia that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, with two minors judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied across Spain since 2005, and Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.

Other communities in the same inventory carry a single statute, among them Cataluña (Ley 11/2014) and Aragón (Ley 4/2018).

LGTBI federation's 2025 radiography of public educational policies across Spain's autonomous communities, covering gender-identity protocols and education legislation in each, places the Comunidad Valenciana with Madrid, Extremadura, Murcia and Navarra among the leaders on educational policy coverage, and records that the Valencian parliament completed its gender legislation.

19177384B97722443848736.name: Buenos Aires
19177384B97722443848736.summary:
Buenos Aires province stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passage by the Chamber of Deputies by 167 votes to 17 and by the Senate by 55 votes to one abstention, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. The 2012 Gender Identity Law remains in force in the province.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. A national decree of December 2024 added consent and medical-judicial requirements for minors' gender-affirming care and is under litigation. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree modifying the Gender Identity Law as it applies to minors, reported by Reuters as banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents, together with a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

The province carries the strongest sub-national negative signal in the country on police conduct. The provincial ombudsman's Gender Violence Office, created by Resolución Nº 100/10, submitted a report to the UN Human Rights Committee for its review of June and July 2016 documenting violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police, or by third parties acting under police cover, against trans and travesti people, in a dedicated section on violence by judicial, state and police agents. The documented incidents occurred in three cities: La Plata, Mar del Plata and Esteban Echeverría, carried out under preventive policing frameworks.

Academic legal analysis identifies a second, indirect instrument of criminalisation. In 2005 Buenos Aires province assumed jurisdiction over drug-sale and possession offences, a devolution that enabled provincial street-offence and drug-law prosecution to become the operative mechanism of indirect criminalisation of travesti and trans women after the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence. A UNLP thesis documents the pattern through microtrafficking enforcement in La Plata's Zona Roja, and Pensamiento Penal records rising criminalisation of trans and travesti women in the province, particularly in that district.

For a trans visitor the operative exposure is police contact: any stop, identity check or street offence in the province engages a documented history of state-implicated violence and of drug and street-offence charges used as a proxy for trans presence. Detention therefore carries a specific, sourced risk rather than a generic one.

Placement in custody is governed by a national rule. In February 2025 the Milei government banned housing trans women convicted of sexual crimes, human trafficking, or any violent crime against a woman in a women's prison. The rule restricts women's-prison housing for trans women in those conviction categories, and no separate trans housing unit or other trans-specific placement rule is recorded; Buenos Aires province has no trans-specific placement rule of its own.

19177384B97722443848736.tangentialFactors:
Violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina reached a documented peak in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a figure described as a record and as averaging one every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes called it an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in the country, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, nonetheless records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.

The provincial pattern sits inside a national deterioration rather than standing apart from it: the December 2024 decree on minors' care and the February 2025 decrees apply countrywide, while the police-conduct findings and the drug-law proxy prosecution are provincial in origin.

17162690B44985096553766.name: Subcarpathian Voivodeship
17162690B44985096553766.summary:
Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in Poland, which stands as the parent framework for Subcarpathian Voivodeship. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals; her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status.

At the voivodeship level the exposure is social rather than statutory. The Subcarpathian Voivodeship council repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution on 20 September 2021, on the same day as the Małopolska and Lubelskie councils, after the European Commission threatened to withhold regional development funds; Subcarpathian Voivodeship replaced the ordinance with a generic anti-discrimination statement. Such documents were declarations of local policy, not criminal statutes, and carried no penalty for visitors.

The county-level era ended in April 2025, when the county of Łańcut, within Subcarpathian Voivodeship, repealed the country's last surviving anti-LGBT resolution at an extraordinary councillors' session. At the peak of the wave, the Atlas of Hate mapping project recorded such documents covering about one third of Poland's territory.

Both the voivodeship repeal and the final county repeal were forced from outside through the threat to regional development funds rather than produced by a change in local attitudes, so the social climate that generated the resolutions is assessed to persist. Harassment exposure remains the operative concern for a visibly trans person at a public event in the county that resisted external pressure until 2025.

The national legal environment is in transition. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

17162690B86810837764805.name: Łódź Voivodeship
17162690B86810837764805.summary:
Łódź Voivodeship stands within Poland's national legal framework. The clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in that framework is detention and the treatment received in custody. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may face both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Polish courts have shown willingness to intervene on that exposure. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities. Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days, while listing sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland alongside physical appearance and foreigner status.

The national legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad. In September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights and called for a recognition framework.

At the sub-national layer, Łódź Voivodeship was one of five voivodeships named in the European Commission's letter of 2 June 2020 to the governors of Lublin, Łódź, Lesser Poland, Podkarpackie and Świętokrzyskie, following the adoption of anti-LGBT resolutions by that year. The Supreme Administrative Court of Poland revoked the Łódź Voivodeship resolution on 12 October 2023. As an earlier instance of the same pattern, the Świętokrzyskie voivodeship council revoked its own resolution on 22 September 2021. By 24 April 2025 all anti-LGBTQ resolutions and all Local Government Family Rights Charters in Poland had been withdrawn or invalidated by court order, including those applicable in this voivodeship.

By 24 April 2025 all anti-LGBTQ resolutions and all Local Government Family Rights Charters in Poland had been withdrawn or invalidated by court order.

17162690B84565288021286.name: Masovian Voivodeship
17162690B84565288021286.summary:
Masovian Voivodeship stands under Poland's national framework, and detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in the country. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status.

The wider legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

The resolution regime that marked the province and the country has been dismantled through the courts. By January 2020 a third of Poland's territory had passed anti-LGBT resolutions. On 6 February 2024 Warsaw's Voivodeship Administrative Court repealed the last remaining document "against LGBT ideology" in the country, and by 24 April 2025 every anti-LGBTQ resolution and Family Charter endorsement had been withdrawn or court-invalidated.

Masovian Voivodeship's own posture runs the other way. In February 2019 Warsaw Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski signed a 12-point LGBT+ Declaration drawn up with LGBT NGOs, pledging equality, non-discrimination and hate-crime response across security, education, culture, sport and employment, and including an intervention hostel and school "lighthouse keeper" projects. No repeal of the declaration is recorded; it stands. The declaration provoked the first anti-LGBT municipal resolution in Świdnik in March 2019 as an explicit counter-reaction, and the administrative-court campaign, led from Warsaw by the national Commissioner for Human Rights and carried through the provincial administrative courts and the Supreme Administrative Court, dismantled the resolution network nationally.

27671186B7584771598694.name: Bauchi
27671186B7584771598694.summary:
Visitors to Bauchi State stand under two overlapping criminal regimes. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, cohabitation between same-sex partners, public displays of a same-sex relationship and the operation of gay organisations, and Human Rights Watch has documented police using it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest. On top of that, Bauchi's Sharia Penal Code remains in force: the UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 confirms the religious penal codes of all twelve northern Nigerian states, Bauchi among them, and records male sodomy as carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Bauchi is the one state where that capital ceiling has actually been pronounced for same-sex conduct. On 28 June 2022 a Sharia court sitting in Ningi local government area sentenced three men, among them 70-year-old Malam Haruna, to death by stoning for homosexuality, holding that they violated Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001. The prosecution was brought by members of the Hisbah Vanguard through their lawyer Adamu Dan Kafi, who told the court the three were arrested committing the offence at Gwada village on 14 June 2022. Reuters reported it on 2 July 2022 as the first time the death penalty had been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria. The presiding judge, Munka'ilu Sabo-Ningi, granted a 30-day appeal window, and the UK Home Office note records that the sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor. Relatives told Punch, which published on 16 July 2022, that the judgment had not been carried out at that point. A further report cited in the same Home Office note placed a death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a Bauchi Sharia court in May 2024.

Courtrooms in Bauchi have themselves been targets of mob pressure. At a sodomy trial in January 2014 at the Tudun Alkali Upper Sharia Court in Bauchi, an angry mob stormed the premises demanding a death sentence. Against that, appellate courts in the state have overturned capital sodomy convictions: Amnesty International's 2004 press release records that the Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed Jubrin Babaji's death-by-stoning sentence, convicted on 25 September 2003 under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, for denial of counsel and a defective confession, following the quashing of Yunusa Rafin Chiyawa's conviction on 14 November 2003, and describes a number of cases in which convictions and death sentences were quashed on appeal.

Gender expression, not identity, is the trigger for arrest in Bauchi. Eighteen men were arrested by Bauchi state police and charged with sodomy for dressing as women, an offence under the Shari'a penal code; the charges were later reduced to vagrancy and the men were held in jail for several years awaiting trial before the pre-trial detention dissolved by the end of 2011. Persons perceived as trans-feminine in Bauchi have been arrested and held under Shari'a charges for years. Whether the proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Violence risk outside the courts is high and documented nationally. The Thomson Reuters Foundation reported in April 2024 on kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, a direct hazard for a visitor using dating apps. Police extortion accompanies enforcement: in March 2025 TimesLIVE reported that a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police was struck in the mouth with a gun butt and released only after paying part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded for looking gay. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and The Dial recorded in February 2025 that six months later no suspects had been charged.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

27671186B50148357657004.name: Kano
27671186B50148357657004.summary:
Kano stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, for all persons including visitors. Over that national layer, Kano State operates its own religious penal code, the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, which took effect on 26 November 2000.

The statutory ceiling in Kano is the harshest available to a trans visitor in the country. Under the Kano Sharia Penal Code, consensual same-sex activity draws 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment where the offender is unmarried, and stoning to death (rajm) where the offender is or has been married. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression and sex characteristics in Nigeria (June 2025) reproduces the same comparison: the Kano code prescribes death by stoning for married or previously married men, and 100 lashes with imprisonment of up to one year for unmarried men. The note confirms that the codes remain in force.

The exposure is not confined to men. The Home Office note records Kano's capital maximum for the offence termed 'lesbianism' as death, alongside Katsina; the other ten states operating Sharia codes punish the same conduct by flogging and up to six months' imprisonment. It also records that Kano's capital maximum applies to same-sex acts between women as well as between men.

Gender expression carries its own criminal exposure. Kano's separate Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law criminalises cross-dressing by men, so attire and presentation are themselves matters of criminal law in the state.

Enforcement is documented, not theoretical. In 2023, eight people convicted of wearing female clothing at a wedding were reportedly flogged in public on Hisbah premises in Kano state. The Hisbah, the state religious police, are recorded in the US Commission on International Religious Freedom's 2019 study of Sharia criminal-law implementation as the most active command among the states surveyed; that study drew on 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 in Kano, Sokoto and Zamfara and recorded Hisbah activity in each.

Nigeria-wide context applies on top of this. The SSMPA criminalises not only same-sex conduct but cohabitation between same-sex partners, public displays of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years, and police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. Human Rights Watch and the Thomson Reuters Foundation document police extortion of people stopped for looking gay and kito gangs that lure victims through dating apps to meetings where they are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail, imprisonment of up to 14 years and the death-penalty risk under Sharia law in the northern states.

27671186B99510750195830.name: Sokoto
27671186B99510750195830.summary:
Visitors in Sokoto State stand under two overlapping penal regimes. Nationally, Nigeria's Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 criminalises same-sex conduct for everyone including tourists, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment; Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, and that police have invoked it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Sokoto State's own religious penal code took effect on 31 January 2001. Male same-sex activity is punished by stoning to death where the offender is or has been married, and by 100 lashes otherwise; sexual acts between women draw ta'azir punishment of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment. Sokoto is listed among the twelve states whose Shari'a criminal codes apply to Muslims, with maximum penalties of death for men and whipping and/or imprisonment for women for same-sex acts.

The code is not a dead letter. On 9 October 2001 the Upper Sharia Court at Gwadabawa in Sokoto State convicted Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu of zina under sections 128-129 of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code and sentenced her to death by stoning, discharging and acquitting the co-accused. She appealed on 26 October 2001 and the Sharia Court of Appeal of Sokoto State quashed the conviction and discharged and acquitted her on 25 March 2002. The sentence concerned zina rather than same-sex conduct, but it establishes that Sokoto's religious courts apply the state Sharia Penal Code in practice, including the capital-punishment framework the code carries for married men's same-sex acts.

The legislative groundwork is documented at state level: an interim committee report was submitted to Sokoto Governor Attahiru Dalhatu Bafarawa on 13 October 1999 and a final report with an annexe draft bill to establish Sharia courts followed on 16 December 1999.

Gender expression carries separate exposure. Northern states also criminalise cross-dressing: Kano imposes up to one year for men who dress or behave as women, and a northern Islamic court imposed 10 lashes for cross-dressing. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. Trans identity itself is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute.

Violence against trans people is documented nationally. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people.

No Sokoto-specific custody finding is available: there is no documented arrest, trial or custody case in the state, no record of where trans prisoners are housed, no trans special unit, and no solitary or segregation practice.

27671186B69054806776702.name: Yobe
27671186B69054806776702.summary:
Yobe State stands under the national framework of Nigeria. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) applies nationwide and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (Version 4.0, June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Yobe is one of the twelve states that adopted Sharia into criminal legislation by 2002, the only states whose Sharia courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond federal law, according to Human Rights Watch's 2004 report. Sharia was established in Yobe in 2000 under Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim, and the state's inhabitants are mainly Muslims, which is how Yobe acquired a parallel religious-criminal jurisdiction for Muslims during the 1999-2002 wave.

For a trans visitor this makes Yobe a jurisdiction-level rather than incident-level risk. The same UK Home Office note (June 2025) states that the federal criminal code penalises same-sex male conduct with up to 14 years' imprisonment and three years for attempts while being silent on women, that the Sharia penal codes of the twelve states apply to Muslims, and that death is the maximum penalty for men in all twelve of them. Penalties for acts between women range from death in a minority of states to flogging and imprisonment. The note's enforcement and Hisbah section records the public flogging in 2023 of a person for cross-dressing, and observes that few secular cases reach court.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. 27671186B90305463766462.name: Gombe
27671186B90305463766462.summary:
Visitors in Gombe State stand under two overlapping criminal regimes. Nationally, the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reaches all persons including tourists, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex relationship and the operation of gay organisations; the UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Gombe is one of the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into its criminal legislation by 2002, as documented in Human Rights Watch's 2004 report, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law. The state's Shari'a Penal Code Law 2001 was signed on 23 November 2001 and criminalises same-sex conduct by men and women beyond the federal code.

The statutory penalties in Gombe are severe. Unmarried men convicted of sodomy face caning of 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment; married men face stoning to death (rajm). The lesbianism offence carries up to 50 lashes plus imprisonment of up to six months. Gombe defines gross indecency in its own formulation as any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour, a formulation broad enough to reach gender non-conformity as well as sex acts.

The UK Home Office note (June 2025) records that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for sodomy for men is death in all twelve states, and penalties for lesbianism range from death to flogging and imprisonment. That note carries a dedicated section on enforcement of Shari'a provisions and the attitude of the hisbah, the morality police. Whether the Shari'a layer formally reaches non-Muslim visitors is not settled by these sources; its practical reach is mediated by arrest practice and morality policing rather than by any exemption for tourists.

Enforcement in Gombe is documented at incident level. In October 2023 the Gombe State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps raided a gathering at Duwa Plaza along the Bauchi-Gombe Expressway that was preparing a same-sex wedding, arresting 76 people. State PRO Buhari Sa'ad told reporters that 59 males were detained, 21 of whom wilfully confessed to being homosexuals, with 17 females present, and that they would be charged to court for a crime of social vice in Gombe State. The Guardian of 23 October 2023 independently confirmed the arrests through Gombe NSCDC Commandant Mohammed Muazu and spokesperson Buhari Saad, who said the remaining males and the 17 females were invited guests and onlookers, and noted officers' concern over the participants' ages.

No trans-specific incident or documented hisbah activity appears in the sources assembled for Gombe. Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed: Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. Absence of records reflects fear of outing and surveillance gaps rather than absence of risk.

27671186B1226853346294.name: Jigawa
27671186B1226853346294.summary:
Jigawa stands under Nigeria's national framework as well as its own state code. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies across the country and, according to Human Rights Watch (October 2016), also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment; police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation and of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity.

Jigawa is one of the twelve northern states that adopted Sharia into their criminal legislation by 2002, a process Human Rights Watch (2004) traces to Zamfara's governor introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000. These twelve states are the only ones where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases. The UK Home Office note states that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Jigawa's own instrument is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, Law No. 12 of 2000, signed on 18 December 2000 and brought into operation on 27 December 2000 (Jigawa State Gazette Vol. 1 No. 12). The Home Office table for Jigawa gives the penalties as death by stoning for married men, 100 lashes plus imprisonment of up to one year for unmarried men, and same-sex acts between women punished with up to 50 lashes plus imprisonment of up to six months. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms the code remains in force and that the Sharia penal layer is the operative criminal frame for Muslims in the state.

The state code reaches conduct the federal statute does not supply independently. Its definition of lesbianism carries up to 50 lashes and up to six months' imprisonment, and Jigawa includes the 'unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs' explanation of the offence — a route to prosecution for women that the federal code, which addresses men's acts, does not provide on its own.

Violence and extraction accompany the legal exposure. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and six months later no suspects had been charged (the Dial, February 2025). TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports a 24-year-old stopped by Lagos police who was struck in the mouth with a gun butt and released only after paying almost half of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed: Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), sentenced on 12 April 2024 to six months for naira abuse and held in a maximum-security prison in Lagos until 5 August 2024; press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison would hold her, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion, and an October 2024 panel found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act.

27671186B54051914323789.name: Kaduna
27671186B54051914323789.summary:
Kaduna State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide with up to 14 years' imprisonment for all persons including tourists. The Act reaches beyond marriage, banning cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years, and Human Rights Watch (October 2016) documents police using it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Kaduna is one of the twelve states where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases. Human Rights Watch (2004) traces that jurisdiction to Zamfara's governor introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, after which by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation.

The state carries two stacked criminal layers, and the secular one is harsher than the federal ceiling. Section 3.1.6 and 8.2.19 of the Home Office note record that Kaduna adopted its own Penal Code in 2017, whose Section 259 punishes 'unnatural offences' including sodomy, lesbianism and bestiality with up to 21 years' imprisonment and a fine, above the federal 14-year maximum.

The Sharia layer is Kaduna's own promulgated code rather than umbrella coverage. Ostien's annotated volume lists the Sharia Penal Code Law 2002, Law No. 4 of 2002, signed into law and coming into operation on 21 June 2002 (Kaduna State Gazette No. 17 Vol. 36, 4 July 2002, pp. A15-A108, bound with the Sharia Criminal Procedure Code). Its annotation records Kaduna as one of only three states whose enacted text states that whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm), with no unmarried or married graduation, while the lesbianism offence is left to ta'azir, discretionary punishment. The Home Office's twelve-state penalties table (section 8.4.3, ILGA-derived) carries Kaduna's row on the same terms: death by stoning as the maximum for liwat, and same-sex acts between women punishable at the discretion of the qadi.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

No trans-specific incident and no documented Hisbah enforcement appears for Kaduna in these sources, and no court-level study samples the state. The evidence for Kaduna rests on its enacted statutes rather than on reported prosecutions.

27671186B53868438251790.name: Kebbi
27671186B53868438251790.summary:
Kebbi stands under the national framework of Nigeria. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The penalties apply to all persons present in the country, including visitors.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry exposure at the border. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Kebbi runs its own religious criminal layer on top of that statute. Its Penal Code (Amendment) Law (Law No. 21 of 2000) was signed into law and came into operation on 1 December 2000, recorded in Kebbi State Gazette Vol. 2 No. 1, Supplement, 31 December 2000. The enacted text provides that whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm), while same-sex acts between women attract 50 lashes and imprisonment of up to six months. The UK Home Office note carries this as Kebbi's own row in its twelve-state Sharia penalties table at section 8.4.3, a dated government confirmation that Kebbi's code extends criminalisation to acts between women and is broader in scope and harsher in penalty than the federal statute for Muslim defendants.

Jurisdiction over that code is personal. Human Rights Watch (2004) records that by 2002 twelve northern states, Kebbi among them, had Shari'a criminal legislation and Sharia courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, and that these were the only states with such jurisdiction. A visitor who is Muslim, or is taken to be Muslim, therefore faces a religious court applying a penal code with a capital ceiling for men's acts; a visitor assessed as non-Muslim is not within that court's criminal jurisdiction, though the national statute still applies.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. Cross-dressing is separately penalised in some states, with Kano providing up to one year in prison or a fine for men who dress or behave as women and sentencing a TikToker to one year in prison in 2025.

Violence against trans people is documented and official response has been slow. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence and extortion against perceived gay people are routine features of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text. Visitors who use dating apps face a separate route to harm: the Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye). She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos and ending with release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

27671186B79778155682183.name: Niger
27671186B79778155682183.summary:
Visitors in every part of Nigeria stand under the national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide and reaches beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Criminal exposure attaches at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (version 4.0, June 2025) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve states that have adopted it as criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is routine. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos and released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Niger State stands under that national framework and adds a second, religious criminal track. Human Rights Watch (2004) documents the wave of Sharia adoption across the twelve states concerned, listing Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara, and tracing it from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated 27 October 1999 and in force 27 January 2000; the provisions remain in force.

Niger State's own Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 (HB.4/2000) was signed on 22 February 2000, came into operation on 4 May 2000, and was gazetted as Niger State Gazette No. 8, Vol. 25 of 9 March 2000. It amends Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State, to review the punishments therein, defines 'adultery' to include sodomy, and inserts section 68A: a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment, with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68, while the ordinary Penal Code punishment applies otherwise.

The state editor's note records that this is not a complete Sharia Penal Code. It amends the Penal Code of 1960 so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims. An outed Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor in Niger State therefore stands under a harsher parallel legal frame than federal law alone, and the June 2025 UK Home Office note confirms the religious layer remains in force and extends criminalisation to acts between women.

27671186B63712480376187.name: Edo
27671186B63712480376187.summary:
Visitors in Edo State stand under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. No source in this inventory applies Sharia criminal law to Edo State.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment: the Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case surfaced in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Edo State's own record is one of lethal community violence against men caught in same-sex acts, with no prosecution recorded in any of the incidents documented here. In May 2018 in Ekpoma, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. The Nigerian Observer's coverage framed the act as 'abominable' and as defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land'.

On 10 June 2010 the Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City, Oredo Local Government Area, that a middle-aged man, Mark Osato Edomwonyi, narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was caught in a same-sex act with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment. A neighbour raised the alarm, Mark fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, and the mob then 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution is recorded in the report, and Mark's whereabouts were still unknown at filing. Lethal mob 'community justice' therefore operates in the state capital as well as in smaller communities, with no documented law-enforcement response.

Edo's police machinery has itself pursued same-sex couples on the ground. The Nigerian Observer reported on 15 August 2008 that police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were caught in the act in a remote community in Edo State in February 2008; a mob mercilessly beat the two for desecrating the community, Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived, and the police arrested Jerry for interrogation. A community lynching attempt was answered by arrest and a wanted declaration rather than by protection.

For national scale, The Initiative for Equal Rights' 2024 Human Rights Violations Report, published in January 2025, records 556 violations affecting 850 victims based on real or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics across Nigeria during the reporting period, and states that these figures represent only a fraction of the true scale.

65028918B93184959873838.name: Aceh
65028918B93184959873838.summary:
Aceh stands under Indonesia's national framework, and the two layers compound each other. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level morality provisions.

Aceh is the only province in the country operating a codified religious criminal law of its own, the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014). It criminalises same-sex conduct under the headings liwath and musahaqah and criminalises close proximity as khalwat. Sentences are imposed by Islamic Shariah courts and policed by the Wilayatul Hisbah religious force alongside secular Satpol PP units, and the punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

The penalty scale runs to 100 strokes for morality offences, and public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences. In August 2025 a Sharia court convicted two men of hugging and kissing and sentenced each to 80 strokes; they were caned in a public park before around 100 spectators, and eight more people were caned the same day. CBS News and AP reported the caning on 26 August 2025. In February 2025 two men were publicly caned in Aceh for a same-sex relationship.

The Qanun does not name transgender people, but enforcement reaches them. A February 2025 round-up at a boarding house detained a waria and a gay student who faced up to 100 strokes under the province's provisions.

A trans visitor has died in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Venue enforcement is documented as well. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Aceh legal scholarship analysing the rise of waria cases through a sharia-law-enforcement lens.
