65028918B88589358118692.name: Lampung
65028918B88589358118692.summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and those punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Enforcement elsewhere takes the form of venue raids: on 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman, an operation Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena called a blatant violation of human rights and privacy, noting that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in 2022. During a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, while Indonesian police deny that violence was used.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women; commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Lampung stands under this national framework. OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation study names Lampung among eight Indonesian provinces — Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, North Sumatera, South Sulawesi, South Sumatera and Yogyakarta alongside it — whose regional regulations discriminate against LGBT people, analysed at both province and district level.

The principal Lampung-specific incident in the sources is a November 2018 operation in which Satpol PP, the regional morals-and-order force, raided three transwomen, detained them at the Satpol PP office and hosed them down at the firefighter building while an officer recorded the act. A UNSW human-rights review of violence against transgender women classifies the episode as police-perpetrated violence.

For a visitor, the exposure in Lampung is documented police contact escalating into recorded humiliation and violence, set against a national environment in which an official decree treats LGBTQ+ people as a security risk and vigilante attacks on trans women are reported. The sources assembled for this province do not support a patterned, continuous campaign of enforcement against visitors in Lampung itself.

On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in Agats, Asmat Regency, alongside ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans.

No trans-specific incident series was identified for West Papua. The risk to a transgender visitor is the amplification of any police contact into unlawful detention and physical violence at rates far exceeding the national norm: a systemic contact amplifier rather than a targeted trans finding, with the probability of escalation documented and elevated.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Within Central Kalimantan itself, no enacted discriminatory bylaw, raid, arrest or incident series targeting transgender people was found. OutRight Action International's Creeping Criminalisation analysis (Katjasungkana and Wieringa, 2022) maps national laws and regional regulations across Indonesia that violate the rights of women and LGBTIQ people, and its eight-province list of discriminatory regional regulations does not include Central Kalimantan.

The operative criminal baseline for a visitor in the province is Indonesia's 2023 Penal Code, passed on 6 December 2022 and in force from 2 January 2026. It criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if an immediate family member lodges a complaint. The code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, but because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under the outside-marriage restriction. Visitor risk in Central Kalimantan therefore follows the national framework rather than any local divergence.

65028918B94007491868798.name: Southeast Sulawesi
65028918B94007491868798.summary:
Southeast Sulawesi stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Visitor risk in this province follows that framework.

OutRight Action International's 2022 mapping of Indonesia's national laws and regional regulations examined regulations in eight focus provinces: Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. Southeast Sulawesi is not among them; the Sulawesi entry in that set is South Sulawesi, a different province. The study finds much overlap between jurisdictions but significant regional variation in the instruments used, including dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

No specific enforcement incident, police action or enacted regional regulation targeting transgender people is recorded for Southeast Sulawesi in the sources reviewed. A qualitative study by Universitas Halu Oleo researchers published in Jurnal Budaya Etnika on 23 December 2024 describes gay life in Kendari, the provincial capital: same-sex communities there live discreetly, and after identifying as gay individuals report becoming more introverted and careful about expressing their feelings to others. The study reports no enforcement incident, raid or local regulation. A trans visitor should therefore expect a discretion-oriented environment rather than visible community presence, while remaining exposed to the national criminal provisions and to the possibility of regional instruments of the kind documented elsewhere in Indonesia.

65028918B6070530336190.name: Special Region of Yogyakarta
65028918B6070530336190.summary:
The Special Region of Yogyakarta stands under Indonesia's national framework, and that framework is hostile to transgender visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, with reporting indicating that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Yogyakarta is not among the two provinces where the Human Dignity Trust records provincial criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity under regional religious law, so the provincial Sharia penalties recorded in Aceh and South Sumatra do not extend to this special region.

Within that national exposure, Yogyakarta presents a regulatory layer that is discriminatory on paper but unproven in operation against transgender people. OutRight Action International's 2022 study 'Creeping Criminalisation' maps national laws and regional regulations that violate the human rights of women and LGBTIQ people, examining regulations in eight focus provinces including Yogyakarta, and finds significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear. The dossier documents no specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted anti-LGBT bylaw targeting transgender people in Yogyakarta itself, and OutRight states its findings are valid for regions beyond its focus set.

The clearest enforcement-adjacent event on record is the closure of the trans-Muslim religious school in this special region. On the night of 24 February 2016, Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah, where trans women study Islam, was closed after the hardline Front Jihad Islam threatened to seal it; the district head justified the closure on the grounds that the school lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site, and the shutdown proceeded on administrative and community grounds with no provincial anti-trans statute cited. Governor Sultan Hamengku Buwono X publicly urged restraint on both sides, describing LGBT people as fellow children of the nation and saying the regional government would study the issue. BBC Indonesia's report describes rising hate speech against LGBT people 'especially in Yogyakarta', and a witness to the closure meeting reported that a Front Jihad Islam leader vowed to keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather.

For a traveller the practical exposure in Yogyakarta is therefore the national criminalisation regime combined with an untested discriminatory regulatory layer and documented local hostility from hardline groups, rather than a provincial anti-trans law with a known enforcement record.

A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled, and reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

National enforcement practice is not limited to prosecution. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and Aceh's punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

OutRight's mapping shows that Yogyakarta's discriminatory regulations are not an isolated local artefact but part of a set shared with Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi and South Sumatra, with much overlap and significant regional variation in the restrictions imposed on transgender people.

76434192B26311534340602.name: KwaZulu-Natal
76434192B26311534340602.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

KwaZulu-Natal stands within that national framework, but documented violence against queer residents persists in its townships. A 2024 Masters criminology thesis supervised at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in Durban, based on in-depth interviews with 15 queer participants drawn from the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation, reports significant victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in KwaMashu Township and examines the adequacy of support, interventions and the safety strategies residents adopt.

Top traditional authority in the province has publicly expressed hostility toward gay and lesbian people. In January 2012 King Goodwill Zwelithini made anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival, prompting demands for an apology; police opened an investigation, the KwaZulu-Natal Premier backed the royal family's account, and the Congress of Traditional Leaders of South Africa (CONTRALESA) said the Pietermaritzburg gay and lesbian network seeking the apology had shown the king disrespect. The South African Human Rights Commission said it would investigate.

Detention raises a separate and more defined set of risks. In 2019 Jade September, a transgender woman held in the male section of Pollsmoor Prison, won an Equality Court case against the Minister of Correctional Services, which held that preventing her from expressing her gender identity was unfair discrimination. The Department of Correctional Services' standard operating procedure for LGBT+ prisoners, reported on in August 2025, requires a safety-risk assessment within the first six hours of admission and stipulates that transgender men and transgender women be detained or transported only with other transgender men or transgender women respectively, alongside respectful search and communication rules. Rights organisations doubt whether the procedure is implemented in practice.

On 14 November 2025 the High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, ruled for Nthabiseng Mokoena, a transgender inmate at Johannesburg Correctional Centre, in litigation against the Department of Correctional Services brought with the assistance of Lawyers for Human Rights (case 2024/070075, judgment delivered 10 November 2025). The court found unfair discrimination and harassment arising from the refusal to allow her to wear feminising attire or be addressed with she/her pronouns, held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at State expense, and ordered the Department to implement the required accommodations, enforce its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and deliver the prescribed medical care.

The South African Human Rights Commission, acting as the National Preventive Mechanism under OPCAT since its designation on 4 December 2024, welcomed the ruling on the day it was delivered, confirming that transgender people are held within the ordinary correctional system and that the judgment affirms their rights to accommodation and treatment in correctional facilities. Because these obligations rest on the Department of Correctional Services and are enforced through national litigation, they bind correctional centres in KwaZulu-Natal as well; a trans visitor or resident arrested in the province enters the same standard operating procedure, though evidence of its implementation in KwaZulu-Natal facilities specifically is not in the record.

Outside detention, exposure remains shaped by everyday hostility and by documents. Where identity documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud, and the route to legal gender recognition under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires pathologising medical evidence and a binary sex classification. Public violence remains documented and ongoing, with the township findings above indicating that constitutional protection is unevenly realised in daily life in KwaZulu-Natal.

76434192B51294388644125.name: Nothern Cape
76434192B51294388644125.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics. The Northern Cape province stands under that national framework, and no provincial statute narrowing it is documented.

The province recorded at least three LGBTIQ+ community members killed during 2024. On 14 May 2024 in Paballelo, Upington, Jo-Ann Isaks, a 27-year-old transgender woman, was found dead in her burning room with multiple stab wounds to the upper body; a family member noticed the flames at about 23:00. On 1 June 2024 in Kimberley, Karabelo Pudumo, an 18-year-old transgender Grade 10 learner at Pescodia High School, was stabbed more than 20 times, allegedly by a man she had been drinking with after he realised she was transgender. The third killing, in September 2024, was of Lazarus Ikaneng Thomas, a 50-year-old gay man.

The violence is severe in method and has drawn sustained community response: more than 300 children and community members attended a memorial for Karabelo Pudumo at her school, and the province's LGBTIQ+ district leader, Jenny Sambok, said the ZF Mgcawu region community was shaken after the Upington killing. Official handling has been uneven. Police in the ZF Mgcawu District opened a murder case in the Isaks matter, described the investigation as at a critical stage, and reported no arrests at that point; the same spokesperson publicly identified the victim by a birth name. An arrest was reported in the Pudumo case, but the reporting outlet could not verify it with authorities.

Everyday exposure outside violence turns largely on documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high. Where identity documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether PEPUDA read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

Detention is a site of elevated risk. Jade September, a transgender woman held in the male section of Pollsmoor, won her 2019 Equality Court case against the Minister of Correctional Services, which held that not allowing her to express her gender identity was unfair discrimination. The Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure that followed requires a safety-risk assessment within the first six hours of admission and stipulates that transgender men and transgender women are to be detained or transported only with other transgender men or transgender women respectively, alongside respectful-search and communication rules. On 10 November 2025 the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, sitting as an Equality Court, ruled for Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena against the Department in case 2024/070075, finding unfair discrimination and harassment over refusal of feminising attire, she/her pronouns and accommodation; the court held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at State expense, and ordered immediate implementation of accommodations, enforcement of the Department's own standard operating procedures, and provision of prescribed medical care. The South African Human Rights Commission, acting as the National Preventive Mechanism under OPCAT, welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025. Reporting in August 2025 records that rights organisations doubt whether the procedure is implemented in practice.

Outside detention, national-level incidents indicate the surrounding risk environment: on 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left severe facial injuries, with an arrest reported, and OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month. Violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

sources.title: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre - Lawyers for Human Rights

The national constitution of 1996 prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006, legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics. This state/province stands under that national framework, and no sub-national statute narrowing it is documented.

The state/province recorded at least three LGBTIQ+ community members killed during 2024. On 14 May 2024 in the Paballelo location of Upington, Jo-Ann Isaks, a 27-year-old transgender woman, was found dead in her burning room with multiple stab wounds to the upper body; a family member noticed the flames at about 23:00. On 1 June 2024 in Kimberley, Karabelo Pudumo, an 18-year-old transgender Grade 10 learner at Pescodia High School, was stabbed more than 20 times, allegedly by a man she had been drinking with after he realised she was transgender. The third killing, in September 2024, was of Lazarus Ikaneng Thomas, a 50-year-old gay man.

The violence is severe in method and has drawn sustained community response: more than 300 children and community members attended a memorial for Karabelo Pudumo at her school, and the local LGBTIQ+ district leader, Jenny Sambok, said the district community was shaken after the Upington killing. Official handling has been uneven. District police opened a murder case in the Isaks matter, described the investigation as at a critical stage, and reported no arrests at that point; the same spokesperson publicly identified the victim by a birth name. an arrest was reported in the Pudumo case, but the reporting outlet could not verify it with authorities.

Everyday exposure outside violence turns largely on documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high. Where identity documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether PEPUDA read with section 9 of the constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

The national human rights commission, acting as the National Preventive Mechanism under OPCAT, welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025. Reporting in August 2025 records that rights organisations doubt whether the procedure is implemented in practice.

76434192B92524600968894.name: Mpumalanga
76434192B92524600968894.summary:
Mpumalanga is a province of the Republic of South Africa and stands under the national framework: the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006, legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, held in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075) that refusing a transgender inmate prescribed gender-affirming health care falls below the required standard of health care and that refusing feminising clothing and accessories is unlawful. Orders compelling the Department of Correctional Services to provide hormone treatment at state expense, permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, implement its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and deliver prescribed medical care were granted, and the South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling the same day. Reporting in August 2025 records that rights organisations doubt whether that standard operating procedure is implemented in practice, so detention remains a site of elevated risk.

Outside prison, everyday exposure is shaped by documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high, and where documents do not match presentation trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing nationally. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane leaving severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month, and violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships. Access to gender-affirming care is uneven: activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in access to gender-segregated bathrooms, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

Provincial official hostility has been stated in durable terms. Meeting at Hazyview in June 2010, the National House of Traditional Leaders and its provincial houses issued a letter saying that while they 'respect' the Constitutional Court's same-sex marriage judgment, 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts'. The letter states they do not support legalisation of same-sex marriages, warns of ostracism and violence, and vows a five-year campaign against it. Reporting in 2016 documents the same body asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause protecting people from discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

Lethal anti-LGBTIQ violence has occurred inside Mpumalanga. Portia Mtsweni, a 25-year-old lesbian, was found dead near Zamani Primary School in Tweefontein in the early hours of Sunday 29 December 2019, half naked with stab wounds. On 2 January about 800 people marched in the Thembisile Hani Local Municipality in protest, organised by Lasiphumakhona LGBTI, the ANC Women's League and others, and the local mayor called on parents, leaders and churches to stand united against gender-based violence.

Police treatment is a live concern for visitors reporting crime in the province. At a Pride Flag Tour held at the eMbalenhle Sasol Club on 18 August, LGBTIQ+ community members led by the Rainbow Seed Institute raised allegations of discrimination and stigmatisation at government institutions, particularly police stations. Participants said they were ridiculed, questioned or treated unfairly when seeking assistance, and one member alleged that after a sexual assault in eMbalenhle months earlier an officer at eMbalenhle Police Station asked why she 'didn't fight back'. Attendees said they fear reporting crimes because of stigmatisation.

76434192B37104984973577.name: Limpopo
76434192B37104984973577.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

Limpopo stands under that national framework, and no statute criminalises a trans visitor's expression of gender identity in the province. The defining risk factor for a trans traveller outside Polokwane and the other towns is the customary-authority layer: chiefs' courts and traditional tribunals adjudicate personal-status and morality-adjacent matters under customary law in the former Bantustan territories that cover much of rural Limpopo, and Human Rights Watch reported in 2012 that the jurisdiction offered no opt-out for the individual brought before it.

Human Rights Watch's reporting of 29 May 2012 stated that the Traditional Courts Bill then before Parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans, and recorded that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, with chiefs' courts punishing lesbians in rural areas. Mamba Online's account of 18 April 2012, by Melanie Judge, reported that the bill debated in provincial public hearings would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in former-Bantustan areas through a separate customary system, that lesbians are punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices with no opt-out, and that those who can are expected to leave rural areas. The same account records that traditional leaders opposed the Civil Union Act of 2006.

For an outed trans visitor in rural Limpopo, the forum a complaint lands before is therefore as likely to be the chief's court as the ordinary court, and an analysis of the legislation at issue warned that it 'establishes a separate legal system' for people in the former Bantustans and threatens to undermine security 'for millions of South Africans living in rural areas', 'particularly for the exercise of gender and sexual rights'. Where police cooperation is already recorded as poor, recourse through the ordinary equality machinery is uncertain in practice.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month, and violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Documents shape everyday exposure. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force, and the cost of affirming one's gender through the process is described as dauntingly high. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud; a 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, held in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075) that refusing a transgender inmate prescribed gender-affirming health care falls below the required standard of health care and that refusing feminising clothing and accessories is unlawful, ordering hormone treatment at state expense, clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, implementation of the Department of Correctional Services' standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and delivery of prescribed medical care. Correctional Services had that procedure before the ruling, but reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice, so detention remains a site of elevated risk.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven, with activists in East London delivering a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 concludes that PEPUDA read with section 9 of the Constitution does not secure equal protection for trans people in gender-segregated bathroom and changing-room access, so facility disputes remain foreseeable for visitors in Limpopo as elsewhere.

76434192B85643022077130.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075), a challenge brought against the Department of Correctional Services with the assistance of Lawyers for Human Rights. The court held that refusing a transgender inmate prescribed gender-affirming health care falls below the required standard of health care, and that refusing feminising clothing and accessories is likewise unlawful. Orders compelling the Department to provide hormone treatment at state expense, permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, implement the accommodations required by its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and deliver prescribed medical care were granted. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling the same day.

Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling; reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice. Detention therefore remains a site of elevated risk for trans visitors and residents despite the binding remedies now in place.

Outside prison, everyday exposure is shaped by documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month. Violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

Within North West province, the principal sub-national legal divergence is the reach of traditional and customary courts. Human Rights Watch's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies the former-Bantustan geography, which includes North West, as standing under a separate legal system; HRW's earlier reporting on the Traditional Courts Bill (29 May 2012) described a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans, offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction, and recorded that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, with chiefs' courts punishing lesbians in rural areas. The Act was declared invalid in Mogale (2023) but suspended and extended, and the replacement Bill (TKLB) has been delayed. No province has religious criminal law, and no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here.

Healthcare access is the sharpest practical constraint on the ground. The trans community in North West cannot access hormone replacement therapy at any public health facility in the province; the North West Department of Health confirmed it has no facilities providing HRT for transgender people in response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International with the South African Human Rights Commission, and residents are forced to travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres to Soweto in Gauteng to obtain it. A visitor dependent on prescribed HRT should expect no provincial public provider and should carry a sufficient supply.

Hate-crime evidence for the province is thin but exists. The Love Not Hate campaign research conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being (2016) records that only three quantitative studies of hate crimes against LGBT people have been done in South Africa: the 2003 empowerment study covering Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and the national campaign study itself. North West is therefore one of only three provinces ever to have received its own representative hate-crime prevalence study.

sources.title: New Report on LGBT Community in North West

76434192B98113213215773.name: Eastern Cape
76434192B98113213215773.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006, legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics. The Eastern Cape has no separate provincial trans statute, ban or enforcement regime; visitors to the province are covered by these national instruments.

Detention in the province runs under a placement rule fixed nationally rather than locally. In Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075), delivered by the Gauteng High Court sitting as an Equality Court on 14 November 2025, the Department of Correctional Services conceded that the regulations to the Correctional Services Act on vulnerable inmates and its own Standard Operating Procedures require inmates to be housed in cells appropriate to their gender identity where feasible and safe, and that those Standard Operating Procedures prescribe single-cell accommodation for transgender inmates. The court ordered single-cell placement or placement with inmates of the same gender identity. That is the operative rule for transgender prisoners in Eastern Cape correctional centres, including St Albans, Mthatha and East London; no province-specific trans placement case is on record. The same judgment held that refusing prescribed gender-affirming health care and refusing feminising clothing and accessories are unlawful, with hormone treatment to be provided at state expense. Reporting in August 2025 recorded rights organisations' doubt that the Department's standard operating procedure is implemented in practice, so detention remains an elevated-risk setting.

Legal gender recognition under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that excludes non-binary people through its binary sex classification; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force, and the cost of affirming one's gender through the process is described as dauntingly high. Where identity documents do not match presentation, trans people in the province face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Access to gender-affirming care in the Eastern Cape is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year, a concrete service bottleneck for a visitor needing continuity of hormone therapy or other prescribed care.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month nationally, and violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships, a pattern that holds in the Eastern Cape's township and rural areas. Within the province, Eastern Cape police arrested four suspects over the killings of two women in Gqeberha on 2 May 2025, in a case that drew public outrage and renewed calls to confront rising gender-based violence.

A further exposure is jurisdictional rather than statutory. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 May 2012 that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans, with no opt-out from customary jurisdiction; it reported that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas. For a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor outside the metro civil-society belt, the practical forum is therefore as likely to be a chief's court as a magistrate's court.

Supports the province's framing of traditional-court rural jurisdiction as the defining risk factor for LGBT travellers off the main cities.

76434192B98113213215773.tangentialFactors:
The Eastern Cape's exposure profile is set less by provincial law than by the interaction of national protection machinery with rural customary jurisdiction and a thin service base. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether PEPUDA read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable at malls, hotels, gyms and workplaces throughout the province.

Gender-based violence provides the ambient crime backdrop. The Gqeberha arrests of four suspects over two women's killings in May 2025 illustrate a provincial pattern of lethal violence against women that is not trans-specific but shapes the risk environment for any visibly gender-nonconforming traveller, particularly after dark and in informal settings such as taverns. The December 2024 assault on Aobakwe Mahlobo in Tshwane is the clearest documented trans-specific hate crime in the recent record and establishes that targeted violence against trans women continues in social venues, with arrest following in that instance.

Comparison with the rest of the country is unhelpful in one respect and instructive in another: the binding remedies created by the Mokoena judgment bind the Department of Correctional Services nationwide, so trans prisoners in Eastern Cape centres hold the same orders as those in Gauteng, but the province has no litigation of its own pressing implementation, which may slow uptake.

76434192B69392740373411.name: Gauteng
76434192B69392740373411.summary:
Gauteng stands under the national constitutional framework of South Africa. The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation; the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court; the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng Division of the High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075), a challenge to the Department of Correctional Services brought with the assistance of Lawyers for Human Rights. The court held that the Department had engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of the transgender inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and by denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, and that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense. Orders were granted compelling the Department to provide hormone treatment at state expense, permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, implement the accommodations required by its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and deliver prescribed medical care. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling the same day.

The Mokoena judgment is the only documented determination of where transgender prisoners are housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving a life sentence, is held at Johannesburg Correctional Centre. She was initially housed in Medium A section, where she could express her gender identity through long hair, makeup and women's clothing, and was later transferred to Medium C section. At the time of the judgment she was housed in C Single Section, a segregated unit of Medium C associated with solitary confinement, and despite requesting a single cell she was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates. The court found that the Department's own standard operating procedures prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where feasible and safe, that no basis existed for refusing her a single cell, and ordered the Department to house her in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity and to enforce its transgender-inmate procedures.

Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling. Reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice. Detention therefore remains a site of elevated risk for trans visitors and residents in Gauteng despite the binding remedies now in force.

Violence against trans people in the province is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman originally from Soshanguve and living in Winterveld, both in the Tshwane area of Gauteng, was assaulted at a local tavern at about 1:30 am after a man began saying gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'. He smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, saying 'I told you I'm gonna kill you', leaving deep cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead that were stitched after treatment at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which MambaOnline reported on 6 January 2025 had shown no progress. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month. Violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Outside detention, everyday exposure is shaped by documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. The cost of affirming one's gender through the process is described as dauntingly high. Where identity documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Access to gender-affirming care across South Africa is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year, a non-Gauteng case that illustrates the national gap between entitlement and service delivery. Academic analysis published in 2024 on whether PEPUDA read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

sources.summary: The SA Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism (14 November 2025) welcomed the judgment of the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075), delivered on 10 November 2025. The court found the Department of Correctional Services engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of the transgender inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, and held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, ordering the DCS to implement accommodations and enforce its own SOPs. Demonstrates an operational Gauteng court remedy, under PEPUDA, for discrimination against a trans person.

sources.summary: The only documented determination of where trans prisoners are housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving life, is held at Johannesburg Correctional Centre: initially housed in Medium A section where she could express her gender identity (long hair, makeup, women's clothing); later transferred to Medium C section; at the time of the judgment she was housed in C Single Section, a segregated/solitary-confinement unit of Medium C, and - despite requesting a single cell - was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates (first two cisgender gay men, then one cisgender male), which DCS justified by overcrowding. The court found the DCS's SOPs prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where feasible and safe and that no basis existed for refusing single accommodation, ordering DCS to house her in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity and to enforce its transgender-inmate SOPs.

This state/province stands under the national framework of the parent country. The national constitution prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation; the national equality statute gives effect to that guarantee through an Equality Court; and a 2024 national hate-crime and hate-speech act explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making the parent country the first jurisdiction to do so; marriage equality followed in 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since a 2003 national statute.

On 14 November 2025 the state/provincial High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in a case against the national Department of Correctional Services over the treatment of a transgender inmate held at the state/provincial correctional centre. The court held that refusing a transgender inmate her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy and refusing feminising clothing and accessories fall below the required standard of care and constitute unfair discrimination and harassment, and that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state/province expense. Orders were granted compelling the Department to provide hormone treatment at state/province expense, permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, implement the accommodations required by its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and deliver prescribed medical care. The national human rights commission's national preventive mechanism welcomed the ruling the same day.

The judgment is the only documented determination of where transgender prisoners are held in this state/province. The inmate, who is serving a life sentence, was initially housed in a section where she could express her gender identity through long hair, makeup and women's clothing, was later transferred to another section, and at the time of the judgment was held in a segregated unit associated with solitary confinement and housed with cisgender male cellmates despite requesting a single cell, a placement the Department justified on overcrowding grounds. The court found that the Department's own standard operating procedures prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where feasible and safe, that no basis existed for refusing single-cell accommodation, and ordered the Department to house her in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity and to enforce its transgender-inmate procedures.

Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling. Reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice. Detention therefore remains a site of elevated risk for trans visitors and residents in this state/province despite the binding remedies now in force.

Violence against trans people in this state/province is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 a 23-year-old transgender woman, originally from one township area and living in another within the state/provincial capital, was assaulted at a local tavern in the early hours after a man stated that gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'. He smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, saying 'I told you I'm gonna kill you', leaving deep cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead that were stitched after treatment at a local clinic. She opened an assault case at the local police station, which reporting on 6 January 2025 recorded as showing no progress. a national rights organisation's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month. Violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in township areas.

Outside detention, everyday exposure is shaped by documents. The 2003 national statute governing legal gender recognition requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of the process, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. The cost of affirming one's gender through the process is described as dauntingly high. Where identity documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 report documents a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Access to gender-affirming care across the parent country is uneven. Activists in a distant town delivered a memorandum to a public hospital over treatment delays running to a year, a case outside this state/province that illustrates the national gap between entitlement and service delivery. Academic analysis published in 2024 on whether the national equality statute read with the constitutional equality guarantee prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

76434192B56312278962278.name: Western Cape
76434192B56312278962278.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

The Western Cape stands under that national framework. Nothing in the sourced material identifies a provincial statute, prohibition, enforcement action or official directive restricting trans people in the province, and no rule of the Province or the City of Cape Town conditions bathroom use by trans people on legal sex or gender markers.

On 19 February 2025 Taswald Ruiters, a transgender woman from Eerste River, was threatened with removal from the Green Point Athletic Stadium in Cape Town after using the women's bathroom. A security guard told her "Look at you, you're a man", ordered her to use the men's bathroom and asserted that he had the final say. The stadium is a public facility operated by the City of Cape Town; the venue was rented that day by Western Province Athletics, which was responsible for the security services. MambaOnline reported the incident on 28 February 2025.

Police were called four times and did not arrive in nearly three hours. The episode therefore records the enforcement-and-response gap a visibly trans visitor can meet in the province's best-resourced metro: the applicable legal protections are national and intact, but the personnel who confronted a trans woman in a municipal facility were contracted security acting without any local rule supporting them, and the public emergency response did not materialise.

The Western Cape High Court appeal decision in 'Khoin v Jenkins in re: Observatory Civic Association v Trustees ... Liesbeek Leisure Properties Trust' [2023] 1 All SA 110 (WCC) recognised intangible heritage in South African heritage law and found a failure to consult First Nations communities. Peter Kantor's case note (2023, PER/PELJ vol. 26) analyses the decision as a cultural-heritage recognition dispute, not a matter of morality or criminal jurisdiction.

19338628B22645672383103.name: Île-de-France
19338628B22645672383103.summary:
Île-de-France stands under the French national framework: national law on identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law and marriage law apply uniformly across the region, and no separate regional regime governs transgender visitors.

The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings, detention and the border. Prison placement follows no statutory rule: where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising through special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations, including placement by birth sex, isolation and exposure during strip searches, with no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform. The opinion rests on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identifies structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention, and it issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October; her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, and placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers.

Documentation is comparatively permissive. Since 2017 transgender people in France may change their legal gender without surgery or any medical diagnosis, and in 2010 France was the first country in the world to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness. Anti-discrimination protection covers sexual orientation since 1985 and gender identity since 2012.

For partner recognition, same-sex civil partnerships (PACS) have been available since 1999 and France legalised same-sex marriage in 2013, becoming the thirteenth country to do so; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

Recorded violence is concentrated in the urban units where Île-de-France sits. The interior-ministry statistics service (SSMSI) Infraction rapide n°53 of May 2025 records 4,800 anti-LGBT+ offences in France in 2024, up 5% on 2023, with crimes and délicts rising 14% per year since 2016. Only about 4% of victims file complaints. Acts concentrate in urban units over 200,000 inhabitants, notably Paris, whose rate of 22 per 100,000 against the national 7 the note attributes partly to non-resident victims and commuters. Recorded victims are more than 70% men.

The 2025 Paris Pride march (Marche des fiertés, 28 June 2025) was classed a sensitive event by the Interior Ministry, with CRS police reinforcements deployed after a far-right homo-patriotes group announced it would join; police were framed as separating the opposing groups. Large LGBT events in the Paris agglomeration now carry far-right counter-presence alongside a heavy security response.

Paris concentrates France's densest LGBTQ infrastructure: as of 2004 the city had 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops, it hosts France's only officially organised gaybourhoods, and it stages the annual Paris Pride parade. The same city carries a targeted-violence history: Bertrand Delanoë, who became France's first openly gay mayor of Paris in 2002, was stabbed that same year during the Nuit Blanche festival by an assailant who told police he hated politicians, the Socialist Party and homosexuals.

19338628B22645672383103.blindSummary:
The state/province stands under the parent nation's framework: national law on identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law and marriage law apply uniformly across the state/province, and no separate sub-national regime governs transgender visitors.

The risks documented for transgender travellers concentrate in two settings, detention and the border. Prison placement follows no statutory rule: where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising through special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. The national custodial-inspection authority examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations, including placement by birth sex, isolation and exposure during strip searches, with no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform. The opinion rests on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identifies structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention, and it issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing a motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in a men's prison in another state/province and kept in isolation since October; her incarceration was put to the national justice minister in oral question no. 219 in the national legislature, and placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. a first-person account published by a national news outlet on 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers.

Documentation is comparatively permissive. Since 2017 transgender people may change their legal gender without surgery or any medical diagnosis, and in 2010 the parent nation was the first country in the world to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness. Anti-discrimination protection covers sexual orientation since 1985 and gender identity since 2012.

For partner recognition, same-sex civil partnerships have been available since 1999 and same-sex marriage was legalised in 2013, making the parent nation the thirteenth country to do so; a national news outlet reported the first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

The national rights-defender authority issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the union's fundamental-rights agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

Recorded violence is concentrated in the urban units where the state/province sits. The interior ministry's statistics service recorded 4,800 anti-LGBT+ offences in 2024, up 5% on 2023, with crimes and délicts rising 14% per year since 2016. Only about 4% of victims file complaints. Acts concentrate in urban units over a small population, notably the principal city, whose rate of 22 per 100,000 against the national 7 the note attributes partly to non-resident victims and commuters. Recorded victims are more than 70% men.

The 2025 annual Pride march (28 June 2025) was classed a sensitive event by the interior ministry, with public-order police reinforcements deployed after a far-right group announced it would join; police were framed as separating the opposing groups. Large LGBT events in the state/province now carry far-right counter-presence alongside a heavy security response.

The principal city concentrates the parent nation's densest LGBTQ infrastructure: as of 2004 it had 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops, it hosts the country's only officially organised gaybourhoods, and it stages the annual Pride parade. The same city carries a targeted-violence history: its mayor, who in 2002 became the parent nation's first openly gay big-city mayor, was stabbed that same year during a night arts festival by an assailant who told police he hated politicians, a major political party and homosexuals.

19338628B95725112529620.name: Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur
19338628B95725112529620.summary:
The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings: detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

The national preventive mechanism told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur stands under this national framework, and the region's own record adds one episode of appearance policing on public beaches. On 1 August 2023 the mayor of Fréjus issued an order prohibiting swimming while wearing 'covering and baggy clothing' on the commune's sea beaches, in force until 17 September 2023 and carrying a €135 fine.

The administrative tribunal of Toulon suspended that order on 5 August 2023, in freedom-of-relief order n° 2302537 brought by the Ligue des droits de l'homme, finding a grave and manifestly unlawful attack on fundamental freedoms: manifestation of religious conviction, freedom of movement, and freedom of dress in public space. It condemned the commune to pay €3,000.

Toulon's order followed the Conseil d'État's ruling of 17 July 2023 on an identical arrêté at Mandelieu-la-Napoule, where the Ligue des droits de l'homme had already contested the ban; observers noted that the Fréjus communiqué justified the prohibition on laïcité grounds while safety was cited publicly, framing religiously marked swimwear as the target. The order no longer operates, so the residual visitor-facing effect on this region's beaches is a signal that visible non-conformity in public dress can attract mayoral prohibition until a court stops it.
