28173009B98838729156012.name: Chechnya
28173009B98838729156012.summary:
Visitors in Chechnya stand under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned since 2023, the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the US State Department advises against all travel to Russia at Level 4 with warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Chechnya's security services operate against LGBT people with a severity not documented elsewhere in Russia. Human Rights Watch (26 May 2017) established that a police purge began in February 2017: men believed to be gay were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured. Some were forcibly disappeared. Others were returned to their families barely alive from beatings, after captors identified them as gay to relatives and urged honour killings. The investigation found that senior regional officials knew of the operation, notwithstanding Ramzan Kadyrov's denial.

The campaign was not confined to 2017. Novaya Gazeta reported on 11 January 2019 that persecution of gay men had resumed, with warnings passed through administrators of LGBT groups on VKontakte telling those still at large to leave the republic; Kadyrov's press secretary Alvi Karimov denied the reports. That account followed the paper's April 2017 investigation into torture and killings of gay men, after which no criminal case was opened.

Detention in Chechnya now carries a further consequence. The Insider (4 September 2024) reported that the SK SOS crisis group had documented Chechen security forces coercing detained gay men into military service: at least seven were sent to fight in Ukraine and at least one was already killed. The methods predate the mobilisation order of 21 September 2022; in early September 2022 six men were detained on suspicion of homosexuality, threatened with fabricated charges and warned they would be sent to the front.

The same machinery is applied generally. An investigation by the Memorial Human Rights Centre, reported by OC Media, describes a mass wave of unlawful detentions across Chechnya in which people are taken to police departments over minor pretexts such as missing insurance documents, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse, and forced to sign military contracts; families have had to recruit two "volunteers" to secure the release of a detained relative.

28173009B24428243574749.name: Dagestan
28173009B24428243574749.summary:
Dagestan stands under the national framework of Russia, where the risks facing transgender and LGBT visitors have sharpened markedly since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these statutes face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and the United States State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The same laws operate inside Dagestan as they do in every other Russian region.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) names the North Caucasus, including Dagestan, as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic campaigns by Chechen and North Caucasus authorities between 2017 and 2024 that involved abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings, and it assesses transgender people and visible advocates as a defined category within that finding.

Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel to Russia. Its advisory warns of violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons and singles out the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan. It also flags frequent terrorist attacks in Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and Stavropol Krai, and states that entry to certain areas and regions requires special permission from the Ministry of the Interior.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, who works in exile, told the Human Rights House Foundation that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He said the situation worsens year on year.

28173009B24428243574749.tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume nationally has risen alongside severity. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda statutes have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those laws brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two further venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and the Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented well beyond the North Caucasus. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 on "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

Dagestan is one of four territories named in the Canadian advisory for frequent terrorist attacks, a security condition distinct from, and additional to, the anti-LGBT enforcement described above. Comparable persecution findings in the region have repeatedly centred on Chechnya, which provides the documented template for the campaigns the Home Office attributes to Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities between 2017 and 2024.

28173009B46612801043871.name: Kabardino-Balkaria
28173009B46612801043871.summary:
Kabardino-Balkaria stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents took effect. The Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation and the expanded propaganda statute, which reaches any public expression justifying gender transition, apply in every region of the country. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings tell LGBT travellers so.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus, including Kabardino-Balkaria, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia. In this region, trans people and public LGBT+ advocates are assessed as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic regional campaigns running from 2017 to 2024, and records that the 2023 extremist designation exposes LGBT+ activity to two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising, with violence spreading beyond the region.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. Working in exile, Isteev attests that conditions in the region deteriorate year on year.

For a trans visitor, the operative risk in Kabardino-Balkaria is therefore the regional one layered on top of the national statutes: security structures applying an extremist designation to any visible LGBT+ presence, in a territory where the state's own asylum authority assesses persecution as likely rather than merely possible.

28173009B7235812138525.name: North Ossetia–Alania
28173009B7235812138525.summary:
North Ossetia–Alania stands under the framework of the Russian Federation, and that framework carries the heaviest anti-trans penalties in Europe. The law signed in 2023 prohibits gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright; the 2013 'propaganda' statute was expanded in December 2022 to cover all ages and any material that presents gender transition to minors as desirable; and in November 2023 the Russian Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT public movement' an extremist organisation, which makes participation in LGBT activism a criminal offence nationwide. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries explicit warnings addressed to LGBT travellers.

Foreign visitors fall directly within these statutes. The expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that could be read as justifying gender transition; foreigners who breach the administrative and criminal codes face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) singles out the North Caucasus, which includes North Ossetia–Alania, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory reading of Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there are found likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with systematic regional campaigns documented between 2017 and 2024, and 2–6 years' imprisonment under the 2023 designation, rising to 6–10 years for organising.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, whose testimony to the Human Rights House Foundation covers this republic, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; he describes the situation as deteriorating year on year. Western travel advisories name North Ossetia–Alania within the wider Caucasus don't-travel area. The practical effect for a trans visitor is that nothing distinguishing about gender presentation, documents or social circles can be assumed to stay private, and that family honour norms and informal security structures can produce detention or removal without any legal process.

28173009B19676032168465.name: Moscow
28173009B19676032168465.summary:
Visitors in Moscow stand under the national framework of the Russian Federation. The July 2023 federal law bans gender transition outright, prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and any legal gender recognition on official documents. The Supreme Court's November 2023 ruling designating the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation took effect on the state's unified list of terrorist and extremist organisations on 22 March 2024, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation.

Moscow is where this framework is enforced most visibly. The Moscow Times' survey of persecution in Russia during 2025, published 23 June 2025 and framed around arrests, club raids and extremism charges, records that Kotov, the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024.

The same reporting line covers Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-extremism designation, reported by the Moscow Times in February 2025. The case concerned organising activity and followed a court ruling in Siberia reported in January 2025, indicating that convictions under the designation have moved from administrative charges to custodial sentences.

Since the March 2024 addition to the unified extremist list, the designation has been used to arrest gay bar owners and to charge people for displaying rainbow-flag symbols. A visitor to Moscow should expect venue raids, identity checks and symbol-based charges to be live risks rather than residual ones.

28173009B76603557910928.name: Orenburg Oblast
28173009B76603557910928.summary:
Visitors in Orenburg Oblast stand under the national framework of the Russian Federation. Since 2023 legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned across the country; the Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation applies in every region; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation.

Orenburg Oblast is the jurisdiction in which that extremism designation first produced a criminal prosecution against a commercial leisure venue. The Central District Court of Orenburg registered the case materials on 10 July 2025, making them Russia's first criminal case brought under the "international LGBT movement" ban; the investigation into staff of the Pose club had been opened in March 2024 and the file was sent to court on 9 July 2025.

The case concluded in June 2026 with Russia's first known convictions for LGBT extremism. Pose owner Vyacheslav Khasanov received seven years' imprisonment and forfeiture of one million rubles, manager Diana Kamilyanova six years and three months, and art director Alexander Klimov two years and three months. The sentences establish that operating, managing or staffing an LGBT-friendly venue can itself be prosecuted as extremist organising, which is the single most direct hazard a trans or LGBT visitor in this oblast faces when choosing where to go out.

36201628B69282955287113.name: NCR
36201628B69282955287113.summary:
NCR (Metro Manila) stands under the national framework of the Philippines: same-sex relations and trans identity are not criminalised, and no provision of national law penalises a person for being transgender. There is, however, no administrative route to legal gender recognition. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, leaving a court order as the only avenue, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. Documents therefore continue to show the sex assigned at birth, and a visitor whose papers do not match presentation should expect that mismatch to be handled by the birth-certificate entry.

National law also provides no anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress for 25 years, so the enforceable protections in the country are sub-national or sectoral rather than national.

Within the region itself, the strongest institutional protection a trans visitor can invoke is Quezon City's gender-inclusive health ordinance, introduced by Councilors Bernard Herrera and colleagues. It requires every city public health facility to provide gender-affirming consultations and counselling, mental-health support, and medical guidance and referrals regardless of gender identity or expression. Mayor Joy Belmonte states that the measure removes longstanding healthcare barriers for gender-diverse and transgender residents. In practical terms, a visitor who needs care and is recognised as trans can enter a Quezon City public hospital or health centre and demand the service on the ordinance's terms, using the city's complaint machinery if refused.

Violence against trans women in the region is documented and recent. Shaina Bayabay, a 29-year-old trans woman in Pasig City, was killed on 1 March 2024; the memorial record classifies the death as violence and the cause as strangulation, and the underlying report states that she was strangled during a drinking session. The Commission on Human Rights has separately described trans killings recorded within a single year as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide, and no dedicated regional machinery for investigating such killings is evidenced.

Detention conditions are materially harsher than the street-level picture. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex. At Manila City Jail, arrivals assigned to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and protection from abuse is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates rather than through any policy. A visitor arrested in the region should expect placement on the basis of the birth certificate, not identity.

36201628B69282955287113.tangentialFactors:
A 2026 travel-risk assessment rates Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers overall at 69 of 100 but scores trans travellers lower, at 62, in the 'Exercise Caution' band, a gap that tracks the difference between the region's visible social tolerance and its thin legal remedies.

Social visibility in the capital is high. Gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy are long-standing, Pride events and nightlife are prominent, and LGBTQ+ themes carry substantial media presence.

Two sectoral rules elsewhere in the country turn on documents rather than identity and are worth noting as the national baseline the region inherits: the armed forces have permitted openly gay and bisexual personnel since 2009 and transgender personnel since 2017, with the uniform policy following the legal gender shown on the birth certificate; and the Code of Professional Responsibility governing lawyers was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, which bears on access to counsel.

Protections outside the region are uneven. SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances cover eight provinces (Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo) and 32 cities and municipalities, while the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers punishes SOGIE harassment with a fine of PHP 20,000 to 40,000 and up to one year's penalty, and the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act reach slurs and ridicule with fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar.

Trans-specific attacks have also been recorded well outside the region, which is the context in which the Pasig killing should be read: Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a river in Cagayan on 23 June 2025 after being reported missing; on the same day a trans woman who was a former journalist and activist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside a clinic in General Santos; a foreign national was arrested in May 2025 on a charge of raping a trans woman at a Batangas resort; and in April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd during a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan, after which the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. A pending gender-recognition bill would open recognition to applicants including consenting minors and allow markers beyond male and female, such as X or nonbinary, and its drafter links the absence of recognition to social exclusion, forced disclosure of trans status and violence.

36201628B88329767373181.name: Central Visayas
36201628B88329767373181.summary:
Central Visayas, the region of the central Philippine islands governed from the Cebu area, stands under the national framework of the Republic of the Philippines. National law does not criminalise same-sex relations or transgender identity, and there is no national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity; the SOGIE Equality Bill has remained pending in Congress for 25 years. Protections that do exist are sub-national, and the region contains an unusually active concentration of them at the provincial and municipal level.

Mandaue City, in metropolitan Cebu, adopted the implementing rules and regulations of its Anti-Discrimination Ordinance in July 2024 in a signing jointly conducted with the city mayor, the KAABAG LGBT Federation and UNDP Philippines. The instrument is operational rather than declaratory: it sets out how the ordinance is to be applied, and a visitor subjected to SOGIE-based discrimination in Mandaue can invoke a functioning local ordinance with a designated federation partner. In the municipality of Carmen in northern Cebu, the Sangguniang Bayan approved a Comprehensive Anti-Discrimination Ordinance on SOGI grounds by unanimous vote in June 2025, days before the close of Pride Month.

The 2026 travel-risk assessment that scores Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers at 69 of 100 but places trans travellers lower at 62, in the 'Exercise Caution' band, describes the capital rather than Central Visayas; no equivalent scoring for the Cebu metropolitan area is sourced here.

36201628B76469343449086.name: Soccsksargen
36201628B76469343449086.summary:
Soccsksargen stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which does not criminalise trans identity or same-sex relations and provides no administrative route to legal gender recognition. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, leaving a court order as the only route, and in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) the Supreme Court held that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. No national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity is in force.

On 23 June 2025 an unidentified gunman shot and killed trans woman Ali Macalintal inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos City. Macalintal was a former journalist and human-rights activist: former deputy secretary general of Karapatan's Soccsksargen chapter and a former anchor-reporter with Radio Philippines Network's DXDX station in General Santos.

Human Rights Watch assessed the shooting as an apparent targeted killing and reported that police were examining her activism as a possible motive. No outcome for the investigation appears in the sources.

The national Commission on Human Rights condemned the killings of two transgender women as marked by cruelty and impunity, naming Macalintal. During Pride Month the same commission characterised the string of killings of transgender women as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide, citing Macalintal alongside 18-year-old student Kierra Apostol and beauty salon owner Ren Tampus.

Bahaghari decried the General Santos killing and separately reported the earlier killing of trans woman Shalani Dolina in Caloocan. Campaigners used the killings to press the Simplified Legal Gender Recognition Bill, and the Commission on Human Rights' Fayda M. Dumarpa pledged the commission's support. The absence of a national statute is the blockage campaigners identify: the SOGIESC Equality Bill has been stuck in Congress for 25 years, and that delay is cited as the direct reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy.

36201628B76469343449086.tangentialFactors:
The June 2025 violence is not confined to Soccsksargen. Kierra Apostol was found dead in a river in Cagayan on 23 June 2025 after being reported missing, Shalani Dolina was killed in Caloocan, and Ren Tampus was gunned down earlier; a foreign national was arrested in May 2025 on a charge of raping a trans woman at a Batangas resort, and in April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd during a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan, after which the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community.

Protections that exist in the Philippines are sub-national or sectoral rather than national. SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances cover eight provinces (Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo) and 32 cities and municipalities; none of the eight named provinces lies in Soccsksargen, and the sources do not identify any Soccsksargen city among the 32.

Detention practice elsewhere in the country shows what protections lose in custody. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex; at Manila City Jail, arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and survival against abuse is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates rather than through policy. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented response at Davao City Jail is administrative segregation, transferring LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex 'to prevent abuse' alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, with three LGBT groupings housed there since the annex was established.

A 2026 travel-risk assessment rates Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers overall at 69 of 100 but scores trans travellers lower, at 62, in the 'Exercise Caution' band. 36201628B47630810559445.name: Central Luzon
36201628B47630810559445.summary:
Central Luzon's clearest documented threat to a trans traveller is trafficking and sexual exploitation in commercial sex venues, not any rule against being transgender. The United States government's Trafficking in Persons Report 2024 states that traffickers exploit victims in tourist destinations and urban areas across the Philippines; in this region the operations on record cluster in one Pampanga city's bar district, where trans women are also concentrated in sex work.

On 17 June 2025 the National Bureau of Investigation announced that its Bataan District Office had arrested five people for human trafficking in Barangay Balibago, Angeles City, including Alvin Baguio, registered owner of Field Sensation's Bar, together with Reden Roa, John Parro, Shirly Calilong and Marilyn Ferrer. The case began with a 19 May 2025 referral from Destiny Rescue Pilipinas Incorporated. Agents ran an entrapment and rescue operation on 1 June 2025 in which 'barfine' transactions ranged from P5,000 to P10,000, and rescued 45 victims including 13 minors, who were turned over to the social welfare agency.

Two months earlier the same NBI office arrested foreign national Shin Ki Jung and accomplices in Angeles City for violations of R.A. No. 11862, the Expanded Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act of 2022, and R.A. No. 7610. A complaint from the husband of a trafficked victim alleged that women had been recruited as Korea-bound performers as cover for work at a club in Angeles City; a rescue operation freed 12 victims including 5 minors, and the arrested subjects were presented for inquest before the Office of the City Prosecutor of Angeles City. The two 2025 operations and the older reporting describe a single sustained market rather than isolated incidents.

Reporting from 2019 by the Preda Foundation, originally The Fuller Project's investigation, found that hundreds of girls are supplied each year in Angeles City to meet demand from foreign men paying for sex, many of them American, in the city that hosted a former United States military base. More than 150 women and girls interviewed for that investigation said they wanted to leave prostitution but did not know how. City-regulated 'entertainers' are required to take weekly STD tests, a measure activists criticised as marketing the sex industry as clean, and advocates warned that a new airport terminal on the city's outskirts could triple visitor numbers and expand sex trafficking.

For a trans visitor the exposure is twofold. Venues where trans women are concentrated in commercial sex work carry the highest violence and trafficking risk in the region, and enforcement operations of the kind conducted in June 2025 can sweep up anyone present, regardless of whether they were targeted. Trafficking provisions under R.A. No. 11862 and R.A. No. 7610 apply to any person in the venue, and none of the regional sources identifies the gender identity of the 57 victims rescued across the two 2025 operations, so no trans-specific figure can be drawn from them.

On protection, Central Luzon lags behind the capital region and Central Visayas. Of the eight Philippine provinces covered by SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances, only Bataan lies in this region, and no city or municipality here appears on the national list of 32 local units with such ordinances. Sectoral protections that do apply region-wide are narrow: the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers punishes SOGIE harassment with a fine of PHP 20,000 to 40,000 and up to one year's penalty, and the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act reach slurs and ridicule with fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. There is no national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity.

The parent framework governs the rest of a trans visitor's exposure. The Philippines does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery, leaving a court order as the only route. A pending bill would open recognition to consenting minors and allow markers beyond male and female. A 2026 travel-risk assessment rates Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers overall at 69 of 100 but scores trans travellers lower, at 62, in the 'Exercise Caution' band.

Detention in this region follows the same national pattern that removes what protections exist on paper. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex: at Manila City Jail, arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and survival against abuse is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates rather than through policy. 36201628B13373758884154.name: Calabarzon
36201628B13373758884154.summary:
Calabarzon stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity and contains no provision of national law criminalising a person for being transgender. The region has no single instrument of its own covering sexual orientation and gender identity; protection depends on ordinances passed by individual provinces and cities inside it.

No national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity exists. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress for 25 years, and in November 2022 the newly elected government rejected United Nations recommendations that included passage of the bill, describing them as unacceptable.

Anti-discrimination ordinances reaching gender identity are in force in parts of Calabarzon: Batangas province (2015), Cavite (2014, extended to cover gender identity by 2018), Batangas City (2016) and Calamba (2017). Coverage runs unit by unit, so the ordinance in effect changes from one city to the next and a visitor crossing a boundary may no longer be covered.

There is no administrative route to legal gender recognition. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses a birth-certificate sex change for trans people, so a court order is the only path, and in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) the Supreme Court held that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. Documents rather than presentation decide how a trans visitor is read at immigration counters, hotels and clinics.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. In August 2025 an LGBTQ pageant winner was found dead in Lipa City with 13 stab wounds days after taking the title, and police worked the case as a homicide. A foreign national was arrested in May 2025 on a charge of raping a trans woman at a resort in Batangas. Murders of transgender and gender-nonconforming persons have been reported in the Philippines since at least 2012.

36201628B63748016552864.name: Cagayan Valley
36201628B63748016552864.summary:
Cagayan Valley stands under the national framework of the Philippines: the country does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity, and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. There is no administrative route to legal gender recognition, because the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses a birth-certificate sex change and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery; a court order is the only mechanism, and a pending bill would open recognition to applicants including consenting minors and allow markers beyond male and female. No national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity exists, the SOGIE Equality Bill having been filed and stalled in Congress for 25 years. Protections are sub-national or sectoral: SOGIE ordinances cover eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities elsewhere in the country, none of them in this region, and penalties for SOGIE harassment exist only through the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers (PHP 20,000 to 40,000 and up to one year) and the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act (PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days and a sensitivity seminar).

Two killings of trans women are documented in this region within the 2024-2025 national series. On 31 July 2024 in Ilagan City, Isabela, a trans woman identified in the monitoring record as G. Cabansag was found dead in a cemetery after an alleged kidnapping and rape; three suspects were identified and the monitored count records the cause as stabbing.

On 23 June 2025 the body of Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman and incoming first-year Business Management student at Cagayan State University-Caritan Campus resident in Zone 7, Centro, Peñablanca, Cagayan, was found floating in the river between Amulung and Iguig, days after she was reported missing. Her mother told 95.7 XFM Tuguegarao she saw visible signs of physical assault and marks of violence on the body. A criminology student of the University of Cagayan Valley, named online as 'Menco de Guzman'/'Sherwin Kyqle', voluntarily surrendered to the Peñablanca police station, admitting that he picked her up on the Saturday night in question but denying involvement.

The killings produced advocacy rather than remedy. Bahaghari chairperson Reyna Valmores Salinas called the Peñablanca killing proof that LGBTQ+ persons remain unsafe and renewed the call for the SOGIESC Equality Bill (House Bill No. 5551; Senate Bill No. 1600), noting that no national anti-discrimination law has passed in 25 years. LGBTQIA+ groups including CSU Crystal at the Cagayan State University-Andrew campus and LGBT Pilipinas Taguig City Inc. demanded a full and thorough investigation, justice and immediate passage of the bill. Campaigners have cited that 25-year blockage as the direct reason the June 2025 killings produced no legislative remedy, and the Commission on Human Rights has described the trans killings recorded in a single year as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

No protective ordinance, institutional-hostility finding or enforcement pattern specific to trans visitors is documented in this region beyond these incidents. The visitor picture is therefore violence without operative local protections, in a region where none of the country's sub-national SOGIE ordinances is recorded as applying.

36201628B91065962446027.name: Western Visayas
36201628B91065962446027.summary:
Western Visayas stands under the national framework of the Philippines, where same-sex relations and trans identity are not criminalised and no provision of national law punishes a person for being transgender. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) forecloses a birth-certificate sex change, the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery, and a court order remains the only route. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress for 25 years, and no national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity exists. Protections are sub-national or sectoral, and one province in this region, Iloilo, is among the eight Philippine provinces with SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances; the national inventory does not specify which of the 32 covered cities and municipalities fall within the region.

No episode of the trans killings documented nationally in June 2025 occurred in Western Visayas: the murder of 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol, the shooting of a trans woman journalist inside a clinic in General Santos, and the arrest of a foreign national in May 2025 on a charge of raping a trans woman at a Batangas resort all took place elsewhere in the archipelago.

Western Visayas' documented episode of institutional gender-expression policing is a university directive rather than a legal measure. In October 2022 Capiz State University enforced a hair-and-uniform directive that excluded students perceived as trans women from the institution. The directive was gendered and binary: students were held to men's haircut rules, and Khaz-JP Padilla, who later graduated from the university, described the effect of the haircut requirement on her confidence ('Why is it that whenever I cut my hair... it feels like I'm losing my self-confidence?'). Padilla transitioned once pandemic-era online classes removed her from the haircut rule's daily enforcement.

An advocacy campaign by a legal-NGO network followed the October 2022 directive and challenged it. The campaign's outcome was recorded at the university's 21st commencement exercises on 7 August 2025, when Khaz-JP Padilla became the first openly trans woman to graduate summa cum laude from Capiz State University and served as batch valedictorian of the social work class with the highest Latin honour. The milestone is attributed to the advocacy campaign that followed the exclusion directive.

As a signal for a visitor, the Capiz episode is indirect. A trans traveller in this conservative provincial region should not expect to encounter the university directive itself, and should not expect the university's current rule set to be verifiable from the sources here. What the episode establishes is that gender expression in the region can be policed by institutional authority, in a setting where the national SOGIE bill's inactivity means no legislative remedy is available for such conduct and where no evidence of an operative local complaint channel accompanies the directive.

36201628B64564033926366.name: Ilocos Region
36201628B64564033926366.summary:
The Ilocos Region stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity and contains no provision of national law criminalising a person for being transgender. It also has no national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity: the SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress for 25 years, a blockage campaigners cite as the direct reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy. Protections are sub-national or sectoral, so what a visitor can invoke depends on the specific locality they are in.

Local instruments of that kind exist within the region. Ilocos Sur is one of eight provinces nationwide with a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance, and Bayambang in Pangasinan is among the 32 cities and municipalities carrying such an ordinance. Bayambang Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023, dated 16 October 2023 and authored by Coun. Benjamin Francisco S. De Vera, protects lesbians, gays, bisexuals, transgenders, queers and intersex persons in the municipality against any and all forms of discrimination solely on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, expression and sex characteristics, and provides penalties for violation.

The ordinance sets an escalating penalty ladder. A first offence carries a fine of at least PHP 1,000 or one month's imprisonment; a second, at least PHP 2,000 or one month and a day to six months; a third, at least PHP 2,500 or six months and a day to eight months; and later violations carry one year's imprisonment plus at least PHP 2,500. Violators must also complete mandatory human rights education. Complaints are filed through the barangay mechanism under the Katarungang Pambarangay provisions of R.A. 7160, the Local Government Code of 1991, giving a person discriminated against in the Pangasinan corridor a defined local complaint route.

The ordinance carries provincial endorsement. Pangasinan Sangguniang Panlalawigan Resolution No. 799-2024, adopted at the session of 19 August 2024 in Lingayen, declared Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023 to conform with the Bill of Rights and with Section 16 of R.A. No. 7160, affirming the municipal instrument at provincial level.

Recourse is not uniform across the region. In the rural parts of two of its provinces, a customary-justice system maintained by Itneg elders, adopted and modified as the Bodong Indigenous Allied Group, operates as an alternative dispute-resolution body alongside Philippine courts and police, so the institution handling a dispute may not be a national court.

Trans-specific exposure remains national in character. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (R.A. 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, a court order is the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A pending bill would open recognition to applicants including consenting minors and allow markers beyond male and female. Transgender women are detained according to birth sex, and violence is documented and recent: in April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd during a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan, and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community.

The resolution is a provincial-level endorsement affirming a municipal anti-discrimination ordinance, giving LGBTQI persons a local legal complaint route in the Pangasinan corridor.

It also has no national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity: the equality bill has been filed and stalled in the national legislature for 25 years, a blockage campaigners cite as the direct reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy. Protections are sub-national or sectoral, so what a visitor can invoke depends on the specific locality.

Local instruments of that kind exist within the state. One of its provinces is among the eight provinces nationwide with a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance, and one of its municipalities is among the 32 cities and municipalities carrying such an instrument. That municipal ordinance, No. 15 of 2023, dated 16 October 2023 and authored by a sitting councillor, protects lesbians, gays, bisexuals, transgenders, queers and intersex persons in the municipality against any and all forms of discrimination solely on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, expression and sex characteristics, and provides penalties for violation.

The ordinance sets an escalating penalty ladder. a first offence carries a fine of at least PHP 1,000 or one month's imprisonment; a second, at least PHP 2,000 or one month and a day to six months; a third, at least PHP 2,500 or six months and a day to eight months; and later violations carry one year's imprisonment plus at least PHP 2,500. Violators must also complete mandatory human rights education. Complaints are filed through the barangay mechanism under the Katarungang Pambarangay provisions of the national Local Government Code of 1991, giving a person discriminated against in the corridor a defined local complaint route.

The ordinance carries provincial endorsement. Provincial Board Resolution No. 799 of 2024, adopted at the session of 19 August 2024, declared the municipal ordinance to conform with the Bill of Rights and with Section 16 of the national Local Government Code, affirming the municipal instrument at provincial level.

Recourse is not uniform across the state. In the rural parts of two of its provinces, a customary-justice system maintained by indigenous elders, adopted and modified as an allied group, operates as an alternative dispute-resolution body alongside national courts and police, so the institution handling a dispute may not be a national court.

Trans-specific exposure remains national in character. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law of 2001 forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, a court order is the only route, and the Supreme Court held in 2008 that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. a pending bill would open recognition to applicants including consenting minors and allow markers beyond male and female. Transgender women are detained according to birth sex, and violence is documented and recent: in April 2024 a drag artist was struck on stage by a man from the crowd during a concert in one of the state's municipalities, and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community.

The resolution is a provincial-level endorsement giving LGBTQI persons a local legal complaint route in the corridor.

The certified copy of the municipality's ordinance protects LGBTQI persons against discrimination solely on the basis of SOGIESC and sets a penalty ladder from fines to imprisonment, with mandatory human-rights education for violators. Complaints are filed through a local dispute-resolution mechanism under the local-government code, giving a visitor in the corridor an actual local complaint route — the operative municipal instrument endorsed provincially.

36201628B64564033926366.tangentialFactors:
A 2026 travel-risk assessment rates Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers overall at 69 of 100 but scores trans travellers lower, at 62, in the 'Exercise Caution' band. That assessment covers the capital, not the Ilocos Region, and no equivalent regional score is sourced here.

Social visibility in the Philippines is high: gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy are long-standing, Pride events and nightlife are prominent in the capital, and LGBTQ+ themes carry substantial media presence. High visibility coexists with the absence of a national SOGIE statute and with documented killings; the Commission on Human Rights has described the trans killings recorded in a single year as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Other sectoral protections operate independently of local ordinances. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers punishes SOGIE harassment with a fine of PHP 20,000 to 40,000 and up to one year's penalty, while the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act reach slurs and ridicule with fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. The armed forces have permitted openly gay and bisexual personnel since 2009 and transgender personnel since 2017, with the uniform policy following the legal gender shown on the birth certificate, and the Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity.

The Bayambang ordinance is narrower than a provincial statute: it binds one municipality, and its provincial endorsement is a conformity declaration rather than a region-wide rule. Elsewhere in the country, recourse has been absent after violence; campaigners cite the stalled SOGIE Equality Bill as the reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy.

36201628B49646111072560.name: ARMM
36201628B49646111072560.summary:
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity and contains no provision criminalising a person for being transgender. No instrument reviewed for this record creates such an offence at regional level either; the visitor-facing risk in the region is structural, arising from which forum hears a dispute rather than from any statute aimed at gender non-conformity.

Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, whose drafting began on 29 March 2019, prescribes the structures and rules of governance of the autonomous region and guarantees religious freedom. Its justice-dispensation clause commits the region to adjudication "in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws", placing civil and religious law side by side inside the region's own governing statute.

The jurisdiction a visitor's dispute reaches is therefore not settled by default. Since Presidential Decree 1083 of 1977, Shari'ah jurisdiction has been confined to personal-status law; a proposal tabled in the Bangsamoro Parliament on 14 July 2026 would recast that limit through a Shari'ah Justice Code of 10 books extending jurisdiction into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and alternative dispute resolution. The proposal rests on the authority of the Bangsamoro Organic Law and the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations. It is not a power in force, and no source reviewed establishes that Shari'ah courts currently prosecute same-sex conduct or gender expression, nor that any such law has passed.

The legal-pluralist marriage regime applies directly to a visitor married to a Muslim spouse. Marriage, divorce, succession and family relations for Muslim residents remain governed by Shari'ah forums, with written-opt-in clauses allowing civil entities to take the same questions. In practice, spouse-status and inheritance questions for such a visitor would run through religious personal-status forums rather than through the civil courts alone.

The reach of those forums is widening. In August 2024 President Marcos Jr. signed a law, passed unanimously by the Bangsamoro Parliament, creating three new Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 circuit courts, extending the Shari'ah court system beyond the Bangsamoro into majority-Christian provinces of northern Mindanao and the Davao region, parts of the Visayas and Luzon, and Metro Manila. The measure carries the Bangsamoro's Shari'ah personal-law regime onto a national footing.

No protective ordinance or civil-rights infrastructure is documented inside the region. The SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances recorded nationally cover eight provinces (Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo) and 32 cities and municipalities, none of them within the Bangsamoro, and the SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress for 25 years, leaving no national statute as a backstop. National sectoral protections such as the Safe Spaces Act, the Magna Carta of Women and the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers apply by force of national law, but the region has no locally enacted SOGIE protection of its own on the record reviewed.

Violence and detention findings for the Philippines at large cannot be assumed to describe conditions inside the Bangsamoro. The documented cases of killings of trans women in June 2025, the arrest in May 2025 of a foreign national accused of raping a trans woman, and the classification practices recorded at Manila City Jail and Davao City Jail all fall outside this region, and no equivalent documentation for Bangsamoro facilities was located.

36201628B49646111072560.tangentialFactors:
The region is the clearest instance of legal pluralism in the national territory: the same conduct could in theory be assessed by civil, Shari'ah or traditional tribal forums depending on the parties and the question, and the July 2026 proposal would widen the religious forum's subject-matter reach well beyond the personal-status boundaries in force since 1977. A visitor's exposure therefore turns on forum allocation, not on a single criminal code.

The trajectory runs toward expansion rather than contraction. The August 2024 law creating three Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 circuit courts, and the 10-book justice code tabled in July 2026, both push religious jurisdiction outward; the region's own Administrative Code already names Shari'ah and tribal law alongside the Constitution as sources of justice.

Comparatively, the protections a trans traveller expects elsewhere in the Philippines are attenuated here. The eight provinces and 32 cities with SOGIE ordinances sit outside the region, the SOGIE Equality Bill has produced no national statute in 25 years, and campaigners have cited that blockage as the direct reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy.

Travel-risk scoring for the country is capital-weighted. A 2026 assessment rates Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers at 69 of 100 while scoring trans travellers at 62 in the 'Exercise Caution' band; that figure describes Manila and does not extend to the Bangsamoro or to its Shari'ah forums.

Documentation of harm is concentrated elsewhere in the country. The trans-specific killings, the drag-artist assault in Bayambang, Pangasinan in April 2024, the jail head-shaving and informal 'wedding' arrangements recorded at Manila City Jail, and the batch transfer of LGBT detainees at Davao City Jail all come from outside this region, so their absence from the record here reflects sourcing rather than a demonstrated absence of risk.

36201628B92932511992503.name: CAR
36201628B92932511992503.summary:
The Philippines does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity, and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. Social visibility is high: gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy are long-standing, Pride events and nightlife are prominent in the capital, and LGBTQ+ themes carry substantial media presence. A 2026 travel-risk assessment rates Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers overall at 69 of 100 but scores trans travellers lower, at 62, in the 'Exercise Caution' band.

The Cordillera Administrative Region, created on 15 July 1987 and comprising Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Kalinga and Mountain Province centred on Baguio, stands under that national framework while adding a second forum. The inter-tribal customary justice system runs alongside the formal court system: bodong and pagta holders resolve criminal and tribal offences with their own holders, sanctions and authority, and Philippine National Police personnel, prosecutors and barangay officials participate in customary-law conflict resolution. A trans visitor therefore faces a structural question of which forum would decide a dispute, rather than a documented trans-specific adverse outcome.

No trans-specific customary ruling, exclusion or punishment relating to gender expression appears in this record. The customary system here is a civil and restorative-justice institution, and no source in the current inventory describes it expanding criminal law over morality or gender expression.

Kalinga, one of the region's six provinces, is the clearest single illustration: its peace-pact system was codified in February 2026 by the provincial government into a 137-page written Pagta, a step its sponsors present as recognition by the national courts. The codification concerns the machinery of dispute resolution generally and is not described as trans-specific.

68945753B94077674833362.name: Daegu
68945753B94077674833362.summary:
Daegu stands under the national framework of South Korea, where gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The armed forces are the exception: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, and transgender people are excluded from military service altogether. Legal gender recognition is available, and on 8 May 2024 a court ruled that requiring sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status violates physical integrity.

Daegu has hosted the country's second-oldest queer culture festival every year since June 2009, a week-long programme of parade and film events usually held in late June. Organisers ran the 2025 edition on central Daegu's Dongseong-ro under the slogan 'We Will Not Be E(r)ased', framing the event as resistance to hate and discriminatory politics. Court filings from the 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 editions show the same pattern: the Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasure Committee sought injunctions against the festival and was dismissed each time.

State-adjacent restriction of the event is recurrent. Police again confined the 2025 march to a single bus-only lane, and in 2023, under then-Mayor Hong Joon-pyo, municipal officials physically blocked the road. In 2026 the Daegu District Court's dismissal of the festival committee's own injunction request was cited as finding the police notice legitimate, on the reasoning that Jungang-ro is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be kept clear for public welfare.

Organised counter-mobilisation is substantial and annual. In September 2025 a Daegu–Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella body convened its 17th 'National Assembly Against Queer', gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at Banwoldang station and along a 450-metre stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans. An estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups maintain a standing 'gay issue countermeasure committee' in Daegu, and opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central street.

Opposition also works through formal complaints. On 8 June 2026 the Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters, comprising the Daegu–Gyeongbuk Parents' Alliance for Protecting the Next Generation, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association, filed a collective petition with the National Human Rights Commission of Korea demanding a change of festival venue, claiming the event risks infringing public welfare and reporting about 34,000 signatures. The petition answers the festival committee's January complaint against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act. Venue restriction and organised anti-queer mobilisation thus continued into the 2026 edition.

For a trans visitor, the practical picture is a visible but contested public presence: the festival proceeds, injunction bids fail in court each year, and no severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources. The surrounding conditions are not benign. South Korea has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on those grounds, and Human Rights Watch records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report.

68945753B85435209225479.name: Daejeon
68945753B85435209225479.summary:
Daejeon stands under the legal framework of South Korea, where gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is lawful. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available in South Korea and the surgery requirement is falling. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled that mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status violates physical integrity, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years, and finding that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. The Supreme Court has also allowed a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

Trans visitors hold a documented, judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court issued a final, unappealed ruling that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed her personal rights, awarding 300,000 won in symbolic compensation against the state.

No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity in South Korea, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on these grounds in Daejeon either. In healthcare, the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Same-sex marriage is not available, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court's 2024 ruling on same-sex partners extended recognition specifically to healthcare rights.

Daejeon's own documented record is institutional rather than visitor-facing. On 7 October 2021 the Daejeon District Court ordered cancellation of the Army's forced discharge of Ssg. Byun Hee-soo, holding that the military should have treated her as female after her legal sex change, that loss of genitalia was not valid grounds for dismissal, and that a fitness-for-duty review should weigh basic rights. It was the first known legal case involving a transgender soldier, and the decision was borne out on her posthumous appeal.

Byun Hee-soo was buried at the National Cemetery in Daejeon on 24 June 2024, a state burial that stands as official honouring while the institutional stance toward transgender service members remains conservative. Some 60 activists protested at the funeral, arguing that the burial was marred by discriminatory treatment. She died by suicide in 2021 after the forced 2020 discharge, the classification of gender dysphoria as a mental disorder, a post-surgery physical-disability finding and court appeals.

The sources record no arrest, enforcement action, or other visitor-facing incident involving a trans visitor in Daejeon. Organised conservative opposition to LGBT rights remains active, Human Rights Watch documented persistent discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report, and that report also assessed the country's overall record for free media and civil society as relatively positive.

68945753B59172752195743.name: North Chungcheong
68945753B59172752195743.summary:
North Chungcheong province stands under the national framework of South Korea, where gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available in South Korea and the surgery requirement is falling. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that forcing surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. The Supreme Court has also allowed a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register. Trans visitors hold a documented, judicially enforced right to public restrooms: on 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court issued a final, unappealed ruling that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, awarding 300,000 won in symbolic compensation against the state.

There is no comprehensive South Korean anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on those grounds. In healthcare the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult. There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner; the Constitutional Court's landmark 2024 ruling extended recognition of same-sex partners' healthcare rights in that specific area.

The province's only trans-specific documented event is the death of Byun Hee-soo, 23, South Korea's first transgender soldier, who was discharged for gender-affirming surgery after her landmark military challenge was rejected in July 2020. She was found dead at her home in Cheongju on 3 March 2021, a counsellor having raised the alarm on 28 February, and her death triggered national debate on the treatment of trans troops.

The handling of that death is the province's distinguishing finding. The initial classification of the death as natural stood for three years before a national review board recognised it as service-related in April 2024.

Aftermath evidence runs in the direction of national protection rather than regional law. Public grief and demands for LGBT protections surged after 3 March 2021, the National Human Rights Commission honoured her, and prosecutors and activists called for an anti-discrimination bill, its eighth introduction since 2007, with a June 2020 draft that included gender-identity provisions; society-wide discourse about responsibility followed.

For a visitor on the ground, no traveler-facing enforcement action, arrest, incident, or hostility directed at visitors is documented in these sources for North Chungcheong, and no repeat-violence data exists for this unit. A trans visitor's exposure therefore tracks the national baseline, with the institutional-handling finding informing rather than elevating the assessment. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.

No visitor document requirements, border-screening practice, or marriage or partner-travel provision is recorded for this province.

68945753B43731078897969.name: Gyeonggi
68945753B43731078897969.summary:
Gyeonggi Province stands under the national framework of South Korea. Gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available and the surgical requirement is falling. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had undergone years of hormone therapy that forcing surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. The Supreme Court has also allowed a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

Trans visitors hold a judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court issued a final, unappealed ruling that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, awarding 300,000 won in symbolic compensation against the state.

South Korea has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation in Gyeonggi carry no statutory protection on those grounds. In healthcare the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the ground that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage in South Korea, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court did issue a landmark 2024 ruling extending same-sex partners a measure of recognition in healthcare.

Within that framework, Gyeonggi's distinctive instrument is student-facing rather than visitor-facing. The province enacted the model student human rights ordinance in 2010 under a progressive superintendent of education, and that ordinance prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. Gyeonggi and Seoul are the only two ordinances in the country that also guarantee the right not to be discriminated against on the basis of pregnancy.

As of 28 April 2024, six regional education offices still enforced comparable ordinances: Gyeonggi, Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju. The Seoul Metropolitan Council abolished the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance on that date, twelve years after adoption, after the ruling People Power Party pushed repeal following an August 2022 campaign by religious groups and parents objecting to the ordinance's sexual-orientation clause.

None of these student protections bind conduct toward a visitor, and no visitor-facing enforcement action, arrest or incident is documented for Gyeonggi Province in these sources. Nationally, Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report records persistent discrimination against LGBT people while noting a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society; Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are broadly positive, organised conservative opposition remains active, and no severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented.

A quoted Gyeonggi-based teacher defended the ordinance against wholesale abolition.

47653553B66835736668351.name: RegiÃ³n del BÃ­o-BÃ­o
47653553B66835736668351.summary:
Región del Bío-Bío stands under Chile's statutory framework for trans people, which is among the more developed in the region. Legal gender recognition has operated since 2019 on a self-determination basis, with no medical or surgical conditions attached. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and since 2012 the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences. Birth certificates also offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Detention carries specific protections. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing trans detainees the recognition of their assumed gender, including placement and segmented housing by gender identity, entry examinations, and rules on access for trans visitors; a standing committee with Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives monitors implementation.

Facility placement is the region's documented failure. On 14 October 2016 Movilh-Biobío filed a formal complaint with the Seremi de Salud, Mauricio Careaga Lemus, concerning the Hospital Traumatológico de Concepción, where patient Hanna Jiménez Carrasco, interned from 28 September to 3 October 2016, was placed and treated as male despite public policy and the legal duty to use her chosen name and social sex. The complaint alleged brutal and illegal discriminatory acts by hospital staff. The national gender-identity statute, Law 21.120, took effect only in December 2019, after the denunciation. For a visitor, an emergency-room or inpatient admission in Bío-Bío therefore carries a documented precedent of gender-mismatched placement.

Regional incident volume is comparatively high. Movilh's XXIII Annual Human Rights Report, published in March 2025 with 2024 data, records Bío-Bío at 5.89% of the national case total, the third-highest share of any Chilean region, with Concepción among the cities recording the most documented incidents at five.

Violence remains a live risk nationally. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing and was described in the national press as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Hostility inside state institutions is also on the record. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging she was relegated to administrative duties, had her private life exposed without consent, and was denied support.

47653553B97418467345315.name: RegiÃ³n de TarapacÃ¡
47653553B97418467345315.summary:
Región de Tarapacá stands under Chile's national statutory framework, which is among the more developed in the region. Legal gender recognition has operated since 2019 on a self-determination basis with no medical or surgical conditions attached. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and since 2012 the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences. Birth certificates also offer a third sex option for intersex children.

The controlling risk for a transgender visitor to Tarapacá is judicial rather than statutory. In early October 2023 the Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled in whole the trial of Jhonatan Cañon for the 2022 murder of trans woman Yuri Pizarro in Tarapacá, holding that the offence of femicidio covers only 'a person biologically female'. The conviction could not stand as framed, which voids the strongest gendered-violence protection available in the penal code within the territory where that court exercises jurisdiction. A trans woman killed in Tarapacá therefore cannot be protected by the charge that carries the heaviest penalty for gender-motivated killing.

Case volume in the region is small in absolute share but rising. Movilh's XXIII Annual Human Rights Report, published in March 2025 with 2024 data, places Tarapacá at about 2% of nationally documented homo/transphobic cases and among the fastest-rising regions, at +18.18% year-on-year, with growth also flagged at +19.51% in the report's period tables. The practical reading is a documented and widening protection gap against gender-motivated violence rather than a high absolute case load.

Detention carries specific protections nationally. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing trans detainees recognition of their assumed gender, including placement and segmented housing by gender identity, rules on entry examinations and access for trans visitors, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives monitoring implementation.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing and was described in the national press as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.
