47653553B84299910343297.name: RegiÃ³n de La AraucanÃ­a
47653553B84299910343297.summary:
La Araucanía is a region of Chile, and trans visitors stand under the national statutory framework rather than any regional variant. Chile's legal gender recognition has operated since 2019 on a self-determination basis with no medical or surgical condition attached; same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences since 2012. Birth certificates also carry a third sex option for intersex children.

Detention conditions are governed by a national protocol signed by the director of Gendarmería de Chile, which guarantees trans detainees recognition of their assumed gender, housing segmented by gender identity, rules for entry examinations and access by trans visitors, monitored by a standing committee with Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives. No regional departure from that protocol is recorded in the sources.

Reported hate-motivated incidents in La Araucanía rose faster than anywhere else in Chile during 2025. Movilh's XXIV Annual Human Rights Report, published in March 2026, names the region first in year-on-year growth, with recorded homo/transphobic cases up 150 percent, against a national total of 3,620 documented cases, 27.1 percent above the 2024 figure. The 2025 national total alone accounts for 23 percent of all cases recorded across the report's 24-year series. La Araucanía nonetheless represented only 1.96 percent of the national case total, so the sharp percentage increase sits on a small base.

Movilh reads the pattern as decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ+ themes receive less public debate, and states that the trend appears aimed at obstructing equality work. The region's formal trans visibility through the law is low: 157 people used Gender Identity Law 21.120 to rectify name and legal sex in its first three years.

Nationally the policy record has stalled. A Chilean advocacy group's annual assessment judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights, the first such reversal since the return of democracy in 1990, attributing the failure of equality and trans-rights bills to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction. Movilh's reporting describes a breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus around LGBTIQ+ rights, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers.

Documented anti-trans violence remains a live risk nationally. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing and was described in the national press as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Institutional hostility has also surfaced in state employment. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging she was relegated to administrative duties, had her private life exposed without consent, and was denied support.

No trans-specific Mapuche customary-law jurisdiction is identified for La Araucanía, and the sources record no state-implicated violence against trans people within the region itself.

Chile's statutory framework for trans people is among the more developed in the region. The policy record has stalled. A Chilean advocacy group's annual assessment judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights, the first such reversal since the return of democracy in 1990, attributing the failure of equality and trans-rights bills to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction. Movilh's 24th Annual Human Rights Report, published in 2025, describes a breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus around LGBTIQ+ rights, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers.

Documented violence remains a live risk. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing and was described in the national press as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Institutional hostility is visible inside state employment. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging she was relegated to administrative duties, had her private life exposed without consent, and was denied support.

For a trans visitor, the risk picture in Región de Arica y Parinacota is the national baseline plus a small deduction. No trans-specific incident, court ruling or enforcement failure originating in Arica y Parinacota is identified in any cited source. The dossier's one hard legal finding, the Court of Appeals of Iquique's annulment of the entire trial over the killing of a transgender woman on the ground that the 'femicide' offence protects only 'a person biologically female', was issued in Tarapacá, not here; it nonetheless supports grouping Tarapacá and Arica y Parinacota as worse than national on shared judicial geography, since it shows the country's strongest gendered-violence protection failing to reach trans women in courts of this part of the country.

Reported caseload in the region sits at the low end of the national distribution. Movilh's XXIII Annual Human-Rights Report on Sexual and Gender Diversity, covering 2024 and published in March 2025, recorded 2,847 cases nationally, up 78.7 %, with Arica y Parinacota holding a 0.84 % share, among the lowest in the country; increases occurred in 11 of the 16 regions. In regions with shares this small a single case can dominate the rate, so the figure should be read as a floor rather than a measure of exposure.

The region's own complaint trajectory has run against the national trend. A local channel for complaints exists. On 14 November 2017 Fundación Iguales announced that Arica became the fourth territory where it provides free legal aid for discrimination cases based on sexual orientation and/or gender identity, through a collaboration agreement with pro-bono lawyer Piera Balbontin Nef covering Arica's jurisdiction. The foundation's legal director said discrimination is greater in regions far from the capital, which is why local legal support matters.

10402087B60477050509260.name: Bayern
10402087B60477050509260.summary:
Visitors to Bavaria stand under Germany's national legal framework. Identity documents, marriage law and anti-discrimination protections in Germany are federal and uniform, and no German state can remove that floor.

Gender-inclusive German is prohibited in Bavarian schools, universities and all state administration since 1 April 2024. The ban implements a declaration by the Söder state government of December 2023, carried out by a cabinet decision amending the language rules of Bavarian public authorities. Critics quoted in the coverage dismiss the measure as symbol politics while noting that it reaches every public counter, registry office and classroom in the state. A visitor dealing with a Bavarian registry office, school or government counter should therefore expect binary gender forms in official communication.

The national Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 November 2024, is the operative document law for a visitor in Bavaria. Adults over 18 declare the change of first name and legal gender themselves before the registry office, subject to a three-month waiting period and a one-year lockout after each change. Those aged 14 to 17 need a guardian's consent or the family court's; for children under 14 only a guardian may declare. The Act passed the Bundestag on 12 April 2024 by 374 votes to 251 with 11 abstentions, the Bundesrat on 17 May 2024, was gazetted on 21 June 2024, and could be registered from 1 August 2024.

Germany has allowed adults to change legal gender since 1980. Same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since 2017, and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is banned nationwide in employment and in the supply of goods and services, with some protections varying from state to state.

Bavaria participates in an organised Länder-level effort to tighten the federal self-ID law. Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt launched a Bundesrat initiative to make the nationwide Self-Determination Act stricter, with Bavaria a partner. The disputed point traces back to the Bundesrat's criticism of 20 October 2023 that the draft let parents decide gender-entry changes for under-14s without counselling, examination or investigation of the child's welfare.

10402087B60477050509260.tangentialFactors:
Several trans-specific exposures reach a visitor in Bavaria without being Bavarian law, because they arise from the national framework. German prisons operate under a statutory binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony reads § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act that way and runs a research project on transgender people in prison. Several other states have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 without press coverage.

Custody placement remains unsettled in practice. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle said that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025, with authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility.

Airport screening has produced documented complaints against federal officers. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which she said officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity, and she characterised the incident as targeted transphobic harassment, giving Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off public argument over registered trans women's access, and reporting on Berlin saunas shows how venues are now treating trans women.

Reporting and support machinery exists for hostility encountered in country. The STOP the HATE campaign site of the Prevention and Empowerment organisation provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, an LSBTIQ* crisis line, emergency guidance and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

10402087B20892132820961.name: Berlin
10402087B20892132820961.summary:
Berlin stands under the national framework of the Federal Republic of Germany: federal constitutional and equality protections apply in every Land, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and no Land can remove that federal floor.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several Länder have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all.

How the exception is applied in practice remains unsettled. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025; authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, and critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law. DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, a finding illustrated by the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted.

The Berlin prison service maintains an official page in German stating that legislation has created a basis for considering trans, inter* and non-binary people held in custody, that prison staff are responsible for taking each detainee's individual needs into account within the legal framework, and detailing gender-segregated placement, intake procedures and counselling and support offers across the city's facilities, including JVA Moabit and JVA für Frauen Berlin.

Screening is a documented flashpoint. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity; she characterised the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and gave Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a debate about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic. Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reported on how Berlin saunas and similar venues now treat trans women, after months of public argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Germany's Pride movement faces a documented rise in attacks. The amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-extremist attacks on Pride events nationally in 2024 and 30 so far in 2025 across roughly 120 parades, including an attack with boiling water, and runs a €100,000 CSD support fund focused on a part of the country. Ahead of the 2025 Christopher Street Day, with hundreds of thousands expected, Berlin's organisers urged participants to be vigilant.

The risk materialised at the capital's own Pride. At the 48th Berlin Christopher Street Day a vehicle drove into a crowd in the Tiergarten area, killing one woman, injuring several people and forcing the event to be cancelled; MANEO offers victim counselling and an anonymous reporting line.

MANEO, Berlin's anti-violence documentation project, recorded 723 LSBTIQ+-hostile incidents in Berlin in 2025, slightly fewer than the 738 documented in 2024, from 1,014 new reports, a new high. Its 12 May 2026 release lists insults, threats and physical attacks in public transport, parks and streets, with Schöneberg, Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Tiergarten most affected, plus 58 attacks on LSBTIQ+ venues, memorials and events.

10402087B85226028911536.name: Hessen
10402087B85226028911536.summary:
Hessen stands under Germany's federal framework. Federal constitutional and equality protections apply to visitors nationwide, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform across the Länder, and no Land can lower that floor.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure. German prisons operate under statutory separation on a binary men-and-women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several Länder have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026.

How the exception is applied in practice remains unsettled. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025; authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, and critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law.

DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, a finding illustrated by the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted.

Registered offences against queer people in Hessen rose from 33 in 2022 to 83 in 2023 and 135 in 2024, an increase of 52 in a single year that Interior Minister Roman Poseck called alarming. Hessen police counted 141 queer-hostile offences in 2025, a more than fourfold rise within four years, which Poseck described as only the tip of the iceberg given a high dark figure.

The 2024 total comprised 16 cases of dangerous grievous bodily harm, seven of bodily harm, 13 of property damage and 26 of insult. Suspects were identified in 46 of the 2024 proceedings and six convictions followed. The ministry attributes part of the responsibility to far-right forces. Poseck cited a January 2026 Kassel tram incident in which a male couple was homophobically insulted, threatened and spat on.

Those numbers must be read with the federal Criminal Police Office's own caveat. Its situation report on the security of LSBTIQ* people, published with the Interior Ministry, introduces a new reporting category that makes Land-by-Land comparison possible but warns that classification changes can inflate registered counts, so part of the rise may reflect better recording rather than a sharper danger.

Protection machinery exists. LSBTIQ* liaison officers have been established at all Hessen police headquarters since 2010 under a framework concept, and the Hessian police keep dedicated contact officers for this hate crime, with the state government promising consistent prosecution.

Screening is a documented flashpoint within Hessen. On 23 November 2024, trans woman artist BASHKKA was screened at Frankfurt Airport where a male security officer refused her a search by a female officer and told her she was 'not a woman'. She filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act, characterising the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and giving Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport. Frankfurt Airport apologised by email, said the security service provider had been instructed to investigate, and promised security staff would be trained on dealing with transgender and gender non-conforming travellers.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a debate about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic.

Reporting and support machinery exists for hostility encountered in country. The STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

10402087B67217417145666.name: Thüringen
10402087B67217417145666.summary:
Thüringen stands under Germany's national framework. Federal constitutional and equality protections apply nationwide, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and no Land can remove that federal floor.

For a trans visitor the sharpest documented exposure is custody. German prisons operate under statutory separation using a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and maintains a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several Länder have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 without press coverage.

How the exception is applied in practice remains unsettled. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025; authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, and critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law.

DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, a finding illustrated by the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted.

Screening is a documented flashpoint under the national framework. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity; she characterised the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and gave Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a debate about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic. Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reported on how Berlin saunas and similar venues now treat trans women, after months of public argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Within Thüringen itself the operative layer is political. In the state election of 1 September 2024, AfD Thüringen, classified by the state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution as right-wing extremist, took 32.8% of the vote, ahead of the CDU at 23.4%, the BSW at 15.8% in its first state election, Die Linke at 13.1% and the SPD at 6.1%. The CDU, BSW and SPD formed the first 'Brombeerkoalition' under minister-president Mario Voigt, a minority cabinet without its own Landtag majority, and it is in this configuration that formal, multi-layered hostility to gender policy in Thüringen is institutionalised.

The Thuringian Landtag has before it an AfD fraction motion, 'Keine Gendersprache an Thüringer Schulen', demanding that the Landtag's existing ban on gender-inclusive language in Thuringian schools be implemented consistently, on the assertion that schools must not be 'a socio-political experimental field'. A separate draft law proposes to dismantle the region's existing equality-policy machinery, arguing that current law 'regularly violates the principle of equal opportunity'. No trans-specific safety finding for Thüringen was documented in the material reviewed.

On 2 June 2026, Thüringen co-signed the Sachsen and Sachsen-Anhalt initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act following the Liebich case, an anti-abuse package framed alongside stronger recognition for trans and inter persons.

14339913B89763821047858.name: Wales
14339913B89763821047858.summary:
Wales stands under the United Kingdom's post-April 2025 Supreme Court regime, which now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the Equality and Human Rights Commission's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. The code is the daily, nationwide consequence of the ruling: a trans visitor in Wales uses facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how lawfully to enforce that division.

Prison placement follows the same rule across the United Kingdom. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, ruled the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory custody guidance unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis; the guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in prisons matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The preceding hearing had been told by the challengers that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard. Any visitor arrested in Wales should therefore expect placement by sex at birth, with contested suicide-risk arguments surrounding that outcome.

Searching and strip-searching follow the same rule. British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, with trans women searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; the prior policy had permitted a trans woman staff member to conduct an intimate search of a woman holding a Gender Recognition Certificate. Police Scotland's interim guidance of 25 June 2025 states that in custody and stop-and-search, any search involving removal beyond a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear is conducted on the basis of biological sex, though where a person's lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

The direction of travel is a court- and watchdog-led rollback rather than executive hostility, and it is contested at international level: on 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.

Wales's own legal framework for a trans visitor is the United Kingdom's: the right to change legal gender has existed since the Gender Recognition Act 2004, discrimination protections cover gender identity as well as sexual orientation, same-sex marriage has been available since 2014, and criminal and entry rules are uniform across the country. Healthcare is the one materially local element: trans adults were historically referred to London clinics until the first Welsh gender identity clinic opened in September 2019.

The devolved Welsh Government has publicly maintained its LGBTQ+ Action Plan through the United Kingdom's post-judgment years. The plan's standing update page was issued answering the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025, and a dedicated young-people's edition was posted in January 2026. That posture signals no devolved hostility, but it does not displace the national single-sex facility, search or prison rules set out above.

sources.summary: Welsh Government LGBTQ+ Action Plan document for young people (posted January 2026): part of the standing devolved inclusion programme whose update page answers the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025.

Welsh Government statutory school guidance "Rights, Respect, Equality" (consultation May 2025): obliges schools to challenge bullying and harassment on sex, gender-reassignment and sexual-orientation grounds, with incident recording/monitoring and a parental escalation route.

sources.title: LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales
sources.summary: The Welsh Government's February 2023 LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales aims to make Wales 'the most LGBTQ+ friendly nation in Europe'. Deputy Minister Hannah Blythyn announced it in the Senedd on 21 June 2022 under the 2021 Welsh Labour–Plaid Cymru agreement. It was built on 61 recommendations from the Independent LGBTQ+ Expert Panel (March 2021) and a 12-week public consultation with 1,328 responses, and it funds a Grassroots Pride Fund. The government pursued a Welsh-specific ban on conversion practices, forming a Working Group on Banning Conversion Practices in December 2022 (gov.wales 'Banning conversion practices in Wales', May 2024). The plan records the UK Government's blocking of the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill in January 2023. Welsh NHS commissioners stated in March 2024 they had no plans to develop a children's gender service, and parents of transgender children called for more help (BBC, March 2024).

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Wales
sources.summary: Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Wales since 1967, the age of consent was equalised in 2001, remaining restrictions were removed in 2003, legal gender recognition has been available since 2004 under the Gender Recognition Act, civil partnerships since 2005, same-sex marriage since 2014, and full adoption rights since 2005, with discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity. Trans adults in Wales were historically referred to London clinics for transgender healthcare until the first Welsh gender identity clinic opened in September 2019 (BBC).

14339913B6930312138089.name: Northern Ireland
14339913B6930312138089.summary:
Northern Ireland stands under the United Kingdom's post-April 2025 Supreme Court regime, which now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. Trans visitors in Northern Ireland therefore use facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how lawfully to enforce that division.

Prison placement follows the same rule across the United Kingdom. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, ruled the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory custody guidance unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis; that guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in prisons matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. Challengers had argued that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard. A visitor arrested anywhere in the United Kingdom should expect placement by sex at birth, with contested suicide-risk arguments surrounding that outcome.

Searching and strip-searching follow the same rule. British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, with trans women searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; the prior policy had permitted a trans woman staff member to conduct an intimate search of a woman holding a Gender Recognition Certificate. Police Scotland's interim guidance of 25 June 2025 states that in custody and stop-and-search, any search involving removal beyond a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear is conducted on the basis of biological sex, though where a person's lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

The direction of travel is a court- and watchdog-led rollback rather than executive hostility, and it is contested at international level: on 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.

Northern Ireland's devolved administration has moved in the same direction on documents of its own. On 8 September 2025 Education Minister Paul Givan requested removal of guidance supporting transgender pupils from the Education Authority website, and the guidance was withdrawn; he argued that it conflicted with departmental policy and with the law in Northern Ireland. The withdrawn guidance had recommended that trans pupils be allowed to use changing rooms matching their gender identity, and teachers' representatives warned that removal ignores the practical realities.

Protection machinery in Northern Ireland has been blocked at executive level. On 14 December 2025 it was reported that other executive parties had blocked Justice Minister Naomi Long's plan to add transgender people as a protected characteristic in Northern Ireland's new hate-crime legislation. Long had sought approval in early November with a response deadline in mid-November, and the bill had carried executive agreement since December 2024. She cited Police Service of Northern Ireland statistics of close to 100 transgender-identity incidents or hate crimes.

82085004B70364588595557.name: Northern Territory
82085004B70364588595557.summary:
The Northern Territory stands under the Australian framework: gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that this protection extends to trans women as women. Marriage equality has applied nationwide since December 2017. No Australian jurisdiction confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, federal identity documents are issued uniformly across the country, and no border friction has been reported for trans travellers entering Australia.

The Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (No. 27 of 2025, assented 30 October 2025; Part 3 commencing 27 July 2026) removes the civil provision that made it unlawful to offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate a person in public on the basis of a protected attribute, gender identity included. Complaints to the NT Anti-Discrimination Commission on that basis lose their statutory footing when Part 3 operates.

The government framed the amendment as restoring freedom of speech and religious freedom, and it also narrows the vilification provision and lets religious schools prefer staff of the same faith. For a visitor, public verbal abuse or humiliation directed at gender expression is deliberately outside Territory civil law at a time when other Australian states have brought equivalent conduct inside theirs.

Protection against motivated violence is thinner at Territory level than the federal baseline suggests. The Northern Territory's own hate-crime statute does not list sexual orientation or gender identity among its qualifying motives; federal coverage of those motives dates only from 2025.

Official posture in Territory-run settings has hardened. The NT government banned rainbow pride flags in public hospitals in February 2025, and in December 2025 issued a policy directive banning gender-affirming healthcare for minors. A trans visitor accompanying a minor, or admitted to a Territory hospital, encounters both rules directly.

ABC News, 17 Oct 2025: the NT government's anti-discrimination amendments passed parliament, framed as restoring free speech and religious freedom — narrowing the vilification provision and letting religious schools prefer staff sharing the same faith; the government had earlier backtracked from scrapping the vilification section. ANROWS research maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights in Australia, naming organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over access to facilities and to records, and pressure to roll back existing rights, alongside systemic discrimination and harassment experienced by trans people. The Tickle v Giggle case itself grew out of organised exclusionary activism, which indicates that the federal protection is contested in practice even where it is settled in law.

Political climate evidence sits on both sides. The Northern Territory voted 60.6% Yes in the 2017 national postal survey on marriage equality, while the 2025 vilification repeal and the February 2025 hospital flag ban show the governing party's current posture toward gender expression in public life.

Detention remains the sharpest residual risk area across Australia. Queensland's inspection standards issued in August 2023 direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, under the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022 in force from 2023, with a discretionary admission caveat and an exception tied to sexual reassignment surgery. That is Queensland practice, not Territory practice.

82085004B21656044714531.name: New South Wales
82085004B21656044714531.summary:
New South Wales stands under the Australian national framework. Gender identity is a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, in force since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that gender-identity discrimination protection extends to trans women as women, awarding compensation against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. Marriage equality has held nationwide since 2017, which governs same-sex couples arriving together, and federal identity documents are uniform across the country.

State law has moved in the same direction. New South Wales passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024, and the Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 took effect on 4 April 2025. Practices causing substantial mental or physical harm are criminal offences punishable by up to five years' imprisonment, and taking a person out of New South Wales for conversion therapy carries up to three years. Anti-Discrimination NSW can investigate complaints from 4 April 2025, with civil referral pathways available.

Visitors face none of the restrictive machinery found in some other jurisdictions: there are no laws confining bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, and no border friction has been reported for trans travellers.

Violence risk is documented rather than theoretical. Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old transgender woman from the Philippines who was visiting Australia, was killed in Wagga Wagga, New South Wales; the ABC reported the investigation on 2 July 2021. The perpetrator pleaded guilty to manslaughter and received a 22-month custodial term, an outcome that indicates a lenient judicial response to fatal violence against a trans woman traveller in this state.

82085004B93533858076668.name: Western Australia
82085004B93533858076668.summary:
Australia treats gender identity as a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, in force since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that gender-identity discrimination protection extends to trans women as women, and awarded compensation against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. Visitors in every state, Western Australia included, stand under that national framework, and marriage and federal documents are uniform nationwide.

State protection in Western Australia runs through a narrower formulation. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 protects the attribute 'gender history', defined by living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex, and the official WA Government guidance states that a person has gender history where they identify as a member of the opposite sex by living or seeking to live as such. Direct discrimination, including treating a person as their former sex, and indirect discrimination are both unlawful under the Act. The binary, medically-inflected wording means a non-binary or gender-nonconforming visitor may fall outside the state-law definition and would rely on federal coverage for a state-level complaint. Western Australia has no state anti-vilification offence, civil or criminal, and no statutory charter binding public authorities.

Complaint eligibility under the state attribute has historically been tied to recognition certificates or a registry change through the Births, Deaths and Marriages framework. On 16 April 2024 Premier Roger Cook and Attorney-General John Quigley announced the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Bill 2024, which repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and abolishes the Gender Reassignment Board, described by the ministers as the only remaining board of its kind in Australia. The Board's functions move to a streamlined administrative process within the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, and applicants are no longer required to undergo medical or surgical reassignment. A statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling, now suffices, and a 'non-binary' sex descriptor becomes available. Stricter rules apply to under-18s through parental consent or Family Court of WA permission, and the Act contains a statutory review clause after three years. The reform implements the WA Law Reform Commission's 2018 recommendations.

The registration reform reshapes the state discrimination attribute itself. The Equal Opportunity Commission's fact sheet records that the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 amends section 4(1) of the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 by deleting the definition of 'gender reassigned person' and inserting a definition tied to recognition certificates under the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 or registration of sex or gender under the amended regime. The Act also repeals the Gender Reassignment Regulations 2001, does not operate retrospectively, and commences by proclamation; once it is in force, gender history complaints must comply with the new registration requirements.

Two complaint routes exist and only one may be used. A complaint may be lodged with the WA Commissioner of Equal Opportunity under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 within 12 months, with acknowledgment of receipt within a week and a free conciliation conference to follow, or with the Australian Human Rights Commission under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 within 24 months, reduced to 12 months for employment matters. Choosing one route forecloses the other.

Visitors encounter none of the restrictive machinery found elsewhere in the world: there are no laws confining bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity in Western Australia, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held nationally since 2017, which matters to same-sex couples arriving together.

Counterweights are documented. The Tickle case grew out of organised exclusionary activism, and ANROWS research maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights in Australia, naming organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over access to facilities and records, and pressure to roll back existing rights, alongside systemic discrimination and harassment experienced by trans people.

Two complaint routes exist and only one may be used. a complaint may be lodged with the state Commissioner of Equal Opportunity under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 within 12 months, with acknowledgment of receipt within a week and a free conciliation conference to follow, or with the national human rights commission under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 within 24 months, reduced to 12 months for employment matters. Choosing one route forecloses the other.

Visitors encounter none of the restrictive machinery found elsewhere: there are no laws confining bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held nationally since 2017, which matters to same-sex couples arriving together.

Counterweights are documented. The Tickle case grew out of organised exclusionary activism, and ANROWS research maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights nationally, naming organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over access to facilities and records, and pressure to roll back existing rights, alongside systemic discrimination and harassment experienced by trans people.

82085004B93533858076668.tangentialFactors:
Western Australia's reform sits inside a wider state-level movement. Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections for gender-diverse people in April 2024, and New South Wales passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. The WA announcement also linked the registration reform to a planned new Equal Opportunity Act and a ban on conversion practices slated for 2025.

Detention is the sharpest residual risk across the country, and the practice Western Australian visitors would meet if detained is set by interstate precedent rather than by any WA instrument in this inventory. Queensland's inspection standards issued in August 2023 direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, a placement rule with a discretionary admission caveat and an exception tied to sexual reassignment surgery; oversight there passed to the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, fully in force from 2023, after a 2009 corrective services procedure was assessed as largely ineffective. Equivalent Western Australian detention placement standards are not covered by the sources assembled here.

The exclusionary activism behind Tickle v Giggle indicates that private and platform-level exclusion can arise even where the statute protects gender identity, and the outcome was a compensation award rather than an injunction preventing exclusion in the first place.

82085004B40257551482390.name: Australian Capital Territory
82085004B40257551482390.summary:
Visitors in every state stand under the national framework: gender identity is a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, and marriage and federal documents are uniform nationwide.

The territory's Human Rights Act 2004 requires public authorities to act compatibly with human rights and enables courts to issue declarations of inconsistency, giving a visitor who encounters discriminatory conduct by a police officer, public servant or public facility a legal review mechanism that common-law states without a charter lack. The territory is also one of four jurisdictions with an explicit self-identification basis for prison placement, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

No region-specific incident series, enforcement pattern or institutional-failure finding was identified in the dossier for this territory; the absence of negative evidence, combined with the structural rights protection and the self-identification custody rule, places it modestly above the national average.

A conversion-practices ban has been in force since early 2021, with offending practices attracting up to a 12-month custodial term or a fine, alongside civil penalties giving a tribunal power to issue orders and order redress; practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition are explicitly not banned. No visitor documents or border-screening practice specific to this territory is recorded in the dossier.

sources.summary: ABC News, 3 Jul 2020: national survey of trans prisoners — experts estimate up to 400 trans and gender-diverse people in Australian cells, often inappropriately housed and at elevated risk of physical and sexual violence; NSW, Victoria, the ACT and Tasmania run explicit self-identification policies while QLD/NT/SA are unclear. ACT-relevant: names the ACT's explicit self-ID prison policy.

The Human Rights Law Centre report 'Ending Strip Searching in Australian prisons' (2026), produced with the trans-community groups Flat Out and FIGJAM, documents strip-searching practice in Australian prisons, including those in the ACT, and its disproportionate harms for trans, gender-diverse and Indigenous prisoners.

sources.title: Human Rights Act 2004 | Acts | ACT Legislation Register
sources.summary: The official ACT Legislation Register lists the Human Rights Act 2004 (A2004-5) as In Force, with the current republished version and a full republication history back to 1 July 2004. Section 31 provides that interpreters may consider international law and the judgments of foreign and international courts and tribunals relevant to a human right. The register also records uncommenced amendments by the Human Rights (Housing) Amendment Act 2025. The Act is the statutory rights framework that ACT public authorities must operate within.

sources.title: Serious barriers in accessing health care for Canberra's transgender community highlighted in new study - ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News reported on 16 April 2022 that the ACT government's LGBTIQ+ Health Scoping Study found serious barriers for transgender and gender-diverse Canberrans: a shortage of primary-care professionals, including GPs, mental-health supports and paediatric specialists with LGBTIQ+ health understanding, resulting in 'excessive wait times, delays from referrals and high costs associated with interstate and international travel'. The article records 20 young transgender people on the waitlist of Canberra's only paediatric endocrinologist, some patients waiting a year for an appointment, GP demand rising 20-40 per cent a year, and the study calling the ACT 'the only jurisdiction not to have a comprehensive gender-focused health service' in private practice or through a publicly-funded gender clinic. The study documents a shortfall of institutional capacity for transgender health care in the ACT.

sources.title: LGBTQ conversion therapy banned in Canberra as Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill passes - ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News reported on 27 August 2020 that the ACT Legislative Assembly passed the Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill, so that from early 2021 conversion practices used on protected persons attract up to a 12-month jail term or a $24,000 fine, alongside civil penalties giving the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal power to issue orders and order redress. The bill was amended before passage after the Association of Christian Schools and the ACT Law Society argued the definition of conversion practice was 'too broad and vague', while practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition were explicitly not banned. The statute is an ACT criminal and civil protection measure.

25490228B8471183517505.name: Castilla y León
25490228B8471183517505.summary:
Castilla y León stands under Spain's national framework. Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition of the acquired gender is possible from age 12 under conditions.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in the region.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months. Both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts apply the aggravation in practice. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied across Spain since 2005.

Castilla y León is the only Spanish autonomous community never to have enacted a regional LGTBI or gender-identity law. For a trans visitor the vacuum is administrative rather than punitive. No criminal ban and no facility restriction exists in the region, national criminal law applies in full, and the severity floor is therefore set by the state. What the region lacks is dedicated machinery: no regional equality office receives complaints, no institutional hate-crime observatory operates, and no region-specific administrative protocol governs responses to gender-motivated incidents.

Legislative movement is under way. The PSOE parliamentary group registered a bill for real and effective equality of LGTBI+ people in Castilla y León on 20 December 2024, explicitly aimed at ending the "sexilio", the out-migration of LGBTI people from the region, and group leader Tudanca urged the fastest possible processing. On 11 June 2025 the Cortes de Castilla y León voted to take the bill into consideration; it runs to 76 articles and answers long-standing demands of regional LGBTI+ collectives. The PP abstained, Vox voted against, and LGBTI advocates fear the process could stall in committee.

Diario de Castilla y Leon (11 Jun 2025): the plenary approved taking the LGTBI equality bill into debate with opposition support except Vox and PP abstention; LGBTI advocates fear the process could stall in committee.

25490228B48808997991554.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Ceuta
25490228B48808997991554.summary:
Ceuta, an autonomous city of Spain, stands under the national framework rather than under any regional statute of its own. Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaces the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The law also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions. With administrative self-declaration, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Ceuta as elsewhere in Spain.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis. Courts are applying the aggravation in practice: a Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300; in Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied since 2005, and Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.

Ceuta has no regional LGTBI or gender-identity statute. The national index of autonomous-community LGTBI legislation states expressly that Ceuta and Melilla have no regional LGTBI statutes of their own and must instead apply the national equality framework and central-government policies. The gap is a statutory one: national criminal law and the national police operate in the city, so the enforcement floor available to a transgender visitor is the same as in the rest of the country.

FELGTBI+'s September 2025 radiography of LGTBI+ policy, prepared with the Universidad de Salamanca, records Asturias, Castilla y León, Ceuta and Melilla as the only Spanish territories still without a specific law on the promotion of LGTBI+ rights. A 2020 precedent study had placed Ceuta and Melilla at the tail of trans-student recognition and protection rankings. The report notes legislative progress in Castilla y León and Asturias in June 2025 and records no equivalent step for Ceuta or Melilla.

Ceuta's border-fence context shapes the environment for LGTBI people there. Europa Press reported on 17 September 2026 that the LGTBI+ association Arcópoli wrote by letter to the Secretary of State for Migration, Pilar Cancela, demanding the urgent transfer to the mainland of LGTBI+ migrants remaining in Ceuta after thousands entered irregularly on 30 and 31 July. Arcópoli called transfer the only effective measure to guarantee their protection and inclusion, cited the extreme vulnerability of people who flee criminalisation and persecution in countries including Morocco, and launched a free remote social, psychological and legal support service for those in Ceuta.

15666254B53975248776023.name: Kelantan
15666254B53975248776023.summary:
Kelantan stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

All 13 states of Malaysia and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintain Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences reach Muslims only. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed such enactments, and three of them also bar women from posing as men. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

Kelantan's own layer was rewritten after litigation narrowed it. In February 2024 the Federal Court struck down 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 on federalism grounds, leaving the federal Penal Code offences fully intact. In August 2026 the Kelantan state assembly passed the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026, replacing those 16 struck-down provisions. The Bill legislates covering of aurat, gender change, and safeguarding the modesty of private parts. Clause 15 mandates that Muslims safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law, and the state's legislative direction explicitly regulates gender-change matters under Islamic criminal law, with enforcement beginning 2026.

The new decency provisions are backed by whipping of three to six strokes, fines up to RM5,000 and imprisonment up to three years. The enactment is in force and is being applied by the Syariah courts. A case in February 2026 was the first Kelantan Syariah Court case involving gender change.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing and gender-change offences do not apply, but the federal Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, with detainees' faces and personal details leaked to pre-tipped media and 31 foreign nationals held among them before their embassies intervened.

Clause 15 mandates Muslims safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law. The state's legislative direction explicitly regulates gender-change matters under Islamic criminal law, with enforcement beginning 2026.

15666254B71460903090065.name: Terengganu
15666254B71460903090065.summary:
Terengganu is one of the 13 states of Malaysia and stands under the federal framework: sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with a maximum of 20 years plus whipping. Sodomy has been criminalised in Malaysian law since 1871. These provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens, so a foreign visitor in Terengganu is exposed to them on the same terms as a resident.

The state layer adds a second offence that reaches only Muslims. Every one of the 13 states, Terengganu included, maintains a Sharia enactment criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Enforcement sits with state Islamic religious departments, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing, which leaves the charge open-ended. A non-Muslim visitor falls outside this layer, but the police powers exercised alongside it do not.

Official messaging in Terengganu is openly hostile. In May 2025 a state executive councillor confirmed that warning signboards against homosexual practices, erected by the Kuala Terengganu City Council at strategic locations including near youth-frequented areas around a state university, were installed deliberately, and said the state wants people to consider such acts "dirty, wrong, and to be avoided". He described instilling hatred of homosexual acts as the point of the campaign.

The documented enforcement pattern against gender nonconformity is raid-based rather than individual. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022; media were pre-tipped, detainees' faces and personal details were leaked, and 31 foreign nationals were held among more than 130 people at one point before their embassies intervened. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, and police raided a second sauna in Penang days later. Queues, venues and any place where gender presentation is conspicuous carry the acute exposure risk for a visitor.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the practical position is that the Sharia cross-dressing offence does not apply, the Penal Code does, and enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon with tourists rarely targeted. The risk that materialises is public outing through an organised raid, and it is not backed by protective machinery: there is no anti-discrimination law, no same-sex marriage, and a transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months, in a case documented under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself" alongside police mistreatment and impunity.

For this record: official state-level endorsement of anti-homosexual messaging — a direct indicator of the hostile official stance a transgender visitor faces in Terengganu.

Thirteen civil-society organisations including Justice for Sisters (May 2025) urged the Kuala Terengganu City Council to remove anti-LGBT signboards, condemning them as discriminatory and a violation of international human rights law; they criticised the Terengganu state executive councillor's defence of the signboards as inciting hatred and discrimination against LGBTQ individuals. For this record: corroborates the official anti-LGBT campaign in Terengganu and documents civil-society pushback with named actors.

15666254B71428205180864.name: Kedah
15666254B71428205180864.summary:
Malaysia criminalises both same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at two levels, and Kedah stands under that national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Every one of the 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya additionally maintains a Sharia enactment criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those state offences reach Muslims only.

Kedah's own instrument is the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014). Section 26 criminalises a male posing as a woman in public, punishable by a fine of up to RM1,000 or up to one year's imprisonment. Female cross-dressing is not an offence under the enactment. Like the other state enactments, it contains no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing, leaving the scope of the offence to the enforcing officers.

The same Kedah enactment criminalises same-sex conduct between Muslims. Section 23 covers liwat (sodomy) and section 24 musahaqah (lesbian sex), each punishable by a fine of up to RM5,000, up to three years' imprisonment, up to six strokes of whipping, or any combination of those penalties. A woman convicted of musahaqah may additionally be committed to an approved home for up to six months under section 52.

Enforcement in Kedah has targeted transgender people as a category rather than as incidental participants. In October 2020 a private birthday party was raided and 30 transgender women were singled out from the gathering and arrested, while the event's organiser was separately investigated for "encouraging vice". A coalition of Malaysian human-rights groups publicly protested the investigation, identifying a pattern of punishing organisers and allies of transgender persons rather than only transgender people themselves.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the Kedah Sharia offences do not apply, but the federal Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented national pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.

65028918B28366581005022.name: West Java
65028918B28366581005022.summary:
West Java stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Sub-national variation sits inside that framework. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and those punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. West Java carries no equivalent religious-law regime, but its police act against LGBT gatherings regardless of whether an offence has occurred.

On 22 June 2025 the West Java Regional Police detained 75 people, 74 men and one woman, at a privately rented villa in the Puncak area of Bogor Regency after a tip from local residents. Police described the event as an LGBT "family gathering" held to avoid detection. Amnesty International reported the arrests on 24 June 2025, called the operation a discriminatory raid and a blatant violation of human rights and privacy, stated that the gathering violated no law, and demanded release and accountability. Tempo reported the arrests on 25–26 June 2025.

Street violence against trans women in West Java is documented and, so far, unprosecuted. Pelangi Nusantara recorded ten attacks on 45 victim-survivors in Bogor between 30 March and 15 July 2026, in which groups of 10–20 men punched, kicked and hurled stones, glass bottles and firecrackers at trans women, stripped some of them naked and filmed the assaults for social media under the account @bogorbersihlgbt ("Bogor clean of LGBT"). No alleged perpetrator has been publicly identified, arrested or prosecuted. A trans-rights activist who accompanied women filing police reports said officers accepted the case but worked on it half-heartedly, and some survivors were too afraid to report. ABC News reported on 15 August 2026 an attack in which men doused a trans woman with what looked like urine on a street in Bogor, one of a wave of attacks; a trans woman quoted in that report said those who previously appeared in public now live in fear.

Activists link the violence to a presidential regulation issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 that lists nonmilitary threats and classifies the "spread of LGBTQ culture" as a risk to be monitored and controlled within national defence policy, and to discriminatory regional regulations. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to the wave of vigilante attacks, with commentators quoted by ABC News stating that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy and that state language legitimises violence against trans women.

Trans travellers have died in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

65028918B4119458748300.name: West Sumatra
65028918B4119458748300.summary:
West Sumatra stands under the national framework of Indonesia. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and those punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. West Sumatra carries no equivalent provincial religious or criminal regime, and its restrictions on LGBT people are written as public-order and administrative measures by cities and regencies.

State and vigilante hostility frame the legal position. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and said the gathering violated no law. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in 2022, was told through his mother in Lima that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release, and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, while Indonesian police deny that violence was used. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists LGBTQ+ people among nonmilitary threats to be monitored and controlled under national defence policy, and reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women.

In West Sumatra, the clearest enacted local anti-LGBT bylaw outside Aceh is Bukittinggi City Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on public order. Articles 43-44 prescribe oral and written warnings, cessation of activities, social rehabilitation programmes, and administrative fines of Rp1,000,000 targeting LGBT people. An academic analysis of the regulation in the AHKAM journal reads it as a response to local religious values and Minangkabau customs, examined through Fiqih Siyasah Tanfidziyah.

Enforcement is real but contested. A 2026 field study of the Perda's implementation records supervision, enforcement and guidance by the local order force (Satpol PP), with sanctions judged of suboptimal effectiveness and rehabilitation hampered because the facilities barely exist. A 2025 study records people swept up in LGBT operations or identified through apps rising from 56 in 2023 to 272 in 2024.

The pattern is spreading to neighbouring regencies. On 13 May 2026 the DPRD of Limapuluh Kota regency finalised a draft anti-LGBT regional regulation (Ranperda) folded into a Public Order and Tranquility (Trantibum) regulation, carrying administrative fines and rehabilitation for LGBT people, with the drafting body's chair stating the stages had reached finalisation. Customary-law actors are pushing parallel measures, including a boarding-house barcode system and proposed nagari regulations on social deviance.

65028918B6690755070061.name: Bali
65028918B6690755070061.summary:
Bali stands under Indonesia's national framework, and that framework is where the legal risk sits. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted anywhere in Indonesia, that provision reaches consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Same-sex marriage remains unrecognised for visitors and residents alike.

The island's own environment is materially milder than the statute book. Travel guidance current to March 2026 describes a "live and let live" basis, records no criminal enforcement against foreign tourists, and names Seminyak (Eat Street and Batu Belig), Canggu and Ubud as the areas with the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly venues. Public displays of affection are advised for all couples as a matter of discretion rather than law. LGBTQ+ travel advisories rate Bali "Exercise Significant Caution," and the Gayborhood guide scores the destination 6.3 out of 10 with a legal score of 2.0, warning that visitors should keep affection quiet despite the tolerant reputation.

Bali has a directly documented death in custody of a trans traveller. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. His mother in Lima was told during a WhatsApp call that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy at national level now treats LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law; commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Bali also hosts a visible trans feminine (transpuan) community, documented in a 2025 peer-reviewed ethnography. The study records real precarity, misrecognition and discrimination alongside organised informal resistance, and rejects a simple victimhood narrative. Visitors should expect a socially tolerant surface operating on custom rather than legal protection.
