65028918B16658067687714.name: Papua
65028918B16658067687714.summary:
Papua stands under the national framework of Indonesia, a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, carry their own provisions against same-sex sexual activity, and in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025 under provincial religious law that reaches anyone present, including foreign visitors. Papua has no equivalent provincial criminal provision in the sourced record, but customary laws may apply alongside the national code.

Identity documents are a documented access point. Since June 2021 the Indonesian Ministry of Home Affairs has run an outreach programme issuing identity papers (KTP) to transgender Indonesians, and Papua is among the provinces where trans residents have received them, alongside Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi and Lampung. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, and the birth sex is printed unless a court order was obtained beforehand. A trans person in Papua may therefore hold correctly issued identity documents while remaining subject to the national framework that criminalises their relationships.

Official policy at national level frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes are codified into law; commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

The detention environment in Papua is documented and severe, though the evidence describes general-population risk rather than trans-specific targeting. A TAPOL briefing of July 2025 records 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military in Maybrat and the Central Highlands between September 2021 and the first quarter of 2025, with almost no consequences; deaths during torture are documented in the operation areas, and the incidents are catalogued on the 'Papuans Behind Bars' database. Victims were mostly males under 24, plus 7 women and 7 minors, and arrests were largely for alleged armed-group links or participation in demonstrations.

The Human Rights Monitor Papua Quarterly Report of 31 October 2025 records killings, arbitrary detentions, torture and arrests of protesters alongside the failure of accountability mechanisms as security forces expand across the territory, with a healthcare crisis under scrutiny. For a trans visitor, contact with security forces in the highland districts therefore carries a documented risk of arbitrary detention and mistreatment with little prospect of redress, and the surveillance and deployment environment raises the chance of being noticed and questioned.

65028918B17554737605304.name: South Sulawesi
65028918B17554737605304.summary:
South Sulawesi stands under Indonesia's national framework, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

A trans traveller died in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Within that framework, South Sulawesi is one of the eight provinces analysed in OutRight Action International's "Creeping Criminalisation" mapping, which documents how provincial and city bylaws criminalise same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity under regional autonomy.

Makassar has been a recurring site of an anti-LGBT bylaw push since at least early 2023, when the city's draft regulation entered the 2023 local legislative programme as a priority for discussion. Two DPRD Makassar members, including PKS-faction member Azwar ST, said the proposal models itself on Perda already passed elsewhere such as Bogor. Constitutional-law expert Bivitri Susanti called such drafts a trend ahead of the political year that risks worsening discrimination and persecution of LGBT people, and noted that the central government does little to stop discriminatory local regulations.

On 27 April 2025, Makassar mayor Munafri 'Appi' Arifuddin reaffirmed his commitment to pushing through an anti-LGBT Perda after a same-sex act at a night entertainment venue went viral. The deputy chair of the DPRD Makassar law-drafting body, Anwar Faruq, voiced support, saying such a regulation is urgently needed to preserve moral order and religious norms.

As of 25 April 2026, the local rule remains a draft (Ranperda) rather than an enacted regulation. The Makassar city government's women's-empowerment and child-protection agency (DP3A) is intensifying LGBT "prevention" through socialisation and education aimed at school-age children alongside case handling, with counselling and a safe house for reported individuals. DP3A head Ita Isdiana Anwar says most reports come from worried families; DPRD Kota Makassar member Muchlis Misbah, citing a Komisi D monitoring meeting showing rising LGBT numbers alongside HIV/AIDS cases, backs the pending Ranperda on HIV/AIDS and LGBT as legal reinforcement.

Available sources record no enacted Perda with specified penalties for South Sulawesi or Makassar, and no mass police raid or wave of violence against trans people documented in the province.

31927357B17004778023462.name: Aguascalientes
31927357B17004778023462.summary:
Aguascalientes stands under the national framework of Mexico. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009. The state's own record on trans-specific legal protection is thinner.

Legal gender recognition remains unfinished at national level and is administered state by state. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many Mexican states now operate administrative recognition procedures, while warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Its state-by-state survey of 11 March 2025 records specifically that Aguascalientes has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people, leaving the state without an administrative mechanism of its own. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

The consequences of non-reform are documented in detail elsewhere. Human Rights Watch's 6 March 2024 report found that delays and refusals of name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. The same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

A court route now exists in Aguascalientes despite the absence of legislative reform. In Amparo en Revisión 430/2025, decided in April 2026 on a project by Minister Giovanni Figueroa Mejía, Mexico's Supreme Court ruled that the requirements in the state's Civil Code for changing the gender marker on birth certificates - judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations - are discriminatory and violate privacy. The Court ordered the state's Civil Registry to grant recognition through a simple, confidential administrative procedure honouring self-perception, issuing a new birth certificate with no marginal notes revealing a prior gender. The ruling's immediate reach is limited to the persons represented by the civil association that filed the amparo, so the administrative route exists on paper without yet applying to the wider public.

Conversion therapy persists in the state despite being prohibited by law. La Jornada Aguascalientes reported on 23 August 2026 that Diversx Laboratorio Cultural Disidente activists Alicia Cruz, Kevin Cruz and Hened Musalem describe operations that continue under the guise of addiction-treatment annexes, and that a person who escaped one such space arrived at the group in the previous year. The same report states that trans women continue to suffer aggression motivated by prejudice. An ENDISEG survey shows that 7.3 percent of the state's population aged 15 and over self-identifies as LGBTI+, the fifth-highest proportion among Mexican states.

Transfemicide remains outside the state's criminal code. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that Mexico City's Congress had approved the Paola Buenrostro law, criminalising transfemicide, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. Aguascalientes belongs to the states that have not adopted comparable reforms. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a national total second only to Brazil's 100. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, prompting LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to prevent and punish violence against trans people, to investigate all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Formal rights and lived safety diverge. Caroline Beer's analysis for LSE USAPP, dated 22 November 2024, concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist on paper but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this is not evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

31927357B35339934753022.name: Baja California
31927357B35339934753022.summary:
Baja California is among the Mexican states that have legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The state congress created the procedure through a 2022 reform to the Civil Code, initially limited to adults. In June 2023 the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation invalidated the 18-years requirement, holding that the law failed to recognise the rights of transgender children and adolescents, and the state congress responded with a further reform in 2024 establishing a procedure for individuals under 18 and extending legal gender recognition to non-binary people.

No criminalisation of trans presence applies. The national framework, as Human Rights Watch set out on 31 March 2025, leaves legal gender recognition to the states and records a patchwork of procedures whose implementation differs sharply; where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation. Baja California sits on the reformed side of that divide.

The counterweight is lethal violence against women and the state's classification of it. The Baja California Attorney General's Office publicly identified Brayan Rivera as a serial perpetrator of feminicides; he was arrested in Downey, California in June 2023 and presented on 6 July 2023 before US Judge Karen L. Stevenson for provisional extradition detention, with probable cause determined on 29 June 2023. At a 7 July 2023 press conference the attorney general linked him to at least three killings in Tijuana: Ángela Carolina Acosta, killed 24 January 2022 in room 404 of the Hotel Cascadas in the city's tolerance zone, Elizabeth on 14 February, and Karen, 28, on 30 August 2021 at the Motel Hacienda Soler; extradition was then estimated at between 15 days and two years.

Under-counting is the pattern rather than the exception. Zeta Tijuana reported on 8 March 2025 that under Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila 1,179 women have been killed in the state while only 110 cases were typified as feminicide. Female economic participation in Baja California stands at roughly 46 to 47 per cent, ranking 14th of 32 states.

Mixed assessment: formal recognition law that now reaches adults, minors and non-binary people, alongside a border-city pattern of lethal violence against women that official statistics under-record.

31927357B33389180120223.name: Baja California Sur
31927357B33389180120223.summary:
Baja California Sur does not criminalise the presence of trans people. The state's elected congress created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition through a 2021 reform to the state Civil Code, and after the Supreme Court of Mexico ruled in June 2023 that excluding children and adolescents from that procedure was unconstitutional, the congress passed a further Civil Code reform in 2024 extending recognition to children, adolescents and non-binary people.

El Financiero reported on 27 June 2024 that the reform approved by the Baja California Sur congress allows minors to change their gender marker and chosen name on birth certificates, with the administrative process described as rapid, free and free of prejudice for trans and non-binary children. The XVI Legislature worked the bill to the terms of the June 2023 Supreme Court ruling that had struck down the adult-only limit.

No incident, prosecution or enforcement pattern specific to Baja California Sur appears in the audited sources. Visitor-facing risk therefore tracks the national baseline: no local legal hostility is documented, and the recognition procedure is resident-facing civil-registry machinery rather than a border, policing or screening control that a visitor would encounter on entry.

31927357B33389180120223.tangentialFactors:
Legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of Mexican equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's 32 states now operate administrative procedures, while warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another and calling on the states without such procedures to adopt them. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

The contrast with a non-reforming state is documented in detail. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that Tabasco has no recognition procedure, that the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gomez remained unsolved, that hate-motivation provisions are absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and that healthcare staff routinely out patients by calling their legal names. Delays and refusals leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

Lethal violence and impunity form the national backdrop. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that over 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, and that Mexico City's congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" on 18 July 2024, criminalising transfemicide with sentences of up to 70 years in one of the deadliest settings for trans people. The statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished.

AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, killings that drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100. Human Rights Watch also recorded a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Inter-American and academic assessments caution against reading statutes as safety. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

31927357B84428150771724.name: Campeche
31927357B84428150771724.summary:
Campeche stands under Mexico's national framework for legal gender recognition, which remains incomplete. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states now operate an administrative procedure for recognizing a person's gender in official documents, while warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another and calling on the remaining states to adopt such procedures.

Campeche's elected congress passed a 2024 reform to the Civil Code creating an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. A trans visitor or resident can therefore have identity documents aligned through an administrative route rather than through litigation, which is the single most consequential legal fact for anyone crossing borders or dealing with police, banking and health services on mismatched documents.

Where recognition is absent or obstructed, the consequences are documented. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" of 6 March 2024 found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, compounding discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

Violence against trans people is a standing national risk. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, killings that prompted LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100. The same period saw a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap. Mexico City's congress passed the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide with a sentence of up to 70 years, making it the second of Mexico's 32 states to do so. The statute is named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and it obliges the attorney-general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community.

Inter-American authorities have pressed the same point. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged Mexican federal and state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

The gap between statute and practice is the recurring finding. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP of 22 November 2024 concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis explicitly cautions that it must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

31927357B65177449444732.name: Chiapas
31927357B65177449444732.summary:
Chiapas operates within Mexico's national legal framework, and no Chiapas statute criminalises or restricts the presence, conduct or dress of trans visitors. A trans traveller to Chiapas commits no trans-specific offence under local law.

Legal gender recognition is the decisive legal gap. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state assessment of 31 March 2025 records that 22 of Mexico's 32 states now operate an administrative procedure for changing name and gender marker on identity documents. Chiapas is not among them; the state had created no such procedure as of March 2025.

The practical consequence for a trans visitor is an identity document that cannot be corrected locally. Where an administrative route does not exist, recognition is available only through the courts, case by case, on a timeline that no short visit can accommodate. Trans people entering Chiapas on documents that do not match their presentation should expect the document mismatch to resurface in routine contacts: checkpoint questioning, hotel and bank registration, pharmacy and clinic visits.

Human Rights Watch documented the surrounding pattern in Tabasco, Chiapas's neighbouring state, in a report of 6 March 2024. In the absence of a recognition procedure there, trans residents face discrimination in employment, health care, education and financial transactions; hospital staff called out interviewees' legal names over waiting-room public-address systems; and the state had no hate-motivation provisions in its criminal code. The report also recorded murders and violence against trans people in Tabasco, including an unsolved killing of a trans activist, and urged the adoption of a simple self-identification procedure. These findings concern Tabasco, not Chiapas, and indicate what document mismatch produces in a state with the same statutory absence.

At national level, protection against the gravest violence remains limited. Mexico City's legislature approved the Paola Buenrostro law in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide with a penalty of up to 70 years' imprisonment; the law takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose killing was never punished, and it obliges the attorney-general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community. Mexico City was only the second of the 32 states to create such an offence, which means Chiapas has no transfemicide statute documented in these sources.

31927357B49801195703560.name: Chihuahua
31927357B49801195703560.summary:
Chihuahua grants legal gender recognition through an administrative procedure run by the state Civil Registry rather than through a statute of its own. The Supreme Court struck down the civil code's requirement of a judicial process in 2019, and the registry has conducted administrative recognitions on that basis since. As of March 2025 the Chihuahua state legislature had enacted no recognition reform.

Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states operate an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure, placing Chihuahua among the majority in practice while remaining outside the group that has codified recognition in state law. Implementation still differs sharply from state to state, so a visitor moving between jurisdictions may meet a different procedure, or none at all.

Partnership recognition is settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised in Chihuahua, and no hostile state or municipal ordinance appears in the sources behind this record.

No incident series specific to Chihuahua is documented here. What a trans visitor should expect in practice rests on the national backdrop, where killings of trans people continue, where delays and refusals in identity-document recognition leave people carrying papers that contradict their lived identity, and where official studies find that progressive legislation is seldom enforced evenly.

31927357B49801195703560.tangentialFactors:
One state legislature has moved to close a gap that Chihuahua has not addressed. Mexico City's Congress approved the Paola Buenrostro law on 24 July 2024, making transfemicide punishable by up to 70 years and making Mexico the second of the country's 32 states to criminalise it. The statute is named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 and obliges the attorney-general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBT community.

Violence against trans people intensified nationally over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, killings that prompted street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI defenders rose across the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Document barriers carry their own violence risk. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents with documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, and set those barriers against killings including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Inter-American authorities have pressed the same point. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that LGBT violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

The distance between statute and practice is the recurring finding. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBT legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this work must not be read as evidence that LGBT people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

31927357B32124965101143.name: Coahuila de Zaragoza
31927357B32124965101143.summary:
Coahuila de Zaragoza stands under the national framework of Mexico, where Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that most states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition while warning that implementation differs sharply between them, and where same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009.

Coahuila is one of the states that has legislated. The 2018 Law on the Civil Registry of the State of Coahuila, articles 124 to 128, established an administrative procedure for recognition of self-identified gender identity; the Human Rights Watch state-by-state tracker of March 2025 records it among the 32 states with such a procedure and links the official gazette text of the reform. The bill reached the plenary of the Congress of Coahuila through proposals from several parliamentary groups and an initiative by former governor Rubén Moreira, and the dictamen was approved unanimously. It reformed article 133 of the Ley para la Familia de Coahuila de Zaragoza and created the Civil Registry law, whose article 2, fraction XI, defines gender identity as the personal and internal conviction.

The procedure is in working use. Ricardo Malacara, director of Coahuila's Civil Registry, stated in March 2023 that roughly 1,500 people had completed the legal gender-identity change before the Civil Registry from early 2019 to March 2023, in both directions, male to female and female to male.

Recognition on paper does not settle the wider risk environment. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, second only to Brazil's 100; a Guardian report of 24 July 2024 states that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022. On 18 July 2024 the legislature of Mexico City made transfemicide a crime carrying sentences of up to 70 years under the Paola Buenrostro law, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to prevent and punish violence against trans people, to investigate LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP of 22 November 2024 concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence. No Coahuila-specific incident or enforcement pattern appears in the sources assembled here, so visitor-facing risk in the state tracks the national baseline rather than a documented local pattern.

31927357B75771156097737.name: Colima
31927357B75771156097737.summary:
Colima is a state of Mexico, and its trans-visitor exposure is set by Mexico's national framework rather than by any local statute identified in the sources reviewed. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised anywhere in the country, and same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction. Nothing in the inventory indicates that Colima has enacted a law targeting trans presence.

Legal gender recognition remains a state-by-state question. The Human Rights Watch report of 31 March 2025 counted, as of March 2025, 22 of Mexico's 32 states that had legislated an administrative procedure, two further states that operate a procedure in practice without having enacted one, six legislatures that have enacted nothing at all, and only seven states that extend recognition to minors. The Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation set binding guidelines for the states in 2022 and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. HRW has called on the states that still lack such procedures to adopt them, and warned that implementation differs sharply from one state to another.

Whether Colima has enacted an administrative recognition procedure, and whether it extends recognition to children, is not established in the material reviewed here. The operative point for a visitor is the national picture: where a state procedure is absent, HRW documents that identity-document mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco.

What an absent procedure means on the ground is set out in the joint HRW and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024, produced from Tabasco, one of the states with no legal gender-recognition procedure. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, the report finds that every document request and every appearance-based scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and that trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. The account is Tabasco's, and the sources reviewed do not carry a parallel study of Colima, but the same procedural vacuum is what a trans visitor without matching documents should expect to encounter wherever Colima's own procedure is missing.

The enforcement backdrop is severe. More than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished in 2022, and impunity for transfemicide is thought to be higher still. Transgender Europe's monitoring counts 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100 in the same period. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. In January 2024, AP reported at least three transgender people killed in the opening weeks of the year, among them the activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.

Transfemicide has begun to be treated as a distinct crime, but only in some states. Nayarit criminalised it first, with penalties up to 60 years, and Mexico City's Congress passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' in July 2024, punishable by up to 70 years; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. Colima's legislature has not been shown in the sources reviewed to have enacted a comparable offence.

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP of 22 November 2024 concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

31927357B33104012885361.name: Guanajuato
31927357B33104012885361.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Mexico is determined state by state, and Guanajuato sits inside that mosaic rather than under a single national statute. As of March 2025, Human Rights Watch counted 22 of the country's 32 states with a legislated administrative recognition procedure, two further states operating one in practice without enactment, six state legislatures that have enacted nothing, and only seven states extending recognition to children. The Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation set binding guidelines for the states in 2022 and extended the right to minors that year, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure. The sources for this record do not state whether Guanajuato's own legislature has enacted such a procedure.

What the sources do place in Guanajuato is documented harm. Human Rights Watch records incidents in the state where a mismatch between identity documents and a trans person's lived gender drove discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market. A visitor should therefore expect document scrutiny at encounters with institutions to be the operative risk, irrespective of whether a recognition procedure exists on paper.

The consequences of an absent or obstructive procedure are set out concretely in the March 2024 Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report on Tabasco, a Mexican state with no legal gender-recognition procedure. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance under scrutiny carries a risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. That report was published alongside the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gómez in Villahermosa, and against a national backdrop in which more than 95% of homicides went unpunished in 2022.

Lethality and impunity frame the wider environment. Transfemicide has been criminalised in only two of Mexico's 32 states: Nayarit, with sentences of up to 60 years, and Mexico City, whose "Paola Buenrostro law" of July 2024 provides up to 70 years. Impunity for transfemicide is thought to run higher than the already extreme national homicide figure. Partnership recognition, by contrast, is settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009.

31927357B33104012885361.tangentialFactors:
The national pattern is uneven rather than uniform, and Guanajuato's position within it is only partly sourced. Six state legislatures have enacted no recognition procedure at all, two operate one administratively without legislation, and recognition of children reaches just seven states. Human Rights Watch called on the states without procedures to adopt them on 31 March 2025 and warned that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, so that identical statutory language can produce very different encounters with a registry office or a clinic.

Tabasco serves as the clearest comparator for what legal silence produces: a March 2024 report documents trans residents there carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, with knock-on effects in banking, health care and dealings with police, in a state where a trans woman was found dead in August 2023. Nayarit and Mexico City sit at the other end of the spectrum as the only two states to have created a transfemicide offence, Mexico City legislating in July 2024 after the 2016 murder of Paola Buenrostro, whose case remains unpunished.

Supranational and federal pressure continues on the same axis. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to strengthen prevention and punishment of violence against trans people, demanded that LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) reaches a compatible conclusion: progressive LGBTQ+ legislation in Mexico is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and the analysis cautions that its findings must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence.

31927357B20618267715210.name: Guerrero
31927357B20618267715210.summary:
Guerrero stands under Mexico's national framework on legal gender recognition, and that framework is the only documented layer for this record. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that recognition is set state by state: 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated an administrative procedure, two more operated one in practice without enactment, six state legislatures had enacted nothing, and only seven states extended recognition to children.

Two higher authorities constrain what the states may do. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states in 2022 and extended the right to minors in the same year, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where a state has not enacted its own procedure, this national framework governs the visitor's expectations.

Human Rights Watch documents the practical consequence of an absent procedure: identity-document mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. Neither of those states is Guerrero, and no Guerrero-specific statute, court ruling or incident record is supported by the vetted sources.

The Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024, examining a Mexican state with no recognition procedure, found that without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request and every appearance under scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation. Trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions as a result. The report's context includes the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and the finding that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.

For a trans visitor, the practical read is that entry into Guerrero means relying on a patchwork: documents issued in a state with a procedure travel with the holder, while local administrative capacity in Guerrero itself is not documented here.

31927357B65869129959700.name: Jalisco
31927357B65869129959700.summary:
Jalisco stands within Mexico's national framework, where legal gender recognition is established state by state rather than by a single country-wide statute. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of the country's 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, that two more operate one in practice without legislative enactment, that six state legislatures have enacted none, and that only seven states extend recognition to children. The sources do not resolve which of those categories covers Jalisco itself.

The parent framework also carries binding judicial and inter-American requirements. In 2022 the Supreme Court of Justice of Mexico set guidelines binding on the states and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where no procedure exists, Human Rights Watch documents identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in the states of Guanajuato and Tabasco.

Tabasco, which has no recognition procedure, supplies the concrete picture of what statutory silence produces. A Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024 found that without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance under scrutiny carries a risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and that trans people are shut out of employment, health services, education and financial transactions. The same reporting context includes the murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa in August 2023 and the finding that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.

The formal existence of rights does not reliably translate into equal treatment. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP, published 22 November 2024, concludes that progressive LGBTQ+ legislation in the country is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, and cautions explicitly that the analysis must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

No Jalisco-specific statute, legislative vote, lethality figure or incident record is supported by the sources for this jurisdiction. A visitor should therefore expect the country-wide pattern rather than verified local protections or verified local hostility, and should treat Jalisco's position on recognition as unresolved rather than favourable or adverse.

31927357B41082348713023.name: Mexico
31927357B41082348713023.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Mexico is a state-by-state matter, not a settled national guarantee. As of March 2025 the Human Rights Watch counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states with legislated administrative recognition procedures, two additional states operating a procedure in practice without legislative enactment, and six state legislatures that have enacted none at all. Only seven states extend recognition to children and adolescents.

Supreme Court guidelines bind the states, and in 2022 the Court extended the right to minors; the Inter-American Court of Human Rights likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure for legal gender recognition. In practice, however, the framework operates unevenly, and where no procedure exists, trans people are left carrying identity documents that contradict their lived gender.

The consequences of document mismatch are documented concretely. The Human Rights Watch report of 6 March 2024, produced with a community inclusion organisation, examined a Mexican state with no recognition procedure and found that every document request or appearance check risks violence, harassment and humiliation, and that trans people are pushed out of employment, health services, education and financial transactions. Identity-document mismatch also drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and in Tabasco.

Violence accompanies the administrative gap. In Tabasco, where the law is silent, the Aug 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa is one of the killings set against more than 95% of homicides nationally going unpunished in 2022. A separate trans woman was found dead in the Carrizal River in Aug 2023, and the wider record includes an Aug 2023 killing of a trans woman in the Carrizal River.

Reported attacks intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in Jan 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in Jun 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Some legislatures have begun to close the specific legal gap. Mexico City's Congress approved the Paola Buenrostro law in Jul 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety.

Inter-American authorities have pressed the same point. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to strengthen efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Partnership recognition is settled at national level: same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

For a visitor, the operative expectation is the national mosaic of recognition procedures rather than any single verified local regime. Caroline Beer's analysis for LSE USAPP of 22 Nov 2024 concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and the analysis explicitly cautions that it must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

31927357B72315499763974.name: Morelos
31927357B72315499763974.summary:
Morelos is a state of Mexico, and the sources vetted for this record carry no Morelos-specific statute, enforcement incident or lethality figure. The operative framework is national. Mexico legislates legal gender recognition state by state, and the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation has set binding guidelines for the states, extending the right to minors in 2022; the Inter-American Court of Human Rights likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure. Human Rights Watch warned on 31 March 2025 that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

As of March 2025, Human Rights Watch counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states with a legislated administrative recognition procedure, two more states operating one in practice without enactment, and six state legislatures that had enacted nothing. Only seven states extend recognition to children. Where no procedure exists, mismatched identity documents drive discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents documented in Guanajuato and Tabasco. A visitor to Morelos is therefore measured against this national position rather than against any locally enacted guarantee.

What legal silence costs on the ground is set out in the Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024, which examined a Mexican state without a recognition procedure. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance that draws scrutiny carries a risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. The reporting period covers the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gómez in Villahermosa, in a country where more than 95% of homicides went unpunished in 2022.

Delays and refusals in name and gender recognition leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. Set against that, transfeminicide has become a criminal category in some state statutes: Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

31927357B15886886594254.name: Nayarit
31927357B15886886594254.summary:
Nayarit stands within Mexico's federal legal framework, and the national picture is uneven. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states have legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, that eight have none, and that two recognise recognition in practice without legislation; the same document records 2019 national Supreme Court guidelines on the subject and notes that only seven states extend recognition to children.

Nayarit is among the states with a statutory route. A 2017 reform of the state Civil Code established an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, allowing adults to change identity documents to match their gender identity. A trans visitor whose documents were issued in Nayarit therefore has a recognition route on the books; the inventory does not document how that procedure is applied in practice, and Human Rights Watch has warned nationally that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Nayarit was the first of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfeminicide, introducing sentences of up to 60 years in early 2024. Mexico City followed in July 2024 as the second, with sentences of up to 70 years under the Paola Buenrostro law, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. The Nayarit statute also allows friends, not only relatives, to identify and claim bodies and to drive investigations, a provision with direct bearing where families disown trans relatives.

The weight to give that statute is limited by the enforcement environment it sits in. In 2022 more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished, and the figure is believed to be higher for transfeminicides. The law records official posture more than proven protection, and Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP on 22 November 2024 reaches the same conclusion at national level: Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and the analysis cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Violence against trans people in Mexico is documented at scale. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months.

Partnership recognition is settled at national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

31927357B98648037880103.name: Queretaro de Arteaga
31927357B98648037880103.summary:
Querétaro de Arteaga stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure, and its state-by-state table lists Querétaro among the six states that have never legislated any such procedure. A trans visitor to Querétaro therefore has no local administrative route to align identity documents with lived identity; the papers carried on arrival are the only identification available, and they cannot be corrected there.

Where recognition is absent, mismatched documents are the documented exposure. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, and it presents Tabasco as the clearest case among the six states whose legislatures still refuse any procedure. The same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Querétaro's Penal Code cuts the other way on one specific point. The reform prohibiting Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual y la Identidad de Género (ECOSIG), commonly called conversion therapies, was published and is in force as of reporting on 20 September 2023, and it sets two to six years' imprisonment, a fine of 20 to 2,000 times the UMA and 50 to 100 hours of community service, treating such practices as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture.

31927357B22618747134228.name: San Luis Potosi
31927357B22618747134228.summary:
San Luis Potosí stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains unevenly implemented. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date, and set out a per-state compliance picture showing that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

San Luis Potosí is among the states that have acted. The state began authorising legal gender changes for transgender people on 17 May 2019, following a 2019 reform of the Civil Registry Law that created an administrative recognition procedure with implementing regulations issued by gubernatorial decree. The state is listed among the states that enacted a gender-identity law in 2019.

Partnership recognition is settled here as well. Same-sex marriage took effect in San Luis Potosí on 21 May 2019, after the state Congress voted 14-12 in favour on 16 May 2019, and joint adoption by same-sex couples has been legal in the state from the same month. Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

The state's hate-crime statutes recognise motivation by gender and sexual preference, which gives trans victims a route to aggravated treatment of an attack. Its local anti-discrimination law bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender but does not name gender identity, leaving a gap in the statutory protection a trans visitor would be able to invoke.

The distance between statute and practice is the recurring national finding. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions explicitly that the work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Violence against trans people is documented at national scale. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, killings that drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Two official responses frame what a trans visitor can expect from authorities. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide, a statute named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished and which activists describe as critical to their sense of safety. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

No region-specific incident, enforcement or ordinance evidence was found for San Luis Potosí, and no border-screening or document-procedure information specific to the state is recorded.

31927357B37261891092938.name: Sonora
31927357B37261891092938.summary:
Sonora is a state of Mexico and stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date, named six legislatures that had enacted none, and warned that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Sonora sits on the recognised side of that divide. The Hermosillo-based daily El Sol de Hermosillo reported on 1 October 2020 that Sonora's Congress approved the state's Gender Identity Law (Ley de Identidad de Género), under which people who identify with the opposite gender can modify their official documentation. The statute is one of the procedures counted in the Human Rights Watch finding that 22 of 32 states have enacted such laws.

Two further protections sit in Sonora's statute book. Sonora's Congress banned conversion therapies (ECOSIG) on 6 December 2022, and the state's hate-crime laws recognize motivation by gender and sexual preference. Sonora also ratified the 2011 constitutional amendment prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

Partner recognition raises no legal barrier here. By 31 December 2022 every Mexican state, including Sonora, had legalized same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling; nationally the institution has been open to same-sex couples since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

The protective reading for a visitor rests on statutes rather than on enforcement evidence. No Sonora-specific incident or enforcement pattern is documented, and no verified local hostility is recorded either.

Violence against trans people across Mexico intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, killings that drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Impunity and uneven enforcement are the recurring findings at national level. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Gaps elsewhere in the country show what the absence of a procedure means in practice. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

31927357B81008000569871.name: Tabasco
31927357B81008000569871.summary:
Extending legal gender recognition to trans people remains the central unfinished task of Mexican equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's states now operate administrative procedures for recognition, while warning that implementation differs sharply between them and calling on the states without procedures to adopt one. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Tabasco is among the states that have not reformed. Human Rights Watch records that Tabasco has no legal gender recognition procedure, placing it among eight states with none; two further states handle recognition in practice only, without a procedure in law. The direct consequence is a permanent documentary mismatch: because no route to recognition exists, trans people's identity documents never correspond to their gender.

The Tabasco finding is documented on the ground in the Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" of 6 March 2024, produced with a local community centre for inclusion. That report found that the absence of recognition curtails trans residents' rights across four socio-economic areas, and that mismatched identity documents invite police stops and institutional mistreatment. For a visible trans visitor the mismatch is the operative trigger: an ID that contradicts presentation is what draws the questioning and mistreatment the report records.

Violence against trans people in Tabasco is documented with a specific case. The March 2024 report records the murder of Karina Gómez, a trans woman, in Tabasco in August 2023. Nationally, AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, killings that drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety. Tabasco has enacted no equivalent measure.

Inter-American authorities have pressed the same point. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

The gap between statute and practice is the recurring finding. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction. No border-screening or entry-document information specific to Tabasco is recorded in the available material.

31927357B88239390016047.name: Tamaulipas
31927357B88239390016047.summary:
Tamaulipas stands within Mexico's national equality framework, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, naming six whose legislatures had enacted none, and warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

For a visitor, Tamaulipas is a no-recognition jurisdiction. The Human Rights Watch state-by-state table of 31 March 2025 records that Tamaulipas has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people, placing it among the eight Mexican states with no procedure, against 22 of 32 that have legislated one; two further states have a procedure in practice only. A trans person whose documents are issued in Tamaulipas has no administrative route to change identity documents to match their gender identity, so the papers the visitor presents to police, banks and clinics will carry a marker that contradicts their presentation.

Criminal law in Tamaulipas moves in the opposite direction. On 18 June 2025 the state Congress unanimously approved reforms to the local Penal Code adding a chapter covering crimes against sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression, and explicitly banning 'conversion therapies'. The chapter carries prison terms of two to six years and fines of up to 2,000 times the local measurement unit, with penalties rising by half where victims are minors, disabled or elderly, or where the conduct occurs in subordinate settings such as family, medical or workplace environments.

As of early 2026 the recognition gap remains open. On 4 February 2026 deputies of Tamaulipas's 66th legislature and LGBT+ civil-society groups agreed a joint agenda to push a Gender Identity Law together with anti-discrimination and health reforms, noting that the initiatives have been pending since June 2025 and that the absent law continues to limit trans people's access to health care, education and employment.

Violence risk follows the national pattern. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, killings that drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Protection machinery exists but is unevenly applied. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

31927357B22008724034476.name: Tlaxcala
31927357B22008724034476.summary:
Tlaxcala stands under Mexico's national framework and adds its own statute on top of it. The state congress's 2019 reform of the Civil Code (Decree D.113, dated 1 October 2019) created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, and the decree text is published on the state congress's own site. The procedure requires no court proceeding, which is the legal basis a trans visitor would rely on to update identity documents in Tlaxcala.

Layered over that, the national Supreme Court's ruling of 17 October 2018 makes a change of name and gender marker available through a simple administrative procedure founded on self-declaration. Document correction therefore does not depend on a judge's approval, on medical evidence, or on a surgical prerequisite.

Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date, and named six whose legislatures had enacted none; Tabasco and Tamaulipas are among them. Tlaxcala falls on the covered side of that divide, but the same reporting warns that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, so a procedure on the books does not by itself establish that a given office will process a request promptly.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since the final states completed legalisation in 2022. Federal law has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2003, a protection that reaches services a visitor uses, from banking to health care.

The sources assembled for this jurisdiction record no Tlaxcala-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern directed at transgender people; the operative rules for a visitor are the state's 2019 decree, the national self-declaration ruling and the federal anti-discrimination statute.

31927357B35199150741361.name: Yucatan
31927357B35199150741361.summary:
Yucatán operates an administrative route to legal gender recognition. A 2024 reform to the state's Civil Registry Law, published in the Diario Oficial of 26 April 2024, created a procedure through which transgender people can update legal gender on identity documents without a court order. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state rundown of March 2025 carries Yucatán on that basis, and the procedure is the fact a trans visitor's document situation turns on when entering or being stopped in the state.

Yucatán sits within the majority of Mexican states that have legislated recognition. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had enacted a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date, and named six states whose legislatures had enacted none. Yucatán is among the 22, not the six.

Marriage equality is settled and has been for a decade. The Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled on 1 July 2013 that two petitioners were able to marry, and the first same-sex couple legally married in the state on 8 August 2013. The Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015, and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán then passed a constitutional amendment permitting same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022.

A ban on conversion therapy has been in effect in Yucatán since 25 August 2021, adopted as a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) prohibition and operating alongside the equivalent ban enacted in Mexico City on 31 July 2020 and in other states. At federal level, same-sex acts have been decriminalised since 1871, and same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009.

31927357B22408340646138.name: Zacatecas
31927357B22408340646138.summary:
Zacatecas operates a legislated route to legal gender recognition. On 23 December 2022 deputies of the state's 64th Legislature approved a reform of the Family Code of Zacatecas on gender identity by 14 votes to 7, after the Justice Committee had issued a positive opinion, establishing the possibility of issuing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity, principally for the trans community.

Human Rights Watch's March 2025 state-by-state feature records the same reform as an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, and adds that in 2023 the director of the state Civil Registry issued guidelines implementing the law; both entries link to the official state gazette. In the Human Rights Watch count of 31 March 2025, 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure, and six had enacted none — Zacatecas is not among the states lacking one.

A protective criminal-law floor applies in the state. On 25 August 2021 the Congress of Zacatecas approved a ban on conversion therapies, or ECOSIG (Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género), by adding fraction VI to article 182 Bis of the state Penal Code, penalising with one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work anyone who incites hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or who promotes such practices. The same session typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity in the state Penal Code.

The document route arrived later than the protective criminal law: the gender-identity initiative debated alongside the 2021 session, which proposed constitutional and Family Code reform, failed to obtain enough votes and remained pending at that time, passing only in December 2022.

Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure and named six whose legislatures had enacted none, while warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another; where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.
