Human Rights Watch's report of 6 March 2024 found that in Tabasco, name and gender recognition delays leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

Violence risk is a standing national concern. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, second only to Brazil's 100. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to prevent and punish violence against trans people and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence. 82249235B96958463903898.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
82249235B96958463903898.summary:
Newfoundland and Labrador stands under the Canadian national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No Canadian jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities. Entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers, and identity documents issued federally can carry an X marker. Healthcare coverage is universal.

Provincial document law is permissive on its face. An amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009, given Royal Assent 13 April 2016, removed the requirement to undergo sex-reassignment surgery before the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration could be changed. The amendment brought provincial law into compliance with an order of a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission, issued in December 2015 on complaints brought by two trans women, and it responded to requests from LGBTQ advocates. The province has therefore operated a surgery-free gender-marker change on provincial records since 2016.

A second amendment, given Royal Assent 23 June 2021 after second reading on 17 June 2021, opened the same route to residents of the province who were not born there, on condition of at least three months' residence. The Government of Newfoundland and Labrador stated that the resulting change certificate carries a $25 fee, counts as official provincial identification, and could be leveraged by the applicant to update records in other jurisdictions, serving as the identification document for people born outside the country. The release also states that the amendments align with earlier changes allowing a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates.

The current official guidance sets the operative conditions: applicants must be 16 or older, or be represented by a parent or legal guardian, with consent of the other parent or guardian for under-16s and written consent of individuals aged 12 to 15, and must have been born in the province or have resided there at least three months. No fee is charged for the change application itself; charges apply only to official copies of the updated documents, at $35 for a new birth certificate or $30 online. The province states that it cannot guarantee a birth certificate bearing an X gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations.

The documented risk signals for a visitor remain weak. Statistics Canada recorded 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents nationally in 2024, up 1% after a 34% jump in 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Newfoundland and Labrador recorded the joint-lowest provincial rate at 5.3 per 100,000, alongside Manitoba, while Ontario recorded the highest at 16.0. The province's 51% rise reflects a move from 19 incidents in 2023 to 29 in 2024, absolute numbers small enough that the rate change is statistically fragile.

Residents of Newfoundland and Labrador change the sex designation on provincial records through the Vital Statistics Act, 2009. Since the 2016 amendment no surgery is required, and since the 2021 amendment the route is available to anyone who has lived in the province for at least three months even if they were born elsewhere. Applications are made for a person aged 16 or over, or through a parent or legal guardian for younger applicants, with the other parent's or guardian's consent and written consent from individuals aged 12 to 15.

The application itself carries no fee under the current official page; charges apply only to official copies of the updated documents, $35 for a new birth certificate or $30 if ordered online. A 2021 government release described a $25 fee for the change certificate. Provincial birth certificates can carry a non-binary X marker, and the province warns that it cannot guarantee that marker will be accepted by other organisations. The change certificate counts as official provincial identification and can be used to update records held elsewhere, including as identification for people born outside the country.

Healthcare coverage is universal under the Canadian framework, and discrimination complaints concerning gender identity or expression have a defined route through the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-motivation provisions.

82249235B3191732862561.name: Prince Edward Island
82249235B3191732862561.summary:
Prince Edward Island stands under the Canadian national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, and entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.

Legal gender recognition in Prince Edward Island carries no surgery requirement. The 2016 amendment to the Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement, replacing it with a declaration of the gender the applicant identifies with supported by a letter from a doctor.

Provincial photo ID can carry an X or a blank gender marker. Since 4 December 2018, Islanders identifying gender on a driver's licence at Access PEI have been able to select "gender not listed" (shown as X) or "prefer not to say" (left blank) alongside male and female, and Prince Edward Island was the first jurisdiction in Canada to offer the blank option.

The formal change of gender designation is restricted to residents. An applicant must have been born in Prince Edward Island and lived in the province for at least three months and must not be in the lawful custody of another person, so a short-term visitor cannot use this route. A legal custodian may apply for a minor under 18 born in the province with at least three months' residence, with written consent of any other custodian or parent and of the child if aged 12 or older. Applications require completed forms including a physician statement and a written statement by the applicant, with signatures arranged before a commissioner of oaths at Vital Statistics.

Healthcare coverage is universal, and discrimination complaints have a defined route: complaints on grounds of gender identity and gender expression are handled under provincial human-rights legislation, and federally under the Canadian Human Rights Act.

Detention is the weakest part of the framework. Since Bill C-16, federal correctional policy requires transgender prisoners to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery; both placement and gender-affirming treatment have been contested in court.

The wider climate is the main caution. Statistics Canada recorded 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents nationally in 2024, up 1% on 2023, at a rate of 12.1 per 100,000 population, down 2% over the year and up 142% since 2018, with eight provinces recording stable or declining rates. Police-reported hate crime has risen for six consecutive years and is up 169% since 2018, with offences motivated by gender identity and gender expression among the fastest-growing categories, and Egale Canada documents an increasingly organised anti-trans movement. The Statistics Canada release of 30 March 2026 reports no Prince Edward Island-specific rate or incident count, and no provincially deviating pattern is documented for the province.

The release reports no Prince Edward Island-specific rate or incident count, and no provincially deviating pattern is documented for the province. sources.title: P.E.I. transgender community applauds ID changes (CBC News)
sources.summary: CBC News, 18 April 2016, reports that the MacLauchlan government tabled a bill to amend the Vital Statistics Act so Islanders can change their gender on official documents by declaring the gender they identify with plus a letter from a doctor, with sex-reassignment surgery no longer required; Pride P.E.I. board member Jesse Macmillan welcomed the move, noting surgery is expensive and the closest provider was in Montreal, and called for a future third gender category, adding that many of his friends in Charlottetown identify outside the binary; a linked item on the article page reports Health PEI would cover the costs of three surgeries for transgender patients. PEI's gender-marker change on provincial documents has worked without a surgery requirement since the 2016 amendment.

82249235B52639524229375.name: Quebec
82249235B52639524229375.summary:
Quebec stands under the national framework of Canada, where gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. No jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, federal identity documents can carry an X marker, and Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers, so entry carries no trans-specific friction.

Provincial law adds a second layer of protection. Quebec's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms has listed gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds of discrimination since 2016, and the enforcement machinery produces results: on 10 June 2024 the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal found that a Montreal bar had discriminated against a trans woman in hiring, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training.

Identity documentation in the province was reshaped by litigation. After a two-month trial heard 29 witnesses, the Quebec Superior Court declared provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people (2021 QCCS 191). The Quebec Court of Appeal largely upheld that decision (2024 QCCA 348), and the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code governing sex designation.

Correctional placement is where the provincial record runs against the protective pattern. On 19 June 2025 Quebec's public security minister announced that transgender inmates in the province would be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety, in a directive issued just after trans woman Levana Ballouz sought a transfer to a women's prison. Advocates say the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. The directive governs detention rather than travel, but it is dated, province-specific evidence of official policy reversing the prior practice of considering gender identity in placement.

The wider climate is measured in police-reported hate crime. Statistics Canada's release of 30 March 2026 on 2024 data counts 4,882 incidents nationally, up 1% on 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, which fell 2% in 2024 and has risen 142% since 2018. Provincial rates spanned 5.3 to 16.0 per 100,000, with eight provinces stable or declining. The release carries no Quebec-specific rate figure, so the assessment of exposure in this province rests on the national series rather than a provincial number.

No Quebec-specific rate figure appears in the release windows, so it supports the record's national-parity assessment. Federal criminal law and the federal human-rights framework apply uniformly in Quebec.

82249235B66370767641120.name: Ontario
82249235B66370767641120.summary:
Ontario stands under the national framework of Canada, one of the safest large destinations for trans visitors. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, and no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities. Entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers, and federal identity documents can carry an X marker.

Provincially the floor is explicit. The Ontario Human Rights Code expressly covers gender identity and gender expression, and the Ontario Human Rights Commission's policy on those grounds states that people are protected from discrimination and harassment in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations. The policy defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender and notes that a chosen name and a pronoun are common ways of expressing it. That is the formal protection a visiting trans person holds in Ontario's workplaces, housing and services, with a defined route for complaints.

Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Most provinces allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender, and Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement, replacing it with a declaration supported by a letter from a doctor. Healthcare coverage is universal.

The risk signal is violence rather than law. Statistics Canada recorded 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents nationally in 2024, up 1% after a 34% jump the year before, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Ontario recorded the highest provincial rate at 16.0 incidents per 100,000 population, above the national figure. Across the longer arc, police-reported hate crime has risen for six consecutive years and is up 169% since 2018, with offences motivated by gender identity and gender expression among the fastest-growing categories; Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report documents an increasingly organised anti-trans movement. Police figures capture only reported incidents, and reporting is influenced by awareness and community trust.

Detention is the weakest part of the framework. Since Bill C-16, federal correctional policy requires transgender prisoners to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Both placement and gender-affirming treatment have been contested in court, including litigation in which lawyer Barbara findlay represented a trans prisoner challenging her placement in a women's institution and the withholding of gender-affirming medical care.

82249235B50381585000441.name: Manitoba
82249235B50381585000441.summary:
Manitoba stands under the national framework: Canada is among the safest large destinations for trans visitors, with gender identity and gender expression protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code as added by Bill C-16 in 2017. No jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, federal identity documents can carry an X marker, and entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.

Provincially, the Manitoba Human Rights Code already prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity. The NDP government has a bill before the Legislative Assembly to extend the Code to gender expression as well, which Justice Minister Matt Wiebe said would bring Manitoba in line with most other provinces and would cover preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing; the bill was scheduled for debate later in 2025. Charlie Eau, executive director of Trans Manitoba, welcomed the amendment.

Manitoba's recorded hate-crime exposure is low relative to the rest of the country. Statistics Canada's police-reported hate-crime release of 30 March 2026 records 4,882 incidents nationally in 2024, up 1% on 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Manitoba posted the joint-lowest provincial rate at 5.3 per 100,000 alongside Newfoundland and Labrador and recorded no increase in 2024, placing it among the eight provinces whose rates were stable or declining. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly across the country, and police figures capture only reported incidents.

Manitoba has enacted trans-specific recognition at provincial level. The legislature passed a bill on 30 May 2024 recognising March 31 as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a backbench New Democrat MLA for Kirkfield Park who is transgender; Oxenham said the day would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary Manitobans that they are supported.

Provincial observance of trans commemorations is established. On 20 November 2023 Manitoba again raised the transgender flag in Memorial Park in Winnipeg for the Transgender Day of Remembrance, an observance first marked eight years earlier, with the flag raised by Logan Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature. Families Minister Nahanni Fontaine and Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara stated that the government supports and upholds the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans. Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson said the day memorialises people murdered as a result of transphobia, violence she said shows no sign of slowing.

82249235B9619254975586.name: Yukon
82249235B9619254975586.summary:
Yukon stands under the national framework of Canada. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, and no jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Most provinces allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers. Healthcare coverage is universal.

Detention is the weakest part of the framework. Since Bill C-16, federal correctional policy requires transgender prisoners to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Both placement and gender-affirming treatment have been contested in court, including litigation in which lawyer Barbara findlay represented a trans prisoner challenging her placement in a women's institution and the withholding of gender-affirming medical care.

No Yukon-specific trans statute, incident series or policing pattern is on record. National criminal law, the national gender-recognition framework and the national protections apply directly in this sparsely populated territory.

The national hate-crime picture sets the background risk. Statistics Canada recorded 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, up 1% on 2023 and up 169% since 2018, at a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents motivated by gender identity or gender expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive annual increase and a rise of 184% since 2020. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, though June 2024 alone recorded 113 incidents against a monthly average near 50.

Reporting capacity is unevenly distributed. Police-reported hate-crime rates run about 2.5 times higher in large metropolitan areas, 13.9 per 100,000, than in smaller towns at 5.5, which bears directly on a sparsely populated territory where local reporting infrastructure and local data are thinner.

The one concrete Yukon incident on record is low-level and symbolic rather than violent: a Pride flag was allegedly vandalized and stolen from Holy Family Elementary School in Whitehorse's Porter Creek neighbourhood over a weekend in June 2024, and a replacement flag was promptly put up. In a statement issued 12 June 2024, Yukon Education Minister Jeanie McLean reaffirmed her commitment to the territory's sexual orientation and gender identity policy, SOGI 123, and said Pride month celebrates the diversity that makes the Yukon vibrant and strong.

Official tone in Yukon runs the other way from the two provinces that have moved against residents. On 30 March 2026 the Yukon Legislature marked International Transgender Day of Visibility, with members rising to speak. Yukon Party MLA Wade Istchenko of Kluane praised the courage, resilience and contributions of transgender, two-spirited and gender-diverse Yukoners, acknowledged that too many people have experienced discrimination, harassment and hate for far too long, and cited a national study showing transgender 15-17-year-olds face 7.6 times the risk of a suicide attempt.

The Northwest Territories stands under the national framework of Canada. Most provinces allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender, and Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act replaced the surgery requirement with a declaration supported by a doctor's letter. The territory's first legislation specifically addressing transgender and non-binary people was open to feedback as of June 2026. The Northwest Territories Legislative Assembly sought comment from police and the Northern Mosaic Network on proposed amendments to the Vital Statistics Act and the Change of Name Act to make the legislation more inclusive for transgender, non-binary, gender-diverse and two-spirit people, including an option for an applicant to request that a name change not be published in the NWT Gazette. Canada is among the safest large destinations for trans visitors, and Nunavut stands directly under that national framework. 14339913B95766344400054.name: England
14339913B95766344400054.summary:
England stands under the United Kingdom's national framework: passport and document rules, entry and visa rules, marriage law and criminal law are uniform across the country, and the single-sex-services rollback operates through the national equality legislation and the national equality watchdog, with no devolved layer between the visitor and those institutions. The national Supreme Court sits in London and the Equality and Human Rights Commission's headquarters are in England, so the machinery that governs a trans visitor's day here is the machinery of the whole state.

The defining judgment is the unanimous ruling of the United Kingdom Supreme Court in For Women Scotland, handed down on 16 April 2025. The court held that "woman" and "sex" in the Equality Act 2010 mean biological woman and biological sex, and that a gender recognition certificate does not entitle a trans woman to the Act's sex-based protections. Lord Hodge said the ruling should not be read as reducing the Act's protection against discrimination for transgender people. That definition governs services, searches and detention allocation for anyone detained in England.

The operative enforcement guidance a visitor meets at venues, on transport and at service counters is the Equality and Human Rights Commission's updated code of practice, issued on 20 May 2025. It advises that services and businesses may ask for a person's birth certificate where there is "genuine concern" about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport "when necessary" for safety. In August 2026 the watchdog's separate code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. Trans visitors therefore use facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how to enforce that division lawfully.

Prison placement follows the same rule. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, ruled the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory custody guidance unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis; the guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in prisons matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The Supreme Court had already held that Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights confers no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex, and that UK-wide ruling governs England's prison and custody decisions. Any visitor arrested in England should expect placement by sex at birth.

Searching follows the same logic. British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, with trans women searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; the prior policy had permitted a trans woman staff member to conduct an intimate search of a woman holding a gender recognition certificate. Police Scotland's interim guidance of 25 June 2025, which applies in Scotland rather than England, states that in custody and stop-and-search any search involving removal beyond a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear is conducted on the basis of biological sex, though where a person's lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

The official baseline for trans-hostile incidents is the Home Office's England-and-Wales hate-crime statistics, published on 9 October 2025: 115,990 police-recorded hate crimes in the year ending March 2025, with the transgender strand down 11% and the sexual-orientation strand down 2% against the previous year. The bulletin cautions that recorded figures understate prevalence, with the Crime Survey estimate at about 176,000 hate-crime incidents a year.

The Supreme Court had already held that Article 8 confers no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex, and that UK-wide ruling governs England's prison and custody decisions. The first minister said the government will consider the judgment.

The UK Supreme Court's April 2025 ruling is the predicate for England's EHRC code and BTP strip-search policy, and a judicial review reported by BBC News on 5 February 2026 tests how far it reaches into prison accommodation UK-wide. In argument, government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy 'Orwellian'.

82085004B13995298844162.name: Queensland
82085004B13995298844162.summary:
Queensland sits within the Australian federal framework. The federal Sex Discrimination Act has protected gender identity since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that gender-identity discrimination protection extends to trans women as women, and awarded compensation against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member; the case arose out of organised exclusionary activism and stands as national precedent on access to services under sex-discrimination law.

There are no laws in Australia confining bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held since 2017, which matters to same-sex couples arriving together. State law in Queensland has moved in the protective direction on several fronts: same-sex conduct was decriminalised in the 1990s reforms, and rights have broadly advanced in line with the national standard.

Queensland enacted the country's first criminal ban on conversion practices, with the Health Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 passing on 13 August 2020. Practices including electro-shock, drug and hypnotherapy aimed at changing a person's sexuality or gender identity are criminalised, with fines and jail time for practitioners. Survivors have told SBS the ban does not reach conversion practices carried out in informal, non-healthcare settings.

Anti-discrimination law was rewritten with amendments commencing on 29 April 2024. The Queensland Human Rights Commission describes a modernised gender identity attribute, protection extended explicitly to non-binary and gender-diverse people, and a broadened definition of gender identity. Serious vilification moved from the Anti-Discrimination Act into the Criminal Code, raising the maximum penalty from six months to three years' imprisonment.

The sharpest adverse measure for a visitor concerns access to care. Since January 2025 new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria are barred from puberty blockers and hormone therapy under a Queensland Health directive dated 28 January 2025, issued under Health Minister Tim Nicholls, which exempts existing patients of the Queensland Children's Gender Service. The ban remains legally contested. Equality Australia has described Queensland as an outlier state.

Detention carries the sharpest residual physical risk. A 2009 Queensland corrective services procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective; oversight passed to the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, fully in force from 2023, and inspection standards issued in August 2023 for Queensland prisons and youth detention centres direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender. Placement is therefore identity-based, with a discretionary admission caveat and an exception tied to sexual reassignment surgery.

82085004B14973555098025.name: South Australia
82085004B14973555098025.summary:
Visitors to South Australia stand under the national framework: the federal Sex Discrimination Act has treated gender identity as a protected ground since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding compensation against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. The precedent binds service providers nationally, including in South Australia.

State law supplies a parallel remedy. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 was amended in 2016 to protect gender identity and sexual orientation, so discrimination on that ground is actionable under South Australian statute as well as federal statute.

Identity documents are the clearest visitor-facing advantage. Since 23 May 2017, under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration (Gender Identity) Amendment Act 2016, a South Australian can change the sex descriptor on a birth certificate with appropriate clinical treatment, with no sex-reassignment surgery required and no forced divorce if married. Non-binary and 'indeterminate' descriptors are available on state birth certificates. With the Australian Capital Territory, South Australia was one of the first two jurisdictions in the country to permit change without surgery.

Violence against trans people is addressed by two specific provisions. Hate-crime sentencing laws that explicitly cover sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex characteristics passed and were implemented in November 2021. The gay-panic defence was abolished on 1 December 2020 and took effect 1 April 2021, removing a mitigation argument that had been available to defendants who killed gay and, by extension, gender-nonconforming victims.

Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2024 passed in October 2024 and has been in legal effect since 1 April 2025, so conversion practices are prohibited rather than merely discouraged.

There is no restrictive machinery aimed at trans visitors. No South Australian law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and relationship recognition is settled: registered domestic relationships date from 1 August 2017 and same-sex marriage has been legal nationally since December 2017, which matters to couples arriving together.

82085004B70793016411369.name: Tasmania
82085004B70793016411369.summary:
Tasmania stands under Australia's national framework, in which the Sex Discrimination Act has treated gender identity as a protected ground since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Gigle that this protection extends to trans women as women, and awarded compensation against a female-only app that had excluded a trans woman member. That holding sets the baseline a trans visitor to Tasmania can invoke.

Criminalisation of male homosexual conduct in Tasmania ended with effect from 14 May 1997. The Commonwealth Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act commenced on 19 December 1994, Tasmania nonetheless retained its Criminal Code provisions, and faced with a likely adverse outcome in Croome v Tasmania it repealed them, becoming the final Australian jurisdiction to do so. The age of consent is 17, a figure shared only with South Australia.

Identity documents carry no surgical hurdle. Gender on Tasmanian birth certificates has been optional since April 2019, the requirement that a transgender person undergo surgery for their gender to be recognised has been removed, and a person aged 16 or over can change their registered gender without parental approval. Birth certificates have issued an 'X' sex descriptor since 2019. The Marriage Amendments Bill passed the House of Assembly on 10 April 2019 after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition, having already cleared the Legislative Council. The Tasmanian Government opposed the amendments and declined to rule out a later repeal.

Partnership recognition is in place for visitors arriving together: same-sex marriage has been available under national law since 2017, and in Tasmania same-sex couples can enter a registered domestic partnership with an optional official ceremony. Equal adoption rights for same-sex couples applied across every state and territory from April 2018.

Facilities and entry carry no restrictive machinery. No Australian law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, and no border friction has been reported for trans travellers.

Counterweights are documented at national level. The Tickle case grew out of organised exclusionary activism, and ANROWS research maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender-diverse rights in Australia, naming organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over access to facilities and to records, and pressure to roll back existing rights, alongside systemic discrimination and harassment experienced by trans people.

82085004B12086860067424.name: Other Territories
82085004B12086860067424.summary:
Australia treats gender identity as a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, in force since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that gender-identity discrimination protection extends to trans women as women, and awarded compensation against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. The Commonwealth statute was amended by the Sex Discrimination Amendment (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Intersex Status) Act 2013, prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status alongside sex, marital or relationship status, pregnancy and breastfeeding across work, accommodation, education and the provision of goods and services.

The external territories have no territory-specific SOGIE statute and no documented divergence from that national framework. Norfolk Island has been part of New South Wales legislation from 1 July 2016 under the Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act 2015 and the Territories Legislation Amendment Act 2016. Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands are jurisdictions where Western Australia laws apply. Jervis Bay Territory stands under the national layer, with no state-level instrument named in the sources. The Sex Discrimination Act applies throughout Australia including the external territories governed directly by Commonwealth law, so a visitor on Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands or Jervis Bay Territory is covered by that statute with no local provision narrowing it.

Availability of the 'X' sex descriptor and anti-discrimination protection on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression extend across the states and territories with concurrent federal protection. Same-sex adult private sexual conduct has been legal nationally since the Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 commenced on 19 December 1994.

Visitors encounter none of the restrictive machinery found elsewhere: there are no laws confining bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held since 2017, which matters to same-sex couples arriving together.

14911670B45290909693812.name: Roraima
14911670B45290909693812.summary:
Roraima stands under Brazil's national framework: same-sex marriage has been legal across the country since the National Council of Justice Resolution of 14 May 2013, joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015, and the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018 removed surgery, hormones or diagnosis as conditions for changing a name and gender marker. These protections rest on national court rulings and national administration rather than on Roraima state statute, and no state-level deviation from them is recorded for a visitor.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held that discrimination and violence motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity constitute a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, carrying imprisonment of one to five years and fines. A legal guide for expatriates confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's on entry and in family matters.

The text of the law does not describe routine experience. OutRight International reports that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, most acutely against trans people, and that enforcement of the protections is uneven in practice. A visitor to Roraima should expect the national picture as it applies outside the major metropolitan circuits: recognised rights on paper, thinner practical enforcement, and greater social friction than the large-city experience suggests.

No third-gender option nationwide, though civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020 and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. First transgender federal legislators (Salabert, Hilton) were elected in 2022.

OutRight International reports that Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections.

An OAB/SP guide for expatriates states that Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper: same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice. Major cities including Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianopolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

14911670B26412867168762.name: Amapa
14911670B26412867168762.summary:
Amapá stands under Brazil's national framework, and no state-level deviation affecting a visitor is documented in the sources. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice resolution of 14 May 2013, adopted 14-1, and joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015. Legal gender change has required no surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018, and gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held that discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity constitutes a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, docketed as ADO 26 and MI 4733, carrying imprisonment of one to five years and fines. That ruling is the operative basis on which homophobia and transphobia are treated as criminal conduct anywhere in the country, including Amapá.

Documents remain the area where a visitor may see divergence. There is no third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry entries marked non-binary or unspecified have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of registry entries to a neutral gender as precedent. Non-binary birth-certificate practice varies from state to state, so the entry a person obtains in Amapá is not guaranteed to match what another state's registry will accept. Trans voters may also register under their lived name and identity before their documents are updated.

Enforcement does not track the statutory text evenly. The country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people, and an expat legal guide updated in April 2026 records that enforcement of the protections is uneven in practice. Major cities such as São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianópolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. For Amapá this translates into the national position carried with a remote-interior discount on services and enforcement, and no state-specific hostility on record. The national survey's per-state table carries a 2022-dated entry recording progress in Amapá on recognition documents.

14911670B46798344041190.name: Amazonas
14911670B46798344041190.summary:
Amazonas stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice Resolution of 14 May 2013, carried 14-1, joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015, and legal gender change requires no surgery, hormones or diagnosis following the Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling of 1 March 2018.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. An expatriate legal guide updated in April 2026 puts the term at one to five years and confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

No Amazonas-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement pattern is documented for a visitor. Registry practice in the state records non-binary or unspecified birth-certificate entries, and name changes are granted on documents there.

There is no third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry non-binary or unspecified entries have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. OutRight International's country report, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions, and that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Enforcement is uneven: major cities are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

Detention carries a specific regime that applies to a visitor held in Amazonas. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 in Rio de Janeiro state prisons interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine, and documents housing in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units; it treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. National norms from 2014 and 2020 permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

14911670B46798344041190.tangentialFactors:
Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress, so the statutory position a visitor relies on is contested at national level rather than settled.

Political visibility has grown alongside the threat. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections; in the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle. Salabert and Hilton became the first transgender federal legislators in 2022.

Violence against trans people is documented in ordinary settings. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists.

Courts have applied the anti-discrimination provisions to commercial conduct. The 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita.

Protection machinery has widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.

The Rio de Janeiro census is one state's data rather than a national finding, but it is the clearest documentation of the gap between the placement rules and the units actually operated. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics.

14911670B1613159902410.name: Rondonia
14911670B1613159902410.summary:
Rondônia stands under the national framework of Brazil, which pairs a broad legal framework for LGBTI people with persistent violence against them in practice. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide under the CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013, adopted by a 14-1 vote, with joint adoption permitted since 2010 and full rights from 2015; the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical, hormonal and diagnostic requirements for legal gender change in its ruling of 1 March 2018; the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation; and federal anti-discrimination provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity to be a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, carrying imprisonment of one to five years and fines, in the ADO 26 and MI 4733 decisions. Constitutional and federal criminal provisions therefore prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on these grounds, and courts have applied them to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

No third-gender option exists on documents nationwide, but civil-registry entries recorded as non-binary or unspecified have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits neutral-gender registry rectification and stands as precedent. Whether Rondônia's civil registries currently record such entries is not established by the sources in this inventory.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions, and Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. A May 2024 investigation documented drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife. In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle; more than 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in those elections overall.

Enforcement is uneven in practice, and the geography of that unevenness matters for a visitor. Major cities such as São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianópolis are described as broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. None of Rondônia's urban centres appears on that list of major cities, so the state's own cities fall in the category the source associates with greater social friction and thinner practical protection.

Legal advances also face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress, and hostile proposals in the national legislature remain a live risk to the current framework. Against that, an analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.

Detention carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region, documenting housing in units operated as masculine with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treating placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

14911670B40722526455680.summary:

14911670B46470234103867.name: Sao Paulo
14911670B46470234103867.summary:

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled in ADO 26 that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. Transphobia is consequently prosecuted on the same footing as racism, and a visitor who faces discriminatory conduct in São Paulo can invoke that provision directly.

No specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists. The 2019 ruling supplies the prohibition, and repeal efforts have been tabled in the National Congress, so the durability of the statutory route is contested even as the constitutional and criminal provisions remain in force. The Superior Court of Justice held in 2023 that nonbinary people may amend their civil records, which bears on how a document carrying a nonbinary marker is read at entry and in services.

São Paulo courts have applied the anti-discrimination provisions to commercial conduct. The 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita. Refusal of service on this ground is therefore actionable in this state.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists. Nightlife carries a documented, targeted risk here that is not captured by the criminal provisions.

The unit led the national ranking in 2024 with 16 killings of travestis and trans people, then fell to 4 recorded killings in 2025, out of the top group. The country's dominant geographic pattern applies: at least 68% of the 2024 killings, 83 of 122, occurred outside state capitals in interior cities, so a traveller's exposure sits more in the interior than in the capital.

Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. LGBTI status is recognised by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted: the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 in Rio de Janeiro state prisons interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region, and documents that travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units. The study treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights, which is the pattern a trans detainee in this country should expect to encounter rather than the text of Resolution 348.

Protection machinery has widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.

Practical friction varies by settlement size. Larger cities such as São Paulo carry legal infrastructure, including counsel experienced in gender-marker and discrimination matters, while smaller cities and rural areas carry more social friction and thinner support.

14911670B30315977547221.name: Parana
14911670B30315977547221.summary:
Paraná is a state of Brazil and stands under Brazil's national framework. Paraná is assessed at the national score: no deviation from the national position has been identified that is material enough to score separately (within ±0.02). A visitor to Curitiba or anywhere else in the state therefore faces the same law as a visitor to any other part of the country.

Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since May 2013, under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, which binds all civil registries after a 14-1 vote, and adoption rights have followed since 2015. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

The Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and in 2023 the Superior Court of Justice allowed nonbinary people to amend their civil records. The age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and lesbian, gay and bisexual people serve openly in the armed forces.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Tribunal ruled that discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines, and transphobia is now punished on the same footing as racism. No specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists behind that ruling, and repeal efforts have been mounted in Congress, so the protection rests on constitutional and criminal provisions rather than a dedicated statute. Intersex people have no specific protections in Brazilian law.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Detention carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine. Rio de Janeiro is one province's evidence of how the national detention rules are applied, not a finding about Paraná's own prison system.

1811400B81659894240990.name: Puducherry
1811400B81659894240990.summary:
Puducherry is a union territory of India with a partial legislature. Legal recognition of gender identity, identity-document rules and welfare policy for transgender people are set principally by the central government, and no Puducherry-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file. The framework that reaches a visitor in Puducherry is therefore the national one.

1811400B80305611676067.summary:
Gujarat stands under the national framework of India, and the source inventory records no Gujarat-specific legal or enforcement deviation material enough to distinguish this state from the national baseline. A visitor therefore faces the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, passed by the Parliament of India in March 2026, which replaces the 2019 Act's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. Self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people fall outside the recognition scheme, and the amendment mandates medical certification for identity recognition, so document practice for a trans traveller rests on that certification.

The amendment removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court of India's 2014 judgment recognising a third gender. Human Rights Watch described the bill as a major setback that strips thousands of rights and increases risk. The government presents the change as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. At the time of reporting in March 2026 the bill had cleared both houses of Parliament and awaited presidential assent.

Entry and stay rest on a mixed baseline. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped openly transgender law student Sakshi Jain although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination, with the Allahabad High Court granting relief in February 2026.

Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. 1811400B26595099860318.name: Bihār
1811400B26595099860318.summary:
Bihār has no state-specific transgender legislation of its own. A trans visitor to the state stands directly under India's national framework, and no source material indicates a deviation in Bihār material enough to score separately from the national position.

That national framework was substantially rewritten in March 2026. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in both houses, amending the 2019 Act, and the measure awaits presidential assent. It removes the right to self-identification recognised by the Supreme Court of India's 2014 judgment declaring transgender people a third gender, and limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme entirely. The amendment also mandates medical certification as the basis for identity recognition on documents.

Rights organisations describe the change as a major setback that strips thousands of people of rights and increases their exposure to harm. Activists including Akkai Padmashali have characterised the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist. The Government of India presents the amendment as widening access to welfare schemes and strengthening protection against trafficking; critics respond that it excludes a large share of transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India's transgender population is estimated at two million.

The entry and stay baseline for LGBT+ visitors remains mixed on other axes. The Supreme Court decriminalised same-sex sexual acts in 2018, and statutory anti-discrimination protection on grounds including sex has been interpreted to encompass gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available anywhere in India, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units for limited purposes.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded transgender people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code. The absence of that protection applies in Bihār on the same terms as elsewhere in the country.

Document and checkpoint friction is documented at several points of entry. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a transgender applicant to sit a medical examination as part of the process; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The high courts remain the strongest protection machinery available. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh after police harassment of a same-sex couple, issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and to education authorities. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people in India, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor to Bihār, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone. Recognition was narrowed nationally in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abusive encounters at railway stations, airports and passport offices were documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of transgender and LGBT+ people.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026. It strips the self-identification route from the 2019 law, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner plus intersex persons, and bases recognition on biological or physical traits. The measure reverses the 2014 Supreme Court ruling that had established self-identification as the standard. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside the listed categories fall outside the recognition scheme.

Certification now runs through medical boards and district authorities, which must certify gender-affirming surgery before identity recognition is granted. A visitor whose documents predate this regime should expect documentary friction wherever recognition is tested.

The amendment also creates offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Human Rights Watch warned on 26 March 2026 that this provision could be used against support networks around trans people.

Presidential assent was still pending in late March 2026. Human Rights Watch urged the president not to sign the bill, and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw it, calling the removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling.

The government presents the narrower definition as a way to target welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection to a defined group. Critics, including rights activists, respond that it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people; India is estimated to have around two million transgender people.

The entry and stay baseline is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018 and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, read to cover gender identity, but same-sex marriage and civil partnership are unavailable, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of more assaults under the new code.

Documented exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact. A trans woman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of a gender check at a Kolkata railway station; trans people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam described degrading custody treatment in interviews recorded in June 2024. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor the practical picture is narrowed recognition from March 2026, removed sexual-violence safeguards from 2024, documented abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters, and high courts that have repeatedly intervened on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.

Sushma v Commissioner of Police bind police conduct and bar conversion therapy. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 26 March 2026. The amendment removes the self-identification route that the 2019 law had provided and that the Supreme Court's 2014 ruling established, and restricts legal recognition to historically recognised socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, together with intersex persons. Recognition now turns on biological or physical traits, with medical boards and district authorities required to certify gender-affirming surgery before an identity is granted. Presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026.

The narrowed scheme excludes trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside the accepted categories. The government presents the narrower definition as concentrating welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection on recognised groups; rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as an attack on the right to exist, and critics warn that many trans and gender-fluid people are left outside any recognition. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, calling the removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling.

The amendment also creates offences including up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to become transgender. Human Rights Watch warns that this provision could be used against support networks and organisations that assist trans people.

Recognition is thin on the ground: of 487,803 transgender persons recorded in the census, only about 32,500 hold identity cards. India is estimated to have around two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender people arrested by the force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024.
