India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex persons, and requiring medical certification of identity. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 26 March 2026, describes the amendment as reversing the 2014 Supreme Court ruling that had established self-identification. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Presidential assent was still pending in late March 2026; Human Rights Watch urged the president not to sign, and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, calling the removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling.

The amendment adds offences carrying penalties of up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Human Rights Watch warns that this provision could criminalise the support networks on which trans people rely.

Recognition coverage is narrow in practice. Of 487,803 transgender persons recorded in the census, roughly 32,500 hold identity cards, against a wider national estimate of about two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.

1811400B75807316846587.name: Madhya Pradesh
1811400B75807316846587.summary:
Madhya Pradesh has no state-specific transgender statute and no documented state-level enforcement series. Legal uniformity across the country sets the deviation at ±0.02, so a visitor to Madhya Pradesh is assessed against the national framework rather than any provincial rule.

That framework was altered on 25 March 2026, when India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of sourcing. The amendment replaces the self-identification route affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2014 with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Critics warn the narrower definition excludes self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Recognition now rests on medical certification. The amendment makes medical-board and district-authority certification mandatory for gender-affirming surgery and conditions identity recognition on medical certification, a direct documents consequence for a trans traveller whose papers rest on that certification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The amendment adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender. People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. The bill was passed amid protests in Mumbai.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.

1811400B77692474244036.name: Chandīgarh
1811400B77692474244036.summary:
Chandīgarh, a union territory of India, is assessed at the national score: the country review identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02). A visitor therefore stands under India's national framework as it stands after the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill passed both houses of Parliament on 25 March 2026, with presidential assent still pending.

The amendment removes the self-identification right affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 judgment and confines legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme altogether. Critics warn that the narrower definition excludes self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people; India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Recognition is conditioned on medical certification. The bill makes medical-board and district-authority certification mandatory for gender-affirming surgery, which converts identity documentation into a clinical process for any trans traveller whose papers rest on that certification. The bill also creates offences carrying up to life imprisonment for 'coercing or alluring' anyone to be transgender, amending the 2019 law. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these offences echo the colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people, and rights activists among them Akkai Padmashali describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist. The government presents the bill as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; the bill was passed amid protests in Mumbai.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters is documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.

The March 2026 amendment reverses a recognition model that had held since the Supreme Court's 2014 ruling and that the 2019 statute had codified, so documents issued before the amendment rest on a legal basis the bill withdraws. Whether existing identity documents remain valid once assent is given is not addressed in the sources.

Documented incidents of mistreatment nonetheless cluster in exactly the settings a traveller passes through, namely railway stations, airport terminals and passport offices.

India's estimated two million transgender people give the recognition scheme a large affected population, and the March 2026 passage was contested in public, with protests reported in Mumbai.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of sourcing. Medical certification becomes a condition of identity recognition. Gender-affirming surgery requires certification by a medical board and a district authority. For a trans traveller whose papers rest on that certification, this is a direct documents consequence: identity papers issued under the old route may not be reissued or amended on the same basis.

The amendment also creates offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. The government presents the bill as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. 1811400B21086746745937.name: Himāchal Pradesh
1811400B21086746745937.summary:
Himāchal Pradesh has no trans-specific statute, enforcement series or documented incident pattern of its own in the available sources; a visitor to the state therefore operates under India's national framework, which Parliament altered on 25 March 2026.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of reporting, with protests held in Mumbai on the day of passage. The amendment replaces the self-identification route established by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling and narrows legal recognition to the male and female categories together with historically accepted socio-cultural identities such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex people. Trans men, trans women and non-binary or gender-fluid people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme.

The amended scheme conditions recognition and surgery on official process. Certification from a medical board and a district authority is required for gender-affirming surgery, and identity recognition rests on medical certification rather than self-declaration. The amendment also adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender, amending the 2019 law. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. Rights activists including Akkai Padmashali describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay remains mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor to Himāchal Pradesh, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.

Haryāna stands under the national framework of India. No Haryāna-specific trans-related statute, enforcement series or incident pattern with a source was identified, so the state is scored at the national position and a visitor's expectations are set by central law.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, amending the 2019 Act, and it awaits presidential assent. The bill ends the self-identification route to legal recognition established by the Supreme Court's 2014 judgment in NALSA v Union of India, confines recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex persons, and otherwise recognises only male and female categories. Trans men, trans women and people who self-identify as gender-fluid or non-binary fall outside the recognition scheme.

Medical certification becomes a condition of recognition. The amendment mandates certification by a medical board and a district authority before gender-affirming surgery, and conditions identity recognition on medical procedure. For a trans visitor whose papers rest on self-declaration, that shift bears directly on how documents are read at entry, at police contact and at any administrative counter in Haryāna.

The amendment also creates offences carrying up to life imprisonment for 'coercing or alluring' a person to be transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these provisions echo the colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. The government presents the bill as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics counter that the narrower definition excludes a large share of trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

National-framework item (applies to Haryāna): India's parliament passed the bill in March 2026, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent. It ends the 2014 Supreme Court self-identification right, narrows recognition to male/female categories plus traditional identities, and makes medical-board and district-authority certification mandatory for gender-affirming surgery. Critics warn the narrower definition excludes self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people; ~2 million transgender people live in India.

10402087B60055985875400.name: Baden-Württemberg
10402087B60055985875400.summary:
Baden-Württemberg stands under Germany's national framework. Federal constitutional and equality protections apply nationwide, identity documents and marriage law are uniform across the Länder, and no Land can remove that federal floor.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison.

Baden-Württemberg's own prison law retains the unrevised 1970s-era placement rules, and the Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 does not name the Land among those with updated provisions. A majority of the German Länder now operate revised rules: a new Art. 17 of Rhineland-Palatinate's prison law has been in force since 1 March 2026, and Bavarian, Saxon and Hamburg provisions have also recently entered into force. Only Bremen's law explicitly references the registered gender entry, while other Länder do so implicitly.

How the exception is applied in practice remains unsettled. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025; authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, and critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law. The transfer indicates that placement follows the civil-registry entry and that exceptions permitting placement contrary to that entry are invoked inconsistently.

DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, a finding illustrated by the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted.

Screening is a documented flashpoint. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity. She characterised the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and gave Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a debate about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic.

Reporting and support machinery exists for hostility encountered in country. The STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation in northern Germany, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

sources.summary: July 2026 report on a convicted far-right extremist holding a legally recognised female gender entry who was transferred from a women's prison to a men's prison after public outcry. The transfer indicates that placement follows the civil-registry entry and that exceptions permitting placement contrary to that entry are invoked inconsistently.

Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 on prison placement for trans prisoners, with bearing on Baden-Württemberg. Placement rules in most Länder have stood unchanged since the 1970s and are now being revised. Since 1 March 2026 a new Art. 17 of Rhineland-Palatinate's prison law is in force, and Bavarian, Saxon and Hamburg rules have also recently entered into force, giving a majority of Länder revised rules. The analysis argues that no constitutional duty exists to anchor placement to the registered gender entry, since a prisoner self-declaration would intrude less on the right to gender self-determination. Only Bremen's law explicitly references the gender entry; other Länder do so implicitly. Baden-Württemberg is not named. Its own prison law retains the unrevised 1970s-era placement rules.

10402087B44391416804171.name: Bremen
10402087B44391416804171.summary:
Bremen stands under the federal framework. The Self-Determination Act (SBGG) took effect on 1 November 2024, having passed the Bundestag by 374 votes to 251. Adults over 18 may change their legal gender by self-declaration without the former medical or court pathway, and the change is entered in the civil registry. Bremen has no trans-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement series of its own; the city-state's registry offices process declarations under the unchanged federal act, and federal criminal law and the general equality act apply without local deviation.

The sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor is custody. German prison administration is a state competence, and Bremen has no placement statute of its own, so the national framework governs inmate placement. All Länder tie placement to the prisoner's legal gender, and § 6(1) SBGG permits state law to override the registry entry; many Länder have enacted exception clauses, some abstract in wording and others criticised as targeting trans inmates specifically. Placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been applied only exceptionally in practice.

The Liebich case shows how the exception works in practice. Marla-Svenja Liebich's gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act; after her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was placed in a men's prison despite her legal registration as a woman, with authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility. A 16 July 2026 France24 wire report on the case records that Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia responded by launching a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal act.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Germany since 1 October 2017 and has no Bremen-specific restriction, so a partner's status travels on the ordinary federal footing.

sources.summary: A 16 July 2026 France24/wire report covers the neo-Nazi prisoner in the 'Liebich' case, placed in a men's prison despite a legal gender change. The case drove Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. The issue is framework-level for every Land, since prison administration and registry offices are Land competences.

Framework analysis (Verfassungsblog, 18 Mar 2026) of German state prison-placement rules under the Self-Determination Act: all Länder tie placement to the prisoner's legal gender; § 6(1) SBGG lets state law override the entry, and many Länder have enacted exception clauses — some abstract (all inmates), some criticised as trans-targeted. Bremen has no placement statute of its own, so this national framework is the operative standard for inmate-placement questions.

sources.summary: German Wikipedia's overview of homosexuality in Germany records that the country's first Christopher Street Days were held in 1979 in Berlin, with 400 partly masked participants, and in Bremen, making Bremen one of the two original host cities of public LGBT street demonstrations in Germany. The overview also documents the federal criminal-law history in which Bremen's current status sits, including the Nazi-era tightening of Section 175a with penitentiary terms of up to ten years and the persecution of men including forced castration in prisons. No Bremen-specific statute or enforcement appears in the overview. Bremen relies on the federal framework.

10402087B45896528657515.name: Hamburg
10402087B45896528657515.summary:
Hamburg stands under the federal framework of Germany. The Self-Determination Act (SBGG), in force since 1 November 2024, allows adults to change legal gender and first name in the civil registry by self-identification, without psychological evaluation or a court order; Hamburg's registry offices process the change, so a trans visitor's documents rest on that national regime rather than on any local instrument.

The Act replaced the earlier court-and-evaluation pathway, brought trans, inter and non-binary status regulation into a single statute, and revised the provisions of the Third Gender Act. Birth-register parent entries still carry the previous gender, so a trans woman may appear as 'father', although a 'parent' option is now available on birth certificates. That registry entry is the administrative anchor on which custody placement turns.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Prison administration is a Land competence, and under the Self-Determination Act the legal gender entry governs placement unless a Land law provides otherwise; constitutional doubts have been voiced about trans-targeted exception clauses (Verfassungsblog, 18 March 2026). Hamburg is among the Länder whose reformed prison-placement rules have entered into force, tying inmate placement to the civil-registry sex entry, so an arrested visitor would enter that machinery at intake.

How the exception is applied remains unsettled. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025; authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, and critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law. The France24 wire report of 16 July 2026 on that placement records that it drove several eastern Länder to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Act. A court-ordered placement of a legally transitioned prisoner in a men's prison at Neubrandenburg in mid-July 2026 (DW/Telegraph, 15-17 July 2026) is the case that anchors that Länder action.

Several states have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all. DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, a finding illustrated by the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted. The Berlin prison service maintains an official page in German with information and contacts for trans, inter and non-binary persons held across the city's facilities.

Screening is a documented flashpoint at ports of entry. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity; she characterised the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and gave Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a debate about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic. Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reported on how saunas and similar venues now treat trans women, after months of public argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

No hostile-offence series, ordinance or event-security finding specific to Hamburg is on file, and no Hamburg-specific enforcement finding on trans prison placement has been recorded. Reporting and support machinery exists for hostility encountered in country: the STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation in northern Germany, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

Framework analysis (Verfassungsblog, 18 Mar 2026) of trans prisoner placement under the Self-Determination Act (SBGG, in force 1 Nov 2024): legal gender entry governs unless state law provides otherwise; constitutional doubts voiced about trans-targeted exception clauses. It anchors the July 2026 Neubrandenburg case (court-ordered male-prison placement despite legal gender change, DW/Telegraph 15-17 Jul 2026) that drove Länder action. 10402087B60782008682549.summary:
The federal Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz, SBGG) governs every step of a trans visitor's stay in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Approved by the federal cabinet in August 2023, passed by the Bundestag in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251 and in force since 1 November 2024, it lets adults over 18 change their legal first name and gender entry by self-declaration with three months' notice and no medical certification. No Mecklenburg-Vorpommern-specific trans statute, placement reform or ordinance is recorded in the sources; the federal framework applies here in full, including to short-term visitors and their documents at check-in and border or identity checks.

The partner baseline is the federal one as well: same-sex marriage with full marital and adoption rights has been available since 1 October 2017, implementing legislation having been passed on 30 June 2017. A married or registered partner travelling with a trans visitor is recognised on those terms in this Land.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure, and it is precisely where this Land is the flashpoint. German prisons operate under statutory separation on a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been applied only in exceptional cases; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of the prison-act provision in force in its own state as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Some Länder have since amended their prison statutes to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026.

According to Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026, prison placement under the SBGG follows the person's legal gender entry unless the applicable state prison law provides otherwise. Whether the exception clauses are abstract (applied to any prisoner where individual risk outweighs interests) or drafted to target trans prisoners specifically is contested among the Länder and is now a live legislative question across the federation.

Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is the jurisdiction in which that exception was applied against the legal gender entry. On 15–17 July 2026 the Landgericht Neubrandenburg ruled that the prisoner known as the Liebich case serve her sentence in a men's prison despite a completed legal gender change; France24 and wire coverage of 16 July 2026 reported the placement as proceeding on that basis. The case drew Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia into a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, so the exposure identified here is not confined to this Land.

The same pattern is documented elsewhere in Germany and sets the expectation a trans visitor should carry into any arrest or prolonged detention. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, illustrating the point with the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted. The Berlin prison service maintains an official page in German with information and contacts for trans, inter and non-binary persons held across the city's facilities — the only facility-level support resource in the sources.

Airport and identity screening is a documented flashpoint for visitors rather than residents. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity; she characterised the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and gave Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off public argument about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic. Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reported on how Berlin saunas and similar venues now treat trans women after months of argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused. A visitor should expect facility operators in this Land to apply similar private or association-level criteria.

Support machinery for hostility encountered in country exists at national level. The STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation in northern Germany, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

sources.title: Studie zu Lebenslagen und Erfahrungen von LSBTIQ* „Queer durch NRW“ (Ministerium für Kinder, Jugend, Familie, Gleichstellung, Flucht und Integration NRW / chancen.nrw)
sources.summary: The North Rhine-Westphalia state ministry records that on 25 April 2025 the Land government published the study „Queer durch NRW – Lebenslagen und Erfahrungen von LSBTIQ*“, the first comprehensive dataset on the living situations of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans*, inter*, queer and non-binary people (LSBTIQ*) in the Land. The study combined quantitative online surveys of more than 5,000 LSBTIQ* respondents, 775 relatives and over 5,000 professionals with qualitative focus groups and expert interviews. It covers discrimination, violence and safety; health, care and ageing; and integration, migration and flight. It was commissioned under Landtag resolution Drucksache 18/6360 to develop the state's „Aktionsplan für Vielfalt und gegen Homo- und Transfeindlichkeit“ on a broader data basis. Land-level findings on discrimination, violence and safety affecting trans* people bear on visitor exposure: the Land enacted no trans statute, and the anti-homo/transphobia action plan now rests on this data.

No trans-specific placement provision for this state/province is on file, so that national standard is what a visitor detained here would face.

10402087B42728698084544.summary:
Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several states have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all.

Rhineland-Palatinate replaced its prison-execution code with § 17, which anchors inmate placement to the legally recorded gender entry and pairs it with a general, abstract exception clause open to all prisoners rather than targeted at trans people as such. A constitutional-law analysis of the provision published on 18 March 2026 treats it as directly governing the placement decision a detained visitor in Rhineland-Palatinate would face, and raises constitutional doubts about the trans-targeted exception clauses other states have adopted instead. Rhineland-Palatinate is the state that carried the reform wave past the point where a majority of the Länder now modernise placement rules that had stood unchanged since the 1970s.

Prison administration is a Land competence in Germany, so the placement rule a detained visitor meets is set by the state holding them rather than by federal law. For a trans visitor the practical import of § 17 is therefore detention-time exposure: placement would key off the civil-register sex entry, subject to the general exception clause.

How the exception is applied in practice remains unsettled. A wire report of 16 July 2026 covers the case of a neo-Nazi prisoner held in a men's prison despite a legal gender change. The chief prosecutor for Halle stated in August 2025 that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake; after her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman, authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, and critics calling the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law. The case drove the eastern Länder to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act.

DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, a finding illustrated by the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted. The Berlin prison service maintains an official page in German with information and contacts for trans, inter and non-binary persons held across the city's facilities.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a debate about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic. Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reported on how Berlin saunas and similar venues now treat trans women, after months of public argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Reporting and support machinery exists for hostility encountered in country. The STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation in northern Germany, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

No other Land-specific trans statute, ordinance, enforcement series or event-security finding survives in the records, so outside detention the visitor exposure tracks the national framework.

10402087B83775792336645.summary:
Saarland has no trans-specific statute, ordinance or placement rule of its own. Prison administration is a state competence while equality and criminal law are federal matters, so a trans visitor in Saarland stands under the German federal position and their exposure tracks that framework.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure. Under § 6(1) of the Self-Determination Act, in force 1 November 2024, placement follows the legal gender entry unless a state law provides otherwise, and the Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 records that no constitutional obligation to follow that entry exists.

Saarland has no separate placement statute. The same analysis cites Saarland's practice of single-cell accommodation with an en-suite shower as a positive model for trans inmates, which is the only Saarland-specific custodial practice in the record.

Saarland's Land constitution, amended in 2011, explicitly includes gender identity alongside sexual orientation in its anti-discrimination provisions, one of only five Land constitutions to carry such a clause. Transphobic hate speech is therefore prohibited in Saarland, unlike in most of Germany. The federal General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006, separately bans discrimination based on gender identity in employment, education, health services and the provision of goods and services.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Germany (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The page records that Saarland's state constitution was amended in 2011 so that its anti-discrimination provisions explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, one of only five Lander constitutions to carry such a clause (Berlin since 1995, Brandenburg since 1992, Bremen since 2001, Saarland since 2011, Thuringia since 1993; Saxony-Anhalt in the public sector since 1997). It further records that Saarland, with Hesse, Berlin, Bremen and Schleswig-Holstein, tabled a joint Bundesrat motion for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019, with Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia agreeing and Bavaria offering modified support. Gives the state-constitutional protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity that a trans visitor stands under within Saarland.

sources.title: Transgender rights in Germany (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The page states that hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned nationwide in Germany, but that some states have laws banning all forms of discrimination in their constitutions - Berlin, Brandenburg, Bremen, Saarland and Thuringia - and that in those states hate speech based on both sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited. For Saarland this is a jurisdiction-specific enforcement difference: transphobic hate speech is prohibited under the state constitution, unlike in most of Germany, and the federal General Act on Equal Treatment (in force since 18 August 2006) bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, education, health services and the provision of goods and services.

sources.title: Jens Spahn will Pseudotherapien gegen Homosexualität verbieten

25490228B84620027724461.name: Canarias
25490228B84620027724461.summary:
Canarias stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 1 March 2023, which applies uniformly across all autonomous communities. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may rectify the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry by simple declaration, with no prior medical diagnosis or gender-dysphoria finding and no requirement of two years of medical treatment; corresponding identity documents are adapted to the new marker. The law also mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, and its transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force.

Recognition is available from age 12 under conditions, and consent for medical procedures is regulated for minors aged 12 to 16. That provision proved contentious in the Congress of Deputies, which passed the law on 16 February 2023. Human Rights Watch placed the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

Access to sex-separated facilities in Canarias rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the Civil Registry is the operative basis for facility rules. A trans visitor whose documents reflect a corrected marker is therefore treated on that basis in practice.

The regional layer is permissive rather than restrictive. Canarias enacted Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014 prohibiting discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising trans persons' rights, and has permitted self-declaration of legal gender since 2021, one of 14 autonomous communities to do so before the national law took effect. The region is also listed among the communities banning conversion therapies, and it created its same-sex couple registry in 2003.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice, though the documented cases come from outside Canarias. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied across Spain since 2005, and Ley 4/2023 enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples. Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries, and Gran Canaria and Tenerife are named internationally known LGBT tourist destinations.

sources.summary: State Law 4/2023 of 28 February 2023 (BOE no. 51, 1 March 2023), the 'Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons' (the 'Trans Law'), applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities, including this one: Title II allows adults to rectify their registered sex marker by simple declaration, with no requirement of prior medical diagnosis or treatment, and provides for corresponding document adaptation. The law further mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, and its transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force.

Human Rights Watch (16 February 2023) reports the Spanish Congress of Deputies' passage of the Trans Law: legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the previous requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The same law expands access to assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing; children from age 12 can obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious. HRW places the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

25490228B81978515469630.name: La Rioja
25490228B81978515469630.summary:
La Rioja stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE no. 51, 1 March 2023), applies uniformly across the autonomous communities, including this one. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaces the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment; Title II allows adults to rectify the registered sex marker by simple declaration and provides for corresponding document adaptation, and transitory provisions govern applications pending at entry into force.

The same law mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and permits recognition from age 12 under conditions, a provision Human Rights Watch reported as contentious. It also prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing, and bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before they can consent.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the Civil Registry is the operative basis for facility rules.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Courts apply the aggravation in practice: a Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300, while in Valencia a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, with two minors judged separately.

La Rioja's own regional trans-rights law of February 2022 already allowed trans people to self-declare their legal gender and granted protective rights to trans visitors and residents, so the national framework layers onto an existing permissive regional base rather than replacing restriction; the regional law remains in force alongside the national Ley Trans.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied across Spain since 2005, and Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.

25490228B56567998760255.name: País Vasco/Euskadi
25490228B56567998760255.summary:
A visitor in the Basque Country stands under the national framework of Spain: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 1 March 2023 as the Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons, applies uniformly across the autonomous communities, and this region has enacted no separate trans statute of its own. Title II allows adults to rectify the registered sex marker by simple declaration, with no requirement of prior medical diagnosis or treatment, and provides for corresponding adaptation of identity documents.

The law also mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, and its transitory provisions govern rectification applications still pending at entry into force. Human Rights Watch, reporting on the passage by the Congress of Deputies on 16 February 2023, described the self-identification route as a simple administrative process replacing the former requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment, and placed the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate conditions for legal gender recognition.

Ley 4/2023 further expands access to assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before they can consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Children from age 12 can obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious during the passage debate.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the Civil Registry is the operative basis for facility rules.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Spanish Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months. Both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based attack has no free-standing offence to charge; Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice. A Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied throughout Spain since 2005. The 2024 national report on LGTBI-motivated offences places this region at the top of the per-capita rates, a figure best read as intensive reporting and counting rather than evidence of danger: the regional government operates its own LGTBI public-order policing and an equality observatory, and no regional statutory rollback exists. Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.

sources.summary: The Basque Parliament passed a law against discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising the rights of trans people, dated 2013, which for the first time incorporated an LGTBI perspective into gender-violence prevention in the Basque education system. Institutional markers predating it include the first Basque Pride march in Bilbao in 1978, the legalisation of the activist collective EHGAM in 1983, and the creation of Emakunde, the Basque Women's Institute, in 1988. A 2017 survey by the Basque Youth Observatory reported that 9 in 10 Basque young people favour same-sex marriage and legal change of sex. Osakidetza, the Basque health service, provided assisted reproduction regardless of sexual orientation and reaffirmed that position in 2013. The Basque Country operates its own non-discrimination legal instruments and equality institutions, including Emakunde, within the national framework.

25490228B94236519555378.name: Galicia

Title II of the law regulates rectification of the registered sex entry by the person's freely expressed will. The procedure is depathologised: no medical diagnosis or treatment is required, the former age-majority requirement for filing has been removed, and identity documents are adapted accordingly.

Article 43 of Ley 4/2023 allows any person aged 16 or over to request rectification directly before the Civil Registry. Recognition is available from age 12 under stated conditions, a provision that provoked political conflict when the law was passed. Title III provides protection and reparation against LGBTIphobic discrimination and violence, and the law mandates measures across administrative, workplace, health and education fields, with public authorities acting within their competences. The education-facing and administrative provisions are implemented by the autonomous communities, the Xunta de Galicia among them.

Human Rights Watch, writing on 16 February 2023 as the Congress of Deputies passed the law, described legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the prior requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment aligned to the sought marker. Transphobic motivation is an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months. 25490228B86140490400531.name: Extremadura
25490228B86140490400531.summary:
Extremadura stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado as BOE-A-2023-5366, which establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. The law mandates measures across administrative, workplace, health and education fields, with public authorities acting within their competences; its education-facing and administrative provisions are implemented by the autonomous communities, and the Extremadura regional government is among the governments that carry them out.

Title II of the law regulates rectification of the registered sex entry by the person's freely expressed will. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route with no medical diagnosis and no requirement of two years of medical treatment, and with corresponding adaptation of identity documents. The former age-majority requirement for requesting rectification has been removed, and recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions. The law also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Extremadura as elsewhere in Spain.

Title III provides protection and reparation against LGBTIphobic discrimination and violence. Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Extremadura records the lowest per-capita rate of hate offences of any Spanish autonomous community in national statistics. That figure reflects how little is counted rather than demonstrated protection, and the low count should not be read as reassurance: a visitor's exposure otherwise tracks the national framework and its enforcement.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied in Spain since 2005.

The provision allowing recognition from age 12 proved contentious. Human Rights Watch places the reform against European and international standards rejecting disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Catalunya.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

A Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Catalunya additionally operates its own statute, Ley 11/2014 of 10 October 2014 (DOGC núm. 6730, 17 October 2014), the autonomous law after which the 2010s wave of Spanish regional LGTBI laws followed. It defines direct, indirect and association-based discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and obliges Catalan public administrations to establish mechanisms so that administrative documentation reflects gender identity. Its protections extend across education, health, employment and sport, including broadening the Observatorio Catalán del Deporte to action against violence and discrimination in sport, and it guarantees same-sex partners' participation in death procedures such as body identification, burial and handling of personal effects.

25490228B80227492032103.blindSummary:

Under its Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions. With administrative self-declaration, the national framework sits among a small group of jurisdictions worldwide operating this route.

The statute applies uniformly across the country's provinces, this one included. Its second title allows adults to rectify their registered sex marker by simple declaration with no requirement of prior medical diagnosis or treatment and provides for corresponding document adaptation; the law also mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, and its transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force. Implementation falls to the provincial government.

A national human rights organisation, reporting on 16 February 2023, records that the reform replaced the previous diagnosis-and-treatment requirements with self-identification through a simple administrative process. The same law expands access to assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before they can consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the national Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from an organic law of 2022 rather than from the 2023 statute. Castilla-La Mancha stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado, applies uniformly across all autonomous communities, including this one, and the source inventory identifies no facility, expression or assembly restriction enacted at regional level.

Document-relevant provision is national and administrative. Because access to sex-separated facilities rests on the gender marker recorded in the civil registry rather than on biological sex, that registry entry is the operative basis for facility rules encountered in the region.

Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision that proved contentious in the law's passage, and Ley 4/2023 also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Penal protection is national. Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and Article 510 hate speech carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Courts are applying the aggravation in practice: a Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo used the transfobia aggravation for the first time in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman and fined the author EUR 300, and in Valencia a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, with two minors judged separately.

Discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics are defined and sanctioned, discriminatory contract clauses are null and void, and the law combats LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing while strengthening protections for unmarried same-sex couples.

Violence risk is documented at national level rather than for this region specifically: a 2026 federation report found that 44% of LGBTI respondents had experienced a hate-motivated incident. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied since 2005, and Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.

25490228B26609846683583.name: Illes Balears
25490228B26609846683583.summary:
Illes Balears stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado, which establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights and applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities. No source in the inventory records a Balearic deviation from that framework.

Article 43 allows any person aged 16 or over to request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route grounded in the free development of personality under article 10.1 of the Constitution. It replaces the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision Human Rights Watch reported as contentious when the Congress passed the law.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules and determines which facilities a visitor may use.

The law defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, and declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void. Human Rights Watch records that it combats LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing and strengthens protections for unmarried same-sex couples.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice. A Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied in Spain since 2005.

25490228B88831207743232.name: Andalucía
25490228B88831207743232.summary:
Andalucía stands under the national framework of Spain: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado, applies uniformly across all autonomous communities and governs the regional position. Any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route grounded in the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Constitution that replaces the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision that proved contentious in the parliamentary passage of the law.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on the gender marker recorded in the civil registry, so a visitor's operative basis for facility rules is the entry obtained through self-declaration rather than any medical documentation.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence, although discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics are defined and sanctioned under Ley 4/2023 itself.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Andalucía's own layer sits on top of that national floor and runs deeper than most Spanish regions. Ley 2/2014, an integral law for non-discrimination on grounds of gender identity, was among the first trans-specific regional laws in Europe. Ley 8/17 of 28 December, in force 4 February 2018, guarantees LGTBI rights and equal treatment for LGTBI people and their families. The regional government approved an equality strategy for 2024-2028 on 26 December 2024.

19177384B98145761763330.name: Catamarca
19177384B98145761763330.summary:
Catamarca stands under Argentina's national framework, and no separate provincial record was located that would change the assessment a trans visitor should carry. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the United Nations described it at the time as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

That statutory position has been narrowed by executive action. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree modifying the Gender Identity Law as it applies to minors and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prisons; Reuters reported that the first decree bans gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

Violence risk is set by national figures. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a rise of 62% year on year and the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, averaging one crime every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims, 142 cases, and gay men for 22%, 50 cases.

Protection machinery at national level has been dismantled. The federal anti-discrimination agency INADI has been closed, the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry eliminated, and trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota dismissed in 2024. Activists interviewed in April 2025 described the trans community's situation as chaotic and desperate, with violence, discrimination and poverty reported as worsened.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020, so that aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.
