Violence, discrimination and poverty affecting the trans community are reported as worsened; this region carries no separate reporting, so the national picture stands as its baseline.

Agencia Presentes (19 March 2026) on the National LGBT+ Hate Crimes Observatory's 2025 report: Argentina recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, up 62% year on year, the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, one crime every 38 hours. 19177384B69455221212116.name: Chubut
19177384B69455221212116.summary:

Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was also the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

Practical safety in the province is set by the national picture. Trans activists interviewed in April 2025 reported that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has worsened since President Milei took office and is worst outside Buenos Aires, in the more conservative interior provinces. 19177384B39000171219781.name: Córdoba
19177384B39000171219781.summary:
What a visitor to Córdoba faces is Argentina's national legal framework, and no source records a provincial rule that departs from it. Law 26.743, promulgated 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and anti-discrimination protection operates through a combination of national and provincial statutes.

That framework has been narrowed by executive decree and the narrowing binds Córdoba as it binds every other province. Emergency Decree 62/2025, issued in February 2025, amends the Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgery and comprehensive hormonal treatment; Decree 61/2025 governs where transgender people are held in the prison system. The Federación Argentina de Lesbianas, Gays, Bisexuales y Trans announced legal action, and constitutional experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called both decrees unlawful and unconstitutional. The decrees' ultimate judicial fate is not recorded in the sources.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented peak in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a 62% rise and a ten-year record, averaging one every 38 hours. Sixty-four of the cases involved institutional violence by security forces, against 17 in 2024; 32% of incidents occurred in police stations or prisons; in 43% of cases the perpetrator was unknown to the victim. Beatings were the main modality and public space the main setting.

Córdoba's own forces are named in that record. Between 18 and 26 November 2025, police of Salta, Córdoba and Buenos Aires provinces intervened in the deaths of three LGBT+ people in eight days, a documented pattern in which this province's police are explicitly identified. The sources do not specify which of the three deaths occurred in Córdoba or the circumstances of any individual case.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court removed in 2020. That gender-motivated aggravation is therefore not being applied in that line of cases.

19177384B45303095947895.name: Formosa
19177384B45303095947895.summary:
Formosa stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world on paper. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passing the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate 55-0 with one abstention, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval; the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010 as the first Latin American country to do so.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention; the outcome of that challenge is not established in the sources.

Protection machinery at the federal level has been dismantled. The national anti-discrimination agency INADI was abolished, and trans people hired under the 1 percent Trans Labor Quota were dismissed.

Violence risk is set by the national picture. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a 62 percent rise year on year and the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, averaging one every 38 hours. Perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space; beatings were the main modality. Institutional violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and 32 percent of 2025 incidents occurred inside police stations or prisons. Forty-three percent of perpetrators were strangers to their victims.

Activists reported in April 2025 that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers had worsened since Milei took office and was worst outside Buenos Aires, in the more conservative interior provinces. Formosa is one of those interior provinces, and the province has no local reporting infrastructure capable of generating separate records, so the national figures are the only available measure of what a visitor faces.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, with an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.

19177384B16625472822217.name: Misiones
19177384B16625472822217.summary:
Argentina's statutory framework remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, passed by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, was promulgated on 24 May 2012 and allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval; the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. The national identity document has offered an "X" marker since 2021. Marriage equality has been available since 2010, and anti-discrimination protection rests on a combination of national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree restricting adolescents' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, a measure reported elsewhere as DNU 62/2025, alongside a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the restriction illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention. The 2012 law remains formally in force, but activists told the Washington Blade in April 2025 that its guarantees are no longer being delivered in practice.

No Misiones-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for transgender visitors. Interior provinces with little local reporting infrastructure generate few records even where the risk is real, so the absence of Misiones material reflects documentation capacity rather than demonstrated safety.

The documented picture is national and deteriorating. At least 227 hate crimes against LGBT+ people were recorded across Argentina in 2025, a 62% increase on the previous year and the worst total of the national observatory's ten recorded years, an average of one attack every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 142 of the 227 victims, or 62.5% of the tally.

Physical violence against bodily integrity made up 147 cases, 64.8% of the total, with beatings the main modality. Perpetrators were predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers acting in public space, and the observatory attributes the surge to the national government's "cultural battle" against LGBTI+ people and to the surrounding hate discourse.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020. 19177384B81563233036116.name: Salta
19177384B81563233036116.summary:
Salta Province stands under Argentina's national framework. Law 26.743, approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated on 24 May 2012, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

That statutory position has been narrowed by executive action. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention. Reuters reported the ban on surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents.

Trans activists interviewed by the Washington Blade in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, described a chaotic and desperate situation. They reported that the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry was eliminated, that trans hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1% of public-sector posts, were dismissed, and that the quota is no longer being implemented. The 2012 Gender Identity Law and the 'X' marker on the national identity document, available since 2021, remain formally in force but are no longer guaranteed in practice, activists said.

Violence reached a documented peak in 2025. Agencia Presentes reported on 19 March 2026 that the national hate-crime observatory recorded at least 227 attacks against LGBT+ people over the year, a rise of 62% year-on-year and the worst of the observatory's ten recorded years, averaging one every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims, 142 of 227. Physical violence against bodily integrity made up 64.8% of cases, 147. Perpetrators were predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space, with beatings the main modality. The observatory attributes the surge to the national government's 'cultural battle' against LGBTI+ people and to hate discourse. The same period saw DNU 62/2025 restricting minors' gender-affirming treatments.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court removed in 2020, so that the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, with an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.

No Salta-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for transgender visitors. Interior provinces without local reporting infrastructure generate few records even where risk is real, so the absence of provincial data reflects documentation capacity rather than demonstrated safety.

19177384B47339545206363.summary:
San Juan operates under Argentina's national framework, and no San Juan-specific source shows a deviation material enough to score separately. The province is therefore assessed at the national position.

Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, remains formally in force. Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations called both measures unconstitutional, argued that abruptly suspending adolescent treatment endangers trans youth, and mounted a judicial challenge; the outcome of that challenge is not recorded in the sources.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people peaked in 2025. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence of Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance removed on appeal in 2020, so that aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

A visitor to San Juan can expect the 2012 Gender Identity Law's recognition procedure to be available on national terms, while the under-18 restrictions of DNU 62/2025 and the prison-placement rules of DNU 61/2025 apply locally as everywhere else in Argentina.

19177384B8726453430521.name: San Luis
19177384B8726453430521.summary:
San Luis stands under the national framework: Argentina's Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passing the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate 55 votes to one abstention, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and an 'X' marker has been available on the national identity document since 2021. The United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010.

For a visitor the operating position has narrowed without the statute being repealed. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei published decree DNU 62/2025 amending Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions, alongside decree DNU 61/2025 altering prison-sentencing law to change the placement of trans detainees. Both decrees apply nationally, to every province, including San Luis. Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measures unconstitutional, argued that abruptly suspending adolescent treatments endangers trans youth, and signalled a judicial challenge.

Activists from organisations named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins told the Washington Blade in April 2025 that the community faces a chaotic and desperate situation, and that the 2012 Gender Identity Law, while still formally in force, is no longer guaranteed in practice.

Milei's Feb 5 2025 decree restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgeries and hormone treatments. The 2012 Gender Identity Law (legal gender change without medical intervention, 'X' DNI marker since 2021) remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed, activists report.

19177384B6836410786482.name: Santa Fe
19177384B6836410786482.summary:
Santa Fe province has no trans-specific statute of its own that the source inventory documents. For a trans visitor, the operative legal picture is Argentina's national framework, which extends to every province. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and has allowed an 'X' marker on the national identity document since 2021.

That statutory position has been narrowed by executive decree. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei published DNU 62/2025, amending Article 11 of the 2012 Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions, alongside DNU 61/2025, which alters prison-sentencing law to change the placement of transgender detainees. Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations interviewed by Agencia Presentes called both measures unconstitutional and said the abrupt suspension of adolescent treatments endangers transgender youth; both decrees face judicial challenge and apply to every province.

Enforcement exposure in 2025 was severe. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours. Cases in which security-force personnel were the perpetrators rose from 17 to 64, a doubling that materially changes what a trans visitor should expect from police contact.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins, described a chaotic and desperate situation under the Milei government. They reported that the national Women/Gender/Diversity Ministry was eliminated, that trans hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law covering 1 per cent of public-sector posts were dismissed, and that the quota is no longer being implemented. They also reported that the 2012 Gender Identity Law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice.

Santa Fe is nonetheless better documented than most provinces on the violence question: the provincial government publishes violent-death statistics that include transfemicidios and travesticidios, and national registers name provincial transfemicide victims. No provincial enforcement series with a source was found in the inventory.

On judicial protection for gender-motivated killing, Argentina's Supreme Court in April 2025 left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated aggravation is therefore not currently applied in that line of cases.

19177384B61792957744675.name: Santiago del Estero
19177384B61792957744675.summary:
Santiago del Estero stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, passed by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, was promulgated on 24 May 2012 and allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. No provincial rule departing from that statute appears in the sources, so a trans visitor's identity documents are not gated by medical approval here.

Violence is the operative visitor concern. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio LGBT+ recorded at least 227 bias-motivated crimes against LGBT people in Argentina over 2025, a record and up on 2024, averaging one every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims (142 cases); 18 trans men were targeted against 5 in 2024, alongside 13 lesbians and 4 non-binary people. Physical violence made up 64.8% of cases (147).

Roughly 32% of the 2025 cases occurred inside police stations or penal institutions, and recorded police involvement jumped from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025. Contact with the police, whether at a stop or in detention, is therefore the setting in which a substantial share of documented harm takes place.

Official posture is adverse at national level. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree restricting minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prisons. Reuters reported the ban on surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents; legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

Argentine trans activists interviewed on 4 April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, described the community's situation as chaotic and desperate, with heightened exposure to violence, discrimination and poverty under the Milei government's policies.

Argentine trans activists interviewed 4 Apr 2025 describe the community as facing a 'chaotic, desperate' situation with heightened exposure to violence, discrimination and poverty; the 2012 Gender Identity Law (legal gender change without medical gatekeeping) remains on the books. This national framework is what a trans visitor stands under in this Argentine province.

National-framework report (Agencia Presentes, 19 Mar 2026) on the Observatorio Nacional de Crimenes de Odio LGBT+ figures: 2025 set a record with at least 227 bias-motivated crimes against LGBT people in Argentina (up on 2024), one every 38 hours; 62.5% of victims (142) were trans women or travestis, 18 trans men (vs 5 in 2024), 13 lesbians and 4 non-binary people; 64.8% (147 cases) were physical violence and 32% occurred in police stations or penal institutions, with police involvement jumping from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025. 19177384B61792957744675.tangentialFactors:
The federal Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry was eliminated under President Milei, and trans employees hired under the Trans Labour Quota Law were dismissed, removing both a policy institution and a visible employment foothold for trans Argentines.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated aggravation is therefore not currently applied in that line of cases, even as the underlying conviction holds.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-state organisations, with an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position. 19177384B7010788354129.name: Tierra del Fuego
19177384B7010788354129.summary:
Tierra del Fuego, an Argentine province, stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passing the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate 55 votes to one abstention on 9 May, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and it remains on the books. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. A trans adult visitor's identity documents are therefore not gated by medical approval on arrival.

The framework has been narrowed by executive action. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree restricting minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, reported by Reuters as a ban on those procedures for adolescents; a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention, so its litigation status is unresolved. The same government eliminated the federal Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and dismissed trans employees hired under the Trans Labour Quota Law.

Practical exposure to violence is the operative visitor concern. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity across 2025, a record, averaging one every 38 hours and up on 2024. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims (142 people), with 18 trans men targeted against 5 in 2024, alongside 13 lesbians and 4 non-binary people. Physical violence made up 64.8% of cases (147).

Police contact is where the exposure concentrates. About 32% of the 2025 cases occurred inside police stations or penal institutions, and recorded police involvement rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025. For a traveler, that is the authorities-contact surface met on any stop, search or detention rather than a background risk.

Argentine trans activists interviewed on 4 April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, described the community as facing a chaotic and desperate situation with heightened exposure to violence, discrimination and poverty under the Milei government's policies.

No Tierra del Fuego-specific deviation from the national position has been sourced material enough to score separately, so the province is assessed at the national score.

17162690B9130125042960.name: Lower Silesian Voivodeship
17162690B9130125042960.summary:
Lower Silesian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland, and no source in the inventory records a local deviation in law or enforcement that would distinguish this voivodeship from the country as a whole. What a trans visitor meets in Wrocław or elsewhere in the province is the Polish national position, including its documented failures in custody.

Detention is the clearest documented risk. In a case published by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Polish law bars such placement wherever a stay would threaten a person's life or health or where the person shows signs of having suffered violence. The Border Guard refused to move or release her despite that bar, and she was released only after the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander; the case page was updated on 28 March 2024. The case also records her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may face both interrupted medical care and unsafe placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene on custody healthcare. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights held that Polish prison authorities violated a trans woman's right to private and family life under Article 8 of the Convention by denying her hormone-replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The Court found that the refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate, while leaving the alleged breaches of Articles 3 and 14 undecided. The judgment binds Poland and governs trans healthcare in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, including Lower Silesian. Poland operates no specialised trans prison section, and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities. Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

The wider legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Donald Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

17162690B71775569625336.name: Greater Poland Voivodeship
17162690B71775569625336.summary:
Greater Poland Voivodeship stands under Poland's national framework, and the sources document no voivodeship-specific deviation from it. Entry is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory records visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days, and lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status.

Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention reported that a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Polish law bars placement wherever a stay would threaten life or health or the person shows signs of having suffered violence; the Border Guard refused to move or release her regardless, and she was freed only after the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication. The case also documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may be exposed to both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying hormone replacement therapy to a trans prisoner held in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The Court left the alleged Article 3 and Article 14 breaches undecided, but held that the refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate. The judgment binds Poland as a whole and is the governing standard for trans healthcare in Polish custody, including in Greater Poland Voivodeship. Poland operates no specialised trans prison section, and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

The protective legal layer is unsettled. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

17162690B77437931625010.name: Pomeranian Voivodeship
17162690B77437931625010.summary:
Pomeranian Voivodeship stands under Poland's national framework, and the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in that framework is detention. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention reported that a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. The Border Guard refused to move or release her despite her identification as a woman and her warning that stopping the medication would harm her; the Border Guard Commander ordered her release only after the legal-aid organisation intervened, citing Polish law, court rulings and international standards, on the ground that continued detention there posed a serious health risk. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months while she was held. The case also recorded her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may face both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Courts have proved willing to intervene against that pattern. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans woman hormone replacement therapy while she was imprisoned, despite hormones having been prescribed to her for almost two years, and awarded EUR 8,000 in damages. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status.

Protection on gender-identity grounds is not yet in force. There is no hate-crime protection covering sexual orientation or gender identity; a March 2025 amendment bill was referred to the Constitutional Tribunal, with hearings held in July and September 2025. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation, and a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, with a second bill following in late October 2024. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024, and the status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

17162690B18723007704312.name: Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship
17162690B18723007704312.summary:
Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland, where legal gender recognition remains court-based and medically gatekept, and where no hate-crime protection on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation is in force. The March 2025 amendment bill that would introduce such protection was referred to the Constitutional Tribunal, with hearings held in July and September 2025.

Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in Poland. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, a citizen on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. The Border Guard refused to move or release her despite her identifying as a woman and warning that stopping the medication would harm her. After the legal-aid organisation intervened citing Polish law, court rulings and international standards, the Border Guard Commander released her on the ground that continued detention there posed a serious health risk. Detained foreign trans women in Poland therefore face placement in male-only facilities until formally challenged, and release can depend on legal intervention.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans woman hormone replacement therapy while imprisoned, despite hormones having been prescribed to her for almost two years, and awarded EUR 8,000 in damages; the Article 3 claim was rejected. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days.

The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. 27671186B81745654473385.name: Cross River
27671186B81745654473385.summary:
Visitors in every state stand under the national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act applies nationwide with up to 14 years' imprisonment for all persons including tourists; additional Sharia criminal law applies in the northern states.

The national law applies here in full — the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (up to 14 years, extends to tourists, bans LGBTQ+ organisations and public expression of identity) plus the inherited criminal provisions; national monitoring recorded 89 extortions, 118 harassment incidents and more than 20 unlawful detentions of LGBTQ+ people by law-enforcement officials in 2024 alone, with detentions for "looking gay" and release on payment of a bribe reported. This division sits outside the twelve northern states that carry a separate religious-law death-penalty regime for same-sex conduct. Dating-app "kito" extortion gangs are a nationwide app-user risk, and foreign government travel advice warns LGBT travellers of arrest, violence and blackmail.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria — Wikipedia
sources.summary: Cross River falls under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 makes same-sex marriage or civil union, and registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or publicly showing same-sex affection, punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment nationwide. The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men (14 years) and gross indecency between men (3 years). The twelve northern states under Shari'a law carry up to a death-penalty maximum: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. Cross River is not among them. The source documents the nationwide 'kito' entrapment-and-blackmail scheme targeting gay men and trans women, police profiling and extortion of people perceived as gay, and mass arrests (42 men in Lagos, August 2017; 53 charged in Kaduna, April 2017; 100+ detained after a Delta hotel raid, June 2018; 67 in Warri, August 2023; 76 in Gombe, October 2023). No anti-discrimination protections exist for LGBTQ people.

sources.title: "Everyone's on the Game": Corruption and Human Rights Abuses by the Nigeria Police Force (Human Rights Watch)
sources.summary: Human Rights Watch's 17 August 2010 report on the Nigeria Police Force documents arbitrary arrests, mass 'raid' arrests, prolonged unlawful detention used as a 'cash cow', and extortion using threats and acts of physical abuse, with bribery the standard price of release. Research was conducted in June and July 2010 in Lagos, Anambra and Kaduna states and the federal capital as case studies of three of Nigeria's six geopolitical zones. The report is national in scope and does not name Cross River. It substantiates the national baseline that police treat suspected same-sex conduct and perceived 'gayness' as an extortion opportunity, with release on payment of a bribe as the documented outcome.

27671186B83907961412659.summary:
Ogun State, a state in southern Nigeria, has no recorded protective statute of its own for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people, and the sources reviewed contain no incident series or documented enforcement divergence specific to Ogun. The national framework applies in full, and it criminalises same-sex conduct far beyond marriage.

The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 is the operative national statute. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that the Act also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have invoked the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at the point of entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that religious criminal law in twelve states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advice for Nigeria, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers that they face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, 14 years' imprisonment under the 2014 Act, and death-penalty risk in states applying religious criminal law.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

The killing of a 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama in August 2024 is the most closely documented case of anti-trans violence in this material. Her beaten body was found on a highway in the national capital hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend, and she had expressed fears for her life in the previous year. Nigerian police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged. Nothing in this material identifies a comparable Ogun-specific incident series.

Extortion and physical abuse by police officers acting on perceived sexual orientation are recorded nationally. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, on the basis of looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its statutory text, a dynamic that applies in Ogun as it does elsewhere in the country.

Visitors and residents who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Detention conditions for transgender detainees are exposed by the case of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to official discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the 2014 Act reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. No sub-national jurisdiction in the sources reviewed departs from that position, and no regional protective law exists for Ogun residents or for travellers passing through the state.

27671186B41407594687181.summary:
Ondo State stands under Nigeria's national framework. Same-sex conduct has been criminalised across the country since 1916, and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, criminalises all forms of same-sex union with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The Act's reach extends to participants and guests at same-sex weddings, according to the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory reported in August 2026.

The Shari'a penalty layer, under which male sodomy can be punished by death, operates only in the twelve states with Shari'a-based criminal codes and does not extend to Ondo. As a state in the southern part of the country, Ondo sits under the secular Criminal Code, where Section 217 makes it a felony for any male to commit or procure an act of gross indecency with another male, in public or in private, carrying three years' imprisonment. The maximum penalty available in the southern states is a life sentence.

No state-specific protective statute, enforcement divergence or recorded incident series has been documented for Ondo. Nigeria provides no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protection and no recognition of same-sex relationships, so a trans visitor has no statutory recourse against refusal of service, police mistreatment or dismissal. Trans identity is not expressly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression remains exposed: proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have been reported, and whether any such proposal has been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Screening and entry carry documented risk. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 records countrywide patterns of arrest, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people, and the FCDO advisory warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation. The same note confirms that the national criminal framework applies in all states, including the 2014 statute, so a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor to Ondo is exposed to the same arrest risk at the point of contact with police as anywhere else in the country.

Delta State stands under Nigeria's national framework: same-sex conduct has been criminal across the country since 1916, and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed in January 2014, criminalises all forms of same-sex union with a maximum federal penalty of 14 years' imprisonment. The statute reaches beyond unions to cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship, the operation of gay organisations, and participants and guests at same-sex weddings. Section 217 of the Criminal Code makes male gross indecency a felony carrying three years' imprisonment. The death penalty is confined to the twelve northern Shari'a states, where male sodomy is punishable under state Zina provisions. No state-specific protective statute exists in Delta.

Delta has a dated record of active enforcement. In June 2018 Nigerian police arrested more than 100 party-goers at a hotel in Asaba on charges that they were gays and lesbians, and by July 2018 those detainees were facing homosexuality-related charges in court. On 27 August 2023 officers from the Ekpan Division in Uvwie Local Government Area raided Teebolus Hotel on Refinery Road, Ekpan, at 9 pm and arrested 67 suspects for allegedly conducting and attending a same-sex wedding ceremony between Daniel Pius, 22, and Maxwel Ohwonohwo, 20. Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the raid followed a confession by a male cross-dresser that he belonged to a gay club travelling to a gay marriage ceremony; the suspects fled on the officers' arrival, 67 were chased and arrested, and drugs and gay marriage ceremonial dresses were recovered. Edafe said efforts continued to arrest fleeing members for possible prosecution. One suspect alleged he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated.

The United States Department of State 2023 human rights report, cited in the UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025, records that on the same date police in Delta State raided a 'white party' organised by the LGBTQI+ community and detained more than 200 individuals, alleging the event was a same-sex wedding; some civil society representatives disputed that account. Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression carries exposure. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in northern states.

27671186B95832466049157.name: Rivers
27671186B95832466049157.summary:
Rivers State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, and the Nigerian Criminal Code as applied in the southern states govern conduct there. These sources record no Rivers-specific statute, incident series or enforcement divergence, so the federal rules are what a visitor to Port Harcourt should expect to face.

The 2014 Act reaches far beyond marriage. It renders same-sex marriage and civil unions invalid and illegal, criminalises registering, operating, participating in or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations, and bans same-sex cohabitation together with any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) sets the penalty band for the organisational offences at 10 to 14 years' imprisonment and records that police used the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest after it passed.

Sex between men remains criminalised under the Nigerian Criminal Code in the south, with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment, and gross indecency carries up to 3 years. Rivers is not one of the twelve northern states where Sharia law operates. The death penalty for male sodomy under state Zina provisions attaches to those northern states, and the UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that Sharia criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women there.

One part of the statute has been struck down. In 2022 a group of Nigerian human rights organisations and activists sued over Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Act, and the court ruled them unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide, which effectively allows LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise freely. The ruling does not decriminalise same-sex conduct, and Nigeria otherwise offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people.

Enforcement against individuals is documented and extortionate. Human Rights Watch describes arbitrary arrest and police extortion as commonplace after the Act, citing eight of the 21 young men arrested but never charged at a birthday party in Ibadan. The only Port Harcourt-specific incident in these sources is that of Daniel, a 21-year-old gay man from Lagos who in January 2015 travelled to the city to meet someone he had contacted on Facebook, was attacked and sexually abused there, and did not report it to the police. That case and the nationwide abuse pattern indicate what a same-sex couple or trans visitor faces in Rivers.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. Detention raises a further question of placement: press coverage at the sentencing of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that assignment between male and female sections was left to discretion.

Trans-specific violence is on the record. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in the national capital hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and six months after the killing no suspects had been charged. Violence by police against perceived gay people continues as a routine feature of enforcement: in March 2025 Lagos police struck Okafor, a 24-year-old stopped for looking gay, in the mouth with a gun butt and released him only after he paid almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in some northern states, and of the Act's reach to helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings.

27671186B96047513549152.name: Kogi
27671186B96047513549152.summary:
Kogi State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reaches far beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation carries criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve Sharia-administering states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Kogi does not administer Sharia, so the federal 14-year maximum is the operative ceiling there.

The statute's construction is settled. The Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014; entering a same-sex marriage or civil union carries 14 years' imprisonment, while registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or making a public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, carries 10 years. The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years and gross indecency with up to 3 years.

Partial constitutional relief exists. In 2022 a coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations won a court ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country, which effectively allows LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise. The ruling does not extend to the conduct and marriage-prohibition provisions. The Constitution contains no specific protections on the basis of sexual orientation, and there are no national anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. The beaten body of the 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama was found on a highway in the capital on 9 August 2024; she had been stabbed a year earlier and had feared for her life, and police opened an investigation. Police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing. Six months after the killing no suspects had been charged, according to the Dial (February 2025). Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are reported as common in Nigeria, especially in the twelve Sharia states.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by police in Lagos, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Official travel guidance reflects the risk. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated Nigeria travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in some northern states, and notes that the Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act also reaches people who help arrange or attend same-sex weddings.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common across Nigeria, including in Kogi, and are especially frequent in northern states.

SaharaReporters (19 Aug 2026): the UK FCDO's updated Nigeria travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation — same-sex activity is illegal with up to 14 years' imprisonment; some northern states under Sharia law can prescribe the death penalty; the Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act also reaches helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings.

27671186B51792679167430.name: Plateau
27671186B51792679167430.summary:
Plateau State stands under Nigeria's national criminal framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the statute reaches beyond the couple: helpers who arrange same-sex weddings and attendees who witness them are also exposed. Sexual orientation and gender expression carry criminal consequences from the moment of entry, and the exposure is not confined to conduct between partners.

Plateau State is a North Central zone state with its capital at Jos and a population of roughly 4.7 million. Two features of its position matter for a trans visitor. It does not carry the concentration of mass arrests and communal tension documented for the wider North Central zone, and Shari'a criminal law does not apply there. In the twelve northern states where Shari'a is in force, same-sex acts between men carry the death penalty under state Zina provisions; Plateau is not among them, so the capital-punishment risk documented in northern Nigeria does not extend to this jurisdiction.

The legal regime is hostile at the level of the whole country. No legal protections for LGBTQ+ people exist in Nigeria, and violence against them is reported as frequent. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated 2026 travel advice for Nigeria warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of the death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in northern states.

One legal complication is worth recording. In a 2022 challenge, a Nigerian court ruled Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act unconstitutional and unenforceable anywhere in the country. The scope of that ruling as applied to enforcement on the ground, including in Plateau, is not settled by the sources available here, and a visitor should not assume the partial invalidation has altered practice.

Trans Nigerians face documented lethal violence and police indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, known as the TikToker Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in the capital hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and six months after the killing no suspect had been charged. Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed, and press coverage of the imprisonment of the prominent transgender woman Bobrisky openly debated which prison section the authorities should place her in, indicating that placement between male and female wings is left to official discretion.

Police enforcement is arbitrary and extortionate. A 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police in March 2025 was struck in the mouth with a gun butt and released only after paying part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded for looking gay. Dating-app users face entrapment: kito gangs lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. Visitors using apps in Plateau face the same national pattern.

27671186B76680224160916.name: Anambra
27671186B76680224160916.summary:
Anambra stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches conduct well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch reported in October 2016 that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Anambra lies outside the twelve states that apply Shari'a criminal law, so the federal penalties apply here in full and the death-penalty provisions for male sodomy under state Zina rules do not reach this state. Same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law at entry, carrying up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Shari'a provisions in those twelve states criminalise same-sex acts between men and between women.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated travel advice for Nigeria, reported by SaharaReporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a in some northern states. The Act also reaches people who help arrange or attend same-sex weddings.

In 2022 a court ruled Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act unconstitutional and unenforceable in any part of the country. The remaining provisions stand, and LGBTQ+ people in Nigeria have no legal protections against discrimination or violence.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters reported in September 2022 that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial recorded in February 2025 that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE reported in March 2025 that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation documented in April 2024 kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

27671186B74554005070963.name: Nasarawa
27671186B74554005070963.summary:
Nasarawa State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) applies across the country and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure on entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory of 19 August 2026, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, states that same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract up to 14 years' imprisonment, and confirms that the federal law extends to people who arrange, attend or conduct same-sex weddings and to those involved with gay groups or organisations. It further warns that some northern states operate Sharia law under which same-sex activity can attract the death penalty, and that breaching curfews or movement restrictions risks arrest and detention.

Trans-specific violence is documented. BBC (9 August 2024) reports that the beaten body of the 33-year-old Nigerian transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama was found along the Katampe–Mabushi expressway in the capital, in a suspected murder, roughly a year after she had said she feared for her life; an investigation was announced, and the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Despite formal constitutional guarantees of non-discrimination and private and family life, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states. Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment: the Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

No source in the current inventory documents enforcement, arrests or facilities specific to Nasarawa State itself; the state-level picture is inherited from the national framework and from incidents recorded elsewhere in Nigeria.

Same-sex sexual acts between men carry up to 14 years' imprisonment under secular law, and the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act makes entering a same-sex marriage or civil union punishable by 14 years' imprisonment while giving 10 years to anyone who 'administers, witnesses, abets or aides the solemnization' of one or supports the registration, operation and sustenance of gay clubs, societies, organisations, processions or meetings. Sharia penal codes apply to Muslims in the 12 northern states, with death as the maximum penalty for men, at least four sharia death sentences imposed since 2022 and none carried out. The note documents tens of LGBT+ arrests per year plus police and Islamic-police harassment including beatings, blackmail, extortion and torture. Sharia does not apply in Abia, a southern state, while the federal penalties and the national arrest climate apply in full.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria – Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's Nigeria article is the national-framework source for Abia: the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act 2013, in force from January 2014, criminalises same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment and also punishes registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations and public displays of same-sex amorous relationships, with a 2022 federal court ruling striking down sections of the Act as unconstitutional. The article lists the 12 northern states operating sharia criminal law for Muslims: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. Abia is not among them, so the sharia provisions do not reach this southern state while the federal 14-year framework and the national climate of arrests and community hostility apply.

27671186B83117616801018.localsOnly:
Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and residents of Abia live under the same arrest climate documented nationally, including community hostility that operates independently of any single prosecution.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024.

Press coverage at Bobrisky's sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to official discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Registration, operation or participation in gay clubs, societies and organisations is itself an offence under the national statute, and public displays of same-sex amorous relationships are separately punishable, which constrains organising and visible community life inside Abia as much as anywhere else in Nigeria.

27671186B91150779192485.name: Ekiti
27671186B91150779192485.summary:
Ekiti State stands within Nigeria's uniform national criminalisation framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches far beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at the border. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advice for Nigeria, updated by 19 August 2026 and reported by SaharaReporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation; of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity; of death-penalty risk under Sharia provisions in some northern states; and of liability for those who help arrange or attend a same-sex wedding. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public.

Enforcement in Ekiti State is documented. Human Rights Watch records that on 21 January 2014, days after the SSMPA was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten by six men in Ado Ekiti, the state capital, who threatened her with 14 years in prison; the report states she was beaten at least twice over the period. In September 2014 a gay man was arrested at the Faguyi bar in Ado Ekiti, his third arrest, and was released after two days in detention after paying 2,000 Naira for himself and 10,000 Naira for a friend. Also in 2014 a 25-year-old gay man was extorted by a state investigator in Ado Ekiti.

Trans-specific violence is documented nationally. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Detention carries a specific placement risk for trans women. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion, and an October 2024 investigative panel found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
