27671186B37873222803025.name: Osun
27671186B37873222803025.summary:
Osun operates inside Nigeria's federal criminalisation framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies across the country and covers tourists and non-citizens as well as residents, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, for cohabitation between same-sex partners, and for any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship.

The statute binds people beyond the couple. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory of 19 August 2026 states that the law also reaches those who arrange or organise same-sex weddings and anyone involved with gay groups, and Human Rights Watch has documented police using the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Same-sex conduct between men is a criminal offence under Nigeria's secular law, with a maximum of 14 years' imprisonment. A parallel Sharia law layer in twelve states carries the death penalty for male sodomy. Under the UK Home Office country note of June 2025, updated April 2026, that layer does not extend to Osun; the federal penalties and the risk of arrest apply in Osun in full.

Trans identity is not expressly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed to it. Nigerians live with proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and the sources available here do not establish whether those proposals have been enacted.

Trans-specific violence is documented and, so far, unpunished. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found along an expressway in the capital, about a year after she had said she feared for her life. Police described the deceased as a man in female clothing. Six months after the killing, no suspect had been charged.

Enforcement by police frequently takes the form of extortion. A 24-year-old man stopped by police in Lagos in March 2025 was struck in the mouth with a gun butt and released only after paying close to half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. People affected describe the same-sex marriage law as a weaponised instrument that generates a climate of hostility independent of its wording.

Dating apps carry documented abduction risk. Kito gangs lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar applications to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of being outed.

Nigeria provides no legal protection for LGBTQ+ people, and the 2014 Act reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. Formal constitutional guarantees of non-discrimination and of private and family life sit alongside mass arrest and detention of LGBTQ+ people, reported most frequently in the states where the Sharia layer applies.

The UK advisory warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, and of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, with death-penalty exposure identified for the states where religious criminal law operates. None of that national exposure is reduced by entering Osun.

27671186B90910891533368.name: Enugu
27671186B90910891533368.summary:
Enugu State lies wholly within Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches conduct well beyond marriage: cohabitation between same-sex partners, public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment. Human Rights Watch records that police have invoked the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest. Trans identity is not expressly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed through that enforcement culture.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation. It states that same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years' imprisonment, that some northern states apply Sharia provisions capable of prescribing the death penalty, and that the same-sex marriage law reaches those who help arrange or attend such weddings. Enugu State is not among the Sharia states, so the death-penalty layer does not apply there.

Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report documents the Act's operation in Enugu State itself. Sharon, a bisexual woman from Enugu State, told the researchers that she married a male friend from high school in July 2015 under family and social pressure and that for as long as she remained in Nigeria she would stay married. The finding illustrates how the statute's prohibition of same-sex partnership pushes people into heterosexual marriages rather than merely punishing them.

Healthcare access is a documented gap in Enugu State. An activist based in Enugu told Human Rights Watch that the major challenge in the state is the rate of HIV and STIs among community members, and that there are no clinics where gay men and men who have sex with men can obtain services without fear of harassment. Many therefore travel to Lagos and other states for care, a journey that itself requires disclosure and carries exposure.

Violence risk for visitors remains elevated across the country. Police have used the Act to stop, beat and extort men perceived as gay, and kito gangs lure LGBTQ+ people through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. Dating-app use in Enugu therefore carries the same entrapment risk documented elsewhere in Nigeria.

27671186B83252759475924.name: Taraba
27671186B83252759475924.summary:
Taraba State stands under Nigeria's national criminal framework. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal in the territory since 1904 in the Northern Region and region-wide from 1916, and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) now carries penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, applicable to all persons present in the country, visitors included.

The SSMPA reaches far beyond marriage. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation, participation in or support of gay clubs, societies and organisations, with prison terms of 10 to 14 years, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. The sources in this inventory do not document any Sharia application in Taraba itself.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised under the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in the national capital hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is routine. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in states that have adopted it. The same advisory records that the SSMPA criminalises attending, organising or promoting same-sex weddings and registering or publicly promoting gay groups.

Enforcement of the SSMPA has been arbitrary and punitive since inception. Human Rights Watch found that its passage was immediately followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detention of LGBT people across the country, including the arrest without charge of 21 young men at a birthday gathering in Ibadan and repeated police detentions reported by interviewees elsewhere.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Taraba itself yields no statute, charge or incident in the available sources. The state's visitor assessment therefore rests on the national pattern: a nationwide SSMPA, documented arbitrary enforcement, and a documented risk of extralegal violence, with no Taraba-specific mitigation sourced.

27671186B90886723034258.name: Ebonyi
27671186B90886723034258.summary:
Ebonyi State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch records that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The Act also criminalises attending, organising or promoting same-sex weddings and registering or publicly promoting gay groups.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Ebonyi is not among the states that have adopted Sharia, so the death-penalty provisions do not apply there; the federal maximum of 14 years is the operative exposure for a visitor in Ebonyi.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Enforcement against LGBTQ+ people is documented nationally. Human Rights Watch found that the SSMPA's passage on 7 January 2014 was immediately followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detention across the country, including the arrest without charge of 21 young men at a birthday gathering in Ibadan and repeated police detentions reported elsewhere. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

If detained, placement between male and female sections is left to discretion. Press coverage of Bobrisky's (Idris Okuneye) imprisonment in 2024 openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in; she was held in a maximum-security prison in Lagos.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters (19 August 2026), warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

65028918B98829509874887.name: West Nusa Tenggara
65028918B98829509874887.summary:
West Nusa Tenggara stands under Indonesia's national framework, and the sources record no sub-national deviation for this province: no enacted bylaw, raid, arrest or incident targeting transgender people in West Nusa Tenggara, and no protective legislation for the province. The province is therefore assessed at the national risk level.

Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. Parliament passed a new Penal Code in December 2022 that took effect on 2 January 2026 and criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with penalties reported at up to two years' imprisonment and at up to one year where an immediate family member lodges the complaint. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, these provisions effectively criminalise all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Aceh applies Sharia law and punishes homosexuality by flogging or imprisonment; in February 2025 two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship. Aceh's punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors, and a trans visitor should treat Aceh as a distinct and more severe jurisdiction.

Venue raids are an established enforcement pattern. On 22 June 2025 police raided a privately rented villa after reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International stated the gathering violated no law. Further raids took place in South Jakarta in February and May 2025.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. His mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release; he died in custody. She alleges police beat him, and Indonesian police deny that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 on the growing repression of Indonesia's transgender community ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes are codified into law.

Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that Aceh and South Sumatra criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Punishments there are imposed under provincial religious law and bind anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. Banten carries no provincial criminalisation of same-sex relations in the sources examined, unlike Aceh and South Sumatra, and no Banten-specific statute, ordinance, raid, protection mechanism or service is documented in anything reviewed. A visitor in Banten therefore stands under the national framework those sources set out rather than under any provincial religious penalty.

Banten is one of nine provinces where the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue identity papers to transgender residents since June 2021, the others being West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua. 65028918B13838862025135.name: Central Java
65028918B13838862025135.summary:
Central Java is a province of Indonesia and a visitor there stands under Indonesia's national legal framework, which the sources record as containing no criminalisation of gender identity itself, no X marker on identity documents, and no legal recognition of same-sex marriage. No provision specific to Central Java that would alter that position for a visitor is documented in the sources.

The national penal code was passed by the House of Representatives on 6 December 2022, signed by President Joko Widodo, and took effect on 2 January 2026. It criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with penalties reported at up to two years' imprisonment under the framework and at up to one year where a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, but because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls within the outside-marriage restriction. Reporting indicates that prosecutions under this provision are selective rather than systematic. The United Nations and other international critics condemned the code for failing to accommodate protections and rights for LGBT individuals and for domestic partnerships.

Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run an outreach issuing identification papers (KTP) to transgender Indonesians. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, and the birth gender is printed on the card unless a court order was obtained beforehand. Electronic identity cards were issued to transgender people in nine provinces. A visitor's documents therefore follow the same two-descriptor system.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes are codified into law; commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy. 65028918B19721185942402.name: West Kalimantan
65028918B19721185942402.summary:
West Kalimantan records no separate LGBTI legislation or enforcement, so the national framework of Indonesia governs what a visitor faces, and no sub-national divergence is documented in the sources.

Indonesia's penal code, signed in December 2022 and in force from 2 January 2026, penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Indonesian law provides no explicit protection of transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and the Constitution does not address sexual orientation or gender identity. On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected a conservative petition 5-4 that had sought to criminalise homosexuality and extra-marital sex, declining to add them to the Penal Code.

Violence against trans people is documented at national scale. Between 14 and 16 July 2026 vigilante mobs attacked trans women across Indonesia. In Bogor, more than fifteen trans women were doused, stripped and beaten, and footage of the attacks was shared online.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among nonmilitary threats, alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction.

A trans traveller has died in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Peruvian Harvard student and trans activist, was arrested on drug charges at an Indonesian airport in 2022 while on honeymoon. During a call his mother was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release; he died in custody. She alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police deny that violence was used.

Venue raids are a documented enforcement route. On 22 June 2025 police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International stated that the gathering violated no law and called the operation a violation of human rights and privacy.

Legal gender recognition is demanding: changing gender markers on documents requires sex reassignment surgery plus judicial approval.

65028918B30999004822283.name: Bengkulu
65028918B30999004822283.summary:
Bengkulu is a province of Indonesia, and trans visitors here stand under Indonesia's national legal and policy framework. No Bengkulu-specific statute, enforcement action, protection measure, service or documented incident directed at trans people appears in the sources; the province is therefore assessed on national conditions.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is not itself criminalised in private in Indonesia outside the provinces with their own provisions. There are, however, no anti-discrimination protections for lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people anywhere in the country.

The amended national penal code, signed in December 2022, took effect on 2 January 2026. Its provision on consensual sex outside marriage is the principal route by which same-sex activity becomes prosecutable, because Indonesia does not permit same-sex marriage and so no same-sex relationship can be registered as marital. Reporting on the provision describes the penalty as up to two years' imprisonment, while the national rights overview in the sources gives up to one year and records that the offence is actionable on the complaint of an immediate family member. The sources do not reconcile the two figures. Prosecutions reported to date are selective rather than systematic, and police and prosecutors have discretion over whether a complaint proceeds.

Legal gender recognition remains the hardest documentary requirement facing a trans visitor. Changing one's gender marker on Indonesian identity documents requires sex-reassignment surgery plus the approval of a judge. A trans person whose documents do not match their presentation carries a documentary exposure at checkpoints, immigration counters and hotels that has no non-surgical alternative route.

Two provinces maintain their own criminal provisions against same-sex sexual activity between men and between women: Aceh, where Sharia law applies and punishments are imposed under provincial religious law, and South Sumatra. Aceh's sanctions reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. In Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Police raids on LGBTQ+ venues and gatherings are a live enforcement mechanism. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering had violated no law. On 11 August 2025 three men were arrested over a Facebook community page.

Vigilante violence against trans people has intensified alongside official framing. A wave of mob attacks on transgender women swept Indonesia between 14 and 16 July 2026; in Bogor more than fifteen trans women were doused, stripped and beaten, and footage of the assaults was circulated online. Reporting from August 2026 ties that wave to a presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025, which lists 'the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture' among nonmilitary threats to be monitored and controlled alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy. Researchers cited in the same reporting document markedly hardened anti-queer public attitudes since 2016.

Hostility in this environment has produced fatal outcomes for foreign trans people. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. Authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release, according to a call made to his mother in Lima. He died in custody. His mother alleges that police beat him; Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Public opinion is strongly aligned with the official position. A 2025 Pew survey found that 93% of Indonesians rated homosexuality morally unacceptable. Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025.

65028918B48178230554278.name: Maluku
65028918B48178230554278.summary:
Maluku stands under Indonesia's national framework. Both audited sources for this province are national in scope and neither records a Maluku-specific ordinance, enforcement action, protection scheme or service, so the assessment below rests on the national picture those sources document.

The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual sexual activity between adults outside marriage. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum of two years' imprisonment, while the national overview notes a term of up to one year where an immediate family member lodges the complaint. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, every sexual act by a same-sex couple falls within the outside-marriage offence, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Criminalisation below the national level is concentrated in Aceh, where Sharia-based penalties reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors: two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship there in February 2025. The Human Dignity Trust profile also lists South Sumatra as criminalising same-sex conduct between men and between women. Neither province is Maluku, and the national overview identifies Aceh as the outlier rather than any eastern province.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

One death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody is directly documented. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. The Diplomat reported in August 2026 that the government is codifying anti-LGBT provisions while vigilante mobs attack transgender women, and commentators quoted by ABC News stated that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Legal gender recognition is available only after sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval, and only the sex descriptors 'male' and 'female' are recognised, with no third-gender option or X marker on Indonesian documents. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing electronic ID cards to transgender Indonesians, operating in nine provinces.

National law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution is silent on both. On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected a petition to criminalise homosexuality by five votes to four.

65028918B43243108525571.name: East Java
65028918B43243108525571.summary:
East Java stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. East Java has no provincial carve-out from this framework.

Indonesian law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex couples have no recognised legal relationship of any kind. A trans visitor whose foreign documents carry a changed gender marker is dealing with a jurisdiction in which legal gender change requires sex-reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, which indicates the standard Indonesian authorities apply to legal recognition of gender.

Violence risk is elevated by official framing and by mob action. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. The Diplomat reported in August 2026 that Indonesia's transgender community faces growing repression, with vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government takes steps to codify anti-LGBT provisions.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in 2022; during a call he was permitted to make, his mother was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody. His mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

The only province-level enforcement signal documented for East Java concerns detention conditions rather than prosecution. In February 2025 a transgender content creator became the first transgender detainee held in the province's women's prison after her file was declared complete on suspected defamation.

65028918B10722647473585.name: Bangka-Belitung Islands
65028918B10722647473585.summary:
Bangka-Belitung Islands stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is assessed as a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to one year's imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The provision applies in Bangka-Belitung Islands as throughout Indonesia.

No anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections exist for sexual orientation or gender identity anywhere in the national framework. Legal gender change requires sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unrecognised, so no same-sex relationship carries legal recognition.

Criminalisation operates at more than one level. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; those punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Enforcement elsewhere takes the form of venue raids: on 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting by The Diplomat in August 2026 describes Indonesia's transgender community facing growing repression, with vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government takes steps to codify anti-LGBT provisions. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

No deviation from this national position has been documented in Bangka-Belitung Islands in either direction, and the province-specific source reviewed yielded no usable finding on trans safety. The national score therefore applies without adjustment.

Three further indicators of the surrounding climate are on record. Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025. The Constitutional Court rejected a petition to criminalise gay sex on 14 December 2017 by 5-4. A 2025 Pew figure found 93% of Indonesians rating homosexuality "morally unacceptable".

65028918B90123187256494.name: Riau Islands
65028918B90123187256494.summary:
The Riau Islands stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is assessed as a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The country overview records the same provision as carrying up to one year's imprisonment when a complaint is lodged.

Two provinces of Indonesia, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; those punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Neither province is the Riau Islands, and no source in this inventory records equivalent provincial criminalisation here.

Enforcement elsewhere in Indonesia takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled, listing "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" alongside terrorism and drug addiction. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks: in July 2026 mobs attacked transgender women in several cities including West Java, with no prosecutions reported, and civil society describes rapidly worsening conditions. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

For the Riau Islands specifically, the inventory records no province-specific divergence from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02), and no unit-specific findings. Private same-sex conduct is not criminalised nationally but attracts no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection, and legal gender change requires sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval. A 2020 raid case documented in the country overview shows how enforcement varies with local bylaws: those held were released because no regional regulation existed.

15666254B97003483933575.name: Kuala Lumpur
15666254B97003483933575.summary:
Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct at the federal level. Sections 377A and 377B of the Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and apply to visitors. Section 377D's "gross indecency" offence carries up to two years. The federal territory of Kuala Lumpur stands directly under this Penal Code, with no local ordinance displacing it.

Every state and the federal territories also maintain Sharia enactments criminalising a man posing as a woman, punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim foreign visitor is not exposed to them; the federal Penal Code, however, applies to that visitor in full.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and conducted in public. On 28 November 2025 police together with Kuala Lumpur City Hall and the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) raided an all-male sauna in Chow Kit, arresting 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were published; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended.

The raid's aftermath carries direct exposure for foreign visitors. A magistrate rejected an extension of remand as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid. On 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

The Human Dignity Trust records enforcement with arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment since the 2018 election, alongside the 28 November operation. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that Jawi had his full licence to carry out enforcement against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences intact, and a High Court had earlier refused to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, drawing on interviews with 73 LGBT people between 2018 and 2021 including residents of Kuala Lumpur, describe state-sponsored discrimination as a defining feature of daily life and call on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, LGBT events and media content are censored, and there is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the practical picture is one of raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but venue-based operations now reach into the capital's nightlife and bath venues without warning, and detainees' identities can be published before any charge is laid.

15666254B50935235229272.name: Sabah
15666254B50935235229272.summary:
Sabah stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with penalties of up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and reach foreign visitors. The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Malaysia, last updated 16 December 2025, further records that transgender people can be targeted through the "gross indecency" offence as well as through state Sharia enactments.

Every state, Sabah included, maintains a Sharia enactment prohibiting cross-dressing and "males posing as females", carrying penalties of up to three years' imprisonment. These state offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim foreign visitor is not exposed to them; the federal Penal Code, by contrast, applies to everyone present in the country.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, reporting on 10 August 2022, documented state-backed discrimination against LGBT people across the federation: arrests, criminal prosecutions at both the federal and state-Sharia level, and a crackdown that has persisted since the 2018 election. The Human Dignity Trust profile likewise reports arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment under these provisions since 2018. The documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public exposure rather than individual stops against visitors.

The Nur Sajat case illustrates the machinery involved. In 2021 a transgender woman faced a religious-affairs arrest warrant and a search operation involving 122 officers. Both reports call for decriminalisation of same-sex conduct and gender diversity; no such reform has been enacted.

The audited sources for this record contain no Sabah-specific findings. Both the Human Dignity Trust profile and the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters report address the national framework and federation-wide patterns, and state expressly that they carry no findings particular to Sabah. The assessment for Sabah therefore rests on the national legal position and the national enforcement pattern.

For a visitor, the practical exposure is the federal layer: arrest under the Penal Code remains possible in law, while enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely the target of individual stops. The acute documented risk arises from venue raids, where detainees are held, identified publicly and prosecuted.

Sarawak is one of the 13 states whose Sharia enactments criminalise cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim visitor is not exposed to that layer; enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded. There is no same-sex marriage and no federal law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Documented enforcement since the 2018 election has been raid-based and public. An October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur produced at least 20 arrests of LGBT people, and an August raid on an LGBT venue detained twenty men. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops. The audited sources record no Sarawak-specific enforcement case, so the national pattern is what a visitor here should expect.

Trans people in Malaysia also face lethal violence. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months, and documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity.

15666254B15173108486297.name: Perak
15666254B15173108486297.summary:
Perak stands under Malaysia's national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of "gross indecency" with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping, and these provisions are not limited to Malaysians. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Every Malaysian state, Perak included, maintains a Sharia enactment criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", carrying up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, while the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops at checks.

A crackdown has been underway since the 2018 election. Police raided a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur in October 2022 with at least 20 LGBT people arrested, an August 2022 raid on an LGBT venue produced twenty male arrests, a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned, and in November 2023 Johor announced plans for conversion-therapy centres.

Queue-and-venue raids carry the sharpest exposure risk for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media had been pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid, the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions on 2 December, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional; the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences intact. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Official hostility is explicit. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the national capital district's Islamic religious department (Jawi) had his full licence to carry out enforcement actions against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled abroad and received UNHCR protection.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months, and documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded, there is no same-sex marriage, and no federal law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. A 2022 Human Rights Watch report, drawing on interviews with 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021, documents state religious authorities harassing LGBT activists and organisations and raiding private events across the federation. The report names no Perak-specific enforcement case, and no Perak-specific evidence appears in the audited sources; the national framework governs visitor exposure here.

15666254B4265207353082.name: Labuan
15666254B4265207353082.summary:
Labuan is a federal territory of Malaysia and stands under the Malaysian national framework: sections 377A and 377B of the Penal Code 1936 criminalise "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of gross indecency, carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping. The provisions apply to any person regardless of gender or consent, are not confined to Malaysian nationals, and therefore reach foreign visitors in Labuan.

The Sharia layer that criminalises cross-dressing and "a man posing as a woman" applies to Muslims only, and a dual court system places Muslims under Sharia jurisdiction while the federal courts handle Penal Code offences. A non-Muslim foreign visitor therefore falls outside the Sharia offences; the federal provisions, which carry the heavier penalties and apply to everyone, are the operative exposure.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded in the Malaysian framework, so a trans visitor cannot obtain documents matching their gender here. No federal law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no same-sex marriage or recognition of same-sex partners.

Enforcement documented since the 2018 election is raid-based rather than directed at individual stops: an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur produced arrests of at least 20 LGBT people, and an August raid on an LGBT venue detained twenty men. A Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned, and in November 2023 Johor state authorities announced plans for conversion-therapy centres.

Human Rights Watch, with Justice For Sisters, interviewed 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021, documenting state-backed discrimination, harassment of LGBT activists and organisations, and raids on private events, alongside a federal penal code punishing oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison.

Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had drawn at least 1,733 attendees by June 2021. Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported in the country, with transgender people particularly vulnerable.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor in Labuan, the practical exposure is the federal Penal Code and the pattern of venue-and-event raids with public outing, not Sharia jurisdiction. The sources reviewed record no Labuan-specific enforcement case and no documented targeting of foreign tourists.

Queue-and-venue operations carry acute exposure for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in the Chow Kit area of Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were published; 17 civil servants identified among those held were suspended. A magistrate rejected the extension of remand for lack of ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point, among them 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. A legal-aid organisation mobilised bailors and counsel. On 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Litigation has narrowed the state Sharia layer without loosening the federal one. A High Court request to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional was refused, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014, filed after 16 trans women were arrested at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Official hostility has been stated in explicit terms. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his full licence to carry out enforcement actions against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists called on him to revoke. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised over a charge of insulting Islam before she fled the country and received UNHCR protection.

Trans-specific lethal violence is documented alongside official indifference. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

28173009B80457268982215.name: Altai Krai
28173009B80457268982215.summary:
Altai Krai stands under the national framework of Russia, and the sources record no regional deviation: the 2023 prohibition on legal gender recognition and on gender-affirming care, the Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, and the expanded "propaganda" statutes apply in full to a visitor in this region.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the baseline a trans visitor here faces: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. A document presenting a gender marker that does not match the traveller's presentation therefore carries direct exposure at any check point where identity papers are examined.

Publicly "promoting" non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is an administrative offence punishable by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeat offences capable of becoming criminal and carrying up to four years' imprisonment. The 2023 extremist designation criminalises support of or activity within the designated movement, and at least 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.

The US State Department travel advisory covering Altai Krai advises against all travel to Russia and states that foreigners found guilty of violating the "propaganda" law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and then deported, and that displaying certain symbols, including the rainbow flag, is a crime.

Enforcement volume is documented by Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025): Russian courts issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols, roughly 98 of them administrative. Since January 2024, 81 people across 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying symbols such as the rainbow flag, and between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges for alleged participation; one died by suicide in pretrial detention, two were sentenced to prison, and 17 cases remain pending or of unknown outcome.

Charges have reached ordinary commercial activity as well. On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three staff of two publishing houses under article 282.2 with running an "extremist organisation" for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes; they face up to 12 years in prison. The enforcement regime described applies nationally and therefore equally in Altai Krai, and the sources report no Altai Krai-specific case.

28173009B16834140201491.name: Republic of Mordovia
28173009B16834140201491.summary:
The Republic of Mordovia stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full and without identified local deviation. Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes to official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that, explicitly, includes anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation, and national government warnings directed at LGBT travellers say so plainly.

The dedicated country dossier for Russia identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02), so the Republic of Mordovia is assessed at the national score. For a trans traveller that position means same-sex marriage is banned, gender transition is banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. Same-sex sexual activity as such is not criminalised.

Penalties are graded and severe. The 2013 propaganda law is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the 2023 extremist designation, participation in the designated movement carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising it carries six to ten years.

Enforcement is active and documented. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols, comprising about 98 administrative cases and 3 criminal cases. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted across 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The volume of enforcement has risen alongside its severity. Cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding June 2025. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's extremist ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars: about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Detention carries lethal risk. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. 28173009B731487536241.name: Khanty-Mansiysk Autonomous Okrug – Ugra
28173009B731487536241.summary:
Khanty-Mansiysk Autonomous Okrug – Ugra stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which applies in full. Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia covering sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the position a visitor actually encounters: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The 2013 'gay propaganda' law is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the 2023 extremist designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years.

Enforcement is active and measurable. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the International LGBT Movement or for displaying its symbols since the Supreme Court designation. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines under those statutes bringing more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel. It states that foreigners found guilty of violating the propaganda law may be arrested and detained for up to 15 days and then deported, that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime, and it carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The UK Home Office note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them. It affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

No deviation from the national position material enough to score separately was identified for this autonomous okrug (±0.02), and the division is therefore assessed at the national score. For a trans traveller that position means same-sex marriage is banned, gender transition is banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, with enforcement risk active rather than theoretical.

28173009B21210279674314.name: Komi Republic
28173009B21210279674314.summary:
The Komi Republic stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full. The sources record no variation in how these laws operate at the level of the republic, and the jurisdiction is assessed at the national score. A trans visitor to Syktyvkar or anywhere else in the Komi Republic faces the same legal position as a trans visitor elsewhere in the country.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed. The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, explicitly including anything "justifying" gender transition. Same-sex marriage is banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year.

Penalties are severe and reach foreigners directly. Anyone who violates these laws faces arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation. The 2013 propaganda law is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the 2023 extremist designation, participation in the designated movement carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising it carries six to ten years.

Enforcement is active and documented. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The speed and physical character of enforcement are documented. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 on a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Travel advisories reflect these risks. The US State Department advises against all travel to Russia for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, at Level 4, Do Not Travel, citing wrongful detention risk, the war, and arbitrary law enforcement, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers that violations can lead to arrest, detention and deportation. 28173009B65133456612022.summary:
Krasnoyarsk Krai stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation in full. The sources identify no deviation from that framework at the level of Krasnoyarsk Krai material enough to score separately, and the division is therefore assessed at the national score.

Under that framework, same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage is banned and gender transition is prohibited outright. Gender-marker changes on official documents are refused, legal gender recognition was banned in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" statute punishes public expression with administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. The expanded law reaches material that "justifies" gender transition. Since the 2023 Supreme Court designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, participation in it carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment and organising carries 6 to 10 years.

Foreigners who violate these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings state this expressly to LGBT travellers. The US State Department's advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and advises against all travel for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention, the war and arbitrary law enforcement alongside its warnings to LGBT travellers.

Enforcement is active and rising. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols, roughly 98 of them administrative and 3 criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. The UK Home Office records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, that the state is able but unwilling to protect them, and it affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. The note also records the national position this division adopts: no regional deviation identified.

28173009B90469334921421.name: Perm Krai
28173009B90469334921421.summary:
Perm Krai, a federal subject of Russia, stands under the national framework documented by the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025): same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections apply. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law barring gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed, and the expanded 'propaganda' law criminalises public expression that 'justifies' gender transition. That law carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to four years in prison.

The Supreme Court of Russia designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation in 2023. Participation carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment and organising 6 to 10 years. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 convictions tied to the designation as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation — one died by suicide in pretrial detention and courts sentenced two to prison — while 81 people across 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols.

Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The speed of the post-designation crackdown was recorded by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented in the sources. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman known as 'Ada' was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Enforcement is expanding in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two preceding years. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life through 2025, including a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as 'a second-class citizen' after the designation.

No enforcement record specific to Perm Krai appears in the sources, so the region is assessed against the national pattern rather than as a separate regime. Survey data cited in the UK Home Office note show respondents in the Volga area, which includes Perm Krai, were more 'closeted' toward relatives than the whole-study sample. The same note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims; Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
