28173009B46424166303156.name: Rostov Oblast
28173009B46424166303156.summary:
Rostov Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the legal position of transgender visitors has been severe since 2023. In that year President Vladimir Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, closing both gender-affirming care and legal gender recognition outright. The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda statute criminalises any public expression that "justifies" gender transition.

Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, administrative detention of up to 15 days, and deportation. The US State Department rates travel to Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, and its advisory carries warnings addressed to LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records that same-sex activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections exist. The propaganda law carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to four years in prison; participation in the designated extremist movement draws two to six years and organisation six to ten.

Enforcement is documented in volume as well as severity. The Home Office note counts at least 139 people in Russia affected by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism convictions as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges over the designation, one of whom died by suicide in pretrial detention and two of whom were sentenced to prison, while 81 people across 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols; Human Rights Watch states that participants face up to 12 years in prison. Cases under the propaganda statutes have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and brought more than 60 million rubles in fines into the state budget over two years (Meduza, 19 June 2025). Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night (The Guardian, 17 January 2024).

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented alongside court enforcement. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

Care access and medical treatment carry their own risk. The Home Office note reports LGBT-legal support clinics operating in the Moscow and Rostov regions, which places such support within reach of a visitor in this oblast. The same note records survey data placing the Southern Federal District, the federal district containing Rostov Oblast, at 27% for reported discrimination by healthcare providers who knew the patient's sexual orientation or gender identity.

Protection machinery exists at the level of asylum rather than entry. The UK Home Office affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims, and Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

28173009B55422170414647.name: Khakassia
28173009B55422170414647.summary:
Khakassia, a republic within the Russian Federation, stands under Russia's national legal framework, and the source record shows no sub-national variation in how that framework is applied. The law signed by President Putin in 2023 prohibits gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, which means neither visitors nor residents of Khakassia can obtain recognised legal gender status, and trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since the same year. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and no statutory discrimination protection exists on grounds of gender identity.

The expanded federal propaganda law criminalises any public expression, explicitly including anything that 'justifies' gender transition. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, advises against all travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers; it states that foreigners found guilty of violating the propaganda law may be detained for up to 15 days and deported, and that displaying rainbow symbols is a crime. The Russian government separately issues its own warnings telling LGBT travellers they face these consequences. These are country-wide federal rules with no sub-national variation.

Following the Supreme Court's designation of the 'international LGBT movement' as an extremist organisation, Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions by 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in that movement or for displaying its alleged symbols, comprising 98 administrative and 3 criminal convictions. At least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024 onward, and three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years in prison. Repeated display of banned symbols carries up to four years in prison.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) applies the refugee convention standard to Russia and finds that LGB people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely for their sexual orientation, while trans people, public LGBT+ advocates and people in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The same note records no division-specific facts for Khakassia.

Enforcement has been swift and physical. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. Cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in two years. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

28173009B62882423633207.name: Arkhangelsk Oblast
28173009B62882423633207.summary:
Arkhangelsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, whose laws set the conditions in force across every region of the country. The sources assembled for this record contain no oblast-specific findings, so the assessment below describes the national climate a visitor to Arkhangelsk enters.

Same-sex activity is not criminalised. Same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment.

Public expression is itself an offence. 'Gay propaganda' charges carry fines up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and repeat offences can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. The November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as an extremist organisation makes participation punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten years.

The US State Department advises against all travel to Russia regardless of any personal characteristic, citing the risk of wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement.

Enforcement volume is documented. Between December 2022 and March 2024, at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, and the UK Home Office assesses that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions tied to the International Public LGBT Movement designation as of 30 June 2025, roughly 98 administrative and three criminal. The Supreme Court ruling of November 2023 entered into force in January 2024 and opened the way to arbitrary prosecutions of LGBT people and their supporters.

Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation; two were sentenced to prison and one died by suicide in pretrial detention. A further 81 people across 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences for displaying banned symbols, with fines up to 2,000 roubles, and repeat displays punishable under the criminal code by up to four years.

Charges reach ordinary commercial activity: on 15 May 2025, investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, an offence carrying up to 12 years.

Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings tell LGBT travellers of this directly.

Participation in the designated extremist movement is punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions tied to the "International Public LGBT Movement" designation as of 30 June 2025, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal. The Supreme Court ruling entered into force in January 2024 and opened the way to arbitrary prosecutions of LGBT people and their supporters. A further 81 people in 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences for displaying banned symbols, with fines up to 2,000 roubles and repeat displays punishable under the criminal code by up to four years.

On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, an offence carrying up to 12 years. The UK Home Office note records that between December 2022 and March 2024 at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, and assesses that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The same note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

A foreign-government travel advisory for Russia carries a Level 4, Do Not Travel rating with warnings directed at LGBT travellers, and states that official support is "very limited" in parts of the country. Enforcement runs on two tracks at once. Administrative cases for displaying banned symbols produced 81 convictions across 98 court cases with fines capped at 2,000 roubles, while the criminal track has moved to multi-year sentences: at least 20 people charged between January 2024 and June 2025, two imprisoned, and a publishing-house case opened in May 2025 that carries up to 12 years. A visitor who is stopped, searched or photographed can therefore be recorded on an administrative file without any conviction following.

The tempo of the post-designation crackdown is documented at national scale. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the preceding two years.

The gap between formal legality and lived exposure is wide. Same-sex activity itself is not criminalised, yet public expression about gender transition, symbols, and now published fiction can be prosecuted, and there is no discrimination protection in housing, healthcare or employment to complain to. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia, and the UK Home Office treats trans people as a particular social group under the refugee convention, which places this jurisdiction in the category of countries generating asylum claims rather than safe destinations.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented in the wider national record. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. 28173009B59972517059449.name: Penza Oblast
28173009B59972517059449.summary:
Penza Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors and has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes to official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, explicitly including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and Russian government warnings address LGBT travellers directly.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the framework applying here: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the propaganda law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The same note records that at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, including convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions, and that trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its alleged symbols, and that 81 people across 98 court cases since January 2024 had been convicted of administrative offences for displaying those symbols, mostly on social media. The 2023 Supreme Court designation enabled criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison and built on the 2013 propaganda law. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity: Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over two years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and quoted a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

28173009B24080199016459.name: Amur Oblast
28173009B24080199016459.summary:
Amur Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the UK government's country policy and information note of June 2025 records that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the Russian constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law signed by President Vladimir Putin banned gender reassignment surgery and the change of gender markers on official documents; trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. A trans visitor has no lawful route to have their documents recognised or amended in Russia, and must travel on documents as issued.

Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded statute expressly reaches anything "justifying" gender transition, which places statements about transition and visible trans self-presentation within the scope of the offence.

The Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation opened criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison, building on the 2013 propaganda law. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in that movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, alongside 81 people convicted of administrative offences in 98 court cases since January 2024 for displaying those symbols, mostly on social media. Charges are brought under both the administrative and the criminal codes.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, including convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. It warns all travellers regardless of personal characteristic of wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement, and notes that foreigners found guilty under the propaganda law face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation.

28173009B94971452660823.name: Kursk Oblast
28173009B94971452660823.summary:
Kursk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the legal position for transgender visitors is prohibitive and has hardened since 2022. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Trans-specific healthcare and legal gender recognition were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and changes of gender marker on official documents was signed.

The expanded propaganda statute reaches foreigners directly. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia, issued at Level 4, Do Not Travel, warns all travellers regardless of personal characteristic of wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement, and states that foreigners found guilty under the propaganda law face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation. The advisory carries warnings specifically directed at LGBT travellers, and national government warnings to that effect are explicit.

A second layer of exposure applies nationwide, Kursk Oblast included. In 2023 the Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation, enabling criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison on top of the 2013 propaganda law. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in that movement or displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, alongside 81 people convicted of administrative offences across 98 court cases since January 2024, most of them for symbols displayed on social media. Charges are brought under both the administrative and the criminal codes, and Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The volume of enforcement is rising with its severity. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, including convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented alongside state action. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which quoted a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

28173009B3082792446388.name: Nenets Autonomous Okrug
28173009B3082792446388.summary:
The Nenets Autonomous Okrug stands under the national framework of Russia, where the risks to transgender visitors are severe and have sharpened since 2022. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025) is the framework this division is scored against, and it contains no division-specific information beyond the national position.

Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia. Same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed. A visitor whose documents carry a marker inconsistent with their presentation has no lawful route to reconciliation inside the country, and no access to trans-specific care.

The Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an extremist organisation in November 2023. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in that movement or for displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. The same reporting found 81 people found guilty across 98 administrative cases since January 2024 under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement.

The expanded propaganda statutes criminalise public expression that justifies gender transition. Penalties reach 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) in fines or 15 days' detention for individuals, and foreigners face arrest, detention and deportation; official national government warnings to LGBT travellers say so explicitly. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding.

Enforcement moves fast. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia. The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

28173009B8796515134902.name: Saint Petersburg
28173009B8796515134902.summary:

sources.summary: The UK Home Office country policy and information note on SOGI for Russia (June 2025) names Moscow and St Petersburg as the large urban centres where survey data suggests LGBT+ people feel more able to be open and where relocation may be a reasonable option. The note records two St Petersburg policewomen fired for allegedly flirting on social media, and an August 2024 Citizens' Watch/Sphere Foundation study of enforcement of the 'propaganda' articles whose respondents included 13% living in St Petersburg. sources.title: Vitaly Milonov - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's biography of Vitaly Milonov documents the city-level origin of the anti-LGBT law a trans visitor to Saint Petersburg stands under. As a member of the Saint Petersburg Legislative Assembly (2007-2016), he is recorded as the principal sponsor of the legislation criminalising 'homosexual propaganda directed toward minors', the city ban enacted in 2012 that the New York Times report 'Anti-Gay Law Stirs Fears in Russia' (29 February 2012) covered. The page quotes his statement that he fully intended to catch Madonna committing a possible offence under it when she visited the city. It also records Milonov stating in 2013 that gay athletes could be arrested at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics if they promoted homosexuality to minors, and his protests against the city's Side by Side LGBT film festival in November 2013.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Russia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's country overview of LGBTQ rights in Russia supplies the federal framework Saint Petersburg is assessed under: a 2013 law criminalises distributing 'propaganda' of 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors, with fines up to 5,000 roubles for citizens, 50,000 for officials, and 1 million roubles plus up to 90 days' suspension for organisations, while foreigners face up to 15 days' detention, a fine up to 100,000 roubles and deportation. Ten regions including Saint Petersburg (2012) enacted regional versions of the ban before the federal law, and Saint Petersburg removed its regional law in 2014, leaving the federal statute in force there. A July 2023 law bans gender transition outright, prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition. A 2010 European Court of Human Rights ruling fined Russia over the systematic refusal of pride-event permits.

28173009B36269087375583.name: Sakhalin Oblast
28173009B36269087375583.summary:
Sakhalin Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors and has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents. The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression, including anything explicitly "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official Russian government warnings tell LGBT travellers of this directly.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets the framework against which Sakhalin Oblast is scored. It records that consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned; that the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an extremist organisation in November 2023; that at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024; that "gay propaganda" offences carry fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention for individuals; and that trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The note contains no information specific to Sakhalin Oblast beyond that national framework.

Human Rights Watch separately documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. Charges in the wider extremism sweep have been brought under both the administrative and the criminal codes.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding. The Guardian documented on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The pattern described above operates nationwide, in every region and every oblast. Sakhalin Oblast is one unit within that national regime, and none of the sources reviewed records oblast-level enforcement figures, local prosecutions or local facilities for this territory.

28173009B21415173479872.name: Saratov Oblast
28173009B21415173479872.summary:
Saratov Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Putin signed the law in 2023 prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that includes, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the US State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The oblast's one region-specific enforcement datapoint is a Saratov court case: in February 2024 a Saratov court fined photographer Inna Mosina 1,500 rubles (about £13.97) for using rainbow-flag imagery in her artwork, recorded by the UK Home Office as the first criminal prosecution under the extremism law. Display of symbols associated with the designated movement is therefore prosecuted in this oblast, and imagery rather than conduct is sufficient to draw a charge.

National enforcement sets the baseline a visitor is measured against. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or display of its symbols since the November 2023 designation, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison, and separately documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. The UK Home Office note counts at least 139 individuals affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement across Russia in 2022-2024.

Document, relationship and care access are closed at national level. Same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were outlawed in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare is described as effectively banned. A trans visitor cannot obtain recognition of their documents in Russia and should expect entry screening, police checks and any interaction with medical services to be conducted against a legal order that treats their status as unlawful.

Physical harm accompanies the legal exposure. The Guardian reported that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, with about 100 patrons at one venue ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two further venues raided the same night. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. BBC Russian documented a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.

Protection machinery exists only outside Russia. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing the country, and the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

28173009B21415173479872.tangentialFactors:

Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Adjacent risks that a trans visitor may mistake for ordinary crime are in fact regime-driven. Detention on extremism grounds has proved lethal in pretrial custody, and forced confinement in conversion-therapy settings has been documented against transgender people held by their own families. Neither is captured by general travel-crime advisories.

28173009B5502896824563.name: Lipetsk Oblast
28173009B5502896824563.summary:
Lipetsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia. Trans-related criminalisation in Russia is legislated centrally and administered by national security bodies, and neither the UK Home Office country policy and information note (June 2025) nor Human Rights Watch's reporting (30 June 2025) contains any evidence specific to this division. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are prohibited.

The propaganda regime reaches expression about gender directly. The expanded law criminalises public expression that includes anything "justifying" gender transition. Under that statute, a visitor who promotes non-traditional relationships faces arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation. The UK Home Office record puts the individual "gay propaganda" fine at up to 400,000 rubles (approximately £3,600), with 15 days' detention as the alternative penalty.

Document markers remain a standing exposure. Any police or hotel document check can force disclosure of a trans person's legal status, because the 2023 ban leaves no route to correct a gender marker, while the extremist and propaganda statutes supply grounds for proceedings on the basis of identity rather than conduct.

The UK Home Office policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including those in the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the Refugee Convention. That finding sets the standard applied to UK asylum claims based on Russian persecution, and Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those leaving Russia.

28173009B2185273376578.name: Magadan Oblast
28173009B2185273376578.summary:
Magadan Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and every source consulted treats that framework as applying uniformly across the country. A visitor to Magadan Oblast therefore faces the same legal exposure as a visitor to Moscow or Vladivostok: the 2023 prohibition on legal gender recognition and on gender-affirming care, the designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation by the Supreme Court in November 2023, and the expanded propaganda statutes.

Legal gender transition and same-sex marriage are banned in Russia, while consensual same-sex activity is not itself a criminal offence. The practical consequence for a transgender visitor is that no document can be brought into alignment with their gender presentation, so any police stop, hotel registration, bank or transport identity check reads as a mismatch between presentation and papers.

The propaganda law reaches public expression explicitly, including material "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who breach it face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation; individual fines under the provision run to 400,000 rubles, roughly £3,600.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols since the November 2023 ruling, with sentences reaching 12 years' imprisonment. It also recorded 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, most of them on social media. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 records at least 139 individuals affected by anti-LGBT law enforcement between 2022 and 2024.

Enforcement volume has risen alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that propaganda-law cases had grown eighteenfold over a decade, with fines under those statutes bringing more than 60 million rubles into state coffers over two years. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's designation, The Guardian reported, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, ordering about 100 patrons at one venue to face walls for search and photography, with at least two further venues raided the same night.

Violence and coercive detention are documented rather than hypothetical. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was held for nine months from summer 2021 at a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping after police responded to a phone she had found. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Official travel guidance reflects the risk. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings addressed specifically to LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the Chechen republic, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. 28173009B42697300509311.name: Ulyanovsk Oblast
28173009B42697300509311.summary:
Ulyanovsk Oblast stands under the Russian national framework, which applies in full and offers no regional deviation material enough to score separately. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. For a visitor this means an identity document carrying an outdated marker cannot be corrected before or during travel, so any police, hotel or transport identity check reads a mismatch.

The 2013 'gay propaganda' law carries administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded statute reaches public expression that 'justifies' gender transition, and foreign nationals who violate it face arrest, detention and deportation; official national government warnings and the US State Department's Level 4 Do Not Travel advisory both address LGBT travellers directly.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation carries 2-6 years' imprisonment and organising 6-10 years under Article 282.2. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or displaying its symbols. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

Enforcement operates inside Ulyanovsk Oblast. Citing an October 2024 OVD-Info report, the UK Home Office records that Ilya Zhuravlev, former head of the dialysis centre in Inza in the Ulyanovsk region, was detained in August 2024 on charges of participating in the activities of the extremist 'LGBT movement' (Part 2 of Article 282.2) and coercion of a person to act of a sexual nature (Part 1 of Article 133). In March 2025 a Ulyanovsk-region doctor, who faced a maximum of one year's imprisonment for alleged sexual coercion, was also prosecuted for 'involving' another man in the LGBT movement and received a three-year sentence.

The UK Home Office note assesses that openly LGBT+ people in Russia are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, with the state able but not willing to provide protection, and records at least 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024. Physical coercion is documented: BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was held for nine months at a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk and forced to take testosterone. The US State Department advisory carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers, and the UK Home Office affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

28173009B91128253561055.name: Vladimir Oblast
28173009B91128253561055.summary:
Vladimir Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and no regional deviation from that framework has been identified. For a visitor the national law applies in full: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. Any police, hotel or transport identity check therefore reads a mismatch that cannot be corrected.

The 2013 'gay propaganda' law is punishable by administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation carries 2-6 years' imprisonment and organising 6-10 years under Article 282.2. Foreign visitors who violate these provisions face arrest, detention and deportation, and official national government warnings to LGBT travellers say so explicitly.

Enforcement is documented and ongoing. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or displaying its symbols; between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. The UK Home Office records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, the state being able but not willing to provide protection.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Physical coercion against transgender people is also documented: BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.

28173009B2687808218031.name: Voronezh Oblast
28173009B2687808218031.summary:

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year and gender-marker changes on official documents are now prohibited. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned.

The 2013 "gay propaganda" law is punishable by administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded statute criminalises any public expression including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the Russian national government has explicitly warned LGBT travellers of this; the US State Department carries a Level 4 Do Not Travel advisory for Russia that contains warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court "extremist" designation of the international LGBT movement, participation in the designated movement carries 2-6 years' imprisonment and organising carries 6-10 years under Article 282.2. Document markers cannot be corrected, so any police, hotel or transport identity check in the oblast reads a mismatch between a visitor's papers and their presentation.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols as of 30 June 2025, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia. The UK Home Office assesses that openly LGBT+ people in Russia are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, the state being able but not willing to provide protection.

28173009B30008444211385.name: Altai Republic
28173009B30008444211385.summary:
The Altai Republic stands under the national framework of Russia, and no sub-national deviation from that framework has been identified in the sources; the territory is therefore assessed at the national score. For a visitor, Russia's laws apply in full within the republic: legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, same-sex marriage is banned, and the expanded propaganda statute criminalises public expression that, explicitly, justifies gender transition.

Penalties under that statute reach administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation in the designated movement carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment and organising it 6 to 10 years under Article 282.2. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention and deportation, and official national government warnings state this expressly to LGBT travellers.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, do not travel, for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention, active war and arbitrary law enforcement. The advisory carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the designated international LGBT movement or for displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Because any police, hotel or transport identity check can set a visitor's documents against their presentation, and because gender-marker changes remain prohibited, document screening is the principal everyday exposure point in the territory. Enforcement volume is rising alongside severity: cases under the propaganda statutes have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding June 2025.

Federal criminal and administrative statutes operate directly in the territory with no local discretion over how they are applied.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender change on official documents took effect. Gender-marker changes on documents remain prohibited, so any police stop, hotel registration or transport identity check can read as a mismatch between a trans visitor's paperwork and presentation.

The propaganda regime carries administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, and repeated offences escalate to criminal prosecution with up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded law reaches any public expression, including material that "justifies" gender transition.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising six to ten under Article 282.2. Foreign nationals who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation.

Official advisories match the legal position. The US State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings addressed specifically to LGBT travellers. Jewish Autonomous Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025) contains no oblast-specific information beyond that national framework, and the division is assessed at the national score. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. No lawful route exists for a visitor or resident to align an official gender marker with their presentation.

The expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, including anything explicitly "justifying" gender transition. Penalties reach fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, and repeated offences risk criminal prosecution. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison; participation carries 2-6 years' imprisonment and organising 6-10 years. Charges are brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The UK Home Office affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

28173009B57398385788417.name: Kalmykia

Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage is prohibited and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people.

The expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression, including anything "justifying" gender transition. Penalties reach fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, and repeat offences risk criminal prosecution. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media, alongside the 257 "gay propaganda" penalties imposed in 2023-24 compared with 22 in 2021-22. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

Raid practice is documented. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and quoted a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that "Ada", a transgender woman, was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (v2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. 28173009B4400867918714.name: Kemerovo Oblast
28173009B4400867918714.summary:
Kemerovo Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and that framework is assessed in full here. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023; the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" extremist in November 2023; and the expanded propaganda statute punishes any public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition, expressly including material that justifies transition. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people, according to the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025).

The penalties a visitor would face are administrative at first instance and criminal on repetition. Fines run to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeat offences risking criminal prosecution. The US State Department advisory adds that a foreigner found guilty under the propaganda law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported, and states that displaying certain symbols, including the rainbow flag, is a crime. That advisory advises against all travel to Russia regardless of personal characteristics.

One enforcement action is documented within Kemerovo Oblast itself. A person already serving a prison sentence there received an additional six-year sentence in February for participating in the "LGBT movement" and for "involving" other prisoners in its activities, RIA Novosti reported, citing the Federal Security Service. No other unit-specific finding appears in the sources: all three are national in scope, and the UK Home Office note contains no division-specific information beyond the national framework, so this oblast inherits the national position with a single corroborating incident.

The national enforcement volume behind that position is documented. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the designated movement or displaying its symbols since the November 2023 designation, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison, as of 30 June 2025. It also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media, and 257 "gay propaganda" penalties imposed in 2023-24 against 22 in 2021-22.

28173009B4400867918714.tangentialFactors:
The trajectory of enforcement is upward on every measured axis. Propaganda penalties rose from 22 in 2021-22 to 257 in 2023-24, a factor of roughly eleven, while the post-designation extremism docket produced 101 convictions carrying sentences as long as 12 years within eighteen months of the Supreme Court's ruling.

The designation operates alongside pre-existing coercion rather than replacing it. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) reported the case of "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping after police responded to a phone she had found. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical raids followed the designation within days. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, ordering about 100 patrons at one venue to face walls for search and photograph, with at least two other venues raided the same night. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The regime places Russia among the most hostile jurisdictions covered by this map, and several foreign governments treat it as such: the US State Department rates travel to Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings addressed specifically to LGBT travellers.

28173009B57295377776076.name: Khabarovsk Krai
28173009B57295377776076.summary:
Khabarovsk Krai stands under the national framework of Russia, which since 2023 has prohibited legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care outright. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as extremist supplies the charge on which courts now convict. The "gay propaganda" statute carries fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia advises against all travel regardless of personal characteristics. It states that foreigners found guilty under the propaganda law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported, and that displaying certain symbols, including the rainbow flag, is a crime. A trans visitor therefore faces administrative detention and removal on top of the underlying penalties that apply to residents.

Human Rights Watch recorded, as of 30 June 2025, 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its symbols since the November 2023 ruling, with sentences reaching 12 years in prison. The same report documents 81 people found guilty in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 since January 2024 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media, which places online posting and shared images within the enforcement surface rather than outside it.

No Khabarovsk Krai-specific trans detention, prosecution or violence figures appear in the inventory. The one local incident it carries is a measure of how gender nonconformity is treated in the territory: a biology and chemistry teacher in Khabarovsk was forced to resign in September after video of him dancing in high heels surfaced amid public controversy, and in October he filed a lawsuit against the Khabarovsk education department seeking reinstatement, a case still ongoing when the UK Home Office documented it.

28173009B30250450380208.name: Bashkortostan
28173009B30250450380208.summary:
Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression, including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Bashkortostan has no division-specific provisions or reporting in the available sources. A visitor to the republic stands under the national framework as applied countrywide, and the UK Home Office note is explicit that no division-specific information about Bashkortostan appears in it.

Under that national framework, same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. The "gay propaganda" law makes public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition punishable by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, and a repeated offence can bring up to four years' imprisonment. Displaying rainbow symbols falls within the prohibition. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an extremist organisation in November 2023; between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws.

The US State Department advises against all travel to Russia regardless of personal characteristics. It warns that foreigners found guilty under the "propaganda" law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported, and that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is itself a crime.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) reports that Russian courts have issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its symbols since the November 2023 designation, with penalties of up to 12 years in prison. HRW also identified 81 people in 98 cases found guilty since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. The 2013 "gay propaganda" law had already made any positive or neutral depiction of non-heterosexual relations an administrative offence.

76434192B57942368908249.name: Free State
76434192B57942368908249.summary:
The Free State province of the Republic of South Africa stands under the national framework set by the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, which prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation. The Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. South Africa was the first country in the world to bar sexual-orientation discrimination, doing so in 1996, and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly extends protection to gender identity and sex characteristics alongside sexual orientation.

Partner status is recognised for a trans visitor travelling with a spouse. The Constitutional Court's judgment of December 2005 compelled Parliament to act, and the Civil Union Act was passed in November 2006 with a National Assembly vote of 229 to 41, legalising same-sex marriage nationwide.

Legal gender recognition is available under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, which allows sex status to be changed in the population registry and therefore on identity documents and passports on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery. The Act demands medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks some people out of recognition altogether, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. The cost of affirming one's gender through this process is described as dauntingly high. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report records a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

The ruling of the High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division sitting as an Equality Court, in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075, judgment 10 November 2025) is binding on the Department of Correctional Services nationwide. The court held that refusing a transgender inmate feminine attire, she/her pronouns and other gender expression, and refusing her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, constituted unfair discrimination, and that hormone therapy forms part of the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e). Orders were granted compelling the Department to provide hormone treatment at state expense, to permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, to implement the accommodations required by its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and to deliver prescribed medical care. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism, which holds the OPCAT monitoring mandate over places of deprivation of liberty, welcomed the judgment on 14 November 2025; the Department had argued that the therapy was cosmetic.

Detention nonetheless remains a site of elevated risk. The Department of Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling, and reporting of August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice.

Violence against trans people is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month, and violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven, and the pattern bears directly on Free State residents: treatment is concentrated in the main cities, so trans people in the province must travel long distances to reach it, private treatment costs hundreds of thousands of rands, and public waiting lists are long. Activists elsewhere in the country have delivered a memorandum to a provincial hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 concludes that PEPUDA read with section 9 of the Constitution does not secure equal treatment for transgender and non-binary people in practice as regards gender-segregated bathrooms, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.
