76434192B57942368908249.blindSummary:
The province stands under the national framework set by the national constitution of 1996, which prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation. The national equality act gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. The parent nation was the first country in the world to bar sexual-orientation discrimination, doing so in 1996, and a hate-crimes and hate-speech statute enacted in 2024 explicitly extends protection to gender identity and sex characteristics alongside sexual orientation.

Partner status is recognised for a trans visitor travelling with a spouse. The Constitutional Court's judgment of December 2005 compelled the national legislature to act, and a civil-union statute was passed in November 2006 with a lower-chamber vote of 229 to 41, legalising same-sex marriage nationwide.

Legal gender recognition is available under an alteration-of-sex-description statute of 2003, which allows sex status to be changed in the population registry and therefore on identity documents and passports on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery. That statute demands medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks some people out of recognition altogether, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. The cost of affirming one's gender through this process is described as dauntingly high. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 civil-society report records a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

The judgment of a high court sitting as an Equality Court in a case against the national correctional department (case 2024/070075, judgment 10 November 2025) binds that department nationwide. The court held that refusing a transgender inmate feminine attire, she/her pronouns and other gender expression, and refusing her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, constituted unfair discrimination, and that hormone therapy forms part of the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment. Orders were granted compelling the department to provide hormone treatment at state/province expense, to permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, to implement the accommodations required by its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and to deliver prescribed medical care. The national human rights commission's monitoring body, which holds the international mandate over places of deprivation of liberty, welcomed the judgment on 14 November 2025; the department had argued that the therapy was cosmetic.

Detention nonetheless remains a site of elevated risk. The correctional department already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling, and reporting of August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice.

Violence against trans people is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. a national LGBTI rights organisation's watch recorded five such murders that month, and violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven, and the pattern bears directly on residents of this province: treatment is concentrated in the main population centres, so trans people here must travel long distances to reach it, private treatment costs hundreds of thousands of currency units, and public waiting lists are long. Activists elsewhere in the country have delivered a memorandum to a provincial hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 concludes that the national equality act read with the equality clause does not secure equal treatment for transgender and non-binary people in practice as regards gender-segregated bathrooms, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

19338628B5758982491638.name: Centre-Val de Loire
19338628B5758982491638.summary:
Centre-Val de Loire stands under France's national framework. Criminal law, the custody rules of the French Criminal Procedure Code, anti-discrimination law, identity-document rules and the law on marriage apply uniformly across French regions, and no source in the inventory records a departure specific to this region.

For a trans visitor the operative exposure is custodial. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, and placement follows the gender inscribed on identity documents rather than lived gender. Trans women whose documents are marked male — the majority, who have not undergone sex-reassignment surgery — are therefore held in men's facilities. Each establishment then improvises its own arrangement: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates.

Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers most in prison. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records an inmate told 'We don't want any women here!' alongside threats of violence, and documents the detention of Kara B., an American trans woman, in conditions Hazan describes as worrying. Accounts collected in the same feature describe heightened vulnerability to assault and to suicide under isolation.

Practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, which argued that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of questioning by French border police at the airport, conducted in front of other travellers.

In everyday movement, accommodation and services, France's oversight bodies record discrimination rather than legal prohibition. The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony, citing the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and setting out guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition the baseline is the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism and custodial-inspection authority, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, following its opinion of 30 June 2010. The review covered some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station.

The mechanism recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform. It explained to the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention, and it issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

The national custodial-inspection authority examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010, alongside ministry and association input. That volume, sustained over a decade, indicates a persistent rather than episodic pattern of complaints.

19338628B74392602121343.name: Grand Est
19338628B74392602121343.summary:
Grand Est stands under the national framework of France. Identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law and marriage law apply uniformly across the region, and the sources record no regional deviation from the national position on transgender rights.

Custody is the sharpest exposure. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, so a trans woman whose identity documents record a male sex, which is the case for the vast majority who have not had sex-reassignment surgery, is placed in a men's facility. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records a detainee hearing other inmates shout "We don't want any women here!" alongside threats of violence.

Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers the most in prison. The same feature documents the case of Kara B., an American trans woman held in conditions described as worrying.

The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 following its opinion of 30 June 2010. It finds that serious violations of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees persist in adult prisons, while no such violations were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. The review covered some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station.

Placement remains contested in the region's own territory. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October; her incarceration was raised in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the prison system cannot guarantee conditions for trans detainees.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of questioning by French border police at an airport, conducted in front of other travellers.

The Défenseur des droits issued a framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out guidance for service providers.

19338628B64983593182368.name: Bretagne
19338628B64983593182368.summary:
Bretagne stands under the national framework of France. Identity-document law, anti-discrimination provisions, criminal law, the prison-placement rules and the marriage statute apply across the country's regions without territorial variation, and no source in the inventory records a Bretagne-specific finding on transgender travellers.

The documented risks concentrate in two settings: custody and the border. In ordinary movement through accommodation, services and public space, France's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Prison placement follows the sex inscribed on the detainee's identity documents. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, and the vast majority of trans women, most of whom have not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, carry documents marked male and are consequently held in men's facilities. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records a trans woman recalling inmates shouting "We don't want any women here!" and threatening violence against her.

Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers the most in French prisons. The same feature describes the case of Kara B., a trans American woman, held in what the controller-general called worrying conditions.

The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism against torture, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, following its opinion of 30 June 2010. It found serious violations of the fundamental rights of trans detainees persisting in adult prisons. No comparable violations were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. The review covered the situations of roughly forty trans detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits to the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station.

The CGLPL told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a further opinion was needed because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because its remit now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

Placement remains contested in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained in connection with opposition to the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was raised in oral question no. 219 addressed to the Keeper of the Seals in the French National Assembly, which argued that the prison system is unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees. Placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women report being questioned publicly about their identity documents. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of questioning by French border police at the airport, conducted in front of other travellers.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. The decision cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline is the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013. CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption have been legal since 2013, with France's first same-sex wedding performed on 29 May 2013, days after the law took effect, and civil solidarity pacts available since 1999. Penal Code article 225-1 has covered gender identity since an 18 November 2016 amendment that replaced the term sexual identity, itself protected since 2012. Homophobic hate speech has carried penalties of up to EUR 45,000 and/or one year's imprisonment since a 31 December 2004 amendment.

It abolished the requirements of sex-reassignment surgery and forced sterilisation, rejected a Senate amendment that would have demanded proof of medical treatment, and requires an applicant to go before a court rather than undergo any medical intervention. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, so a court order is the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A pending bill would open recognition to applicants including consenting minors and would allow markers beyond male and female, such as X or nonbinary; its drafter links the absence of recognition to social exclusion, forced disclosure of trans status and violence.

No national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity exists. Non-discrimination bills have been filed since 1999 without enactment, and the SOGIESC Equality Bill has been stuck in Congress for 25 years, its latest version Senate Bill 1600, which would prohibit denial of admission, denial of public and health services, and infliction of physical harm or verbal abuse based on SOGIE. Campaigners cite that blockage as the direct reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy. Two civil-union bills filed since 2022 face religious-conservative opposition.

Protections that do exist are sub-national or sectoral. SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances cover eight provinces (Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo) and 32 cities and municipalities, with further ordinances at barangay level. Two access rules turn on documents rather than on identity. The armed forces have permitted openly gay and bisexual personnel since 2009 and transgender personnel since 2017, with the uniform policy following the legal gender shown on the birth certificate. The Code of Professional Responsibility governing lawyers was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. 36201628B47773222326566.summary:
The Zamboanga Peninsula stands under the national framework of the Philippines. Consensual same-sex relations are legal and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender, but legal gender recognition is unavailable: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. The Family Code defines marriage as between a man and a woman, so same-sex marriage is not recognised, and no national anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity.

The local legal floor in this division is set in part by Zamboanga City, the peninsula's regional center, which enacted its own anti-discrimination ordinance in 2020 and is named among the more than 20 local governments with such ordinances. Non-discrimination ordinances operate at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels across the country. The other provinces and cities of the peninsula are not sourced individually, so equivalent protection outside Zamboanga City is unresolved.

Violence against trans women is documented and recent. On 23 June 2025 Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman and student at Cagayan State University in Peñablanca, was found dead in a river in Cagayan province with visible signs of physical assault; a person who admitted picking her up the previous night surrendered to police and denied killing her. The same day Ali Macalintal, a trans activist and former journalist, was shot by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos, and Shalani Dolina was killed in Caloocan earlier in 2025. The Commission on Human Rights has described the trans killings recorded in a single year as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide. All three killings occurred outside this peninsula, but they are the clearest available indication of what a trans visitor to the country should expect.

Detention strips away most of what protection exists on paper. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex. At Manila City Jail, arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and safety is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates rather than through policy. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented response at Davao City Jail is administrative segregation, transferring LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex 'to prevent abuse' alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, with three LGBT groupings housed there since the annex was established. These facilities are outside the peninsula; no jail practice specific to the peninsula is sourced.

Public space is governed by statute rather than by identity. The Safe Spaces Act 2019 criminalises homophobic and transphobic slurs, with fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found a majority of Filipinos opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, a division of shared facilities a trans visitor may be challenged over. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed repeatedly since 1999 and has never passed; campaigners cite its 25-year blockage as the direct reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy, and the latest version was filed in 2022 as House Bill 5551 and Senate Bill 1600.

36201628B13149248482964.name: Bicol Region
36201628B13149248482964.summary:
The Bicol Region stands under the national framework of the Philippines. Consensual same-sex relations are legal and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender, but there is no route to legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) the Supreme Court held that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. The Family Code confines marriage to a man and a woman, and no national statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity; the SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress since 1999.

Inside the region, Albay province, which lies wholly within Bicol, enacted a province-wide sexual-orientation and gender-identity anti-discrimination ordinance in 2022, making it one of nine provinces nationwide with such protection. The ordinance is a provincial instrument and does not establish a floor for the rest of the region; whether other Bicol provinces, cities or municipalities have enacted comparable ordinances is not sourced here.

Protections that reach a visitor nationally are sectoral. The Safe Spaces Act 2019 covers homophobic and transphobic slurs, with fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar; the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers punishes SOGIE harassment with a fine of PHP 20,000 to 40,000 and up to one year's penalty. In schools, the Anti-Bullying Act 2013 and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy (2017, reiterated 2022) cover sexual orientation and gender identity, though a 2017 Human Rights Watch investigation recorded bullying and discrimination against gender-diverse students across Philippine schools while noting that law offered few remedies at the time.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a river in Cagayan on 23 June 2025 after being reported missing; on the same day a trans woman who was a former journalist and activist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside a clinic in General Santos. A foreign national was arrested in May 2025 on a charge of raping a trans woman at a Batangas resort, and in April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd during a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan. The Commission on Human Rights has described the trans killings recorded in a single year as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Detention removes what protections exist on paper. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex: at Manila City Jail, arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and survival against abuse is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates rather than through policy. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented response at Davao City Jail is administrative segregation, transferring LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex 'to prevent abuse', alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens.

Public opinion is a live factor in how documents and facilities are treated. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found that only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions and that a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, so toilet and changing-room use in the region rests on local practice and the disposition of staff rather than on a settled legal rule. A 2026 travel-risk assessment rates the national capital 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers overall at 69 of 100 but scores trans travellers lower, at 62, in the 'Exercise Caution' band.

36201628B29919658129037.name: Eastern Visayas
36201628B29919658129037.summary:
Eastern Visayas, six provinces in the eastern central Philippines, stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which applies uniformly across the region; the sources record no regional deviation from that framework, and the region is assessed at the national position.

Consensual same-sex relations are legal nationwide and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. Same-sex marriage is not recognised: the Family Code defines marriage as between a man and a woman. Transgender people cannot change their legal gender. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery.

No national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity exists. The SOGIE Equality Bill was filed in 1999 and has remained pending in Congress for roughly 25 years. Protections are sub-national: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances operate at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels elsewhere in the country, and the parent framework records eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities with such ordinances. Whether any local government inside Eastern Visayas has enacted one is not established by these sources.

Two executive measures exist on paper without effect. Executive Order 100, signed 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, and Executive Order 51 (2023) amended it to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee; neither had been implemented as of 2025.

Public opinion bears on facilities access. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22% support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed transgender women's access to women's toilets, a position with direct consequences for restroom use in public buildings across the region.

Violence against trans women is documented and recent. Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman, was found dead with signs of physical assault in a river in Peñablanca, Cagayan province on 23 June 2025, having been reported missing since 22 June; her mother reported the disappearance to local police. The chairperson of Bahaghari, the national LGBT alliance, called the killing part of a pattern of violence against Filipino trans women and renewed calls for the SOGIESC Equality Bill. The case occurred in Cagayan Valley rather than Eastern Visayas and is evidence of the national climate a visitor here moves through.

36201628B97761566458517.name: Northern Mindanao
36201628B97761566458517.summary:
Northern Mindanao stands under the national framework of the Philippines: same-sex relations are lawful, no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender, and no national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity exists. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress for 25 years, so the only binding protections a visitor can rely on are sub-national ordinances, sectoral statutes and the courts.

Local protection across Mindanao is thin. By mid-2019 only four local government units in the entire territory had passed pro-LGBT ordinances, according to MindaNews. Documentation for Northern Mindanao specifically is sparse, and the absence of a regional signal does not establish that no divergence exists.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable anywhere in the country. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. Same-sex marriage is not recognised: the Family Code confines marriage to a man and a woman. Access rules therefore turn on documents rather than on identity, including the armed forces' uniform policy, which follows the gender shown on the birth certificate.

Official machinery exists on paper without effect. Executive Order 100, signed 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, and Executive Order 51 of 2023 added a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee; neither had been implemented as of 2025.

Facilities access is contested in public opinion rather than settled by law. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found a majority of respondents opposed trans women's use of women's toilets, alongside 22% support for same-sex civil unions.

Violence against trans women is documented and recent. Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman, was found dead with signs of physical assault in a river in Peñablanca, Cagayan province on 23 June 2025, having been reported missing the previous day; her mother had reported the disappearance to local police. The chairperson of Bahaghari described the killing as part of a pattern of violence against Filipino trans women and renewed calls for the SOGIESC Equality Bill. That case sits in Cagayan Valley, outside Northern Mindanao, and is evidence of national climate rather than of conditions in this region.

Detention removes most of what protection exists on paper. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex: at Manila City Jail, arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and safety is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' rather than through policy. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented response at Davao City Jail is administrative segregation, transferring LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex 'to prevent abuse'. Schools are a further documented site of harm: a 2017 Human Rights Watch investigation recorded bullying and discrimination against gender-diverse students across Philippine schools.

One sub-national complication touches the region directly. Lanao del Norte, which lies within Northern Mindanao, has adjacent Muslim personal-law courts operating, so personal-status questions there may be handled under a religious legal framework rather than the general civil one.

The 25-year blockage of the SOGIE Equality Bill is cited by campaigners as the direct reason that two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy, which indicates that a violent incident in this territory is unlikely to trigger a change in the governing rules.

Other recent trans-specific incidents elsewhere in the country include the shooting of a trans woman who was a former journalist and activist inside a clinic in General Santos on 23 June 2025, the arrest of a foreign national in May 2025 on a charge of raping a trans woman at a Batangas resort, and the striking of drag artist Taylor Sheesh on stage in Bayambang, Pangasinan in April 2024, after which the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community.

Social visibility is high nationally: gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy are long-standing, Pride events and nightlife are prominent in the capital, and LGBTQ+ themes carry substantial media presence. Sectoral statutes also apply: the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers punishes SOGIE harassment with a fine of PHP 20,000 to 40,000 and up to one year's penalty, and the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act reach slurs and ridicule with fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar.

The Code of Professional Responsibility governing lawyers was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. The armed forces have permitted openly gay and bisexual personnel since 2009 and transgender personnel since 2017, with the uniform policy following the legal gender shown on the birth certificate.

Legal gender recognition requires a court order, since the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A pending bill would open recognition to applicants including consenting minors and would allow markers beyond male and female, such as X or nonbinary.

Detention removes what protections exist on paper. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented response at Davao City Jail is administrative segregation, transferring LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex 'to prevent abuse', alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, with three LGBT groupings housed there since the annex was established. At Manila City Jail, arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and survival against abuse is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates rather than through policy.

Schools are a further documented site of harm: a 2017 Human Rights Watch investigation recorded bullying and discrimination against gender-diverse students across Philippine schools while noting that law offered few remedies at the time.

36201628B99380759663697.name: Caraga
36201628B99380759663697.summary:
Caraga records no region-specific law or regulation bearing on trans people. A visitor there stands under the national framework of the Philippines, where same-sex conduct is legal and no provision of law criminalises a person for being transgender. The Caraga entry in the sourced reference material carries no separate finding on LGBT rights, so the national position governs in full.

Identity documents cannot be brought into line with a trans visitor's presentation. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A court order is the only route, so the marker a visitor carries at hotels, checkpoints and counters will remain the one assigned at birth.

No national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity exists. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed repeatedly since 1999 without enactment, and protection runs only through local ordinances: eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities nationwide hold SOGIE anti-discrimination rules. Within Caraga, Butuan City, the regional capital and the most likely first port of call, adopted a non-discrimination ordinance in 2016, and Agusan del Norte and Dinagat Islands are among the covered provinces. Whether the remaining Caraga localities are covered is not resolved by the sourced material.

National recourses do exist for hostile speech. The Safe Spaces Act and the Magna Carta of Women reach slurs and ridicule with fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar; the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers punishes SOGIE harassment with a fine of PHP 20,000 to 40,000 and up to one year's penalty.

Shared facilities remain contested. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, alongside 22% support for same-sex civil unions. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised, the Family Code defining marriage as between a man and a woman.

Detention removes what protection exists on paper. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex; at Manila City Jail, arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and survival against abuse is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' rather than through policy. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented response at Davao City Jail is administrative segregation, transferring LGBT detainees to the City Jail Annex to prevent abuse.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent nationwide, though no incident in Caraga is recorded in the sourced material. Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a river in Cagayan on 23 June 2025; the same day a trans woman, a former journalist and activist, was shot inside a clinic in General Santos. A foreign national was arrested in May 2025 on a charge of raping a trans woman at a Batangas resort, and in April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage in Bayambang, Pangasinan.

Entry and visa rules specific to trans visitors are not covered by the sourced material.

36201628B99380759663697.tangentialFactors:
A 2026 travel-risk assessment rates Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers at 69 of 100 but scores trans travellers lower, at 62, in the 'Exercise Caution' band. Caraga itself is not scored.

Executive Order 100 s.2019, signed 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, and Executive Order 51 s.2023 added a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee. Neither had been implemented as of 2025, so the machinery a visitor might expect to reach does not function on the ground.

Campaigners attribute the absence of legislative remedy after two killings in June 2025 to the SOGIE Equality Bill's 25-year blockage in Congress. The Commission on Human Rights has described the trans killings recorded in a single year as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Social visibility is high and long-standing, with gender-diversity traditions carried under local names such as bakla and tomboy, prominent Pride events and nightlife, and substantial LGBTQ+ media presence. That visibility coexists with the lower trans-specific risk score and the documented 2025 killings.

A 2017 Human Rights Watch investigation recorded bullying and discrimination against gender-diverse students across Philippine schools while noting that law offered few remedies at the time. Schools are a further documented site of harm alongside streets and detention.

47653553B40993810137393.summary:
RegiÃ³n de Antofagasta stands under Chile's national legal framework, which the dedicated country dossier (Outright International, published 12 March 2026) sets out in full and against which it records no Antofagasta-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding and no division-level information. A trans visitor to the region therefore faces the national rules: same-sex marriage and joint adoption legal since March 2022; the criminal code's treatment of sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences since 2012; legal gender recognition on a self-determination basis since 2019, with no medical or surgical conditions attached; and a third sex option on birth certificates for intersex children since 2006.

Documented abuse in the region is rising faster than the national average. Movilh's XXIV Annual Human Rights Report (HECHOS 2025), published in March 2026, places Antofagasta at 2.09% of nationally documented abuse cases, a year-on-year rise of 45.45% in 2025 and the second-largest regional increase recorded, behind one region that grew by 150%. Across Chile the report counts 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025, an increase of 27.1% and the highest annual figure in 24 years.

Antofagasta is part of a general national pattern rather than an exception. Of the 16 regions Movilh tracks, 14 recorded increases in 2025 and only ValparaÃ­so (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) recorded falls. Movilh reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions where public debate is less visible, which makes a moderate regional share an indicator of documented harm diffusing outward rather than evidence of a quieter local environment.

The policy environment has also moved backwards at national level. In the 2025-26 rollback, the Chilean congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill, an action condemned by civil society groups and by Chile's national ombudsman for children.

Región del Maule stands under the national framework of Chile, where legal gender recognition has operated since 2019 on a self-determination basis under Gender Identity Law 21.120 (introduced 2013, enacted 2018, operative 2019). 68945753B85747362819570.name: Gangwon
68945753B85747362819570.summary:
Gangwon province stands under the national framework of South Korea: gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life, and no province-specific ordinance or enforcement pattern targeting trans visitors is documented in these sources. The rules a visitor meets in Gangwon are the national ones.

Legal gender recognition no longer depends on surgery. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that determining gender change by surgery is contrary to law and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are now reference only, not criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity. That ruling is the standard applied in Gangwon, where no province-specific case is documented. The Supreme Court has separately allowed a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

Trans visitors have a judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 2 July 2024 a Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, ruling that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights. The court held comfortable restroom use to be a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that barred a transgender student from its restroom forms part of the national standard applied in Gangwon, where no specific incident is documented.

Restroom avoidance is a documented national pattern rather than a local one. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink to do so, and 36% forwent restroom use entirely.

The armed forces are the exception to South Korea's non-criminalisation: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld it in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether. This bears on a visitor only insofar as it applies to nationals serving, not to civilians.

There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity in South Korea, so accommodation, services and employment carry no statutory protection on these grounds. The National Human Rights Commission flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023 after the Ministry of Health and Welfare refused to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

No same-sex marriage exists, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner; the Constitutional Court's 2024 ruling extended recognition only to same-sex partners' healthcare rights. Organised conservative opposition remains active, and Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in South Korea alongside a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.

68945753B82824634329413.name: North Jeolla
68945753B82824634329413.summary:
North Jeolla province has no separate local legislation on gender identity or gender expression. The framework a visitor stands under is the national one of South Korea: being transgender is not criminalised, consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal, and the only criminalisation in this field sits in the armed forces, where Military Criminal Act article 92-6 punishes consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available in the province and no longer depends on surgery. On 8 May 2024 the Yeongdong regional court approved a change of registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is contrary to law to determine gender change on the basis of surgery and that judicial guidelines prescribing surgery are now reference material rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life in accordance with their gender identity. Because the ruling applies province-wide as national law, a visitor to North Jeolla can seek court approval to change registered sex through the local courts on the same terms.

Trans visitors have a judicially enforced right to use public restrooms. On 22 July 2024 an appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a 3 million won claim, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change had been approved in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights. The court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. That ruling binds North Jeolla as national law.

The practical difficulty trans people report in this area is documented. A 2021 survey by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea of 591 transgender respondents found that 41 per cent used a restroom belonging to a gender other than their own, 39 per cent avoided food and drink in order to reduce restroom needs, and 36 per cent simply went without using a restroom. In 2021 the Daegu District Court, Pohang branch, awarded 7 million won in damages against a beauty academy that had prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom.

Against that protection, the wider legal environment carries gaps that matter to a visitor. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity in South Korea, so services, employment and accommodation offer no statutory protection on those grounds. The Ministry of Health and Welfare has declined to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult, and the National Human Rights Commission flagged this blind spot in November 2023. There is no same-sex marriage, which affects a visitor travelling with a partner, although the Constitutional Court issued a landmark 2024 ruling extending recognition of same-sex partners' rights in the specific area of healthcare.

No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources, and no incident involving trans people is documented within North Jeolla itself. Organised conservative opposition to LGBT rights remains active, and Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in South Korea while noting a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society.

68945753B5424648896322.name: South Jeolla
68945753B5424648896322.summary:
South Jeolla has no separate local ordinance on gender identity or gender expression, so a visitor to the province stands under South Korea's national framework. Being transgender is not a criminal offence in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, a provision the Constitutional Court upheld in 2023, and transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available without surgery. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are now reference rather than criteria; the court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity.

Trans visitors have a judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 22 July 2024 a Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, holding that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed her personal rights, and that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 Daegu District Court ruling at the Pohang branch had already awarded 7 million won against a beauty academy that barred a transgender student from its restroom.

Facilities remain a practical risk rather than a legal one. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found 41 per cent used a restroom of a different gender, 39 per cent avoided food and drink to do so, and 36 per cent went without using a restroom at all.

There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation in South Jeolla carry no statutory protection on these grounds. The National Human Rights Commission flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023 after the Ministry of Health and Welfare declined to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner, although the Constitutional Court's 2024 ruling extended recognition of same-sex partners' healthcare rights in that specific area. Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in South Korea alongside a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society, and organised conservative opposition remains active. No severe incident involving a trans visitor in South Jeolla appears in these sources.

68945753B5424648896322.tangentialFactors:
South Jeolla is one province among South Korea's seventeen first-level administrative units, and the rules that shape a trans visitor's expectations here are national rather than provincial: the criminal-law position, the document-change procedure, the restroom ruling and the absence of an anti-discrimination statute apply identically across the country. South Korean citizens can petition a family court to change their registered sex, and since the May 2024 Yeongdong ruling the courts no longer treat sex-reassignment surgery as a prerequisite; hormone therapy and a demonstrated life lived in the acquired gender have supported applications, and judicial guidelines requiring surgery now serve only as reference. The Supreme Court has also permitted a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

Transgender people are excluded from military service, and service members who have sex with a partner of the same sex face up to two years' imprisonment under Military Criminal Act article 92-6, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023. A gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017.

Residents have a damages remedy where police or institutions obstruct restroom access: the 300,000 won award finalised in July 2024 ran against the state, and the 7 million won award of 2021 ran against a private beauty academy. The National Human Rights Commission of Korea accepts complaints and has publicly pressed the Ministry of Health and Welfare on hospitalisation guidance for transgender patients.

Employment, housing and access to services are unprotected on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation because no comprehensive anti-discrimination law is in force. Same-sex couples cannot marry, though the Constitutional Court's 2024 decision gives same-sex partners standing in health-insurance decisions.

68945753B53856725499604.name: Jeju
68945753B53856725499604.summary:
Jeju stands under South Korea's national framework. South Korea does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, a provision the Constitutional Court upheld in 2023 after a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available on Jeju and the surgery requirement has fallen. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that conditioning gender change on surgery is contrary to law and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are now reference material rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity. The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change nationwide, including on Jeju, and the wire report records no specific case on the island. The Supreme Court has separately allowed a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

Trans visitors have a judicially enforced right to public restrooms. A person transitioning from male to female who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020 was advised by police to avoid women's public restrooms; the Seoul Central District Court ruled on 2 July 2024 that this advice infringed personal rights, and on 22 July 2024 the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal, finalising 300,000 won in damages against a 3 million won claim. The court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% avoided facilities out of fear, and a 2021 damages award compensated a student barred from academy restrooms. These national rulings govern Jeju, where the reporting describes no specific incident.

Protection machinery on the ground is thin. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on these grounds. In healthcare, the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court did issue a landmark 2024 ruling extending same-sex partners a measure of recognition in healthcare.

For a visitor on the ground, Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are broadly positive, but organised conservative opposition is active and Human Rights Watch records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report, which also notes a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. The principal trans-specific protection on the ground is a finalised court judgment on restroom access. On 22 July 2024 an appellate court dismissed the national government's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change had been approved by a court in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights. The court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The judgment is unappealed and serves as the national framework against which the metropolitan city is assessed.

The practical conditions behind that ruling are documented. A 2021 survey by the national human rights body of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% avoided facilities out of fear. Earlier relief exists at private level: a 2021 damages award against a private academy that barred a student from school restrooms.

Legal gender recognition is available and the surgical requirement has fallen. On 8 May 2024 a provincial court approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that conditioning gender change on surgery is against the law and that court guidelines requiring surgery now serve as reference rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. The Supreme Court has separately allowed a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on these grounds. In healthcare the national human rights body flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the national health ministry rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, stating that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage, which affects a visitor travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court did issue a 2024 ruling extending recognition of same-sex partners' healthcare rights in that specific area.

Organised conservative opposition is active nationally, a leading international human rights organisation records persistent discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report, and there is no national anti-discrimination statute to counter it, although the same report notes a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.

1875124B91024374055933.name: La Libertad
1875124B91024374055933.summary:
La Libertad region stands under Peru's national framework: trans identity is not a crime, but the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents requires restroom entry to be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Hate-crime provisions in Peru's Penal Code carry no LGBT coverage after Congress voted in 2017 to strip those protections, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, without them.

La Libertad appears in the Public Ministry's Observatory of Criminality study of intentional deaths of LGTB people between 2012 and 2021 with 84 criminal complaints covering 88 victims and 72 identified suspects. La Libertad ranks second in absolute count with 10 of the 88 deaths, level with Lima Norte and behind Lima's 12, with the region's cases centred on Trujillo. Six fiscal districts account for 58% of the deaths: Lima (12), La Libertad (10), Lima Norte (10), Lima Este (7), Lima Sur (6) and Callao (6). La Libertad's roughly 3% share of national population against an approximately 11.4% share of these deaths gives a per-capita lethality around 3.8 times the national average, a concentration not explained by population alone.

Regionally, Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR, dated 6 September 2024 and published in El Peruano on 7 November 2024, states that every travesti, transsexual and transgender person in La Libertad has the right to formal, dignified and productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions without discrimination on grounds of gender identity or its expression, and recognises the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability. The ordinance cites constitutional equality guarantees and article 323 of the Penal Code, which treats discrimination as a crime, and recommends that local governments issue municipal ordinances recognising gender identity and fundamental rights.

Elsewhere in Peru, enforcement of the bathroom restriction reaches private and public life: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's complaint against a gym that enforced it, and television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told congresswoman Susel Paredes to 'go use the men's room'. Recorded violence against trans people is rising and under-counted: 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed between 2020 and 2023, and a 2024 report co-authored by trans journalist Gianna Camacho found trans women most affected while stressing that recorded figures are a sub-registry.

Two protective rulings sit against that record. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of trans woman and activist Azul Rojas Marín, Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history. The Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 holds that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard against which Peru's bathroom law and the removal of hate-crime coverage stand in clear conflict.

1875124B58976419670313.name: Tacna
1875124B58976419670313.summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but a visitor to Tacna faces a legal regime with no gender-identity-recognition law and no hate-crime statute. Anti-trans violence can only be prosecuted as ordinary homicide, and the 'hate crime' label applied by investigators carries no separate legal consequence. Peru's Congress removed LGBT protections from the Penal Code's hate-crime provisions in 2017, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. Peru's compliance is contested. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights carried the case of Azul Rojas Marín to the Court, and in December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of the trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. Per BBC News Mundo it was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and the Inter-American Court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history.

Restrictions on trans people's use of public spaces are now legislated and are enforced beyond state facilities. In February 2025 a congressional committee approved unanimously, for plenary debate, the dictamen of bills on bathroom access presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru found the provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity and implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Enforcement reaches private life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected; its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected. The Public Prosecutor's Office identified 84 criminal complaints on LGTB deaths between January 2012 and May 2021, most victims gay men at 55.8% and trans women at 36.4%.

On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of the 'Los 5 Titos' hostel on Arias y Aragüez street in central Tacna. The autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the upper airways. She entered the hostel with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone roughly two hours later carrying a white bag; the body was discovered by hostel staff when the rental time expired. Police were analysing surveillance footage inside and outside the hostel to trace the suspect's escape route and held camera footage and taxi-driver testimony, but per the audited reporting no suspect had been identified, and the case was being investigated as a possible hate crime. Her family and local LGBT collectives held a vigil on 23 May 2025 demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives.

Activists note a recently promulgated legislative proposal by congressman Alejandro Muñante restricting access to public bathrooms on grounds of sexual orientation, further tightening the space trans visitors and residents occupy in the region.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Per BBC News Mundo it was the country's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and the Inter-American Court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Restrictions on trans people's use of public spaces are now legislated. In February 2025 a congressional committee approved unanimously, for plenary debate, the dictamen of bills on bathroom access presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the national Catholic university found the provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people and implicitly frames them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising with trans women most affected; its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected. The Public Prosecutor's Office identified 84 criminal complaints on LGTB deaths between January 2012 and May 2021, most victims gay men at 55.8% and trans women at 36.4%.

On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of the 'Los 5 Titos' hostel on Arias y Aragüez street in the state/province. The autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the airways. She entered with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone roughly two hours later carrying a white bag; staff discovered the body when the rental time expired. The state/province police were analysing surveillance footage inside and outside the hostel to trace the suspect's escape route and held camera footage and taxi-driver testimony, but per the audited reporting no suspect had been identified, and the case was being investigated as a possible hate crime. Her family and local LGBT collectives held a vigil on 23 May demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives.

Activists note a recently promulgated legislative proposal by congressman Alejandro Muñante restricting access to public bathrooms on grounds of sexual orientation.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 the national health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a capital city constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

13589884B77991835419453.name: Atlántico
13589884B77991835419453.summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention. A Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

The sharpest risk sits where armed groups operate, including in territories under their control. In the department of Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through flyer campaigns targeting "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots", and threatened a further wave. Trans women in that department reported few options beyond sex work; Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after receiving death threats from armed men, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. In the department of Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Targeted killings of trans people continue in the country's ordinary, urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025. A 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. One report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

Atlántico sits inside that national pattern. Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 annual report, "Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia", records 270 LGBTIQ+ victims nationally in 2025, a 63% increase over 2024, of which 165 were homicides, meaning one LGBTIQ+ person was killed every 32 hours. The report describes the violence as a continuum running from discrimination through intrafamily violence (1,531 cases), sexual violence (628 cases) and threats (1,184 victims) to homicide and impunity, and documents its territorial expansion into territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, criticising the state response as insufficient.

For the Atlántico department the same report documents 54 intrafamily-violence cases, 41 sexual offences, 12 discrimination cases, 8 digital-violence cases, 69 threats, 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders and 8 lethal-violence cases. It designates Barranquilla, the department's main hub, and the nearby municipality of Soledad as territories with a "high" threat level for this population. Publimetro Colombia reported the finding under the headline of increasing violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Atlántico and Colombia.

Impunity is the operative condition. The report finds that threats show near-total impunity, with 99.8% of cases never advancing past the investigation stage, and names this failure of investigation and prosecution as the structural feature of the crisis rather than an incidental gap.

One institutional commitment is on record: the department's development plan, and Barranquilla's, commit coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, police and judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violence against LGBTIQ+ people.
