Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans nationals change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". National high court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on self-recognition without a surgical requirement. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and a comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe, and it is the national picture against which this state/province is assessed. The national oversight office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and one count put hate-crime killings of trans people at 13 in the first quarter of 2025 alone. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was beaten in broad daylight in a metropolitan area in April 2025, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek, and died the following afternoon with no one arrested; her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia, and the head of state/province ordered an urgent investigation.

Where armed groups operate, the threat is organised and announced. In one state/province, armed groups gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulated "social cleansing" flyers against trans women, forcing her to relocate twice after death threats; in a further state/province, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". an activist quoted in the reporting states that the national prosecution service does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases. Reported totals for that pattern include 41 trans women killed nationally in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024.

Protection machinery exists alongside that failure. In July 2023 the national transitional justice jurisdiction indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence against them as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; a national court has also ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several national cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that killings are rising.

No finding specific to this state/province on law, enforcement practice or incidents affecting trans people appears in the sources available for this entry. The assessment therefore rests on the national framework and the national pattern of violence and prosecution, which apply throughout the country including this state/province.

13589884B75246552958907.name: Meta
13589884B75246552958907.summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Meta Department stands under Colombia's national framework. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016, same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2015, and a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation. Legal gender recognition has been available since 1993 on the basis of self-recognition, and since a rule change approved in June 2015 trans Colombians change the sex marker on government identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, and a comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

No source in the record reports any Meta-specific legal provision, enforcement practice or incident involving trans people. The assessment for the department therefore rests on the national pattern, which the sources describe as severe and worsening.

The gap between the written framework and enforcement is documented at national level. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Where armed groups operate, the violence takes the form of announced campaigns. In Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns publicised through flyers targeting "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots" and threatened a further wave; the Guardian's investigation of 30 July 2024 recorded that armed groups gave the trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed, and trans women in that department reported few options beyond sex work. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". The Guardian also quoted an activist stating that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases, and reported 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024.

Targeted killings of trans people also occur in ordinary urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025; a 28-second video of the assault circulated from 5 April showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. An international broadcaster reported on 6 August 2025 that anti-LGBTQ attacks were surging across the country, covering a wave of assaults through the Millerey case and attacks on same-sex couples.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern, and a Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

13589884B23733272568917.name: Cundinamarca
13589884B23733272568917.summary:
As a department of Colombia, Cundinamarca stands directly under the national legal framework, and the sources in the record carry no finding on law, enforcement practice or recorded incidents specific to this department. A visitor's expectations therefore rest on how the national rules apply and on the enforcement record documented elsewhere in the country.

Legal gender recognition runs through an administrative channel rather than a court. Since 1993 a person may change the gender marker on a Colombian birth certificate, with current options of F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero), and the process is notarial, requiring no surgery and no court ruling; the sources state that this route applies equally in Cundinamarca. Decree 0732 of 2026, signed by outgoing justice minister Jorge Iván Cuervo on 9 July 2026, obliges public notaries to complete the request within five business days, makes the first request and any simultaneous name change free of charge, and shields the change history from public disclosure. A Constitutional Court ruling of 4 February 2022 ordered the government to offer the nonbinary option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws. Since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia carry three gender options: male, female and X. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

The violence record available to a visitor is national. The sources count 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight more between February and April 2024, and a CNN article of 6 August 2025 covers a wave of attacks against LGBTQ+ people in Colombia following the killing of Sara Millerey. No source in the record places such an incident in Cundinamarca.

13589884B56780975975491.name: Tolima
13589884B56780975975491.summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia, of which Tolima is a department, is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

Courts have also intervened directly in detention, ruling on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty and protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Targeted killings of trans people continue in ordinary urban settings. El País English edition (14 April 2025) reports that Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek; she died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon and no one had been arrested. The same report states that hate crimes killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, and that her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was"; President Petro ordered an urgent investigation.

The sharpest risk sits where armed groups operate. The Guardian investigation (30 July 2024) documents armed groups in Caquetá giving trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulating "social cleansing" flyers against trans women, and quotes an activist saying the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings as ordinary cases. The report gives 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

No finding specific to Tolima on law, enforcement practice or incidents for trans people appears in the sources. The two incident reports available concern Antioquia and Caquetá, other departments elsewhere in Colombia. Nothing in the record marks Tolima as materially different from the national picture, and nothing marks it as safer; the department is assessed against the national transfemicide and armed-group baseline set out above.

13589884B76435085510886.name: Cesar
13589884B76435085510886.summary:
Cesar operates under Colombia's national legal framework, and no Cesar-specific finding on trans law, enforcement practice or incidents is available for this department. The rules a trans visitor therefore faces in Cesar are the national ones, which are among the more developed in the region on paper and considerably weaker in application.

Legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises recognition without a surgical requirement, and since a rule change approved in June 2015 the sex marker on government identification has been changed by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official who defended that change described the examinations as profoundly invasive of privacy rights and rooted in unacceptable prejudice. The markers available on Colombian birth certificates and identity documents are F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero), with trans and non-binary markers carried on national identification from November 2025 and three gender options (male, female, X) on passports issued within Colombia since August 2023. These routes apply equally in Cesar, and no surgery or court ruling stands between a visitor and correct documents.

Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, same-sex marriage has been available since the national court's April 2016 ruling, same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2015, and trans people have served openly in the armed forces since 2015. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The enforcement gap is severe and is the operative risk. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of that year. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that killings are rising. An activist quoted in a July 2024 investigation stated that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases.

13589884B66570655136682.summary:
La Guajira stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America and is what a trans visitor in this frontier department meets directly. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The source inventory identifies no La Guajira-specific legal, document, entry, screening, facilities or care finding that departs from that national position, and no enforcement deviation material enough to score separately; the department is assessed at the national score.

What distinguishes La Guajira is who controls conduct on the ground. The department sits in the country's frontier belt where "orden público" regimes mean armed groups rather than departmental police effectively regulate conduct. In March 2024 armed groups in Guajira posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

A 2025 report by Caribe Afirmativo documents the territorial expansion of violence and the insufficiency of the state response, with trans women displaced from such departments because of their gender identity by the same armed actors that displace others. National context reaching this department: the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one count recorded 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone.

Targeted violence continues in ordinary urban settings as well. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025; a video of the assault went viral from 5 April showing her with fractured limbs in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

13589884B83777567082486.name: Valle del Cauca
13589884B83777567082486.summary:
Valle del Cauca sits under Colombia's national framework, which is among the more developed legal regimes for trans people in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route under which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025. These instruments are national; the sources located for this department contain no departmental ordinance, statute or enforcement series of its own.

The department's safety picture is worse than the national average. Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 assessment places Valle del Cauca among the departments where what it describes as a territorial expansion of violence applies: killings have spread outward from established hotspots while the state response has remained insufficient. Lethal anti-trans violence in Colombia now occurs openly in urban settings as well as in territories held by armed actors. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, on 4 April 2025; a video of the assault went viral from the following day and she died that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, and even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation no arrest had been made.

Official recorded figures are high. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone, and the state ombudsman counted at least 25 trans women murdered between January and September 2025. Caribe Afirmativo recorded one LGBTIQ+ person killed every 32 hours across 2025, a 63% increase over 2024 (270 killings against 164), with trans women accounting for 18% of the 2024 homicides. One report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, and EL PAÍS cited additional killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper in the same period. Earlier counts reported 41 trans people killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight trans women killed between February and April 2024.

The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025. He praised the government's legal reforms and stated commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise. Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide: in July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

13589884B61455559641217.name: Quindío
13589884B61455559641217.summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Quindío is the national Colombian one, and it is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention. A Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The source inventory contains no Quindío-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding. Nothing in it deviates from the national position far enough to be scored separately, so the department is assessed at the national score, and the findings below are national context that a visitor to Quindío should expect to carry across departmental lines.

The gap between the statutory framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025. The Guardian reports 41 trans people killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024.

Lethal anti-trans violence is not confined to remote territory. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight on 4 April 2025 in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín; the assault was filmed and the 28-second video went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim, before she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". Police questioned local residents and President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, but no one was arrested, and solidarity events were held in several cities.

The sharpest risk sits where armed groups operate, including in territories under their control. In Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through flyers on the street and via WhatsApp, naming "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots" and "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, and threatened a further wave. Three armed men gave a trans woman and local election candidate one week to leave town; she hid for a week, then fled at night. A second trans woman said a friend of hers was killed, and Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after death threats from armed men. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Trans women in these departments reported few options beyond hairdressing or sex work, with discrimination narrowing their livelihoods to those two trades.

The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity.

13589884B22408468869829.name: Vaupés
13589884B22408468869829.summary:
The department of Vaupés stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

Day-to-day conduct in Vaupés is regulated by a different layer of authority. The department operates under an orden público regime in which armed groups rather than the departmental police hold effective control, and a 2025 national LGBTIQ+ report documents the territorial expansion of violence against LGBTIQ+ people together with the insufficiency of the state response, noting that trans women are displaced from their regions by the same armed actors that displace other residents. No department-specific enforcement or incident data for Vaupés was located.

A trans visitor should therefore expect the formal protections of the national framework to depend in practice on actors who are not the police, and should read the documented armed-group targeting of trans women in other Colombian departments as the operative model of risk. Lethal anti-trans violence in the country has occurred in broad daylight, been filmed by bystanders, and ended without an arrest even after a presidential order to investigate.

13589884B85526028135750.name: Risaralda
13589884B85526028135750.summary:
Risaralda falls squarely within Colombia's national legal framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on self-recognition without a surgical requirement, marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025. At least 41 trans women were killed nationally in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, and 13 in the first quarter of 2025 alone. Of 155 criminal investigations into LGBTQ killings, only three reached a verdict in the period reported, roughly 2 per cent, against an overall homicide-conviction rate of about 9 per cent.

Where armed groups operate, the risk is organised rather than incidental. In Caquetá department, armed groups circulated "social cleansing" flyers on the street and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign still running despite the 2016 peace agreement. Three armed men gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; she fled at night after hiding for a week. Trans women in Caquetá reported few options beyond hairdressing or sex work, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. In Guajira department, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Targeted killings also occur in ordinary urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, in April 2025; a 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands flailing in a creek unable to swim before she drowned, and she died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon. No one was arrested although police interrogated local residents. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, solidarity events were held in several cities, and her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was".

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

No source isolates Risaralda from this national pattern, so the national figures and the armed-group threat profile are what a visitor to the department should expect to face.

13589884B51885004571697.summary:
Guaviare Department stands under Colombia's national legal framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds has been prohibited by statute since 2011, the Constitutional Court opened same-sex marriage in April 2016, and adoption by same-sex couples has been available since 2015. Legal gender recognition rests on Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993, and since June 2015 a trans Colombian changes the sex marker on government identification by signing a document before a notary rather than submitting to judicially ordered bodily or psychiatric examination. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

A national LGBTI policy text addresses rights in public education, health care, prisons and the status of victims of the armed conflict, and its victim-protection provisions engage directly with the risk pattern described below.

The violence a trans visitor faces is set at national scale. Reporting current to mid-2025 counts nearly 50 queer and trans people killed in Colombia that year to date; 41 trans people were killed in 2023, and eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024. One account counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone.

Impunity is the defining feature of that toll. Of 155 criminal investigations into LGBTQ killings, only three reached a verdict in the year covered by the reporting, a conviction rate of roughly 2 per cent against 9 per cent for homicides generally.

Armed groups operating despite the 2016 peace agreement drive the most acute risk. In Guajira, flyers posted from March 2024 carried kill lists of named individuals under wording that identified "homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans" as targets. In Caquetá, "social cleansing" flyers circulated on the street and through WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. Trans women in Caquetá reported few options beyond hairdressing or sex work, and Tatiana Cespedes, a 51-year-old trans woman, was told by three armed men that she had one week to leave town or be killed; after hiding for a week she fled at night.

Targeted killing is not confined to territories under armed-group control. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia in April 2025 and drowned after being beaten with fractured limbs; President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Some conflict-period violence has been prosecuted as an international crime: in July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging gender persecution as a crime against humanity.

No source in the current inventory reports a Guaviare-specific incident, facility, enforcement action or protection mechanism. The assessment for Guaviare is therefore the national pattern of armed-group threat and investigative failure, combined with the thin institutional reach characteristic of Colombia's smaller peripheral departments.

13589884B16144547040567.name: Caquetá
13589884B16144547040567.summary:
Caquetá is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025, and a Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one report counted 13 trans people killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, welcoming the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that rising killings must be addressed urgently.

Targeted killing of trans people also occurs far from conflict zones. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, on 4 April 2025; the assault was filmed and the video went viral the following day, and she died that afternoon. Police questioned local residents, but no one was arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Her mother, Sandra Borja, stated that her daughter was killed for being who she was, and solidarity events were held in several cities.

Inside Caquetá the threat environment is armed-group control. In July 2024 The Guardian documented armed groups running a "social cleansing" campaign: flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, and further waves of flyers were threatened. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men that she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night. A second trans woman reported that a friend of hers had been killed. Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after receiving death threats from armed men. Armed groups also circulated warnings on phones targeting trans women, and trans women in the department reported fleeing it. Discrimination narrows trans women's livelihoods in Caquetá mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and several reported few options beyond sex work.

Lethal violence against trans people is recorded at scale nationally: 41 trans people were killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

13589884B18807997781037.summary:
The Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework. The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025. The courts have also intervened directly in detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was", and solidarity events were held in several cities. One report counted 13 trans people killed by hate in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, and the same reporting records the stabbing death of a trans woman sleeping rough.

In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

The source inventory records no incident, law or enforcement finding specific to Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina. A trans visitor to the islands is therefore assessed against the national position: the recognition framework set out above, and a national pattern of lethal anti-trans violence in which no arrest was recorded even after an investigation was ordered at the highest level.

1875124B3772980127380.name: Puno
1875124B3772980127380.summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but national legislation now restricts trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. Puno, as a Peruvian department, is bound by all of these measures: they are national in scope and the sources record no Puno-specific application, exemption or enforcement practice.

The operative restriction is the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow exceptions for situations involving medical attention, custody, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The same package bans inclusive restroom signage such as 'women in their diversity' and, according to the Inter-American Advisory Opinion record, determines restroom entry by sex assigned at birth, which reaches trans youth as well as adults.

The legislative sequence is documented. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante of Honor y Democracia; the measure stood at committee stage at that date. On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote, after which it entered into force as national law. The stated trigger for the original bills was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez airport.

Enforcement is expected to rest on the personal judgment of security staff, including checks of identity documents, which LGBTI activist Gianna Camacho identified as the practical consequence of the rule. Legal gender recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so a trans visitor's documents frequently do not correspond to presentation, and restroom access becomes the point at which that mismatch is tested. The policy has already reached private premises: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced it.

Hostility is not confined to signage and access. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. On the floor of Congress, congressman Lizarzaburu made dehumanising comparisons about trans people, as recorded by the human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru.

Violence against trans people is documented and, by the account of report co-author Gianna Camacho, substantially under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and stressed that published figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law, so a bias-motivated assault against a trans visitor falls outside the hate-crime aggravation that other regional systems provide.

The constitutional framework points the other way. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. IDEHPUCP, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, argues that the restroom provision breaches the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, that its aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, and that UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Speech and association are constrained as well. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports that the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The measure stood at committee stage in February 2025 and, as national law, binds Puno.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) states that on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions, and argues this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The analysis addresses the national framework that governs Puno and records no Puno-specific finding.

The state/province, as a state within the national framework, is bound by all of these measures: they are national in scope, and the sources record no jurisdictional application, exemption or enforcement practice.

The operative restriction is the April 2025 national law on the right to sexual integrity of children and adolescents. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow exceptions for situations involving medical attention, custody, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The same package bans inclusive restroom signage such as 'women in their diversity' and determines restroom entry by sex assigned at birth, reaching trans youth as well as adults.

The legislative sequence is documented. On 20 February 2025 the national legislature's Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante of the Honor y Democracia bloc; the measure stood at committee stage at that date. On 2 April 2025 the legislative Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote, after which it entered into force as national law. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at the country's main international airport.

Enforcement is expected to rest on the personal judgment of security staff, including checks of identity documents, which LGBTI activist Gianna Camacho identified as the practical consequence of the rule. Legal gender recognition in the state remains long, costly and invasive, so a trans visitor's documents frequently do not correspond to presentation, and restroom access becomes the point at which that mismatch is tested. The policy has already reached private premises: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced it.

Hostility is not confined to signage and access. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of the national legislature, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. On the legislative floor, congressman Lizarzaburu made dehumanising comparisons about trans people, as recorded by a national university's human-rights institute.

Violence against trans people is documented and, by the account of report co-author Gianna Camacho, substantially under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in the state with trans women most affected, and stressed that published figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was the state's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per a national news outlet, the regional human-rights court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the court through the regional human-rights commission.

The national legislature voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April constitutional-committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left the state one of only three jurisdictions among its neighbouring states lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law, so a bias-motivated assault against a trans visitor falls outside the hate-crime aggravation that other systems provide.

The constitutional framework points the other way. The regional human-rights court held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The national university's human-rights institute, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, argues that the restroom provision breaches the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the state constitution and article 1.1 of the regional human-rights convention, that its aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, and that international reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Speech and association are constrained as well. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 the state's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings, and in July 2025 a constitutional court in the seat of government, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

1875124B82769317880582.name: Tumbes
1875124B82769317880582.summary:
Tumbes stands under Peru's national framework: trans identity is not criminalised, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. There is no documented local mitigation for this border department, and the national restroom rule applies to public facilities including transport hubs, which matters because the bill was triggered by a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez airport.

On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. Exceptions cover custody situations, places where medical attention is required, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities; the package also bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage and inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', subject to narrow listed exceptions. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents carries this mandate, so trans people including trans youth are barred from facilities matching their gender identity.

The legal analysis of IDEHPUCP at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte dated 15 April 2025, argues that article 5 directly violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. IDEHPUCP has separately found the provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people and has recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Practical enforcement is expected to rest on front-line staff. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warned that bathroom access would come to depend on security personnel's personal judgment, including identity-document checks, and noted there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The restriction reaches private life as well: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on Willax TV presenter Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Because identity documents frequently do not match a trans person's presentation and legal gender recognition remains long, costly and invasive, an ID check at a restroom door or a border checkpoint carries a concrete risk of outing. Peru's entry and screening arrangements are national, and nothing in the sources documents a Tumbes-specific carve-out.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. That binding regional standard sits against the April 2025 statute, and the Inter-American framework also underlay the Rojas Marín litigation.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Hate-crime protection is absent. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

One case reached a judgment. Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. 1875124B61751373376494.summary:
Lambayeque has no trans-specific ordinance, municipal rule or local enforcement pattern on record; a visitor in this department is bound by Peru's national framework. The parent framework is mixed. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The operative restriction on public facilities was approved in stages during 2025. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions covering custody and situations where required, including accompanying minors, the elderly or people with disabilities, and obliging venues not to post ambiguous restroom signage. The plenary of Congress approved the fused text on Wednesday 2 April 2025 as Article 5.1 of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes and waived a second vote. The stated trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport.

The Pontifical Catholic University of Peru's human-rights institute IDEHPUCP reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. Activist Gianna Camacho argues that enforcement would fall to security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

Enforcement already reaches private life. The consumer-protection body INDECOPI dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit under SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI. On television, presenter Ana Maria Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to go use the men's room.

Violence figures are national and rising, and recorded totals are a floor rather than a count. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 assassinations of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian, with trans women most affected. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, twelve of them trans women. Killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, and in 13 of the 19 killings in 2023. The observatory's co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, states that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One documented case illustrates the pattern of abduction and killing: in February 2023 the 31-year-old trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano was kidnapped from central Lima by the Los Gallegos extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot. Two killers were arrested in March 2023.

Hate-crime machinery does not reach these offences. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan Leon, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marin, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack; it was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

1875124B1797874831789.name: Amazonas
1875124B1797874831789.summary:
Amazonas stands under Peru's national framework: the department has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern, and none of the sources covering this territory contain Amazonas-specific content. What a trans visitor faces in Amazonas is the national statute book, national policing and national monitoring data.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities. On 20 February 2025 the Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliging venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The stated trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved the fused text of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes and waived a second vote. Its Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex, which bars trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Enforcement reaches private premises as well as public buildings. IDEHPUCP recalls SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, in which a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, where bathroom assignment was grounded on the sex recorded in the DNI. Activist Gianna Camacho argues that enforcement of the national restriction would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

National monitoring is the only violence data available for this territory. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 LGBTI homicides and 170 rights-violation cases across 2020-2023, the homicide victims comprising 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian; 19 killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women, and the killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023.

The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. IDEHPUCP recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

1875124B15182629165166.summary:
ANCASH DEPARTMENT STANDS UNDER THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK. No trans-specific regional ordinance, departmental decree or incident series for Ancash appears in the source inventory; every available item is national in scope, and the framework below is what a visitor to Ancash is scored against.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

In February 2025 the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting entry into public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than a person's birth sex, with narrow exceptions covering custody situations and cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliging venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho argued the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

The plenary of Congress approved the fused text of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes on 2 April 2025 and waived a second vote; its Article 5.1 bars persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex, and the same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. The same law's vague child-protection articles, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru read Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The institute also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu, and found the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people while implicitly framing them as harassment risks. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Enforcement reaches private life as well as state facilities. Consumer-protection body INDECOPI, in SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI. On television, presenter Ana Maria Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; among the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian, and 19 killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women. Killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. The 2024 report's co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan Leon, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marin, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive. The 2026 status of the bathroom restriction is unconfirmed in available sources, and no source in the inventory records any Ancash-specific enforcement action or incident.
