For residents, gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, which bears directly on whether a person can present documents matching their lived gender when restroom access is policed by identity papers.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are also constrained for residents. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. 1875124B73300566086976.name: El Callao
1875124B73300566086976.summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity. Its national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. El Callao stands under that national framework: no region-specific trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding appears in the sources, so what a trans visitor faces in this department is what the national rules deliver.

The governing instrument is the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents. Its Article 5.1 prohibits any person from entering or using a public sanitary facility designated for a sex other than their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities. The plenary of Congress approved the text and waived a second vote on 2 April 2025. The same package obliges venues not to post ambiguous or inclusive restroom signage. The bills were merged and approved by unanimity in the Comision de Mujer y Familia on 20 February 2025, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante of Honor y Democracia; the stated trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport.

Enforcement rests on individuals judging appearance and documents. Activist Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, states that security staff would have to check the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. The restriction already reaches private premises: the consumer-protection body INDECOPI, in SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, which had grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases across 2020-2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women. Killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. A 2024 report co-authored by Gianna Camacho found hate crimes rising with trans women most affected and stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One case illustrates the pattern of targeted killing: in February 2023 the 31-year-old trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano was kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot. Two killers were arrested in March 2023.

Peru's crime-registration systems do not incorporate sexual orientation or gender identity, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

1875124B80189625477090.name: Ucayali
1875124B80189625477090.summary:
Ucayali stands under the national framework of Peru, which does not criminalise trans identity but has legislated in 2025 against trans people's use of public facilities matching their gender identity. On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from a second vote a law whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow exceptions for custody situations, places where medical attention is required, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The same package bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage, including inclusive wording such as 'women in their diversity', and its vague child-protection articles enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational content.

The legislative origin of that restriction is traceable. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, and the measure passed the plenary in April 2025. A July 2023 social-media complaint over the gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez International Airport in Lima set the process in motion. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warned at the time that restroom access would come to depend on the personal judgement of security staff, including identity-document checks, and noted that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The Pontifical Catholic University of Peru's human-rights institute IDEHPUCP concludes that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the law rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers when UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Hate-crime protection for LGBT people is absent from Peru's law. Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. That outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in its hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and, according to its own researchers, under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected; its co-author, trans journalist and human-rights defender Gianna Camacho, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women again the most affected group.

Enforcement reaches private as well as public life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the 2025 bathroom policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'; Congressman Lizarzaburu made dehumanising comparisons about trans people on the floor of Congress, a record captured by IDEHPUCP.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

A trans visitor to Ucayali should therefore expect to face the national restroom restriction as applied wherever security staff or building rules determine access, with no hate-crime coverage in the Penal Code to fall back on, and with official violence figures that are acknowledged to understate the problem.

No source in this inventory records a regional ordinance, an incident series, a facility rule or an enforcement pattern specific to the state/province; the binding text is national, and the practical question for residents is how security staff and building administrators apply article 5 to regional public facilities.

The evidence that exists about everyday enforcement is drawn from elsewhere in the country and is consistent with the national pattern. a national consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, which suggests that complaints about access restrictions are unlikely to succeed through that channel. Activists and researchers warn that restroom access will turn on the personal judgement of security staff, including identity-document checks, and that no record supports the premise that trans women have assaulted anyone in women's restrooms.

Civil society and academic institutions carry much of the documentation. a human-rights institute at the national Catholic university published the legal analysis of article 5 by named researchers, and documented the dehumanising floor remarks of a serving member of the national legislature. Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, co-authored the 2024 report on rising hate crimes and stressed that the published figures are only a sub-registry, meaning residents in the state/province should not read the absence of local records as the absence of local incidents.

Two state/province actions have been favourable to trans residents: the June 2024 removal of pathologising gender-diversity terminology from official health guidance, and the July 2025 ruling of a constitutional court in the national capital striking down an anti-equality decree after an activist challenge. Both were obtained outside the legislative process and neither has been shown to have been implemented regionally.

Likewise unsourced is whether the June 2024 health guidance has been implemented in Ucayali health facilities, whether the July 2025 Lima constitutional ruling has been applied regionally, and how the raised obscenity sentence and article 4 media ban are being used against identity-related content in the region.

1875124B61678101818850.name: Junín
1875124B61678101818850.summary:
No department-level trans statute, ordinance, enforcement finding or incident series for Junín appears in the inventory, so the department stands under Peru's national framework and the national assessment governs what a trans visitor to Junín should expect. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The restroom restriction moved through Congress in two steps. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody situations, where medical attention is required, or when accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and with a parallel ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The immediate trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport. On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote the fused text, whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', subject only to narrow listed exceptions. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by biological sex, barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Enforcement rests on private judgment at the door. Activist Gianna Camacho, co-author of the 2024 hate-crime report, warns that access would come down to security staff assessing identity documents on their own discretion, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The legal analysis of Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte at IDEHPUCP, the human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, concludes that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. IDEHPUCP also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The restriction reaches private and public life alike. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI recorded 54 murders of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases across Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims at 30, against 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, including 12 trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty such as multiple gunshots and stabbings; the 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 complaints in 2020 alone. The inventory recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of Rubí Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans sex worker, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. A 2024 report co-authored by Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and she stresses that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

Impunity has been broken once. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The absence of hate-crime protection is a matter of record. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

1875124B3070334250121.summary:
Huancavelica stands under Peru's national framework. The region has no recorded trans-specific law, ordinance, enforcement pattern or incident of its own, so what a trans visitor to Huancavelica faces is the national position: no criminalisation of trans identity, but statutory restriction of access to public facilities, no hate-crime protection, and rising recorded violence.

Peru's Congress has legislated directly against trans people's use of public facilities. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents mandates that restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Hate-crime protection for LGBT people was stripped from the Penal Code in 2017, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

The restriction reached committee stage in February 2025. Infobae Perú reported on 20 February that the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. Exceptions are narrow: custody, situations requiring medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The text also bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory and warned that restroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity checks, noting there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The institute finds the provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by implicitly framing them as harassment risks, resting on a stigmatising stereotype that UN reporting contradicts, since trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Peru's constitutional baseline points the other way. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Report co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stresses that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One 2023 killing illustrates the pattern: in February 2023 a gang abducted trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and killed her in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme.

Madre de Dios has no distinct trans-specific law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement record in the material reviewed for this dossier; the national framework therefore governs what a trans visitor to the department faces. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, removed hate-crime protection for LGBT people from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women continues to rise.

Restroom access is restricted nationally. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission approved unanimously a merged dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante of Honor y Democracia, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. The text lists narrow exceptions for custody, required medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The bill followed a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the text and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex'. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents carries the same requirement into force for trans people, including trans youth, and the legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Enforcement is expected to rest on the judgement of individual security staff. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that access to restrooms would depend on staff discretion, including checks of identity documents, and notes that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The restriction reaches private life as well: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television the presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, to 'go use the men's room'.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, holds that the restroom provision violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The institute states that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers, and cites UN reporting showing that trans people are more often victims than aggressors. It also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases across Peru for 2020-2023, with trans women accounting for more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, 12 of them trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 complaints recorded in 2020. A 2024 report on rising hate crimes found trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stated that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One case sets a legal precedent for the region. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024), covering the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian; killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty (multiple gunshots, stabbings), and the 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination (61 denuncias in 2020). 1875124B5984096006894.localsOnly:
Residents of Cusco live under the same national restrictions as visitors, without an exemption for habitual presence. Restroom entry is determined by 'biological sex' under the April 2025 law, so a trans resident faces the security-staff and identity-document assessment described above in shopping centres, gyms, cinemas, health facilities and municipal buildings, as well as in workplaces. The consumer-protection body's dismissal of a complaint against a gym that applied the policy indicates that administrative channels offer little recourse for these disputes.

Inclusive signage is banned, which removes 'women in their diversity' and comparable wording from shops, public bodies, schools and event materials. The vague child-protection articles of the same law, including the article 4 ban on media and advertising content, expose residents who produce artistic, educational or identity-related material to censorship, and the obscenity minimum sentence rose from three to four years.

Two protective developments are on record for residents. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Because LGBT provisions were removed from the Penal Code in 2017, a resident who is assaulted because of their gender identity has no hate-crime coverage under that statute; the Azul Rojas Marín judgment came through the Inter-American system after decades of litigation rather than through ordinary domestic hate-crime prosecution.

1875124B63771233756824.name: Apurímac
1875124B63771233756824.summary:
Apurímac stands under the national framework of Peru. No Apurímac-specific trans statute, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding appears in the sources attached to this record, and all three are national in scope; the operative rules for a visitor in the department are therefore the laws and enforcement patterns recorded at national level.

The most direct legal exposure concerns public restrooms. Bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, were merged and approved unanimously by the congressional Women and Family Commission on 20 February 2025; the measure bars trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their sex at birth, with exceptions only for custody, situations requiring medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and it bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The congressional Plenary approved and exempted from a second vote on 2 April 2025 the bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', and it was enacted as Law 32331 on 13 May 2025. The package followed a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at the Jorge Chávez airport.

The IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru concludes that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

In practice, access to restrooms now turns on the personal judgment of security staff, potentially including identity-document checks, a consequence flagged by LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho; she also notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The restriction reaches private premises as well as public facilities: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Hate-crime protection is absent. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome leaves Peru one of only three countries in South America, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian; killings rose to 19 in 2023, of whom 12 were trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty. Among the cases is the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising with trans women most affected, and co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

Accountability has come once, after long litigation. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

1875124B34173194899706.name: Arequipa
1875124B34173194899706.summary:
Arequipa department has no region-specific trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding on record. All three attached sources are national in scope, and as national measures they bind the department. The operative legal frame for a visitor to Arequipa is the national one.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The facility restriction is in force. The Commission on Women and Family approved a dictamen covering bills 6506 and 8457 on 20 February 2025, barring entry to public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to one's birth sex, with exceptions only for custody, medical care, or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and requiring unambiguous signage. The Congress plenary approved the package on 2 April 2025, exempt from a second vote, as article 5 of the law strengthening the right to sexual integrity of children and adolescents; the wider package was enacted as Law 32331 on 13 May 2025. A trans traveller using a public restroom in Arequipa therefore faces a live national legal exposure.

Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho warned that the measure would leave security staff to judge people by personal criteria, such as requesting their national identity document. Enforcement of the restriction reaches private as well as public life: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told congresswoman Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report counted 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women most affected and hate crimes rising; its co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry. The report recounts the February 2023 kidnapping of trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her murder in Carabayllo with approximately 30 gunshots at the hands of the 'Los Gallegos' gang, the bodies showing gunshots, stab wounds and throat-slitting that indicate extreme hate.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three countries in South America, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity' is banned, inclusive language has been prohibited in the legislature, and official health guidance no longer pathologises gender diversity after the June 2024 revision, which improves the terms on which trans patients are treated. Minimum sentences for obscenity rose from three to four years under the April 2025 law.

1875124B3524833739478.name: Loreto
1875124B3524833739478.summary:
Loreto is a department of Peru and stands under the national framework: Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

No trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement finding for Loreto appears in the sources. Every attached item is national in scope, and as national law the restrictions below apply in Loreto.

Facility access is restricted by statute. On 2 April 2025 the Congress plenary approved, exempt from a second vote, the dictamen of the law strengthening the right to sexual integrity of children and adolescents, whose article 5 bars from public sanitary facilities anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex, with exceptions limited to accompanying or assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. The February 2025 committee stage covered bills 6506 and 8457, which would bar entry to facilities destined to the sex opposite one's birth sex, with exceptions for custody, medical care or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and would require unambiguous signage. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The restriction reaches private life as well as public facilities. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, to 'go use the men's room'. Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho warns that security staff would judge people by personal criteria, such as requesting their DNI, so the practical effect is broader than the text of the rule.

Hate-crime protection is absent. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The TLGBI Rights Observatory recorded 54 killings of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women most affected and hate crimes rising. In February 2023 trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped in central Lima and murdered in Carabayllo with approximately 30 gunshots at the hands of the 'Los Gallegos' gang; the body showed gunshots, stab wounds and throat-slitting indicating extreme hate. The observatory's co-author Gianna Camacho states that recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One protective outcome is on record. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack; it was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history.

25984515B95172477822815.name: Adana
25984515B95172477822815.summary:
Adana Province stands under the Turkish national framework without any province-specific overlay: the source record contains no Adana provision on gender identity, documentation, policing or facilities, and no local enforcement data either. What a trans visitor meets in Adana is therefore the countrywide position, set at national level.

The baseline is permissive on its face. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, the year gender reassignment surgery became lawful. A visitor whose passport marker has been changed abroad or at home can present that document without the change itself constituting an offence.

The direction of travel runs the other way. A leaked draft omnibus justice reform, the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would enable criminal charges against LGBT people across Türkiye; Human Rights Watch described it as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. The measure is national, contains no province-specific provisions, and would apply in Adana if adopted. Istanbul activists held a press conference against the draft on 28 October 2025.

Two further gaps bear directly on a visitor. Türkiye has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so there is no statutory complaint to make against a hotel, clinic or officer who treats a trans guest differently. Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition at all: marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unavailable, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as individuals. A partner travelling alongside a trans visitor has no recognised standing in any Turkish proceeding.

LGBT people are also barred from serving openly in the military, a restriction that falls on residents rather than tourists but that shapes the official attitude a visitor encounters at any checkpoint where identity is examined.

25984515B90872828599679.name: Adıyaman
25984515B90872828599679.summary:
Adıyaman Province stands under the national framework of Türkiye, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — together with systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. There is no Adıyaman-specific carve-out from any of this: the provisions that govern a visitor's exposure are national.

The government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Under that framing a leaked draft omnibus justice reform, the 11th Judicial Package, would enable criminal charges against LGBT people nationwide; Human Rights Watch reported it on 29 October 2025 as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades, and Istanbul activists held a press conference against it on 28 October 2025. The package contains no province-specific provisions and would apply to Adıyaman unchanged if adopted. Its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Street-level enforcement shows what that looks like in practice. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor in Adıyaman, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care, which bears directly on a visitor who needs hospital contact while in the country.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: The national framework of Türkiye applies to every visitor to Adıyaman Province. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1858 under the Ottoman penal code, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, when gender reassignment surgery became legal. Türkiye has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military. Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition: marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unavailable, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as individuals. These provisions are countrywide, with no Adıyaman-specific content.

25984515B90872828599679.blindSummary:
The province stands under the national framework of the parent nation, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. A national human rights monitoring body recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — together with systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. There is no province-specific carve-out from any of this: the provisions that govern a visitor's exposure are national.

The national government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language a international human rights organisation identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Under that framing a leaked draft omnibus justice reform, the 11th Judicial Package, would enable criminal charges against LGBT people nationwide; the organisation reported it on 29 October 2025 as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades, and activists in a major city held a press conference against it on 28 October 2025. The package contains no province-specific provisions and would apply here unchanged if adopted. Its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Street-level enforcement shows what that looks like in practice. During 2025 police in a major city stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in one urban district and held them at a central police station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of a regional human rights convention. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

The parent nation requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor in the province, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people nationally is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in a large city by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 trans and LGBTI+ pride week in that city by a truth and memory centre found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner was found dead in a cell at a women's prison on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from national human rights association branches in six cities demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by an opposition legislator on 12 December 2025, confirmed that trans prisoners are placed according to their registered sex and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Transition-related care is tightening. A health ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a provincial health directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required electronic reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care, which bears directly on a visitor who needs hospital contact while in the country.

25984515B90872828599679.tangentialFactors:
The pattern documented for Türkiye is longstanding rather than a product of the current legislative moment. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Türkiye, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Because every instrument cited here is national, the risk surface in Adıyaman is expected to track the countrywide pattern rather than diverge from it: the absence of provincial provisions in the draft package, and the absence of any Adıyaman-specific legal text, both point the same way.

25984515B90872828599679.localsOnly:
Legal baseline for residents: legal gender change has been possible since 1988, when gender reassignment surgery became legal. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1858 under the Ottoman penal code. These provisions are countrywide.

Türkiye has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military. 25984515B26209284550223.name: Afyonkarahisar
25984515B26209284550223.summary:
Afyonkarahisar stands entirely under Turkey's national legal and policing framework on LGBTI+ matters. The draft omnibus justice package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 contains no Afyonkarahisar-specific provision, and no provincial record exists that would make this province either more protective or more hostile than the country-wide picture. A visitor to Afyonkarahisar is subject to the same national rules, the same document regime and the same street-level policing practice documented elsewhere in Turkey.

The leaked '11th Judicial Package' would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people. Conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', including its so-called 'promotion', would carry up to three years in prison; participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies would carry up to four years, and because same-sex marriage is not legal in Turkey such ceremonies are by definition symbolic. Human Rights Watch called the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. The measure had not been enacted when reported, but authorities have already been documented acting against trans people as though comparable prohibitions were in force.

The same draft would restrict gender-affirming care: the minimum surgery age raised from 18 to 25, permanent infertility imposed as a condition, medical professionals fined or imprisoned for up to seven years, and transgender patients facing up to three years for care falling outside the new limits. Rights groups assess that these limits would push transition care into underground settings.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy', records 313 violations of the right to liberty, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total and consisting mostly of detentions, alongside 336 violations of the right to assembly and 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51. The torture figure is linked mainly to peaceful assembly, and the report documents event-specific bans together with violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings. These are national figures; no Afyonkarahisar-specific finding appears in the source.

The same report records six right-to-life violations in 2025, three of them counted as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. These totals are compiled from media and civil-society reporting because the Turkish state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so the true figure cannot be verified from official records.

Hostility has been institutionalised under a 'Year of the Family' banner: instructions issued to public institutions, hate speech from senior officials, censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events. The source presents this as national practice rather than a choice available to any province, which means it applies in Afyonkarahisar as it does in Istanbul or Ankara.

Two national rules bear directly on a trans visitor's exposure at any checkpoint. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance, and police conducting 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) stops have required trans women to produce documents. Any such interaction is an occasion on which passport details can be compared against presentation. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for GBT checks before release; that city-level pattern is one illustration of a national practice, not a separate local regime.

Two further national measures shape what a trans person faces if detained. Trans prisoners are placed according to registered sex rather than gender identity, confirmed by the death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 and by the parliamentary question filed by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option on gender-related medical-board reports and required electronic reports, a change assessed as risking the profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy', records six right-to-life violations, three classified as hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the most affected. The figures are compiled from media and civil-society reports because the state maintains no official hate-crime statistics. The same report records 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51, mostly linked to peaceful assembly, together with 336 assembly violations and 313 liberty violations, a roughly 2.5-fold increase in liberty violations composed mainly of detentions.

The asymmetry is visible in individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the attacker was released while Yaşam herself was referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention outcome as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Assembly remains a flashpoint. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Türkiye places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, including a trans man held in a women's prison.

The Prison Insider country profile on Türkiye, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and drawing on ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. 25984515B97476213604692.name: Antalya
25984515B97476213604692.summary:
Antalya stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than left to residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 of them recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

A leaked draft omnibus justice package from October 2025, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality". It would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 on condition of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who provide such care. Human Rights Watch called the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it.

The Kaos GL report "A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy", presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at its launch, documents senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner, creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, with regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

The draft package contains no province-specific provisions, and the surviving record carries no Antalya-level breakdown. Neither a more protective nor a more hostile local regime can be established for this province; the documented national picture applies here unchanged.

For a visitor, the practical exposure point is the identity-document checkpoint. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Any such stop is an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation, and foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints must produce original documents.

Street-level enforcement elsewhere in Turkey shows how these stops are used. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafes in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police issued no fines but documented them anyway, and that enforcement was being applied before the new law had been passed.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

25984515B63739470532168.name: Aydın
25984515B63739470532168.summary:
Aydın province stands under the national framework that applies across Turkey, and that framework has been revised to place documented LGBT people under sustained legal jeopardy. The Turkish Ministry of Health announced new reporting rules in September 2025 that require hospitals to record the gender of transgender patients in official e-reports rather than allowing them to enter an "other" option, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular listing "gender reassignment" as an official cause for medical-board referral. The stated purpose was to tighten transition-related care; the practical effect is that every clinical encounter leaves a documented marker of a trans patient's status.

Human Rights Watch described the measure as an attempt to silence doctors, and that concern sits alongside a wider tightening reported by Kaos GL in its 2025 monitoring, which found anti-LGBTI+ hostility institutionalised as explicit state policy, with senior officials issuing hate speech and instructions to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner. Regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom during the same period.

The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Under that framing a draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people was before the government as of October 2025. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Street-level enforcement in Istanbul illustrates that point. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The passport-carrying rule for foreigners compounds these risks. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor in Aydın's coastal towns, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Turkish rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison — and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited here as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

25984515B40051660631000.name: Aksaray
25984515B40051660631000.summary:
Aksaray stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than left to residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 of them recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

A leaked draft omnibus justice package from October 2025, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality. It would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 with a requirement of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who provide such care. Human Rights Watch called the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it. The measure had not been passed when reported, but authorities have acted as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at its launch, documents that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as explicit state policy under a Year of the Family banner, with senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and with regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

Street-level enforcement illustrates the gap between pending legislation and practice. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafes in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for General Information Gathering background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to her.

Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, and Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation, creating a direct outing risk for a visitor whose appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

The surviving record for this province is entirely national-level and carries no Aksaray-specific breakdown. Neither a more protective nor a more hostile local regime can be established from the inventory, and the documented national picture applies here unchanged.

25984515B60965754972902.name: Ardahan
25984515B60965754972902.summary:
Ardahan province stands under the national framework of Turkey. The documentation available for this jurisdiction is national in scope, and the draft instrument described below contains no Ardahan-specific provisions; without any provincial breakdown in the record, the national picture governs what a trans visitor to Ardahan should expect to face.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft omnibus justice package, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality". Human Rights Watch called the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades.

The draft reaches ceremonies and medical care as well as public conduct. It would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, with penalties of up to four years in prison. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, attach mandatory permanent infertility to that care, and punish the health professionals who perform it. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft.

The package had not been enacted at the time of reporting. Kaos GL's 2025 report, whose findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, documents that hostility toward LGBTI+ people had already hardened into explicit state policy during the year, carried under a "Year of the Family" banner by senior officials whose hate speech and instructions to public institutions created a climate encouraging human-rights violations.

For a visitor, the practical point of contact with that policy is the identity check. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, and any police stop becomes an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation, with an outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match the gender marker recorded in the document.
