25984515B679661827679.name: Batman
25984515B679661827679.summary:
Turkey presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors, driven by hostility that has become formal state policy rather than residual prejudice. A leaked draft omnibus justice package from October 2025, the '11th Judicial Package', would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 with a requirement of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch called the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades; 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record. The association's report, 'A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy', documents anti-LGBTI+ hostility institutionalised as explicit state policy under a 'Year of the Family' banner, with senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom. Findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at the launch.

Street-level enforcement illustrates the gap between statute and practice. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them.

Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation, creating a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison — and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Batman province carries no province-specific provisions in any of this material. The surviving record is entirely national-level and carries no provincial breakdown, so neither a more protective nor a more hostile local regime can be established here; the documented national picture applies in Batman unchanged.

The national picture therefore applies in Bayburt unchanged.

25984515B39892287187022.name: Bilecik
25984515B39892287187022.summary:
Bilecik province stands under the national framework applicable across Turkiye, and the sources carried for this record contain no Bilecik-specific law, enforcement practice or local ordinance. Whatever local variation exists is undocumented here, so the national picture is what a visitor to Bilecik should expect to encounter.

The most consequential pending measure is the leaked '11th Judicial Package', a draft omnibus justice package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. If adopted as drafted it would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', and would punish participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with up to four years in prison. The draft carried in the inventory makes no provision specific to Bilecik, so its reach would be uniform.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25 and require permanent infertility as a precondition, while imposing penalties on health professionals who provide such care. Human Rights Watch described the package as one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. Fifteen Turkish LGBT organisations and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at its launch, finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people has become explicit state policy rather than residual prejudice, with senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner creating a climate that encourages human-rights violations. Regulatory and supervisory bodies are documented as systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

At street level, foreign visitors are required to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance, and police stop-and-check practice has been applied to trans people in public spaces even where the pending draft has not been enacted. Any such interaction places passport data alongside physical presentation, which is the principal outing risk facing a trans visitor in Bilecik or elsewhere in Turkiye.

25984515B43512589741592.name: Bingöl
25984515B43512589741592.summary:
Bingöl is a province in eastern Turkey with no documented provincial divergence from the national legal position on trans people. No province-specific ordinance, separate legal system or distinct enforcement pattern has been recorded for Bingöl, so a trans visitor here stands under the same national framework that applies across Turkey, including the draft package described below.

That framework is hostile by design. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 on a leaked omnibus draft, the '11th Judicial Package', which would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour it defines as 'contrary to biological sex and general morality'. Participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony would carry penalties of up to four years' imprisonment. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25 and attach a mandatory permanent-infertility condition, while punishing health professionals who carry out such care. Human Rights Watch called the measure one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades; 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it. The package had not been enacted as reported, but its drafting establishes the direction of travel for anyone assessed against Turkish authorities.

The Kaos GL 2025 report, 'A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy', presented at its launch by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, records that anti-LGBTI+ hostility has been institutionalised as explicit state policy. Senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner created a climate encouraging human-rights violations, while regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

For a trans visitor the practical exposure points are checkpoint identity checks, in which original photo identification must be produced and compared against presentation, and any contact with police under 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) practice. Both are national patterns; the only regional-grade note specific to the east concerns security practice rather than law, namely emergency-era policing and elevated police presence.

25984515B19802935753104.name: Bitlis
25984515B19802935753104.summary:
Bitlis province stands under the national framework of Türkiye, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors, driven by hostility that has become formal state policy rather than residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record, together with systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people.

The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Under that framing a draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people was before the government as of October 2025. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that the leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package would amend the national penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", criminalise participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to 4 years in prison, and raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 with a mandatory permanent-infertility condition. Health professionals who perform such care would face punishment under the draft. Human Rights Watch called it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades, and 15 Turkish LGBT groups together with the Turkish Medical Association oppose it.

Kaos GL reported that its 2025 report, "A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy", documents anti-LGBTI+ hostility becoming institutionalised as explicit state policy: senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, while regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. Findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at the launch.

Street-level enforcement illustrates how this operates. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

That document obligation is general: Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, an asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Türkiye places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Türkiye, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, risking the profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

25984515B96039700866385.name: Bolu
25984515B96039700866385.summary:
Bolu is a province of Türkiye and sits entirely under the national framework that governs LGBT rights across the country. The pattern is one of documented, institutionalised state hostility rather than informal prejudice. Kaos GL's 2025 human-rights monitoring recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, including 299 detention decisions of which 256 were recorded through formal channels and 43 were taken off the record.

A leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package, reported in October 2025, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', with penalties of up to three years in prison, and would criminalise participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years. Human Rights Watch described the draft as one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it. The measure had not been passed when reported, but enforcement of prohibitions that exist only on paper is already documented in practice.

The draft also reaches transition-related care. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, and make permanent infertility a condition of eligibility. Health professionals who perform such care would face penalties including fines and prison terms of up to seven years, and patients would face terms of up to three years.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, found that hostility became explicit state policy during the year: senior officials issued hate speech, instructions were issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The report documented six right-to-life violations, three of which rights organisations classified as hate-motivated killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected. It also recorded 89 cases of torture or ill-treatment, up from 51 the previous year.

Street-level enforcement illustrates the practical effect of that policy. In one large city in 2025, police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the streets, in shops and in cafés and held them at a police station for 'General Information Gathering' background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One woman detained stated that police took no fines but documented her anyway, and noted that the new law had not been passed even as its prohibitions were being applied to her.

Foreign visitors carry a specific exposure at every checkpoint. Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any interaction with police in Bolu province is therefore an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation, creating a direct outing risk for a trans visitor whose passport gender marker does not match how they appear.

Violence in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is asymmetric. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in the Bakırköy district of Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Prison conditions remain among the most severe points of risk for any trans person detained in Türkiye. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025. Turkish rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in six cities demanded an independent investigation. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Türkiye places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, with a trans man held in a women's prison.

The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening at ministry level. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a provincial health directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording an 'other' option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

The national Criminal Code remains in force as written, while a leaked draft omnibus package would add explicit prohibition of conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with penalties of up to three years in prison, and up to four years for taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony. The draft had not been adopted when reported, and its pending status has not prevented authorities from behaving as though the prohibitions already operate.

Enforcement ahead of legislation is the central operational risk. In 2025 police stopped roughly twenty trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in a major urban district and held them at a police station for 'General Information Gathering' background checks before release. Rights lawyers argue such checks breach Article 5 of the Convention on Human Rights. One woman detained reported that officers imposed no fines but documented her anyway, and noted that the new law had not yet been passed even as it was being enforced against her.

Checkpoint interactions carry a direct outing exposure for anyone whose presentation does not match their passport. Foreign nationals are required to produce original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 national lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response is asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in a major city by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was referred for arrest, a sequence activists treat as evidence of state policy.

Transition-related care is being restricted through administrative regulation. a Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a provincial health directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required electronic reports to be issued, placing trans patients in a named, trackable category in official records.

The draft package would push further, raising the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 with a mandatory permanent-infertility condition, penalising providers and exposing patients to prison terms. Fifteen national LGBT groups and the national medical association have publicly opposed the draft.

Pride organising remains a flashpoint. Monitoring of a national LGBTI+ pride week by a national truth and justice documentation centre found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the 2025 event, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Prison exposure, should a trans visitor be detained, is governed by placement on registered sex. a transgender prisoner was found dead in a cell at a women's prison on 1 December 2025. Rights organisation branches in several provinces demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported psychiatric evaluation of four transgender inmates shortly before the death, a delayed medical response, prosecutors and crime-scene investigators attending two days later, and no witness statements taken. The case, raised in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirmed that trans prisoners are placed according to registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison.

a national prison-conditions profile prepared with a civil society association in the penal system, drawing on international LGBTI+ data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches of LGBT detainees, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other prisoners, no policy or staff training on LGBT needs, transfer practices that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaint systems that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

The draft package has been described by Human Rights Watch as one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades, and a national LGBTI+ human rights report launched in early 2026 finds that hostility became institutionalised in 2025 through senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner, with regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

A national LGBTI human-rights association (24 Feb 2026 annual report): hostility became explicit state policy (presidency-centred, implemented via a family-focused ministry); six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings with trans people most affected, eighty-nine torture or ill-treatment cases (up from 51), 313 liberty violations (about 2.5x), counted from media cases as the state keeps no hate-crime statistics.

25984515B5155931768473.name: Bursa
25984515B5155931768473.summary:
Bursa stands under the national framework of Türkiye, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than left to residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, together with 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

A leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" and would punish taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with up to four years in prison. Human Rights Watch calls it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. The draft had not been passed when reported, yet authorities have acted as though its prohibitions were already in force.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25 and impose a mandatory permanent-infertility condition, exposing health professionals who provide such care to penalties. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the measure. A separate Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option on gender-reassignment medical-board reports and required e-reports to be issued, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, "A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned Into State Policy", presented at its launch by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, finds that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as explicit state policy during the year. Senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, while regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The government frames its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals".

Street-level enforcement reaches visitors directly. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, and Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Detention compounds the risk. Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities: the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and the case raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison. Prison Insider's country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer, and no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners.

Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. 25984515B57743432888015.name: Çorum
25984515B57743432888015.summary:
Çorum province stands under the national framework applicable across Türkiye, and that framework presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years in prison, and would allow charges against anyone taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, carrying up to four years. Under civil-code article 40 the same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 and impose a permanent-infertility mandate, with providers facing fines and up to seven years and patients up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected, and Human Rights Watch called for withdrawal; the measure had not been passed when reported.

Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, published 24 February 2026 under the title "A Major Siege", finds that hostility toward LGBT people became explicit state policy during 2025, driven by "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions. The report documents 313 right-to-liberty violations, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total and mostly detentions, alongside 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51, and six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people most affected. Türkiye keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on media monitoring rather than state records.

Enforcement already runs ahead of the pending legislation. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue these checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee stated that no fines were issued but that the women were documented anyway, and that enforcement was being applied before any new law had been passed. Foreign nationals stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, and Turkey requires foreigners to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, every checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response asymmetric. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025. The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, binary and heteronormative administration with no staff training on LGBT needs, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints mechanisms that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, risking the profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to care.

For Çorum specifically, the source inventory records no province-specific enforcement, incidents or facilities. The province is assessed against the national picture: the draft package, the detention pattern, the document-carrying requirement and the prison and healthcare rules apply here as they do elsewhere in Türkiye, and a visitor should expect checkpoint document checks and official record-keeping to behave as described above rather than as a local variant.

The measure had not been passed when reported, but authorities have acted as though the prohibitions were already in force.

25984515B99670107521163.name: Diyarbakır
25984515B99670107521163.summary:
Diyarbakır is the largest city of Türkiye's south-east and stands under the national legal framework that Human Rights Watch and Kaos GL document as actively hostile to trans people. Official framing around "the family" and "public morals" is the stated basis of that policy, and enforcement has run ahead of legislation that remains unenacted.

A leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years' imprisonment, permit charges against anyone taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony carrying up to four years, and, under civil-code article 40, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 together with a permanent-infertility mandate. Providers would face fines and up to seven years; patients up to three. Fifteen LGBT organisations and the Turkish Medical Association objected, and Human Rights Watch has called for the draft's withdrawal. As of the reporting date the package had not been enacted, so it is not yet the law under which a visitor is charged, but it defines the direction of the regime.

Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, "A Major Siege", published 24 February 2026, records 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total and predominantly detentions, 89 violations involving torture or ill-treatment against 51 the previous year, and six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people most affected. The report describes hostility becoming explicit state policy under "Year of the Family" instructions. Türkiye keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so these totals rest on media coverage and NGO monitoring and understate the underlying figure.

Diyarbakır is the site of the strongest anti-trans killing case in Türkiye's record. On 14 September 2024, the day of a national anti-LGBT "Great Family Gathering" rally, two men attacked two trans women with sharp objects in the Kayapınar district. Sudenaz Uran was killed at the scene and her friend was injured. The defendants recorded the killing and the recording entered the case file. On 19 December 2025 both were sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment for the intentional killing of a woman. During the trial the Family and Social Services Ministry's application to intervene was accepted while the local bar association's LGBTI+ commission's application was rejected, placing the state on record as guardian of "the family" and the victims' own representatives outside the courtroom.

That sentencing outcome cuts against the general pattern without displacing it. Six anti-LGBT deaths were recorded nationally in 2025 and only three were classified as hate killings, and the single strongest homicide-justice result produced anywhere in the country came from a court in this province, not from the national institutions.

Checkpoint identification is the routine exposure for a visitor. Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. In the country's largest city in 2025 police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release; one woman stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway. The source inventory supplies no equivalent checkpoint count for Diyarbakır, so the national identification rule and the capital's pattern are the operative warnings here.

Police presence in Diyarbakır is structurally elevated. The city carries a conflict-era security legacy of state-of-emergency legacies and the village-guard system, with high police density and detention powers held in routine use. Any stop, document check or GBT-style questioning in this setting should be treated as a documented identification event rather than a routine formality.

Placement of trans detainees follows registered sex. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near the national capital on 1 December 2025, and the case confirmed that Türkiye places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, including a trans man held in a women's prison. Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın coordinated a demand for an independent investigation after other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Transition-related care is contracting. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. A trans patient in Diyarbakır can therefore expect medical records to carry a visible gender marker, and the draft package's proposed floor of 25 with an infertility mandate would narrow care further if enacted.

25984515B87415935832289.name: Düzce
25984515B87415935832289.summary:
Düzce stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been converted into documented state practice. The province's own record yields no distinct local finding, so the assessment below rests on the nationwide regime a visitor to Düzce is subject to, including at police checkpoints, in medical facilities and in document controls that apply equally in interior provinces.

Turkish law itself is not the immediate hazard. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since the 1858 Ottoman penal code, and legal gender change has been available since 1988. Turkish marriage law, however, gives same-sex relationships no recognition and provides no civil unions, domestic partnerships or joint adoption, and no comprehensive statute bans discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBT people are barred from open service in the armed forces.

The operative danger is a pending legislative package. A Human Rights Watch release of 29 October 2025 reported that the leaked 11th Judicial Package, an omnibus draft amending the penal and civil codes, would criminalise conduct deemed "contride to biological sex and general morality" with sentences of up to three years. The same draft would sharply restrict gender-affirming healthcare by setting a minimum age of 25 and imposing onerous eligibility conditions, and would expose both trans people and the professionals who treat them to criminal charges. The government's stated justification for the package is protection of "the family" and "public morals". The draft also carries unrelated measures, including longer sentences for children and mechanisms for removing online content.

Draft status has not prevented anticipatory enforcement elsewhere in Turkey, and visitors should expect checkpoint and document interactions to be conducted on that footing. Turkish media reported in early 2026 that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex"; that specific provision was ultimately left out of that year's judicial reform package, while the broader package's fate is treated below as unresolved.

Public assembly is restricted in practice. Amnesty International records that Pride events and other LGBTQ gatherings were repeatedly disallowed across Turkey through 2024 and 2025, with police detaining participants who assembled regardless. A trans visitor present during a Pride period should expect dispersal orders and identity checks rather than protected assembly.

25984515B68163725002210.name: Edirne
25984515B68163725002210.summary:
Edirne Province is governed by the national law of Türkiye, and no Edirne-specific policing, document, facility or violence findings appear in the sources reviewed. The province is therefore covered here by the national framework alone, which has been tightening rather than loosening.

A leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years' imprisonment. The same package would raise eligibility for gender-affirming healthcare to a minimum age of 25 subject to onerous conditions, and would allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals who treat them, with fines and sentences for providers and up to three years for patients. The government's stated justification is protection of "the family" and "public morals". Turkish media reported in early 2026 that the government was also considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of that same category of behaviour, though the provision was not included in that year's judicial reform package.

Hostility is carried as declared state policy. In May 2025 President Erdoğan announced a "Decade of Family and Population" covering 2026 to 2035 at the International Family Forum, with explicit anti-LGBTI rhetoric. The European Commission's Türkiye Report 2025 concludes that the country's laws and their implementation do not properly protect LGBTQ people.

Document checks are a recurring exposure. Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Reported police practice in 2025 included stopping trans women in streets, shops and cafés and holding them at a police station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release; legal experts cited in that reporting argue the checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee stated that no fines were issued but she was documented anyway, before the draft law had even passed. Foreign visitors stopped in such encounters must produce original identity documents, which places passport gender markers directly in front of the officer.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was referred for arrest, a reversal activists read as evidence of a policy of hate. Pride events were disallowed in 2024 and 2025, with police detaining participants.

Transition-related care is tightening through regulation as well as legislation. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required electronic reports. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care, and the draft package would compound this by pushing eligibility to 25 with a permanent-infertility mandate.

Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 and confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison. For LGBT detainees generally, prison conditions are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement, including arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, ineffective complaints that can attract further violence, and administration operating on a binary basis with no staff training to identify LGBT needs.

25984515B73855241915553.name: Elazığ
25984515B73855241915553.summary:
Elazığ province stands under the national framework of Turkey, where homosexuality has been decriminalised since 1858 and gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, and where discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in law. The same framework withholds recognition of same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions and same-sex adoption, and bars LGBTI people from serving openly in the military. In the 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49, ahead only of Azerbaijan and Russia.

Legislative risk is live rather than hypothetical. A leaked omnibus draft law dated 29 October 2025, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with penalties of up to three years, would sharply restrict gender-affirming healthcare by imposing a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility conditions, and would allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care. The government's stated justification is protecting "the family" and "public morals". The package also carries unrelated measures, including longer child sentences and online-content removal. As of early 2026 the government was considering criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality".

Elazığ has its own documented record of organised hostility. On 19 December 2022 an anti-LGBT hate rally was held at Cumhuriyet (Republic) Square under the banner "LGBT sapkınlıktır" ("LGBT is perversion"), with ruling AKP deputy mayor Nazif Bilginoğlu in attendance. The rally statement denounced consensual same-sex relationships and "homosexual marriage" as a "revolting loss of reason" in Western states, deployed the terms "perverse" and "degenerate mentality", and tied its gender and sexual themes to Turkey's denunciation of the Istanbul Convention. The event is evidence of state-facilitated, locally active anti-LGBT mobilisation in this province, and it bears directly on the reception a visibly LGBT traveller can expect here.

Nationally, Pride events have been repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed since 2015, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. Any visible LGBT presence in public space in Elazığ is therefore assessed against a pattern of official intolerance that is enforced, not merely declared.

25984515B21238382887484.name: Erzincan
25984515B21238382887484.summary:
Erzincan province sits under the Turkish national legal framework with no province-specific ordinance, incident or court decision on record, so the national picture governs what a trans visitor faces here. The framework is contradictory on its face: homosexuality has been decriminalised since 1858, gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited by law. Those provisions coexist with a documented pattern of enforcement hostility.

Same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions and same-sex adoption receive no legal recognition, and LGBTI people are barred from serving openly in the military. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Türkiye placed 47th of 49, ahead only of Azerbaijan and Russia.

The sharpest threat to a visitor comes from a leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. The omnibus draft would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", carrying up to three years' imprisonment, and would sharply restrict gender-affirming healthcare by raising the minimum age to 25 and imposing onerous eligibility conditions. The package would allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care. The government's stated justification is protecting "the family" and "public morals". The same draft carries unrelated measures including longer child sentences and online-content removal.

In early 2026 the government was reported to be considering going further and criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality". The legislative status of either measure is not established in the sources available here.

Pride marches have been banned and forcibly dispersed by the authorities since 2015, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. ILGA-Europe reported on 7 December 2020 that 19 human rights defenders faced prosecution for taking part in a peaceful Pride march at Middle East Technical University in Ankara in May 2019, which shows that even a campus march can draw criminal charges. That exposure for LGBT advocacy is the national freedom-of-assembly climate a visitor in Erzincan would be judged against.

Under the national framework, checkpoint and identity-document checks are the recurring point of contact between a trans visitor and the state. Foreign nationals are required to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance, and any stop becomes an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation. Regular police identity checks (GBT) applied to trans women in Istanbul through 2025 illustrate how such encounters are used for documentation even without charges.

25984515B50530672954016.name: Erzurum
25984515B50530672954016.summary:
Erzurum province sits wholly inside Türkiye's national legal framework; no separate provincial regime applies to trans visitors, and the criminal code, civil code, Health Ministry regulations and police practice operating in Istanbul or Ankara operate identically here.

A leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with penalties of up to three years, would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 under onerous eligibility conditions, and would allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care. The government's stated justification is protection of "the family" and "public morals". The package also carries unrelated measures including longer sentences for children and online-content removal. The draft had not been enacted as reported, and authorities have in places acted as though its prohibitions were already in force.

The baseline legal position is less restrictive than the enforcement environment suggests. Homosexuality has been decriminalised since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and trans people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, the same year gender-reassignment surgery was legalised. A court action to close the Lambda Istanbul association was overruled by the Constitutional Court, which kept the organisation open.

Recognition stops there. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and joint adoption are not recognised; LGBT people are barred from serving openly in the military; and no comprehensive national law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Türkiye 47th of 49 countries.

Street-level policing is the immediate hazard for a visitor. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Foreign nationals are required to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance, so any stop is an occasion on which a passport is compared against presentation.

Lethal violence is documented and the state response is asymmetric. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 43 of them taken off the record. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with trans people disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was referred for arrest.

Pride events remain flashpoints nationwide. Pride has been banned in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police deploying tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. Poyraz, a transgender prisoner, was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025; branches of the Human Rights Association in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation after accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers described a prolonged medical delay, prosecutors entering the prison two days later and witness statements going untaken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, risking the profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to care.

25984515B57211123653900.name: Giresun
25984515B57211123653900.summary:
Giresun province stands under the national framework of Türkiye, which Human Rights Watch describes as moving from residual prejudice toward codified hostility. A leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, reported on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise LGBT conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, and would criminalise same-sex ceremonies with up to 4 years. The same package would raise the eligibility age for gender-affirming healthcare from 18 to 25, impose mandatory infertility and repeated-evaluation conditions, expose providers to fines and up to 7 years' imprisonment, and expose patients to up to 3 years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected to the draft.

The draft had not been enacted as of the October 2025 reporting, but its pending status does not describe the operative baseline. Türkiye has decriminalised homosexuality since the Ottoman penal code of 1858 and has permitted legal gender change and gender-reassignment surgery since 1988, so a trans visitor enters a country where transition is lawful on paper while advocacy and public expression are the targets of the current legislative push.

Entry and stay interactions carry an outing risk that follows from the absence of protective machinery. Türkiye has no comprehensive national law banning discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions or joint adoption, and bars LGBT people from openly serving in the military. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Türkiye 47th of 49 countries.

Public visibility is the most exposed activity. Pride events have been banned in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police deploying tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants. A visitor attending or near any Pride-related gathering in Giresun should expect the same enforcement pattern applied nationally.

25984515B36227448932647.name: Gümüşhane
25984515B36227448932647.summary:
Gümüşhane Province stands under the national framework of Turkey, which governs visitors in Gümüşhane. The sources record no provincial legal divergence from that frame in Gümüşhane, so a trans visitor to the province should expect the national pattern of law, document handling and policing rather than any local variant.

Homosexuality has not been treated as a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman Empire's 1858 penal code. Transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, and gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988 subject to court-approved procedures.

No comprehensive law in Turkey prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition: the law defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, which makes same-sex marriage legally impossible though not criminalised, and the gender recorded on a trans person's civil-registry record determines their marriage eligibility.

A leaked omnibus draft known as the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise LGBT conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with up to 3 years' imprisonment, criminalise same-sex ceremonies with up to 4 years, raise the age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 with mandatory infertility and multiple-evaluation conditions, and punish providers with fines and up to 7 years' imprisonment. Fifteen LGBT groups and the national medical association object to the measure. It had not been passed as of that reporting.

Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police using tear gas and water cannons. Amnesty International reported restrictions and excessive force against Pride protesters in 2015 and again in 2024.

25984515B57889067347253.name: Hakkâri
25984515B57889067347253.summary:
Turkey's national legal framework governs Hakkâri Province, with no separate provincial layer of trans-specific law. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman Empire's 1858 penal code, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988; gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since that year, subject to court approval.

The framework offers a trans visitor little protective depth. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and it recognises no same-sex relationships. Marriage is defined by law as a union between a man and a woman, which makes same-sex marriage legally impossible though not criminalised, and marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in a person's civil-registry entry rather than on trans status. Documentation, not presentation, is the operative fact in any registry or checkpoint interaction.

As of 29 October 2025 a leaked omnibus draft known as the 11th Judicial Package was before the government. Human Rights Watch reported that it would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise LGBT conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years' imprisonment, criminalise same-sex ceremonies with up to four years, raise the age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 with mandatory infertility and multiple-evaluation conditions, and punish providers with fines and up to seven years' imprisonment. Fifteen LGBT groups and the national medical association object to the measure. Its pending status does not suspend existing police practice.

Hakkâri's divergence from the national baseline lies in security practice and social climate rather than in law. The province is a conflict-affected area carrying state-of-emergency legacies, a village-guard system and a high police presence, and it is assessed as among the most conservative parts of the country. A visitor should expect the national pattern of document checks and police discretion to be applied more intensively here than in Istanbul or the western coast.

25984515B95117543422129.name: Hatay
25984515B95117543422129.summary:
Hatay Province stands under the national framework of Türkiye, where hostility toward trans people has been consolidated into state policy rather than left to social prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, including 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — alongside systematic intrusion into the privacy of LGBT people. Nothing in the sourced material distinguishes Hatay from this national pattern, and no Hatay-specific incident is documented in the inventory.

A leaked omnibus draft known as the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise LGBT conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with up to 3 years' imprisonment, criminalise same-sex ceremonies with up to 4 years, raise eligibility for gender-affirming healthcare from 18 to 25 with mandatory infertility and repeated-evaluation conditions, and expose providers to fines and up to 7 years and patients to up to 3 years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected. Amnesty International records that three draft packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible; none was ultimately submitted to parliament.

The absence of enacted legislation has not restrained enforcement. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on streets, in shops and in cafés in Beyoğlu and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that no fines were issued but that she was documented anyway, and that the new law had not passed even as it was already being applied to her. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk wherever appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Every checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events are suppressed as a matter of routine. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still continuing at year's end. Governors have extended bans to LGBTI-focused events generally since October 2018; police dispersed the 2015 and 2016 Istanbul parades with water cannon and tear gas, and on 14 June 2019 the Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya prides were all banned. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

The Erdoğan government frames its position as protecting 'the family' and 'public morals', language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma. A February 2026 press report stated the government was considering a law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex' with one to three years' imprisonment; that measure was not included in the 12th judicial package.

Legal recognition is partial and unprotected. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' leaking publicly.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Coordinated by Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın, rights groups demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025. The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, no policy or staff training to identify LGBT prisoners' needs, binary and heteronormative administration, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints mechanisms that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required e-reports to be issued, risking profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

The depth of the regime predates the current government. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it predates the legal changes made after 2018 and stands as historical evidence of the pattern's duration rather than a statement of current law.
