25984515B20089439873245.modelContext: Iğdır: Azerbaijani-majority border province; secular-Alevi elements; low salience.
25984515B20089439873245.blindSummary:
The province stands under the national framework of the parent nation, and the assessment for a trans visitor is drawn from that national record. No source in the current inventory reports conditions specific to this province, so the findings below describe the regime a visitor would encounter anywhere in the state/province, including at checkpoints, in police contact and in access to care.

Hostility is documented as state policy rather than residual prejudice. a national LGBTI+ human rights report recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in the same year, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected.

Legislative criminalisation has been repeatedly drafted but not enacted. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise LGBT conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years' imprisonment, criminalise same-sex ceremonies with up to four years, raise the age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 with mandatory infertility and multiple-evaluation conditions, and punish providers with fines and up to seven years' imprisonment; 15 LGBT groups and the national medical association objected. Amnesty International's country report for 2025/26 records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during that year, which would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, none of which was submitted to parliament. a February 2026 press report stated that the national government was considering a law criminalising publicly encouraging behaviour contrary to biological sex with one to three years' imprisonment; that measure was not included in the 12th judicial package. Pending status has not stopped enforcement: the government's stated justification of protecting the family and public morals is identified by Human Rights Watch as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma.

Street-level enforcement is the immediate risk for a visitor. During 2025 police in the largest city stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in a central district and held them at a named police station for General Information Gathering background checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the regional human-rights convention. One of the women stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that enforcement was being applied before the new law had passed. Foreign nationals stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents, and the state/province requires foreigners to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints with fines of up to 3,000 in local currency and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation, creating a direct outing risk.

Violence against trans people is met with an asymmetric state/province response. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in a district of the largest city by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Public assembly is blocked. Amnesty International records that in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the capital city's LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still continuing at year's end. Since October 2018 provincial governors have extended event bans to LGBTI-focused gatherings generally; pride in the largest city was banned repeatedly, with police dispersing the 2015 and 2016 parades using water cannon and tear gas, and three cities' prides all banned on 14 June 2019. Monitoring by a truth and memory centre of the 2025 trans and LGBTI+ pride week in the largest city found violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. In December 2025 a provincial court ordered the dissolution of a young LGBTI+ association, ruling that it had shared obscene images incompatible with society's moral values that could encourage or promote LGBTI identities.

Detention carries specific danger. a transgender prisoner was found dead in a cell at a women's prison near the national capital on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from human rights association branches in six provinces demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by an opposition MP on 12 December 2025, confirmed that the state/province places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, with a trans man held in a women's prison. a prison-monitoring country profile, prepared with a civil society penal-system association using international LGBTI data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, binary and heteronormative administration with no policy or staff training to identify LGBT prisoners' needs, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. a national health ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a provincial health directorate circular that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the other option and required electronic reports to be issued, risking profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Entry and status basics have not changed: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the imperial penal code of 1858, transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised.
25984515B20089439873245.tangentialFactors:
The pattern documented in 2025 is longstanding rather than novel. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth, not as a statement of current law.

Adjacent to the criminal-law risk is the military regime. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the Turkish military: conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classed under a definition of homosexuality as a psychosexual illness, must provide photographic proof, and risk their unfit report leaking publicly. This is a resident-facing exposure rather than a visitor one, but it illustrates how classification machinery feeds official records.

The drafting activity of 2025 and early 2026 shows a legislature testing boundaries through publication rather than passage. Three packages were made public in 2025 without being submitted to parliament, and a further criminalising proposal reported in February 2026 was left out of the 12th judicial package. Enforcement, by contrast, has proceeded through police practice, event bans and administrative circulars that require no statute.

Regional comparison is limited by the inventory: the documented enforcement actions are concentrated in Istanbul and İzmir, and no reporting covers Iğdır or the eastern provinces. Whether GBT-style stops, pride bans and association dissolution are applied with the same frequency in Iğdır is not sourced here.

25984515B9026957888422.name: Isparta
25984515B9026957888422.summary:
Isparta province stands under the national framework of Turkey. No Isparta-specific statute, incident, police action or court case appears in the sources behind this record, so the assessment below describes national law and national enforcement as they apply in Isparta alongside every other province.

A leaked omnibus draft known as the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend Turkey's penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality at up to three years' imprisonment, and would criminalise same-sex ceremonies at up to four years. The same package would restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over, conditioned on infertility and repeated evaluations, and would expose medical providers to fines and up to seven years in prison. Fifteen LGBT groups and the national medical association object to it.

Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records the enforcement a visitor would meet in any province. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans on the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, and more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained. A court overturned the Istanbul governorate ban in November 2025 as disproportionate and unlawful, yet prosecutions of 92 people for taking part in pride marches were still continuing at the end of the year. In December 2025 an Izmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had acted outside its stated purpose and shared obscene images incompatible with the law.

Three draft law packages aimed at LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and would make legal gender recognition nearly impossible. None was submitted to parliament, and the leaked October package likewise remained unpassed, but the declared intent has not waited on enactment to shape how authorities act.

Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so a trans visitor stopped, questioned or refused service has no statutory protection to invoke. Identity documents are compared against presentation at every checkpoint interaction, and the absence of any equality guarantee removes the legal ground on which a complaint would stand.

25984515B58862484177861.name: Kahramanmaraş
25984515B58862484177861.summary:
Kahramanmaraş stands under Turkish national law, and the source inventory records no Kahramanmaraş-specific statute, incident or court case concerning trans people. What a trans visitor faces in the province is the national framework as it operates elsewhere in Türkiye.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal code to imprison for up to three years anyone who incites or promotes conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, criminalise participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with penalties of up to four years, and restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over under mandatory permanent infertility, exposing providers to fines and up to seven years and patients to up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected to the draft. The package is national legislation and applies to the province; it had not been enacted when reported.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy', records 313 liberty violations, roughly 2.5 times the previous year and mostly detentions, together with 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 and mostly linked to peaceful assembly, and six right-to-life violations of which three were recorded as hate-motivated killings with trans people most affected. Because the state keeps no hate-crime statistics, these figures are counted from media and civil-society reports.

Identity checks are the ordinary point of contact between a trans visitor and the authorities. On 31 July 2025 police in the Beyoğlu district of Istanbul carried out mass ID roundups of trans women, recording their names and filming video. Foreign nationals are required to produce original photo identification at transit checkpoints, so any stop becomes an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation.

25984515B55399473509250.name: Karabük
25984515B55399473509250.summary:
Karabük province stands under the national framework of the Republic of Turkey, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — together with systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. No Karabük-specific incident appears in the sources; the province is governed by the same national laws, ministries and police practice described here.

The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Under that framing a draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people was before the government as of October 2025. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

The leaked omnibus draft, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 as the "11th Judicial Package", would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. Same-sex marriage is not legal in Turkey, so such ceremonies are symbolic, which bears on travelling with a partner. The draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, impose mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, and penalise healthcare professionals performing such interventions with fines and up to seven years in prison, while trans people receiving care deemed illegal would face up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention.

Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring review finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy: "Year of the Family" instructions were issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ association was closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members, and artistic events were cancelled or banned. The same review records six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations up from 51 the previous year, and freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

Street-level enforcement illustrates how the pending draft is already applied. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The passport-carrying rule for foreigners compounds these risks. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Turkish rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison — and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care, with online framing contested as an "LGBT opening".

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited here as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

25984515B36972543372669.name: Kastamonu
25984515B36972543372669.summary:
Kastamonu province stands under the national framework of Turkey: the criminal law, health regulation, identity-document rules and detention practice that determine what a trans visitor faces are set at national level and apply in Kastamonu as elsewhere. No statute, enforcement action, incident or court decision specific to Kastamonu appears in the sources assembled for this record.

On 29 October 2025 Human Rights Watch reported a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, that would amend the penal code to imprison conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality for up to three years, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies for up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; health professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention.

The draft had not been reported as passed, but the prohibitions it contains are already being applied. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in that reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not been passed even as it was being applied to them.

Foreign nationals must carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. For a trans visitor in Kastamonu, every checkpoint stop is an occasion on which a passport gender marker is compared against presentation. That is the most direct outing risk in the province.

Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people has become explicit state policy rather than residual prejudice: "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years with criminal cases against 11 of its members, and artistic events cancelled or banned. The review records roughly 313 violations in the year, about 2.5 times the previous total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — 89 torture or ill-treatment violations against 51 the prior year, six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings in which trans people were the most affected, and freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

Under that framing the Erdoğan government has repeatedly invoked protection of "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people.

25984515B36972543372669.tangentialFactors:
Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies. A visitor considering public visibility in Kastamonu should read that as the ceiling on assembly tolerance nationwide.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth, not as a statement of current law.

25984515B36972543372669.localsOnly:
Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Residents of Kastamonu also live under the national policy measures recorded in 2025: "Year of the Family" directives to public institutions, closure of an LGBTI+ association with criminal cases against 11 members, and cancellation or banning of artistic and broadcast events.

25984515B30869354278170.name: Kilis
25984515B30869354278170.summary:
Kilis stands under Turkey's national framework, and no provincial law, incident or court case specific to Kilis appears in the surviving sources for this record. What a trans visitor faces in Kilis is the country-wide regime: as of October 2025 a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal code to imprison conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, subject to mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; Human Rights Watch warns the measure would push treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention. The draft had not been enacted when reported, but enforcement has not waited for it.

Kaos GL's 2025 national monitoring found hostility toward LGBTI+ people hardening into explicit state policy, with "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years with criminal cases against 11 of its members, and artistic events cancelled or banned. The same review recorded roughly 313 violations overall, about 2.5 times the previous year, with 299 detention decisions, 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings in which trans people were most affected, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations up from 51 the prior year, and freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

Practical exposure at checkpoints is unchanged: Turkey requires foreign nationals to produce original photo identification, and every stop is an occasion on which documents are read against presentation. Foreign visitors stopped in the street have been held for background checks without fine, documented anyway, while the pending legislation was still unpassed.

25984515B11362042972294.name: Kırıkkale
25984515B11362042972294.summary:
Kırıkkale is a military-industrial conservative province with no province-specific statute, ordinance or incident series in the record. A trans visitor here stands under the same national framework that binds every Turkish province, and that framework has tightened rather than loosened.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft omnibus reform, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal code so that acting "contrary to biological sex and general morality", or promoting such conduct, carries up to three years in prison through an amendment to article 225 on indecent acts. The same draft would restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over under onerous eligibility criteria and would expose both trans people and the professionals who treat them to criminal charges. Human Rights Watch described the package as one of the decade's most alarming rights rollbacks and urged its withdrawal.

The draft was justified in the government's stated terms of protecting "the family" and "public morals". That framing matters operationally: three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, and none was ultimately submitted to parliament, yet the announcements themselves have shaped how authorities behave. A February 2026 newspaper report separately recorded that the government was considering a law criminalising publicly encouraging "behavior contrary to biological sex", with one to three years' imprisonment.

The standing law is comparatively permissive on paper. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender recognition has been available since 1988. There is, however, no comprehensive statute prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so the protections a visitor might expect elsewhere simply do not exist here.

Enforcement in 2025 was heavy. Authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches in June 2025, police used unlawful force against peaceful protesters, and more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained. In November a court overturned the Istanbul governorate's ban as disproportionate and unlawful, but prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at year's end. Pride events have been banned in Istanbul and most other cities in most years, with tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions deployed against those who defied the bans; on 14 June 2019 the 7th Izmir Pride, the 3rd Antalya Pride and the 27th Istanbul Pride were banned by the cities' governors.

Organised LGBTI life is also under direct legal pressure. In December 2025 an Izmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, finding that it had pursued activities outside its stated purpose and shared "obscene" images incompatible with the law.

Two further exposure points bear on a visitor's daily conduct. Same-sex marriage is not recognised; a 2012 request to include it in the constitutional writing process was rejected by both the AKP and the MHP, so travelling with a partner carries no legal standing. And openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service, with the armed forces' health regulation classifying homosexuality as a "psychosexual" illness rendering members unfit, and conscripts who declare homosexuality required to provide photographic proof — a documentation demand with obvious privacy consequences for anyone entering that system.

25984515B10334298996421.name: Kırklareli
25984515B10334298996421.summary:
Kırklareli Province has no province-specific statute, ordinance or incident series in the record. The legal position of a trans visitor in Kırklareli is set entirely by the national framework that governs every province of Turkey, and no Kırklareli-specific deviation from that framework is documented.

The national baseline is mixed on its face and hostile in practice. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman Empire adopted a new penal code in 1858, and trans people have been able to change their legal gender, following surgery, since 1988. Against that, Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military, and same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition in the form of marriage, civil union or adoption.

Legislation in waiting is the principal threat. A leaked draft omnibus reform circulated in October 2025 as the 11th Judicial Package would amend article 225 of the penal code on 'indecent acts' so that acting or promoting conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' carries up to three years in prison, would restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over under onerous eligibility rules, and would allow criminal charges against trans people and the professionals who treat them. Human Rights Watch, which reported the draft on 29 October 2025, described it as one of the decade's most alarming rights rollbacks and urged withdrawal; the government's stated justification is the protection of 'the family' and 'public morals'. The measure had not been enacted when reported, but enforcement has not waited for it.

Street-level enforcement already resembles the pending regime. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' background checks before release; legal experts cited in that reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and one detainee stated that no fines were issued but the women were documented anyway. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance, so any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which a visitor's documents can be compared against their presentation.

The recorded violence is lethal and state response is asymmetric. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 of them through formal channels. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected; in August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker, who was released while the victim was referred for arrest.

Pride events remain a flashpoint: authorities have banned Pride in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, using tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions, and monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through that year.

Custody and health records carry their own exposure. Trans prisoners in Turkey are placed according to registered sex, and a trans prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, with rights groups demanding an independent investigation and lawyers reporting delayed medical response, prosecutors entering two days later and witness statements not taken. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular, barred hospitals from recording an 'other' option on gender-related medical-board reports and required e-reports, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th out of 49 assessed countries.

Criminalisation has a long baseline that is often misread as protection. Homosexuality has not been an offence in Turkey since the Ottoman Empire adopted a new penal code in 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender, following surgery, since 1988. These provisions do not amount to a rights framework: Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military, and same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition, whether marriage, civil union or adoption. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Turkey 47th of 49 assessed countries.

Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, published on 24 February 2026 and titled for that year's governmental framing as the year of the family, records 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025, roughly two and a half times the 2024 figure and mostly detentions, alongside 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year and concentrated in assemblies, and six violations of the right to life, three of them hate-motivated killings, with transgender people most affected. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft omnibus reform, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal code so that acting contrary to biological sex and general morality, or promoting that conduct, carries up to three years in prison by amending article 225 on indecent acts. Human Rights Watch described it as one of the most alarming rights rollbacks of the decade and called for its withdrawal. In July 2025 police in Istanbul's Beyoğlu district rounded up roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés, held them at a police station for identity checks, recorded their names and filmed video, and gave no official reason. Transition-related care is being tightened through administrative channels. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a circular from the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the other option and required electronic reports to be issued. Hostility now operates as documented state policy rather than as residual prejudice. a national LGBTI+ human rights report published in February 2026 records 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025, roughly two and a half times the 2024 figure and mostly detentions, alongside 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year and concentrated in assemblies, and six violations of the right to life, three of them hate-motivated killings, with transgender people most affected. The same report finds that the head of state/province and senior officials' designation of LGBTI+ people as deviant or as a threat raised the motivation of state officials and produced third-party impunity, that a new Family Ministry has become the implementing ministry, that one LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed, that platforms and broadcasters were penalised or withdrew content, and that artistic events were cancelled. No official hate-crime statistics exist, so documented cases rest on media reporting.

a draft legislative package now stands at the centre of the risk assessment. a national human rights organisation reported in October 2025 that a leaked draft omnibus reform, the 11th judicial package, would amend the penal code so that acting contrary to biological sex and general morality, or promoting that conduct, carries up to three years in prison by amending the article on indecent acts. The same draft would restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over under onerous eligibility conditions, including infertility requirements and repeated evaluation, and would expose both transgender people and the medical professionals who treat them to criminal charges. The draft was described as one of the most alarming rights rollbacks of the decade, with a withdrawal called for. The government's justification rests on protecting the family and public morals.

Enforcement has already moved ahead of that pending legislation. In mid-2025 police in the capital's main entertainment district rounded up roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés, held them at a police station for identity checks, recorded their names and filmed video, and gave no official reason. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such stops violate Article 5 of the regional human rights convention. Trans women held during those round-ups stated that they were released without fines but documented all the same, at a point when the draft law had not been passed.

Checkpoint interaction carries a specific document risk. The parent nation requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 local lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any police stop becomes an occasion on which original documents are compared against presentation, which is an outing risk in itself.

Pride events have been a flashpoint for a decade. Authorities have banned Pride in major cities in most years since 2015, responding with tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions of participants.

For a trans visitor who is arrested or falls ill, custody and healthcare conditions are governed by registered sex and by segregation. National rights groups, coordinated from branches in six cities, demanded an independent investigation after a transgender prisoner was found dead in a cell at a central women's prison on 1 December 2025; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirmed that trans prisoners are placed according to their registered sex, since a trans man had been held in a women's prison.

a national prison-system profile, prepared with a civil society association and drawing on international LGBTI+ data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches of LGBT detainees, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals to transfer to hospital out of fear of other male prisoners, an absence of policy or staff training on LGBT prisoner needs, an administration operating on binary and heteronormative terms, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaint procedures that are ineffective and can invite further violence.

Transition-related care is being tightened through administrative channels. a health ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a provincial health directorate circular in a mid-sized interior city that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the other option and required electronic reports to be issued. The change risks profiling transgender patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

25984515B86381770870747.name: Kocaeli
25984515B86381770870747.summary:
Kocaeli, a province of Turkey, stands under the national framework set out for the country. Turkey presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors: hostility has been formalised as state policy, the national government frames its position as protecting 'the family' and 'public morals', a draft package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people was pending as of October 2025 while authorities acted on equivalent reasoning, police stop trans women on the street for background checks and require foreigners to produce original identity documents at transit checkpoints, hate-motivated killings continue against an asymmetric state response, trans prisoners are placed by registered sex, and transition-related care is being narrowed by Health Ministry regulation. No statute, court decision, enforcement incident or provincial documentation specific to Kocaeli appears in the sources assembled for this record, so the assessment a visitor should carry into the province is inherited from national law and nationwide policing practice.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal code to imprison conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality for up to three years, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies for up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25 and condition it on permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Clinicians performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns that enactment would force treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention.

National monitoring for 2025 gives the enforcement picture a visitor joins on arrival. Kaos GL recorded roughly 313 violations across the year, about two and a half times the previous year's total, including 299 detention decisions, six right-to-life violations of which three were classified as hate-motivated killings with transgender people the most affected, and 89 torture or ill-treatment violations against 51 the year before. Freedom-of-expression violations rose from 216 to 540.

The hostility is administered rather than merely expressed. Kaos GL documents 'Year of the Family' instructions issued to public institutions, the closure of an LGBTI+ association with criminal cases opened against eleven of its members, and the cancellation or banning of artistic events. A visitor in Kocaeli meets the same national security apparatus described in that monitoring, and every document check is an occasion on which papers can be compared against presentation.

25984515B78139731385057.name: Konya
25984515B78139731385057.summary:
Konya stands within the national framework of Turkey, and the danger a trans visitor faces there is set by that framework rather than by any local instrument. No Konya-specific statute, incident, or court case is documented in the sources consulted for this entry; the findings below apply country-wide.

Turkey presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. Under a stated policy of protecting "the family" and "public morals", a leaked omnibus draft known as the 11th Judicial Package was reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the penal code to imprison conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality for up to three years, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies for up to four years.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, and condition it on permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed it. Human Rights Watch warns the measure would push treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention. It had not been enacted when reported, and its pending status has not stopped authorities acting as though equivalent prohibitions were already in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring found that hostility toward LGBTI+ people in Turkey became explicit state policy. "Year of the Family" instructions were issued to public institutions, one LGBTI+ association was closed with criminal cases opened against eleven of its members, and artistic events were cancelled or banned. The same review recorded six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations against 51 the previous year, roughly 313 violations overall, about two and a half times the 2024 total, 299 detention decisions, and freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

Street-level enforcement supplies the practical dimension. Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in 2025 in the Beyoğlu district and held them for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release; one detainee reported that no fines were issued but the women were documented anyway, with enforcement applied before any new law had passed. Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention. Every document interaction is an occasion on which papers can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Prison conditions govern any prolonged contact with the authorities. Trans prisoners in Turkey are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities; a transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, with accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reporting four transgender inmates sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before, delayed medical staff, prosecutors entering two days later, and witnesses not interviewed. The case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025. A Prison Insider profile prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and ILGA World data documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer, binary administration with no staff training on LGBT needs, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

a national monitoring organisation's 2025 review found that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy. "Year of the Family" instructions were issued to public institutions, one LGBTI+ association was closed with criminal cases opened against eleven of its members, and artistic events were cancelled or banned. The same review recorded six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations against 51 the previous year, roughly 313 violations overall, about two and a half times the previous year's total, 299 detention decisions, and freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

25984515B47044460443496.name: Kütahya
25984515B47044460443496.summary:
Kütahya province stands under the national framework of the Republic of Turkey, and no Kütahya-specific evidence of trans-specific enforcement, violence or legal practice was located in the source inventory. What a trans visitor to Kütahya faces is therefore the national regime as it is applied across the country's interior provinces, where the conservative social environment compounds a legal order that offers no comprehensive protection on grounds of gender identity.

Turkey presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. The government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting 'the family' and 'public morals', language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma.

Draft legislation would extend that regime further. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that the leaked omnibus 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' carry up to three years' imprisonment, and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years. It would amend civil-code article 40 ('Changing Sex') to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, with mandatory infertility requirements and evaluation by a government-approved hospital, and would imprison care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three. Three draft packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, which would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible; none was submitted to parliament. Amnesty International records that authorities have acted on the substance regardless: as of October 2025 the 11th package had not been passed, yet enforcement patterns were already being applied.

Street-level enforcement illustrates the gap between pending law and present practice. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One woman detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to her.

Foreign visitors are drawn into these encounters directly. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. A foreign passport is thus produced at any stop, and the gender marker within it is compared against the holder's presentation — a direct outing risk at every checkpoint interaction, in Kütahya as in holiday destinations.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

The national legal order offers no standing protection. There is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military, and same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 — a route that the 11th Judicial Package would narrow substantially, raising the age threshold to 25.

Public assembly is prohibited rather than merely restricted. Pride parades have been banned by local authorities since 2015, Istanbul's 2015 to 2018 parades having been banned and dispersed. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Organised LGBTI life is under direct legal pressure. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. In September 2026 police detained dozens in raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists under a 'Decade of Family and Population' crackdown.

Prison exposure follows registered sex. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison — and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025. The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, binary and heteronormative administration with no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints procedures that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

25984515B80837210717778.name: Malatya
25984515B80837210717778.summary:
Malatya falls entirely under Turkey's national framework, and no statute, police directive, court decision or incident specific to Malatya appears in the sources consulted. What a trans visitor faces in the province is what the central authorities have built nationally: a documented escalation of hostility that monitoring organisations record as state policy rather than residual prejudice.

The most consequential item is the leaked omnibus "11th Judicial Package", reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts "contrary to biological sex and general morality" carry up to three years' imprisonment, and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years. It would amend civil-code article 40 ("Changing Sex") to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, add a mandatory infertility condition and a government-approved hospital evaluation, and imprison care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three. The package had not been enacted when reported; three separate draft packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 and none were submitted to parliament, yet monitoring shows authorities acting on the assumptions behind them.

That assumption is visible in routine policing. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped some twenty trans women in streets, shops and cafés and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release, with no fine but with their details documented. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Kaos GL recorded 313 violations against LGBTI+ people in 2025, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions, 256 taken through formal channels and 43 off the record.

Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry photo identification at transit checkpoints including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Any stop in Malatya is therefore an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation, with the outing risk that comparison creates.

Violence is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, which activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Official framing supplies the licence. The Erdoğan government has repeatedly cast its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma; family-year directives issued from the head of state during 2025 accompanied broadcast and arts-event censorship and the closure of a rights organisation.

25984515B80837210717778.tangentialFactors:
Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. Those facts sit alongside the absence of any comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, which leaves a visitor without a domestic remedy if refused service or stopped on those grounds.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service. Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised, so a visiting spouse or partner has no legal standing in Turkey regardless of marital status at home.

Pride events have been flashpoints for a decade. Local authorities have banned pride parades since 2015; Istanbul's 2015–2018 parades were banned and dispersed. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at year's end. Monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

The legislative picture shifted during 2026. The 12th judicial reform package passed that year dropped provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, though these carry no legal marital status. In early 2026 Turkish media reported that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex"; it was not included in that year's package. In September 2026 police detained dozens in raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists under a "Decade of Family and Population" crackdown.

Two decades of external reporting reach the same conclusion about depth. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it predates the legal changes made after 2018 and stands as historical evidence rather than a statement of current law.
25984515B80837210717778.localsOnly:
Transition-related care is tightening for residents. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Legal gender recognition remains formally available but contested. Three draft law packages made public during 2025 would have criminalised expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and made legal gender recognition nearly impossible; they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

Organisation is under direct legal attack. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images incompatible with "society's moral values" that could "encourage or promote" LGBTI identities.

Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and witness statements were not taken. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that Turkey places trans prisoners according to registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, binary and heteronormative administration, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints processes that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

25984515B30119007363221.name: Mardin
25984515B30119007363221.summary:
No measure, incident or institution specific to Mardin concerning transgender visitors is documented in this edition's sources. What a trans visitor to Mardin faces is the national framework of Türkiye, and no local authority in the province is recorded adding bans, checkpoints or enforcement programmes of its own.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts described as contrary to biological sex and general morality carry up to three years imprisonment, and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years. The same package would amend civil-code article 40 to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from eighteen to twenty-five, with mandatory infertility conditions and evaluation at a government-approved hospital, while imprisoning care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three. The package is national in scope and would apply in Mardin as elsewhere.

Drafting activity continued into 2026. A February 2026 press report described legislation under consideration that would criminalise public advocacy of behaviour contrary to biological sex with one to three years imprisonment; that provision was not included in the 12th judicial package. Amnesty International recorded that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, criminalising expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and making legal gender recognition nearly impossible, and that none was ultimately submitted to parliament. The gap between drafting and enactment has not governed enforcement: in 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly twenty trans women in streets, shops and cafés in Beyoğlu and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for background checks, without fines but with documentation, before release.

The statutory baseline is permissive on its face. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. Marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in the civil registry, so a trans person who has legally changed the registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow ranking placed Türkiye 47th of 49.

Public assembly is a documented risk. Amnesty International recorded that in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, that police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, that more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, that three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June and released on 8 August pending trial, and that prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at year's end. Pride events have been banned in most years since 2015, with tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions used against those who defied the bans.

Transition-related care is tightening on two fronts. In June 2025 the health ministry's medicines agency banned prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under twenty-one, despite existing law permitting access from eighteen; a Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 additionally barred hospitals from recording the "other" option in medical-board reports and required e-reports, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records.

Organisational space is contracting. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association for sharing images deemed obscene and incompatible with society's moral values. In September 2026 coordinated raids under the 'My Family is Safe' crackdown involved 162 suspects, nine associations and thirteen businesses.

25984515B33535290178113.summary:
Mersin province records no local statute, police programme or administrative ban directed at transgender visitors in this edition's sources. What a trans visitor to Mersin faces is the national framework of Türkiye, applied here without any provincial counterweight: no local authority in Mersin is documented adding protection, and none is documented adding restriction of its own.

Under Türkiye's national law the position on legal gender is unchanged since 1988. A person may change registered gender only after sex-reassignment surgery, a medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive statute prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no remedy exists against the denial of housing, employment or public service on those grounds. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are unavailable.

The pending national criminalisation package is the principal open threat. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus 11th Judicial Package would amend penal code article 225 so that acts deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality carry up to three years' imprisonment, and that same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies carry up to four. Civil code article 40, governing the change of registered sex, would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, require a government-approved hospital evaluation and impose mandatory infertility conditions. The package would imprison care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three. The provisions had not been enacted when reported, but police enforcement of the new framework was already being applied in practice in other provinces.

Checkpoint document checks are the routine mechanism by which a visitor's documents can be compared with their presentation. Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. In Istanbul in 2025 police held roughly twenty trans women at a police station for background checks without issuing fines, detaining them to record their details. That pattern of undocumented record-keeping is the enforcement model a Mersin visitor should expect to encounter at any checkpoint interaction.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal, and the state's response is asymmetric. In 2024 a trans woman was knifed in an Istanbul district by a seventeen-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Rights organisations treat that inversion as evidence of institutional policy rather than isolated error.

Mersin appears in the national record in one connection. When a transgender prisoner was found dead in a women's prison near the national capital on 1 December 2025, coordinated demands for an independent investigation came from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the facility two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Türkiye places trans prisoners according to their registered sex; a trans man had been held in a women's prison.

Transition-related care is tightening on the clinical side. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a provincial health directorate circular in Kayseri that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording an other option and required electronic reports. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Visible LGBT assembly is effectively closed nationwide. Istanbul Pride was banned for the tenth consecutive year in 2025, and many other cities impose comparable bans, which means the same restriction governs assembly in Mersin-area cities. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.
