25984515B57226385500606.name: Muğla
25984515B57226385500606.summary:
Muğla, the province containing Bodrum, Marmaris and Fethiye, stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised into state policy. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus measure, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts "contrary to biological sex and general morality" carry up to three years' imprisonment and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years. The same draft would amend civil-code article 40, titled "Changing Sex", raising the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 and adding mandatory infertility evaluation and approval by a government-approved hospital, while imprisoning care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three.

The draft was national-level in scope and contained no province-specific provisions for Muğla. Its pending status has not stopped authorities from acting on its logic: Kaos GL recorded 313 violations against LGBT people in 2025, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

Legal gender recognition exists. Turkey has permitted transgender people to change their legal gender since 1988, but only through sex-reassignment surgery, a medical examination and court permission. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are unavailable. Because Turkish marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, a person who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender.

The 12th judicial reform package, passed in 2026, removed the provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people that had been in the bill. It made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, though such ceremonies carry no legal marital status.

Enforcement patterns are national and reach resort-province institutions. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 records that the Erdoğan government made anti-LGBT hate speech a core part of its election campaign, that the ninth successive ban on Istanbul Pride week events in June 2024 was accompanied by police arrests of those who attempted to assemble, that authorities regularly and arbitrarily ban other events by LGBT groups, and that local authorities around the country have increasingly cancelled concerts by artists openly supportive of LGBT rights. The television regulator RTÜK has justified fines on digital platforms for LGBT-related content as violating "societal and cultural values." Any visible LGBT assembly in Muğla is therefore an assembly under a regime that bans such events as a matter of routine.

Street-level checks create a direct document risk. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One woman detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to her. Foreign nationals are required to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın coordinated demands for an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees rest on segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it predates the legal changes made after 2018 and stands as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

25984515B88478081264350.name: Muş
25984515B88478081264350.summary:
Muş province stands under the national framework of Türkiye. No Muş-specific ordinance, incident or court decision is documented for the province, so what a trans visitor faces in Muş is what the national sources record for the country as a whole.

The baseline is permissive in narrow terms and hostile in every operative one. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender recognition has been available since 1988, but no comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised. A visitor's partner, marriage or transition status therefore carries no protective weight in dealings with Turkish authorities.

Criminalisation is pending rather than enacted, and the distinction has not slowed enforcement. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft judicial-reform package, the 11th Judicial Reform, would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people and described it as one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against the provisions targeting LGBT people. Amnesty International records three draft law packages targeting LGBT people made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBT identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible. None of the three was submitted to parliament.

Assembly is the sharpest street-level exposure. Since 2015 local authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches, with police using water cannon and tear gas against participants in the 2015 and 2016 Istanbul parades. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at the end of the year.

The parent framework also governs the interactions most likely to occur on a visit. Foreign nationals are required to produce original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance, and police continue to conduct "General Information Gathering" (GBT) identity checks in which trans women have been held and documented without charge. Any such stop compares a visitor's documents against their presentation. Trans prisoners are placed according to registered sex, and a Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 barred hospitals from recording the "other" option in gender-related medical-board e-reports, tightening the official record around trans patients.

25984515B18723924091225.name: Nevşehir
25984515B18723924091225.summary:
Nevşehir province operates under Turkey's national legal framework. No province-specific ordinance, incident or court decision has been recorded for Nevşehir, and the sources supporting this record are national in scope; the assessment below is therefore the national picture as it would be encountered in a tourist district of Cappadocia, where a tourism economy sits alongside regional conservatism.

The legal baseline is mixed but thin. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so a trans visitor who is refused service, turned away or stopped has no statutory complaint to make. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, which means marriage or partnership status carries no weight in entry, accommodation or next-of-kin matters.

Legislative pressure is documented and unresolved. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft judicial-reform package, the 11th Judicial Reform, would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people and described it as one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against the provisions targeting LGBT people. Amnesty International records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public in Türkiye during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, and that none were ultimately submitted to parliament. Press reports in early 2026 said the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex"; that provision was not included in the year's judicial reform package.

Enforcement has outpaced legislation. Under the parent framework, Kaos GL recorded 313 violations in 2025, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 43 of them taken off the record. In Istanbul in 2025 police stopped around 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee stated that no fines were issued but that she was documented anyway, and that enforcement was already being applied although the new law had not passed.

Checkpoint document checks are the central outing hazard. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. A foreign visitor stopped at such a checkpoint must produce a passport whose gender marker may not match their presentation, making every routine stop a possible disclosure.

Pride events remain suppressed. Since 2015 local authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches, with police using water cannon and tear gas against the 2015 and 2016 Istanbul parades. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025.

Violence is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

A judicial act in December 2025 shows the hostility extending to organised LGBT life. An İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images incompatible with "society's moral values" that could "encourage or promote" LGBTI identities.

25984515B59741408878569.name: Niğde
25984515B59741408878569.summary:
Niğde stands under the national framework of Turkey, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions (256 through formal channels, 43 off the record) alongside systematic intrusions on the privacy of LGBT people.

There is no comprehensive law in Turkey prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised, so a visitor travelling with a spouse or partner has no legal status for that relationship on arrival. Homosexuality has been decriminalised since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender recognition has been available since 1988.

Documents are the sharpest day-to-day exposure. Foreign nationals must carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Every checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation, and in 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in Beyoğlu and held them at Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" checks before release. Legal experts cited in that reporting argue the checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights; one of the women stated that no fines were issued but she was documented anyway, and that enforcement was already being applied although the new law had not been passed.

Criminalisation is pending rather than enacted, and the gap has not constrained practice. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft judicial-reform package, the 11th Judicial Reform, would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people and called it one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; activists held a press conference in Istanbul against the provisions on 28 October 2025. Amnesty International records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, and that none was ultimately submitted to parliament. A press report in February 2026 described draft legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex" with one to three years' imprisonment.

Pride events are systematically prohibited. Marches have been banned in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions used against participants. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police used unlawful force against peaceful protesters, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images incompatible with "society's moral values".

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

If a visitor is detained overnight or longer, the conditions follow registered sex rather than presentation. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to registered sex, with one trans man held in a women's prison. Prison Insider's country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, no staff training to identify LGBT prisoners' needs, binary administration, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints that are ineffective and can invite further violence.

No Niğde-specific source covers any of these points, and no provincial deviation from the national picture is documented; the assessment rests on national reporting.

Legislative criminalisation remains pending rather than enacted, but is being enforced as though in force. Amnesty International records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible; none were submitted to parliament. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft judicial-reform package, the 11th Judicial Reform, would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people and described it as one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; activists held a press conference in the largest city on 28 October 2025 against the provisions targeting LGBT people.

The reported terms of that package are severe: up to three years for conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, up to four years for same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies, the gender-care age floor raised to twenty-five with mandatory infertility conditions, and removal of civil-status recognition of gender change. The principal national LGBTI report of February 2026 characterised the preceding year's hostility as explicit state policy, citing 'Year of the Family' directives, censorship instructions, one organisation closed and three hate-motivated killings.

Street-level enforcement illustrates the gap between statute and practice. During 2025 police in the largest city stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in a central district and held them at a police station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the applicable regional human-rights convention. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them.

Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents. Foreign nationals must carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 in local currency for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation, creating a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in a district of the largest city by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner was found dead in a cell at a women's prison on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from human-rights branches in six provinces demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by an opposition MP on 12 December 2025, confirmed that trans prisoners are placed according to their registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison.

Transition-related care is tightening. A national health ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a provincial health directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

25984515B63638727958144.name: Osmaniye
25984515B63638727958144.summary:
Osmaniye province has no documented trans-specific ordinance, enforcement programme or local institution of its own in the sourced material. What a trans visitor to Osmaniye faces is the national framework of Türkiye, which applies here without local modification.

Under that framework, homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender change has been available since 1988. No comprehensive statute prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised. The draft legislative package leaked in October 2025 would have gone considerably further: Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that the 11th Judicial Reform package would pave the way to criminal charges against LGBT people, calling it among the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades, and LGBT activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against its provisions. Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records three draft packages targeting LGBT people made public during 2025, which would have criminalised expression of LGBT identities and consensual same-sex relations and made legal gender recognition nearly impossible; none was submitted to parliament.

The drafting record since then is contested in the sources and should be read as unresolved. A February 2026 press report described a proposed law criminalising publicly encouraging "behaviour contrary to biological sex" with one to three years' imprisonment, and that provision was not included in the 12th judicial package passed in 2026; the same account states the LGBTI-discriminatory provisions of the draft judicial package were removed in 2026. The direction of travel nonetheless remains restrictive rather than protective, and enforcement has not waited for legislation.

Document checks are the sharpest daily exposure for a visitor. Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Police practice of subjecting people to "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background stops, documented in Istanbul in 2025 against roughly 20 trans women held at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station without fines but with records created, means any stop can become a comparison between passport gender marker and presentation. Openly LGBT people are also barred from military service, classified under a definition of homosexuality as a "psychosexual illness", required to provide photographic proof, and exposed to the leaking of their "unfit report".

Public assembly is restricted. Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and most other cities in most years since 2015, in some years using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. In June 2025 blanket bans were issued against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans Pride marches, police used unlawful force against peaceful protesters, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at year's end.

Transition-related care is narrowing. In June 2025 the Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency, under the Ministry of Health, banned the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21.

sources.summary: Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Rize included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classed under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' leaking publicly. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied bans. In 2026 the draft judicial package's LGBTI-discriminatory provisions were removed; the page records a February 2026 press report of a proposed law criminalizing publicly encouraging 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison, which was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill (the 12th judicial package).

sources.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)
sources.summary: Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26): in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images on social media that were incompatible with 'society's moral values' and could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. The report also records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalize any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible to obtain - though they were ultimately not submitted to parliament. In June 2025 the Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency (Ministry of Health) banned the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21.

25984515B30494634933389.name: Sakarya
25984515B30494634933389.summary:
Sakarya is a province in Turkey's Marmara region and stands under the national framework: no Sakarya-specific statute, enforcement programme or local ban concerning transgender visitors is documented in the sources assembled here, and nationwide provisions govern the province's residents and visitors alike.

The most consequential pending measure is the leaked 11th Judicial Package, a 66-page draft amending the Turkish Penal Code, the Civil Code and six other laws, leaked to Turkish media in mid-October 2025 and analysed by Amnesty International in a November 2025 factsheet. Human Rights Watch's release of 29 October 2025 sets out its terms: conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' would carry up to three years' imprisonment, participation in same-sex ceremonies up to four years.

For trans visitors and residents the draft's care and recognition provisions matter most. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, impose mandatory infertility conditions and multi-stage evaluations, imprison providers with sentences of up to seven years and patients with up to three years, and raise the minimum age for legal gender recognition procedures from 18 to 25 with further conditions added. Amnesty International warns the package would criminalise LGBTI+ people and those advocating for their rights and would severely restrict or make impossible trans and gender-diverse people's access to gender-affirming healthcare.

This is the third set of proposed legal amendments targeting LGBTI+ rights in 2025; the earlier two stalled in Parliament. The draft's status as a proposal rather than enacted law has not been treated by rights organisations as diminishing its effect, and fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association have formally objected.

Standing law already shapes what a trans visitor faces. Homosexuality has been decriminalised in Turkey since 1858 and sex-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, but legal gender recognition still requires a court's permission under Article 40 of the Civil Code, with the applicant at least 18, unmarried and holding a medical report from a state-designated hospital. A passport or identity document that reflects a pre-transition presentation therefore sits against a recognition regime that is judicial, conditional and slow, and any checkpoint or hotel registration check is an occasion on which document and presentation are compared.

The Turkish military bars homosexuals from service and classifies homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness, an official characterisation that indicates how state institutions frame gender and sexual non-conformity.

Sakarya sits within a province-level pattern of public-space restriction elsewhere in the country: Istanbul Pride drew roughly 100,000 participants in 2013 and 2014 before local authorities banned the parades outright for 2015 to 2018. Public assembly of LGBT people has been treated as a matter for provincial administration rather than central law.

25984515B31080883995775.name: Samsun
25984515B31080883995775.summary:
Samsun is a province on Turkey's Black Sea coast, and no province-specific rule, ban or enforcement programme governing transgender visitors is recorded there. What a trans visitor to Samsun faces is the national framework, which applies in the province as in every other.

That framework is contradictory on its face. Homosexuality has been decriminalised in Turkey since 1858 and sex-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, yet legal gender recognition still requires a court's permission under Article 40 of the Civil Code, with the applicant at least 18 years old, unmarried, and holding a medical report issued by a state-designated hospital. A visitor whose passport marker does not match their presentation is therefore dealing with a country in which recognised gender change is possible but slow, court-gated and medically conditioned.

The direction of travel is restrictive. A 66-page draft known as the 11th Judicial Package was leaked to Turkish media in mid-October 2025; it would amend the Turkish Penal Code, the Civil Code and six other laws. Human Rights Watch reported that the package would criminalise conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with terms of up to three years, and penalise participation in same-sex marriage or engagement ceremonies with up to four years.

For trans people specifically, the draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, add mandatory infertility conditions and multi-stage evaluation hurdles, and expose providers to up to seven years' imprisonment and patients to up to three. Amnesty International's November 2025 factsheet concludes that the proposals would severely restrict, or make impossible, trans and gender-diverse people's access to gender-affirming healthcare, and would criminalise LGBTI+ people and those who advocate for their rights.

Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association have objected to the draft. Amnesty records it as the third set of proposed legal amendments targeting LGBTI+ rights in 2025, the earlier two having stalled in Parliament. The proposals are nationwide and would apply within Samsun as in every other province.

25984515B34503670046284.name: Siirt
25984515B34503670046284.summary:
Siirt province stands under the national framework of Turkey, and no Siirt-specific ban, enforcement programme, incident or local institution concerning transgender visitors is documented in the audited sources. What a trans visitor to Siirt faces is the country-wide regime, applied by national ministries, provincial governors and police stations that operate the same powers throughout the country.

That regime is actively tightening. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, carrying up to three years' imprisonment, with participation in same-sex ceremonies punishable by up to four years. The same package would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from eighteen to twenty-five, attach mandatory infertility conditions and multi-stage evaluation hurdles, and imprison providers of such care for up to seven years and patients for up to three. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association object to the measures.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report for 2025/26 records that three draft law packages targeting LGBT people were made public during 2025, seeking to criminalise LGBT identity expression and consensual same-sex relations and to make legal gender recognition nearly impossible. None was ultimately submitted to parliament. A related proposal to criminalise publicly encouraging behaviour contrary to biological sex, carrying a one-to-three-year sentence, was also omitted from the 12th judicial package. The pattern across these drafts is of measures announced and enforced in substance before, or without, enactment.

The settled law remains comparatively old. Homosexuality was decriminalised under the Ottoman penal code in 1858 and legal gender change has been available in Turkey since 1988. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military.

Pride events are prohibited rather than merely policed. Governors blocked the Istanbul parades held between 2015 and 2018, and on 14 June 2019 the governors of Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya banned all three cities' prides. In June 2025 blanket bans were issued against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches; police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still continuing at the end of the year.

Civil society faces closure. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had circulated images incompatible with society's moral values.

25984515B86660708585065.name: Sinop
25984515B86660708585065.summary:
No measure, incident, arrest, ban or institution concerning trans visitors is documented in Sinop in the audited sources. What a trans visitor to Sinop faces is the Turkish national framework, and no local Sinop authority is recorded adding enforcement or prohibitions of its own.

Sinop stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than left to residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 43 of them taken off the record. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of them classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected. The government's stated posture of protecting "the family" and "public morals" supplies the rhetorical basis, identified by Human Rights Watch, for legitimising stigma of LGBT people.

Street-level enforcement operates ahead of the law. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly twenty trans women in the Beyoğlu district, in shops and cafés, and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" checks before release. Legal experts cited in that reporting argue the checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detained woman reported that no fines were issued but that she was documented anyway, and that enforcement had begun although the new law had not yet been passed. Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which places presentation and passport gender marker in direct comparison.

The Human Rights Watch release of 29 October 2025 reports that the leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", carrying up to three years, and participation in same-sex ceremonies up to four years. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 with mandatory infertility conditions and multiple evaluation hurdles, and would imprison providers for up to seven years and patients for up to three. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association object to the package.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records three draft law packages made public during 2025 that would criminalise LGBTI identity expression and consensual same-sex relations and render legal gender recognition nearly impossible. None was submitted to parliament. The same report documents that in June 2025 blanket bans were issued against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, that police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, that more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and that prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at year's end. In December 2025 a court in İzmir ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, holding that it had shared "obscene" images incompatible with "society's moral values". Amnesty records no incident in Sinop itself.

The national profile compiled on Wikipedia places these measures against a longer legal history. Homosexuality was decriminalised in 1858 under the Ottoman penal code, and legal gender change has been possible since 1988, while same-sex marriage is not recognised and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military. Governors have repeatedly blocked Pride events: parades in Istanbul were banned by local authorities across 2015 to 2018, and on 14 June 2019 the governors of Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya banned all three cities' Pride marches. The same source records a proposal to criminalise publicly encouraging "behavior contrary to biological sex" with a one-to-three-year sentence, which was ultimately not included in the 12th judicial package.

Prison conditions compound the risk for anyone detained. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before, that medical staff arrived after a prolonged delay, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to registered sex. Rights group reporting compiled by Prison Insider with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer, with complaints that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening as well. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records.

25984515B33997294820892.name: Sivas
25984515B33997294820892.summary:
No Sivas-specific statute, enforcement programme, incident or institution concerning transgender visitors is documented in the sources assembled for this edition. What a trans visitor to Sivas faces is the national framework of Türkiye, and no local authority in the province is recorded adding prohibitions of its own.

That framework includes a draft legislative threat at the level of penalty. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that the leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, carrying up to three years, with participation in same-sex marriage ceremonies or celebrations carrying up to four years. The same package would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from eighteen to twenty-five, attach mandatory infertility conditions and repeated evaluation hurdles, and imprison care providers for up to seven years and patients for up to three. Fifteen LGBT organisations and the Turkish Medical Association objected to the measures.

The settled baseline underneath that draft is older and mixed. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Türkiye since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and trans people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, subject to sex reassignment surgery, medical examination and court permission. Against that, no comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised, and openly LGBT people are barred from military service under a health regulation that classifies homosexuality as a psychosexual illness.

Enforcement against LGBT assembly is documented and repeated. Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions used against participants who defied the bans. In June 2025 the Istanbul governorate issued blanket bans against both the LGBTI and the Trans Pride marches; police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at the end of the year.

Organisations face dissolution as well as prosecution. In December 2025 a court in İzmir ordered the Young LGBTI+ Association dissolved, finding that it had circulated obscene images incompatible with society's moral values that could encourage or promote LGBT identities. Blanket bans combined with case-by-case prosecutions under Law No. 2911 constitute the enforcement climate that provincial authorities in Sivas operate within.

Two further national indicators round out the picture. Press reports in early 2026 recorded that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of behaviour contrary to biological sex, and Türkiye placed 47th of 49 countries in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking.

25984515B4318484465943.name: Tekirdağ
25984515B4318484465943.summary:
Tekirdağ province records no province-specific statute, enforcement action, incident or institution concerning transgender visitors. What a trans visitor to Tekirdağ stands under is the national framework of Turkey, and that framework is documented as a structured and deliberate danger rather than residual prejudice.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that the leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years' imprisonment, and participation in same-sex ceremonies with up to four years. The same package would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, attach mandatory infertility and repeated-evaluation conditions, and imprison providers for up to seven years and patients for up to three. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected. Same-sex marriage is not recognised in Turkey, so the ceremony provisions apply to symbolic events rather than legal unions.

Street-level risk is document-driven. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped around 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release; legal experts cited in that reporting argue the checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women stated that no fines were issued but that she was documented anyway. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention, so every stop is an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of them classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Public assembly is suppressed. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans pride marches in Istanbul, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force and more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained; three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025.

Detention and imprisonment carry their own documented hazards. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions. Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex: a transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and the case raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Prison Insider's country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, binary administration, and complaints that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

25984515B20532508270601.tangentialFactors:
The parent framework for Türkiye documents a scale of enforcement that a visitor to Tokat should expect to be reachable anywhere in the country: 313 recorded violations in 2025, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, and 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

Street-level identity checks are a national practice rather than an Istanbul peculiarity. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in Beyoğlu and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

Carrying original photo identification is separately mandatory for foreign nationals at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention. Every checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

Compared with jurisdictions that hold statutory non-discrimination protection, Türkiye offers none on sexual orientation or gender identity, and the pending draft package would move in the opposite direction by adding penalties rather than removing them.

25984515B20532508270601.localsOnly:
Residents seeking legal gender recognition must undergo surgery and obtain court approval; the procedure has been available on that basis since 1988. There is no statutory non-discrimination remedy available to residents discriminated against on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no relationship recognition exists beyond marriage, which is closed to same-sex couples. Civil unions and adoption are unavailable.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Pride organisation carries a documented risk of police force. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

25984515B1589724669162.name: Trabzon
25984515B1589724669162.summary:
Trabzon province carries no trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation in the available record. The absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence from the national position, not as evidence of safety for a trans visitor: the Turkish national framework applies to Trabzon in full.

Turkey does not presently hold a passed criminal statute against trans identity or same-sex conduct, but a leaked omnibus reform draft reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 would amend the penal code to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years' imprisonment and participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with up to four. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, mandate permanent infertility assessment and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, and expose both the healthcare professionals performing such care and the patients receiving it to criminal prosecution, with pretrial detention possible. The measure had not been adopted when reported. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed it, and Human Rights Watch called for its withdrawal.

The pending status of the draft has not prevented authorities from acting as though prohibitions were already in force. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafes in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in that reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police imposed no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not passed even as enforcement was already being applied to her.

Checkpoint interactions carry a direct outing risk for trans visitors. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any stop becomes an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation. For a visitor whose appearance does not match a passport gender marker, that comparison is the central practical hazard in Trabzon as elsewhere in the country.

The state response to violence against trans people is asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender people the most affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Rights groups treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate rather than an isolated failure.

Transition-related care is tightening through administrative rule. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required electronic reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Detention conditions are governed by segregation and placement on registered sex. Trans prisoners in Turkey are held in gendered facilities matching their registration, and a transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. A visitor who enters Turkish custody faces a system in which gender confirmation is not accommodated in facility assignment and in which complaints processes are documented as ineffective.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

25984515B47484816256121.name: Tunceli
25984515B47484816256121.summary:
Tunceli stands under the national framework: Turkey presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors, driven by hostility that has become formal state policy rather than residual prejudice. No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for Tunceli itself. That absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence, not local permissiveness.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus reform draft, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal code to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years in prison, and participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with up to four. The draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, mandate permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, and expose both healthcare professionals performing such care and patients to criminal prosecution, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; Human Rights Watch called for its withdrawal. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Kaos GL's Human Rights Report 2025, titled "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds LGBTI+ hostility became explicit state policy, with instructions issued to public institutions under the "Year of the Family" banner. It documents 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings with trans people the most affected, 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, 313 right-to-liberty violations — about 2.5 times the previous year — with 299 detention decisions, freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540, and 40 right-to-association violations including the first closure of an LGBTI+ association in many years.

Street-level enforcement elsewhere in Turkey illustrates how the framework operates before it is enacted. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, creating a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

25984515B95251525471141.name: Uşak
25984515B95251525471141.summary:
Uşak is a province of Turkey and its trans visitors stand under the national framework documented across the country. No province-specific trans-related source exists for Uşak, so the absence of a documented local ban or local incident is not evidence of permissiveness; the national pattern is the operative expectation.

Turkey's danger to trans visitors is structured and documented rather than residual. Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", records hostility toward LGBTI+ people converted into explicit state policy, with "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years, restrictions on expression and artistic freedom, and events cancelled or banned.

The same monitoring counted 313 liberty violations in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 89 torture and ill-treatment violations up from 51, and private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, a category that includes obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy. It also recorded 61 travel bans against trans people, a direct freedom-of-movement restriction that bears on travel planning, and six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected group.

A leaked omnibus draft, the "11th Judicial Package", was before the government as of October 2025 according to Human Rights Watch. It would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years' imprisonment, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, conditioned on mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years' imprisonment, patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would push treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

Enforcement has not waited for legislation. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on streets, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in that reporting argue the checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee reported that no fines were issued but the women were documented anyway, and that the new law had not passed even as its prohibitions were being applied. Istanbul is a single data point illustrating a nationwide practice rather than a separate local regime.

Any checkpoint interaction carries a document risk. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. A visitor whose appearance does not match the passport gender marker can be outed at the moment documents are compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees rest on segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

25984515B28392380114016.name: Van
25984515B28392380114016.summary:
Van is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework: the country's penal code, migration rules, health regulations and prison administration apply here in full, and no trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for Van itself. That absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence, not local permissiveness.

A leaked omnibus measure identified by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 as the "11th Judicial Package" would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, conditioned on mandatory permanent infertility assessment and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years, patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warned it would drive treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest. As reported, the draft had not been passed; its pending status has not prevented authorities elsewhere from acting as though equivalent prohibitions were already in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 review characterises hostility as explicit state policy rather than residual prejudice: "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years, restricted expression and artistic freedom, and events cancelled or banned. The monitoring counted 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected; 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year; 313 liberty violations, roughly two and a half times the prior year, carrying 299 detention decisions; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; and 61 travel bans.

For a visitor, the most likely contact with this machinery is a street checkpoint. Turkish authorities require foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release, an practice legal experts cited in the reporting argue violates Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One woman stopped stated that no fines were issued but that she was documented anyway, and that enforcement was already being applied ahead of any new law. Every such interaction is an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation, and any mismatch between passport gender marker and appearance is an outing risk.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required electronic reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care; anyone relying on hormone therapy in transit should expect records to carry a gender marker consequence.

25984515B28392380114016.tangentialFactors:
Prison conditions are a live risk for any trans visitor detained in Turkey. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Coordinated by Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın, rights groups demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to registered sex, with a trans man held in a women's prison, and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The pattern has depth. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's continuity rather than as a statement of current law.

25984515B19658467647683.name: Yozgat
25984515B19658467647683.summary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for Yozgat province. That absence records the absence of documented divergence from the national position, not local safety: the rules set out below reach Yozgat unchanged.

Yozgat stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward LGBTI+ people has hardened into formal state policy. Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family", records instructions issued to public institutions under that banner and, for the first time in years, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation; expression and artistic freedom were restricted and events cancelled or banned.

The same review counts 313 liberty violations in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year, alongside 299 detention decisions; 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year; 61 travel bans; and private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, among them obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy. Six right-to-life violations were recorded, three of them hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the most affected group.

A leaked omnibus draft, the "11th Judicial Package", was reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years' imprisonment, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, behind mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years' imprisonment, patients up to three, with pretrial detention possible.

Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft. Human Rights Watch warns that it would drive treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

Document checks are a standing exposure for a trans visitor anywhere in Turkey. Foreign nationals must produce original photo identification at transit checkpoints, and police stops for background checks were used against trans women in Istanbul in 2025. Every such interaction is an occasion on which a passport gender marker is compared against presentation, and fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira are attached to non-compliance with the identification rule.

Lethal violence and asymmetric state response are documented nationally. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025; rights groups demanded an independent investigation, and opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.
