25984515B41137800759750.summary:
Şırnak province yields no trans-specific statute, enforcement series or documented incident in the available sources. The assessment therefore rests on the national framework of Turkey, which applies in full within the province, and on the passport and checkpoint rules that bind foreign visitors there.

A leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, was reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, behind mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years, patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warned it would push treatment underground. The measure had not been enacted as of that reporting, but authorities have acted against LGBT people as though equivalent prohibitions were already operative.

Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", records 313 liberty violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the previous total, with 299 detention decisions; 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected; 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; and 61 travel bans.

Checkpoint interaction is the principal everyday exposure for a visitor. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in Beyoğlu and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Any stop becomes an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation, a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people is met with asymmetric state response. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was referred for arrest. Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex in gendered facilities: a transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and the case raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported four transgender inmates sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, delayed medical staff, prosecutors entering two days later, and witness statements not taken.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, risking profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to care.

19177384B49506124846693.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
19177384B49506124846693.summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743 passed the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate by 55 votes to one abstention on 9 May 2012, was promulgated on 24 May 2012, and allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. Emergency decree DNU 62/2025, published in February 2025, modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for people under 18, which Reuters reported as a ban on surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. Decree DNU 61/2025 of the same month re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty and invites the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere; it bars people who have legally changed their gender from being held in women's prisons when detained for sexual offences or violence against women.

National protection machinery has been dismantled. The national administration eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs, and has moved to restrict the twelve-year-old Gender Identity Law. Buenos Aires-based activists told the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current government took office, with harassment and hate speech rising nationally.

Violence reached a documented peak in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity across the year, a ten-year record averaging one every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes data published on 19 March 2026 puts 32% of those crimes inside police stations and penal facilities, records security-force violence rising from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and shows trans women and travestis concentrating 62.5% of victims, 142 cases, with most perpetrators drawn from security personnel and unknown assailants.

The operative risk on the ground is police identification and detention. On 18 September, six months after an unlawful detention, officers from police station 18 carried out fresh detentions, arrests and arbitrary identifications of travestis and trans women, writing several of them up under article 81 of the City's Contravention Code for lacking documents and arresting one. Activists described the operation as a new episode of illegal persecution.

Judicial protection against gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

The city has operated its own anti-discrimination law since 1996, hosts a large visible LGBTQ scene and tourism economy, and concentrates the administration of the national employment-quota law alongside the national femicide registry, making it where a state response is most likely to be present. FALGBT and legal experts called both February 2025 decrees illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

14911670B90188072957077.name: Santa Catarina
14911670B90188072957077.summary:
Santa Catarina stands under the national framework of Brazil, where same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change, spousal and residence categories treat same-sex and opposite-sex couples identically, and a 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling (ADO 26) makes discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds punishable as equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989. A visitor's entry, documents and family status are therefore handled on the same footing as any other traveller's.

In one respect Santa Catarina runs worse than the rest of the country. It is the only Brazilian state to have enacted a statutory bathroom restriction, and it is the venue of a nationally decisive refusal: staff at a Florianópolis shopping centre barred a trans woman from the women's restroom, where she urinated on herself in front of shoppers and had to travel home by public transport. On 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Tribunal rejected her appeal, leaving such refusals lawful under ordinary private-premises rules. The concrete exposure a visibly trans visitor faces is in shops, restaurants and transport hubs across the state.

Foreign partners are protected in practice. A Florianópolis judge of the 1st Civil Court, M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva, blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived more than ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian. Foreign same-sex marriages are recognised for immigration purposes, including the spousal residence permit.

Florianópolis itself is named among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural parts of Santa Catarina may present more social friction, although legal rights are identical nationwide.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's March 2026 country overview records that LGBTIQ people in Brazil still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions, and guarantees apply equally to visitors in Santa Catarina.

Since 2020 people in Santa Catarina have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific law prescribes this. In Florianópolis, judge M. C. Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 under CNJ Resolution 175/2013, and a 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989.

Constitutional guarantees and federal criminal provisions adopted after the 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling prohibit discrimination and hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity. A deeply conservative Congress has nonetheless generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal the marriage equality recognised by the Supreme Court in 2013. These guarantees apply nationwide and cover visitors in Santa Catarina. In September 2025 the government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee, a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019, for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy. The Superior Court of Justice ruled that nonbinary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity.

A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names Florianópolis among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction, though legal rights are identical nationwide. Foreign same-sex spouses and partners are treated identically for visa and residence categories, including the spousal residence permit, and foreign same-sex marriages are recognised for immigration purposes. Joint and second-parent adoption are confirmed by STF RE 846.102 (2015). Gender-marker changes proceed without surgery. ADO 26 (2019) criminalises homophobia and transphobia as equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989.

82249235B24619009834807.name: British Columbia
82249235B24619009834807.summary:
British Columbia stands under the Canadian framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation and hate-propaganda provisions of the Criminal Code, both carried by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in British Columbia, and sexual orientation has been covered federally since 1996. Courts have applied these protections consistently.

British Columbia has no hostile provincial legislation. It was the first jurisdiction in Canada to write sexual orientation into its human-rights code, in 1992, and it is routinely assessed as the country's most progressive province on LGBT issues; Vancouver's Davie Village remains the established social centre. No province or territory restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Legal gender recognition operates on a self-declaration basis. Transgender people may change their legal gender in every province and territory, British Columbia included, under rules that vary from place to place; Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act replaced the surgery requirement with a declaration supported by a doctor's letter. Federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.

A 2021 amendment to the Criminal Code, in force since 2022, made Canada the first country in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide, for minors and for adults. Coverage of health care is universal.

The visible risk to a visitor is the hate-crime climate rather than the statute book. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in Canada in 2024, up 1% on 2023 after a 34% rise the year before; the total is up 169% since 2018, a more than doubling, while the population rate fell 2% to 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, and religion-motivated incidents were essentially stable at 1,342. Offences motivated by gender identity and gender expression remain among the fastest-growing categories over the longer arc, and Egale Canada publishes an analysis of the 2024 data affecting 2SLGBTQI people. The national figures carry no British Columbia breakdown.

Hostility is also visible in British Columbia itself. In 2023, coordinated disruptions repeatedly targeted public drag-storytime events at libraries: Coquitlam Public Library postponed or cancelled on several occasions, including a protest at its Town Centre branch on 14 January 2023 and a postponement on 13 October 2023, citing public-safety risk, while the counter-gathering that followed became the largest queer gathering the Tri-Cities had seen. At a Richmond library event with no police on site, a man pushed through the crowd to photograph attendees.

Detention is the weakest part of the national framework. Since Bill C-16, federal correctional policy requires transgender prisoners to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Both placement and gender-affirming treatment have been contested in court, including litigation in which lawyer Barbara findlay represented a trans prisoner challenging placement in a women's institution and the withholding of gender-affirming medical care.

Two provinces have moved against residents. Alberta and Saskatchewan have enacted policy rollbacks affecting trans people living there, including school-facing measures on names, pronouns and notification of parents. These rules govern residents rather than visitors, but they mark the direction of provincial politics running alongside the human-rights statutes.

47653553B5611469222723.summary:
Región de Valparaíso stands under the national framework of Chile, which is among the more developed in the region. Legal gender recognition has operated since 2019 on a self-determination basis, with no medical or surgical conditions attached, and Gender Identity Law 21.120 extends name and gender changes on all official documents to people aged 14 and over. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and since 2012 the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences. Birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children, available since 2006.

Detention carries specific protections. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing trans detainees the recognition of their assumed gender, including placement and segmented housing by gender identity, entry examinations, and rules on access for trans visitors; a standing committee with Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives monitors implementation.

The policy record has stalled. A Chilean advocacy group's annual assessment judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights, the first such reversal since the return of democracy in 1990, attributing the failure of equality and trans-rights bills to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction. Movilh's 24th Annual Human Rights Report, published March 2026 and covering 2025, describes a breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus around LGBTIQ+ rights, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers.

Documented violence remains a live risk. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing and was described in the national press as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Institutional hostility is also visible inside state employment. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging she was relegated to administrative duties, had her private life exposed without consent, and was denied support.

Regional evidence places Región de Valparaíso at the centre of recorded anti-LGBTI discrimination in Chile. By a wide margin it is the country's highest-incidence region: in 2024 it concentrated 51.32% of all national recorded cases, with Región Metropolitana second at 25.12%, and the regional total was up 80.93% over 2023. In 2025 recorded cases fell only in Región de Valparaíso and Región Metropolitana while all other regions rose. Movilh reads that pattern as a decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ themes have less visibility and debate, not as a local improvement; the report carries a full per-region and per-commune series for 2002-2025.

Valparaíso and Viña del Mar's port-university culture is bohemian in character, and criminality in the region is general rather than gender-targeted. Protection machinery does exist locally: Valparaíso hosted the first Encuentro de Oficinas Municipales de Diversidad in 2022, and San Antonio, in Región de Valparaíso, was among the founding comunas of the Red de Municipalidades por la Diversidad, Inclusión y No Discriminación (Red Diversa), created in 2014 and grown beyond 60 municipalities by 2024. All assessments here are relative to the national picture in Chile.

13589884B3780741375954.name: Antioquia
13589884B3780741375954.summary:
Antioquia department stands under Colombia's national legal framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry trans and non-binary markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Antioquia contains the city at the centre of the country's most alarming recent record on anti-trans violence. On 4 April 2025 in Bello, a city in Antioquia near Medellín, the 32-year-old trans woman Sara Millerey González Borja was beaten and thrown into a waterway in broad daylight while onlookers filmed her. The video went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured limbs flailing in a creek unable to swim. She died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, solidarity events were held in several cities, and protests followed. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello during 2025; the first two victims were gay men. Her mother Sandra Borja stated that they killed her for being who she was.

Care access in the same episode is documented: a clinic reportedly did not treat her as an emergency because she had not been shot. One report counted 13 trans people killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone, alongside 41 transgender women killed in 2023 and eight more between February and April 2024.

Where armed groups operate, the risk is structured rather than incidental. In the department of Caquetá, where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement, armed groups distributed flyers on streets and on WhatsApp announcing a 'social cleansing' plan naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and threatened a further wave; trans women there fled after death threats. In the department of Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording 'All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans'. In Caquetá, trans women reported few options beyond sex work; Tatiana Céspedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after death threats from armed men, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed.

Protection machinery exists and has been used. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern, and a Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

13589884B40908771570386.name: Bogota Capital District
13589884B40908771570386.summary:
Bogotá Capital District stands under Colombia's national framework, which the sources describe as among the most developed in Latin America for trans legal recognition. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender change on the basis of self-recognition without surgical or psychiatric requirements, reinforced by a 2012 ruling allowing change through the civil registry without family court authorisation; since a rule change approved in June 2015 that route runs through a notary rather than judicially ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Colombian identification documents carry four markers, female (F), male (M), trans (T) and non-binary (NB), available on the national identity card from November 2025.

Consensual same-sex activity has been legal in Colombia since 1981. Same-sex marriage became available in April 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples in November 2015, and a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation. Rulings T-033 of 2022 and T-527 of 2024 protected the recording of gender identity in official documents. A comprehensive trans law was still before the legislature in 2025, and both national overviews note that prejudice and discrimination against LGBTI people remain present in a considerable part of the population.

The enforcement gap in that framework is severe and documented by official sources. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025 and warned that institutional reform and daily lived experience are disconnected, with killings rising and discrimination requiring urgent action.

Bogotá Capital District is the centre of the country's best-documented trans community and its trans-specific services. Red Comunitaria Trans, a trans community organisation, reported police shouting at, baton-beating and shooting at trans sex workers in the early hours on a central street of the district, and the district mayor's office took up the case.

Lethal violence against trans people is also documented inside the district. Two trans women were killed within hours of each other on the night of 2 January 2026, and a 32-year-old trans activist was found dead in the eastern hills of Bogotá in December 2023.

For a visitor, the operative screening reality is mass identity-check operations in the central districts. In San Bernardo in April 2025, more than 200 officers were deployed for a security operation; in Santa Fe in January 2026, over 1,200 uniformed officers conducted operations including background and migrant control. A visibly gender-nonconforming person moving through central Bogotá is therefore likely to be stopped and identity-checked in routine practice.

National lethal violence illustrates what such encounters can precede. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín on 4 April 2025, beaten with fractured legs, arms and hands, left flailing in a creek unable to swim, and drowned; a 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April. Her mother, Sandra Borja, stated that her daughter was killed for being who she was. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities.

Some conflict-related violence against LGBTI Colombians has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that the violence constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

Detention is the point at which courts have intervened most directly on trans rights. A Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system, and a 2012 ruling held that a transgender woman imprisoned in Bogotá could choose her own hairstyle and makeup.

sources.summary: Wikipedia's Colombia overview is the national framework every visitor to Bogotá Capital District stands under: consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981; the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016 (making Colombia the fourth Latin American country to do so); adoption equality came in 2015; a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; and transgender people have had a right to change legal gender recognised since 1993, reinforced by a 2012 Constitutional Court ruling allowing civil-registry change without a family court. The national top government lawyer's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in the country between January and May 2025, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025. 25490228B43154843394848.name: Comunidad de Madrid
25490228B43154843394848.summary:
Madrid is one of Europe's principal LGBT urban centres: the Chueca district is the community's epicentre, the annual Pride event (MADO) in late June or early July draws millions of attendees, and daily life offers substantial anonymity for LGBT visitors. The same source records that homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence remain significant problems in the city, and that marginalised groups including trans people and migrants face additional barriers.

The national framework a visitor's documents stand under is Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, which establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The statute also carries broad anti-discrimination guarantees, employment and health measures, and an LGTBI equality strategy. Human Rights Watch described it in February 2023 as a hard-won victory after years of activism.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis. Courts apply the aggravation in practice: in Vigo a Tribunal de Instancia used it for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300; in Valencia a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Madrid was among the first Spanish regions to adopt its own gender-identity law, passing it in 2016 alongside the Islas Baleares and the Región de Murcia, after Extremadura in 2015. That regional statute sits above the national floor set by Ley 4/2023 and was amended by Ley 17/2023. On 27 December 2023 two community laws, Ley 17/2023 and Ley 18/2023, amended the 2016 gender-identity law and the regional anti-LGBTBI law on the stated ground of protecting freedom of expression and academic freedom, stripping the provisions that obliged educational institutions; the resulting restrictions sit in the school environment and do not touch a visitor's public conduct, documents or entry.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied across Spain since 2005, and the country is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly in the world.

19338628B30439183828151.name: Bourgogne-Franche-Comté
19338628B30439183828151.summary:
Bourgogne-Franche-Comté stands under the French national framework. Rules on identity documents, anti-discrimination, criminal law, marriage and gender recognition are set by national statute and apply uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions, so the legal rules a visitor faces in this region are the same ones that apply elsewhere in France.

Detention carries the sharpest documented risk. France has no statutory rule governing where a trans prisoner is held: placement follows the gender inscribed on identity documents, and each facility improvises, using special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describes trans women incarcerated on that basis as falling into a legal grey area, punished beyond their alleged crimes, with accounts of heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

The CGLPL, France's national custodial-inspection authority, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations of fundamental rights across all places of detention: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty. The recommendations also extend to intersex and non-binary detainees, and the national preventive mechanism told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the earlier one produced no marked improvement and because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, which argued that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of questioning by French border police at the airport, conducted in front of other travellers.

In everyday movement, accommodation and services, France's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition. The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony, citing the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and setting out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition the baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

Rules on identity documents, anti-discrimination, criminal law, marriage and gender recognition are set by national statute and apply uniformly across all state/province under the parent nation's jurisdiction, so the legal rules a visitor faces in the state are the same ones that apply elsewhere.

Detention carries the sharpest documented risk. The national framework has no statutory rule governing where a trans prisoner is held: placement follows the gender inscribed on identity documents, and each facility improvises, using special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describes trans women incarcerated on that basis as falling into a legal grey area, punished beyond their alleged crimes, with accounts of heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

The national custodial-inspection authority examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations of fundamental rights across all places of detention: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty. The recommendations also extend to intersex and non-binary detainees, and the national preventive mechanism told an international prevention association that a new opinion was needed precisely because the earlier one produced no marked improvement and because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in a men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the head of the national justice ministry in oral question no. 219 in the national legislature, which argued that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under legislative scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of questioning by border police at the airport, conducted in front of other travellers.

In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the national oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition. The national equal-rights ombuds issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony, citing the union's fundamental-rights agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people nationally report identity-related discrimination, and setting out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition the baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported the first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

19338628B36302232233914.name: Hauts-de-France
19338628B36302232233914.summary:
Visitors in Hauts-de-France stand under France's national framework: criminal law, identity-document rules, anti-discrimination law and marriage law apply uniformly across the region, and the country's oversight bodies record the same pattern of risk everywhere.

Prison placement is the region's documented contact point with trans-visitor risk. Under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender inscribed on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities. Controller-general Adeline Hazan, the national detention inspector-general, identifies transgender detainees as the group that suffers the most in prison.

The BuzzFeed News investigation of 12 January 2018 documents that practice in the region directly. Paola, transferred in 2014 to the correctional facility at Lille, was met by detainees shouting that they did not want any women there, was attacked with a knife by a fellow inmate, and spent two days in solitary confinement. The same investigation records Kara B. held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 protest trial in the capital, and the Ministry of Justice counted 13 transgender detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016.

The national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 covering every place of deprivation of liberty and built from referrals received since 2010 concerning transgender detainees. It finds that assignment to establishments or wards, male or female, is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and that search procedures for persons whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation.

That opinion recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, and urges research funding. It faults the administration for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules, and the CGLPL issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty after concluding that its 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement.

Placement remained current practice in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October; her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, and placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline is the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

65028918B14696209246677.name: Jakarta Special Capital Region
65028918B14696209246677.summary:
The Jakarta Special Capital Region stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; those punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Venue raids are a standing enforcement instrument. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveler in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Jakarta is the most heavily raided venue in Indonesia for LGBTQ+ gatherings, and the capital's raid series is the clearest documented instance of the national pattern. Police arrested 141 people over a "gay sex party" in Jakarta in May 2017, detained 144 at the Atlantis Gym sauna on 21 May 2017 with ten subsequently charged, and arrested 51 at a Central Jakarta sauna in October 2017 with six charged. All of those cases were pursued under the pornography law.

The same pattern continues in the current period. Police detained 56 people at a hotel in South Jakarta on 1 February 2025, nine at another South Jakarta hotel on 24 May 2025, and 75 at a private villa near the capital on 22 June 2025. Offences charged in these operations can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment under Indonesia's broadly worded Pornography Law.

Arrests in these raids are made without naming detainees and without judicial proceedings, according to Amnesty International's 24 June 2025 press release. Amnesty International Indonesia's deputy director called the villa operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy that exemplifies the hostile environment for LGBTI people in Indonesia, and demanded the release of those arrested.

There is no LGBT-specific statute and no general anti-discrimination law in Indonesia, so police action in Jakarta operates on pornography and morality provisions rather than any LGBT-specific offence. A visitor therefore faces exposure through broadly worded national laws applied at the discretion of police, not through a named prohibition.

1811400B15614733245507.name: Mahārāshtra
1811400B15614733245507.summary:
India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, and the framework stands over Maharashtra as it does over every other state. The bill amends the 2019 law, removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex people, and makes medical certification a condition of recognition. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the scheme.

Human Rights Watch, in a news release of 26 March 2026, calls the amendment a huge setback. It objects to the new offences of "coercing or alluring" a person to be transgender, provisions it describes as reminiscent of colonial-era laws that punished transgender people for presenting as women. Rights activists including Akkai Padmashali characterise the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist.

The recognition gap is documented numerically. India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, while about 32,500 hold the identity cards on which access to social security schemes depends. Critics warn the narrower definition excludes many transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people from welfare benefits. Lawyer N Kavitha Rameshwar calls the medical-certification requirement an attack on the privacy and dignity of the individual. The government answers that the narrower definition targets people facing extreme and oppressive discrimination and prevents exploitation and trafficking.

Approval status is stated in the sources only as far as both houses of Parliament, with presidential assent still pending at the time of reporting; the final legislative status is not confirmed here. Whatever the outcome of assent, the amendment reverses the Supreme Court's 2014 ruling on third gender and self-determination, and India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The entry and stay baseline remains mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel: a trans woman alleged groping by a Railway Protection Force constable at a Kolkata railway station during a gender check, transgender detainees described degrading treatment in Railway Protection Force custody in Assam in interviews recorded June 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student at Chennai International Airport in November 2024 despite her PAN card, and passport authorities required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination until the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

In Maharashtra itself, the sharper screening mechanism is at public-festival gates rather than in statute. After the Vishva Hindu Parishad publicly urged garba organisers not to admit non-Hindus and to check Aadhaar cards, organisers in Nagpur imposed Aadhaar verification, security checks with separate "male and female" boundaries, and a ritual bow before a Varaha avatar as conditions of entry. An identity-checked, religion-screened gate places a gender-nonconforming visitor under examination by officials who have no business asking, and it is occurring in named cities rather than statewide.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. A UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

Parliament narrowed recognition in 2026 and the 2024 criminal-code rewrite dropped gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences, while high courts have repeatedly intervened: the 2021 guidelines, the February 2026 relief on passport medical examinations, and judicial acknowledgement of same-sex couples as family units.

Screening exposure varies sharply by setting. Statute-based risk is national, but the outing mechanism documented within the state/province is a festival entry gate in one city combining religion-based identity verification with binary security lanes, which is a different and more situational risk than a police station or an immigration counter.

Compared with the national baseline, the state/province distinguishing factor in these sources is the public-festival access screening rather than any state/province-specific statute; the state/province-specific criminal, document and recognition rules are those of the national framework.

1811400B23625213884851.name: Delhi
1811400B23625213884851.summary:
Delhi stands under India's national framework. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Human Rights Watch reported on 26 March 2026 that the bill removes the right to self-identification, limits recognition to those groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates offences of coercing or alluring a person that could criminalise the support systems trans people rely on. Human Rights Watch calls the bill a major reversal of hard-won rights and has urged the president not to sign it.

BBC News reported that the amendment bill has been approved by both houses of Parliament and awaits presidential assent, reversing the self-identification route established by the Supreme Court's 2014 ruling. The government argues the narrower definition will make welfare benefits, job reservations and healthcare support more targeted while strengthening protection against exploitation and trafficking. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel has asked the government to reconsider, citing privacy and dignity.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units. An estimated two million transgender people live in India, and the national documentation position is thin: the last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, of whom roughly 32,500 hold the identity cards required to access social security.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender, and trans people arrested by the force in Assam recounted degrading custody treatment in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.

HRW calls it a major reversal of hard-won rights and urges the president not to sign it. India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for social security. This national documentation gap bears directly on Delhi as the capital, and the source records no Delhi-specific event.

BBC News reported that the 2026 amendment bill has been approved by both houses and now awaits presidential assent, removing the right to self-identify in a reversal of the 2014 Supreme Court ruling. 68945753B55100681051852.name: Seoul
68945753B55100681051852.summary:
South Korea does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available and the requirement of surgery is falling. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that forcing surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. The Supreme Court has also allowed a transgender person with minor children to change their gender in the family relations register.

Trans visitors have a documented, judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court issued a final, unappealed ruling that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, awarding 300,000 won in symbolic compensation against the state.

There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on these grounds. In healthcare, the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court did issue a landmark 2024 ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights, extending a measure of recognition in that specific area.

For a visitor on the ground, Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are broadly positive, but the surrounding context requires care: organised conservative opposition is active, no national anti-discrimination law exists, and Human Rights Watch records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report, which also notes a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.

The Seoul Central District Court, presiding judge Chung In-jae, dismissed the state's appeal and ruled partially for the plaintiff in a damages action against the state on 2 July 2024, awarding 300,000 won (about $240) of the 3 million won claimed; the judgment became final because neither party appealed (Korea Times, 22 July 2024). The court held that a police officer's advice to a person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed personal rights, and stated that the right to comfortably use restrooms is a fundamental and universal human right.

The conditions underlying that ruling are quantified by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea's 2021 survey of 591 transgender respondents: 41% had used a restroom of another gender out of fear of mistreatment, 39% restricted food and drink to avoid entering public restrooms, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. Courts outside the capital have reached the same result against private actors: in 2021 the Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court awarded 7 million won in damages against a beauty academy that barred a transgender student's restroom use.

Recognition has liberalised nationally, not only in the capital. On 8 May 2024 the court in Yeongdong approved male-to-female gender-marker change for five transgender people without sex reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that every human being has the right to live according to their gender identity. The national court guidelines that previously required surgery have been downgraded to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them (Yonhap, 8 May 2024). The ruling sits outside Seoul and bears on this jurisdiction as evidence of the national judicial trend.

31927357B30293642818187.name: Quintana Roo
31927357B30293642818187.summary:
Quintana Roo stands under Mexico's national framework, where extending legal gender recognition to trans people remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a recognition procedure by that date, while six states (Aguascalientes, Chiapas, Durango, Querétaro, Tabasco and Tamaulipas) had reformed nothing, leaving trans residents carrying documents permanently mismatched to their lived identity. The same feature documents coercive detention and border scrutiny risks for travellers whose documents contradict their presentation, a hazard that falls hardest where recognition procedures are absent or obstructed.

Quintana Roo is among the states that enacted legal gender recognition in 2020, so a visitor's documents are not automatically a point of friction at the state level. Same-sex marriage has been permitted in the state since 2012: two marriages performed in Kantunilkín in November 2011 were annulled by the governor in April 2012, then reinstated on 3 May 2012 once the state conceded that its Civil Code sets no gender requirement. The state congress legalized adoption by same-sex couples in August 2022, and the state ratified the 2011 federal constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination.

Protection machinery inside the state is explicit. The Quintana Roo penal code punishes crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender as hate crimes. On 15 December 2023 the Quintana Roo congress, following Morelos, banned conversion practices, prohibiting and sanctioning 'Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género' (ECOSIG), commonly called conversion therapies. Practitioners face two to six years in prison and fines of 1,000 to 2,000 times the daily UMA value, and the reform applies across the state, including the tourist corridors of Cancún and the Riviera Maya.

31927357B30293642818187.tangentialFactors:
Partnership recognition is settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction. Cancún is counted among the country's principal gay-tourism destinations, which shapes the commercial surface a visitor meets without altering the legal framework described above.

Violence against trans people intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap. Mexico City's Congress approved the 'Paola Buenrostro law' in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety.

Inter-American authorities have pressed the same point. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Where recognition is delayed, the consequences are concrete. The Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, set against killings including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

The gap between statute and practice is the recurring national finding. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

15666254B89722251658211.name: Selangor
15666254B89722251658211.summary:
Selangor stands under the national framework of Malaysia. At federal level, sections 377A to 377D of the Penal Code criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping; the Human Dignity Trust country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records that these provisions have been enforced in recent years, apply to both men and women, and are usable against transgender people. They are not limited to Malaysian citizens and reach foreign visitors.

At state level, every one of the 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

Selangor is the state where the religious-enforcement apparatus has been most publicly exercised against gender expression. In 2021 the transgender cosmetics entrepreneur Nur Sajat failed to appear in a Selangor Sharia court to answer criminal charges of "insulting Islam" grounded in her attire; the state religious department issued a warrant for her arrest and announced that it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, then sought her extradition from Thailand. She was permitted to remain under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, in a report released on 10 August 2022, cite the deployment as evidence of how far Malaysian authorities go to enforce rigid gender norms.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. In 2021 the Federal Court struck down provisions of the Selangor Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding state power, on federalism grounds; the Penal Code offences remain fully intact. A Selangor Sharia court has also sentenced five men to six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane.

State-backed restriction is ongoing. A crackdown on LGBT people has run since the 2018 election, and at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021; Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters found such programmes to internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Selangor Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.

15666254B42356713390762.name: Johor
15666254B42356713390762.summary:
Johor stands under the national framework of Malaysia, which criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at two levels. Sections 377A to 377D of the federal Penal Code punish same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping, apply to men and women alike, and are not limited to Malaysian citizens. In November 2023 the Johor government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people. No protective or tolerant regime specific to Johor is on record, and public-morality offences in the state are enforced through its religious authorities, the channel Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters document as driving state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia.

Malaysia provides no legal mechanism for gender recognition, so identity documents are read as issued, and the country has neither same-sex marriage nor an anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.

15666254B45695250728659.name: Malacca
15666254B45695250728659.summary:
Malacca stands under Malaysia's national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the Federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise same-sex sexual activity with a maximum of twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping, and section 377D, 'outrages on decency', criminalises gross indecency in terms the Human Dignity Trust records as usable against transgender people. These offences are not limited to Malaysian citizens and reach visitors in Malacca.

The Sharia layer reaches Malacca as well. Every one of Malaysia's thirteen states maintains an enactment criminalising cross-dressing or 'a man posing as a woman', with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those offences apply to Muslims only, are enforced by state Islamic religious departments, and contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing. Three of the thirteen states also bar women from posing as men.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and sixteen Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact; a High Court had already refused to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014, following the mass arrest of sixteen trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement is documented as active rather than dormant. The Human Dignity Trust profile, last updated in 2024, records evidence of the law being enforced in recent years and a crackdown on the LGBT community since the 2018 election. The Human Rights Watch report of 10 August 2022, produced with Justice For Sisters, concludes that pervasive official antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity shapes law enforcement, judicial outcomes and public discourse.

Transgender people in Malaysia are documented as particularly vulnerable to physical and verbal abuse, against a backdrop of consistent reports of discrimination and violence. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months, and case documentation records police mistreatment and impunity. In 2021 the prominent transgender woman Nur Sajat was prosecuted in Selangor and fled the country after threats of arrest, subsequently receiving UNHCR protection; 122 religious officers had been mobilised against her for 'insulting Islam'.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor in Malacca, the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, with media pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked; more than 130 people were held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened, and a magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground. Police raided a second sauna in Penang days later.

There is no same-sex marriage, no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination law in Malaysia. Visible gender nonconformity in Malacca is exposed to the same public-morality and religious enforcement that operates nationwide, and the heritage-tourism setting offers no recorded protection.

27671186B76269877687363.name: Abuja Federal Capital Territory
27671186B76269877687363.summary:
Abuja Federal Capital Territory stands under Nigeria's national framework with no territorial carve-out. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforces colonial-era offences of "carnal knowledge against the order of nature" punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment, and its own provisions carry 10 to 14 years for same-sex cohabitation, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advisory, as reported by Sahara Reporters, adds that the law reaches people who help arrange or conduct same-sex marriages and criminalises activities involving gay groups and organisations.

The same advisory warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, and states that some states operating under Sharia law can impose the death penalty. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that police have used the 2014 Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest, and that the statute reaches far beyond marriage.

A trans visitor should treat the territory as a place where a documented killing has gone unpunished. On 8 August 2024 the beaten, bruised body of 33-year-old transgender TikToker "Abuja Area Mama" was found along the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in the Banex/Wuse II area of Abuja, hours after she posted a final video and having previously expressed fear for her life. A police statement described the victim as "a man fully dressed in female clothing with no means of identification". The Abuja police chief, Benneth Igweh, ordered a thorough and discreet investigation; six months later no suspects had been charged. A petition of nearly 6,000 signatures demands investigation of the killing as a hate crime, and a human-rights group has sued the national government and the police for failing to investigate, seeking a court order compelling investigation and prosecution after multiple petitions were ignored.

Everyday enforcement is extortionate and violent. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, which makes dating apps an active entrapment vector rather than a social convenience.

Gender presentation carries exposure independent of identity documents. There is no legal route in Nigeria to change gender. Cross-dressing is banned under Sharia law in twelve states and in the Nigerian military, and Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live under fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available. Police in the Area Mama case recorded her as a man in female clothing, indicating how an officer's report can fix a trans person's legal status at the scene.

Detention carries a further uncertainty: placement between male and female sections is left to official discretion. Press coverage at the sentencing of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in.
