1875124B65618634887963.name: Lima
1875124B65618634887963.summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national framework has recently moved against trans people's access to public space. On 2 April 2025 the Plenary of Congress approved, exempt from a second vote, the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, later promulgated as the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents. Article 5 of the text prohibits entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated, with listed exceptions. The provision passed after a February 2025 approval, unanimously, by the Women and Family Commission on the Muñante initiative, and it also bars inclusive signage of the kind the international airport in Lima had installed, signage reading "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity".

IDEHPUCP, the human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, published an analysis of the rule on 15 April 2025 by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte. They describe it as direct legislation conditioning basic rights on "biological sex" and as a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle, and note that trans people, though the rule frames them as aggressors, are more often the victims of violence and discrimination. LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho, quoted on the February 2025 approval, called the measure discriminatory and described what enforcement would amount to in practice: security staff deciding on their own judgement whether a woman entering a restroom is trans, and demanding her national identity document (DNI).

That enforcement mechanism reaches private business and public life in Lima. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that applied the policy. On television, Willax TV presenter Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to go use the men's room. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Violence against trans people in Peru is documented and, on its own figures, under-recorded. The TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report, published by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, recorded 54 murders of LGBTI people and 170 reports of rights violations between 2020 and 2023. More than half of the dead were trans women (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. 2023 was the year with the most homicides, 19, and in 26 of the 54 killings no suspects were identified. In central Lima, on 12 February 2023, the "Los Gallegos" extortion gang abducted the transgender sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, from jirón Chancay and killed her with roughly 30 gunshots. The report flags state inaction: no official system records victims' sexual orientation, and hate crimes go unsanctioned. Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender and a co-author of the 2024 hate-crime research, has stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

Two convictions and one legal reversal sit alongside the violence record. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly twenty years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, according to BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights. In July 2025 a constitutional court in Lima, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

The country's protections were weakened on paper well before the bathroom law. In 2017 Peru's Congress voted to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. The April 2025 law also constrains speech and association: vague child-protection articles, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

25984515B47806653651907.name: Ankara
25984515B47806653651907.summary:
Ankara stands within Turkey's national framework, where hostility toward LGBTI people has hardened into explicit state policy rather than residual prejudice. Kaos GL's annual report "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", launched in 2025, places the hostility at the presidency, identifies the Ministry of Family as the implementing ministry, and records censorship of broadcasts, cancellation or banning of artistic events, and the closure of an LGBTI+ association for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members.

The same report documents six violations of the right to life during the year, three of them recorded as hate-motivated, with transgender people the most affected. It records a rise in torture and ill-treatment violations to 89 from 51 the previous year, and states that the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics.

The leaked draft "11th Judicial Package", reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years' imprisonment, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years, and courts could order pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft. The package had not been enacted when reported, and its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

25984515B12971548112787.name: Eskişehir
25984515B12971548112787.summary:
Eskişehir stands under the national framework applicable in Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes with articles criminalising behaviour "contrary to biological sex and general morality" and its "promotion", carrying up to three years' prison through an amendment to the indecent-acts provision. The same package would impose sharp restrictions on gender-affirming care, including a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility requirements, and could expose trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists to charges. The government justified the measures as protecting "the family and public morals".

Eskişehir is one of the country's few interior cities with a functioning Pride tradition, and that tradition has been suppressed by force. In June 2021 police blocked the city's first Pride parade. Duvar English reported that officers reached the assembly area hours before the scheduled start time and carried out identity checks; organisers were not permitted to hold a press meeting or conduct the march, and police detained 20 people on the grounds of violating the ban on the march. The intervention came days after police actions against Pride events in Istanbul and Ankara, and Turkish authorities have repeatedly banned Pride events in recent years on security and public-order grounds.

The legal baseline residents and visitors encounter is mixed. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and trans people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, subject to surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised.

Pride has been banned in most years since 2015, with participants facing police attacks. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries. In early 2026 Turkish media reported that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex"; that provision was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package.

25984515B63001774148772.name: Gaziantep
25984515B63001774148772.summary:
Gaziantep stands under the national framework of Turkey in full, with no documented local divergence in either direction: a visibly trans visitor to the province faces the same legal exposure, the same document checks and the same enforcement climate as elsewhere in the country, applied by provincial authorities under national law.

The most serious pending threat is a leaked 11th Judicial Package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour "contrary to biological sex and general morality" and its "promotion", carrying up to three years' imprisonment through an amended indecent-acts provision, and would sharply restrict gender-affirming care through a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility requirements. Human Rights Watch states the package could support charges against trans people themselves, against care providers, against civil-society organisations and against journalists, and that the government justified it as protecting "the family and public morals".

Enforcement in Gaziantep rests on the same meeting-and-demonstration law applied elsewhere. Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records that in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans pride marches, that police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and that more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still continuing at the end of the year.

Official hostility is stated in terms that operate before any charge is laid. Turkish authorities must carry, and foreign visitors are required to produce, original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Police stop-and-check practice against trans women, documented in Istanbul during 2025, involves detention for "General Information Gathering" background checks in which documents are compared against presentation; a foreigner stopped in Gaziantep is exposed to the same comparison.

Violence risk is documented rather than incidental. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in Turkey during 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. The pattern of state response is asymmetric: in August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker, who was released while the victim was referred for arrest.

Human Rights Watch states the package could support charges against trans people themselves, against care providers, against civil-society organisations and against journalists, and that the government justified it as protecting "the family and public morals".

Enforcement in the province rests on the same meeting-and-demonstration law applied elsewhere. Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records that in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans pride marches, that police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and that more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still continuing at the end of the year.

Official hostility is stated in terms that operate before any charge is laid. Foreign visitors are required to produce original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 national lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Police stop-and-check practice against trans women, documented during 2025, involves detention for "General Information Gathering" background checks in which documents are compared against presentation; a foreigner stopped in the province is exposed to the same comparison.

Violence risk is documented rather than incidental. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence during 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. The pattern of state/province response is asymmetric: in August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in a national city by a 17-year-old attacker, who was released while the victim was referred for arrest.

25984515B18786507826220.name: İstanbul
25984515B18786507826220.summary:
İstanbul stands under the national framework in force across Turkey, where hostility toward LGBTI+ people has been formalised as state policy. Kaos GL's 2025 annual report, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", records that pattern operating in İstanbul directly, including intensified practices of sealing or closing the homes of LGBTI+ residents that obstruct access to housing.

The same monitoring counts six violations of the right to life across Turkey in 2025, three of them recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people the group most affected. Torture and ill-treatment violations nearly doubled, rising to 89 from 51. One LGBTI+ association was closed and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members. The state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on civil-society monitoring rather than on government record-keeping.

Street-level policing in İstanbul targets trans women specifically. On 31 July 2025 police in the Beyoğlu district stopped around 20 trans women for identity checks, recorded their names and filmed video of the encounters; those stopped described the operation as profiling. Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which makes every check an occasion on which a passport gender marker can be compared against presentation.

Public assembly is closed to LGBTI+ people in the city. The Governorship of İstanbul has denied permission for and locally banned pride parades on security and public-order grounds since 2015, with the 2016 to 2018 bans stated explicitly. Police used water cannon against the march on 29 June 2015. Suppression escalated thereafter: blockades and tear gas in 2021 with 25 arrested; 373 arrested in 2022; 113 arrested in 2023; and 11 arrests in 2024, three of them minors.

The 2022 operation is documented in detail. On 26 June 2022 riot police dispersed the march at Taksim Square, blockaded streets in the nearby Cihangir neighbourhood and shut down public transport to the square, detaining 373 people including AFP photojournalist Bülent Kılıç, who were released after a night in custody according to Kaos GL. The district governor's offices of Kadıköy and Beyoğlu had banned all LGBTI+ Pride Week events for seven days beforehand, and eight further people were detained at a Pride march in İzmir.

Organisers' adaptations have not reopened the space. In 2024 İstanbul Pride was moved to non-Taksim public spaces and organisers issued fake meeting calls to thwart police, after which 11 people were arrested, three of them minors. The scale of what is now prohibited is established by the 2014 march, which drew more than 100,000 participants and remains the largest LGBT event in Turkey's history.

The İstanbul figures sit inside a national pattern of detention. Kaos GL's report, the Truth Justice Memory Center's Pride monitoring and NGO coordination through Human Rights Association branches are the working evidence base, which means figures can be contested by authorities in a way that state-recorded data would not be.

25984515B59477790330217.name: İzmir
25984515B59477790330217.summary:
İzmir stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward LGBT people has hardened into documented state policy. The Kaos GL report "A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy" records 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year, with detentions, arrests and criminal cases against Pride participants identified as the main reasons. The same report documents 89 torture or ill-treatment violations and six violations of the right to life, three of them recorded as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. For the first time in many years an LGBTI+ association was closed and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members for human rights advocacy.

A leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality and its promotion with up to three years' prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. It would amend Civil Code Article 40 to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing interventions deemed illegal would face fines and up to seven years' prison, trans people receiving such care up to three years, and courts would be able to order pretrial detention. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns that it would push treatment into unregulated underground settings. The draft had not been reported as enacted, and its pending status has not stopped authorities from acting on its logic.

Document checks are the routine point of contact between a trans visitor and the security forces. On 31 July 2025 police in the entertainment district of Istanbul carried out a mass roundup of trans women, recording their names and filming them without giving any official reason. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identity at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any stop therefore becomes an occasion on which a passport is read against presentation, which is a direct outing risk for a visitor whose appearance does not match the gender marker.

İzmir's own record cuts against its reputation as the country's most secular city. The 13th Pride Week and its events were banned, and in May and June 2025 police broke up Pride-related public events with batons, tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets. A visible trans community operates here, but visibility has attracted the same coercive response documented in Istanbul, and Pride organisation itself is treated as a target for prohibition rather than a protected assembly.

66186276B86072070009793.name: Puerto Rico
66186276B86072070009793.summary:
Puerto Rico is a US territory, and the full United States federal framework applies on the island: statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, screening, federally funded care and federal custody. The territory's own legislation does not soften that framework; in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and the January 2025 executive order eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents presents a marker that may not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened further for one category of traveller: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Airport screening follows federal Transportation Security Administration procedure at Puerto Rico's airports. All luggage is screened and may be hand-searched; prosthetics including breast forms are treated as medically necessary items and are not subject to the three-liquid rule, and medical equipment is admitted through the checkpoint after screening. The National Center for Transgender Equality's guidance advises packing strategies that reduce the frequency of invasive searches, and a visitor should expect screening to be conducted on those terms.

Care access during a visit cannot be assumed. The January 2025 order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in Puerto Rico, and the territory's own statute compounds it: in July 2025 the governor signed a ban on trans youth care that reporting describes as the most severe such restriction in any US jurisdiction.

The 2025 law was pushed through non-public hearings and is deliberately vague, so clinicians and affirming parents who facilitate hormone therapy or top surgery risk prosecution. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the "risks" of trans-affirming care. The Health Secretary, Carlos Mellado...

This is federal TSA procedure and applies at Puerto Rico airports.

Rossello announced SB1253 ('clarify religious freedom principles') and SB1254 (conversion-therapy ban with pastoral exemption); LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allies said the pair would open discrimination doors, criticizing the religious-freedom carve-out as license to refuse service on orientation/gender-identity grounds.

Road to marriage equality in PR ran through federal court.

Washington Blade (18 Mar 2019): the pro-statehood NPP caucus in the PR House blocked a floor vote on SB1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors; Sen. Zoe Laboy (co-sponsor) dissented publicly. Conversion-therapy ban died in the House despite Senate passage and governor support.

Washington Blade (13 Jun 2019): Gov. Rossello asked lawmakers to withdraw SB1253/SB1254 amid sustained opposition; his April announcement had included a pastoral-capacity exemption for clergy in the conversion-therapy ban. Record of LGBT advocates defeating the religious-freedom bill pairing.

Erin in the Morning (2025): PR enacted a trans youth care ban pushed through non-public hearings; law is deliberately vague so doctors and affirming parents facilitating HRT or top surgery risk prosecution; mandates Education/Health department campaigns on 'risks' of trans-affirming care; Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments allowing puberty blockers and continuation of existing HRT, but the enacted text is the most extreme care restriction in US jurisdictions per the report.

sources.title: Executive Order 14168 ("Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government") - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Executive Order 14168 (signed 20 January 2025) directs US federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognize only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by placing transgender inmates in facilities congruent with their sex assigned at birth rather than their asserted gender identity. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order violates the Prison Rape Elimination Act's requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided on an individual safety assessment. Federal custody rules apply in Puerto Rico as a US territory. No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit, or ruling was located.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002, but after the U.S. Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 struck down all state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute. In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for it, and threatened doctors who violate the ban with up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine, and permanent loss of their licenses; the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court. An anti-discrimination bill (House Bill 1725) passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 and would have barred discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, public transportation and public facilities, business transactions and housing, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. The 2013 law that did pass (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities remain uncovered. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018, and a similar 2019 bill was withdrawn by Rosselló on 13 June 2019 after House approval amid protests. Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the U.S. federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. 2020 was the first year anyone in Puerto Rico was charged with a hate crime: Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged after Bonilla confessed that he and Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island. In 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488 (signed 29 May 2013) extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.

SYN-ASM.name: American Samoa
SYN-ASM.summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies: EO 14168 on binary sex classification in documents, federal facilities and care funding; EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding; and EO 14201 on athletic participation, the last paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all United States identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents; and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker, available from 2022, has been eliminated for new applications. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, with the policy contested in federal courts.

Marriage recognition is unsettled in practice. The Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it, so the territory declined a formal ban before Obergefell. In July 2015 the territory's attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was still under review, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the CNMI moved to apply it. In January 2016 the newly confirmed District Court judge Fiti Alexander Sunia told the Senate he had not read Obergefell, that the district court does not deal with the ruling, and that he would not perform same-sex weddings absent a change in local law. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that Obergefell does apply and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied, while recording that no same-sex couple has applied to date and setting out a litigation route through the High Court of American Samoa, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, and then the US Department of the Interior. As of July 2024 an on-island survey by Miami University professor Daniel Hall was still testing whether the local ban would survive a 14th Amendment challenge, indicating that the ban is treated locally as operative and its durability as an open question, more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of marriages performed elsewhere.

Trans people in the territory have obtained protection through national enforcement machinery. In September 2023 the US Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, and in June 2023 a federal civil action had cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Social conditions differ from the legal picture. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, are described in university research material as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, with colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of indigenous gender identities; the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, re-anchored to cultural pride. Travel guidance describes homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture, in contrast to Fiji, while noting that Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism and that reserved behaviour by people of all orientations is expected. Fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified at the 2003 committee hearing that Samoan fa'afafine do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing.

sources.summary: The UH Manoa libraries research guide on Pacific gender identities, last updated 2026-07-23, states that the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride: 'we are fa'afafine Samoa'. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent (2015-07-10): American Samoa was then the only US territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied — its AG said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

sources.title: American Samoa Senate rejects bill outlawing same sex marriages (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. The territory therefore deliberately declined a formal marriage ban before Obergefell, and the hearing records contemporaneous local fa'afafine views on the question.

sources.title: American Samoa judge objects to same sex marriage (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. The exchange shows that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise that the ruling did not automatically apply.

sources.title: The Ambiguity that Isn't: Why Same-Sex Marriage Is Legal in American Samoa (Harootunian & Lawrence, American University JGSPL vol 33 iss 2 (2026) pp 163-207)
sources.summary: 2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. The article is the most recent dated authority on whether the 2015 ruling is operative in American Samoa, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality.

sources.title: Survey conducted on-island focuses on local same sex marriage ban (Samoa News, Asi Andrew Fa'asau, Pago Pago)
sources.summary: Samoa News reported in July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether American Samoa's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment. The survey also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question (collectivistic vs individualistic orientation; linear vs polychronic time). As of mid-2024, nine years after Obergefell and more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of outside marriages (Dec 13 2022), the local ban is treated on-island as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.

SYN-ASM.tangentialFactors:
American Samoa was the only US territory that had not moved to apply the 2015 federal marriage ruling, alongside which Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands had already done so; no marriage licence application had been made in American Samoa at that point either.

Contemporary travel commentary contrasts the territory with Fiji, describing homophobia as rampant there while presenting homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture, and notes that the fa'amatai chiefly system structures social life across both Samoan nations. Local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin has called the Samoan islands the homeland of fa'afafine culture. Accommodation in the territory skews toward business travel, with hotels such as Tradewinds in Pago Pago.

Guidance for trans and nonbinary travellers on document rules is published by Lambda Legal, covering which documents to consider, how name and gender changes interact with national records, and the current status of document updates; HRC's 2025 travel guidance sets out the passport posture for trans travellers under the same executive order. SYN-GUM.name: Guam
SYN-GUM.summary:
Guam stands under the full United States federal framework as an unincorporated US territory. United States passports and other federal travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X gender marker was eliminated by a January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents faces a mismatch between document and presentation at entry.

Screening at Guam's airport follows federal Transport Security Administration procedure. The agency's body-scanner and pat-down protocols can disclose a trans traveller's status to officers; travellers may request an alternative screening method and escalate problems on the spot, and most trans travellers pass screening without incident.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in Guam, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed.

In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports, a rule that applies to arrivals here.

Guam recognises same-sex marriage. Chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down the territory's prohibition on 5 June 2015, following an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero after they were denied a licence; the ruling took effect at 8am on 9 June 2015 and made Guam the first US territory to recognise such marriages.

The guide covers pre-flight packing, document and screening mismatches, the right to request alternative screening, and how to escalate airport problems. Most trans travellers pass screening without incident. TSA screening procedures apply in Guam as a US territory.

SYN-GUM.tangentialFactors:
A January 2025 executive order bans transgender troops from serving openly in the United States military and directed Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to submit an implementation plan within 30 days, framing trans identity as 'radical gender ideology'. Guam hosts a large permanent United States military presence, so the exclusion reaches a substantial share of the island's residents and workplaces rather than a marginal group.

The federal measures on markers, screening and military service bear directly on an island whose economy and society are shaped by that permanent basing, which also concentrates federal employers and federally funded providers in a small jurisdiction.

Guam's 2015 marriage ruling shows the territory courts have at times moved ahead of, or independently of, the federal political branches on recognition, even as the document, screening and funding rules imposed from Washington now govern entry and care here.

Trans service members and applicants within Guam's substantial military community are barred from serving openly under the January 2025 order.

Residents have been able to marry a same-sex partner since 9 June 2015, under the ruling of the United States District Court for the District of Guam.

SYN-VIR.name: United States Virgin Islands
SYN-VIR.summary:
The U.S. Virgin Islands stands under the full United States federal framework, and that framework sets what a trans visitor faces at the border. United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker was eliminated by executive order in January 2025, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents faces a mismatch between document and presentation at entry. Airport screening follows federal procedure: Transportation Security Administration body scanners can flag trans bodies and trigger secondary screening and pat-downs, and travellers may request alternative screening or decline the scanner.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed. In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

The territorial layer runs the other way. The Virgin Islands human-rights law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, and in March 2017 the Attorney General ruled that the territory's anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, an official interpretation extending territorial protections. Same-sex marriage has been legal since a 2015 territorial Superior Court ruling struck down the denial of marriage licences to same-sex couples, later settled nationwide by federal recognition. The historic sodomy statute, applied from 1957, has been replaced. None of this alters federal document rules, federal screening, or federal funding decisions, and no territorial statute softens them.

The contrast between layers is the main turbulence a visitor should expect. Territorial protections on gender identity and the 2017 Attorney General interpretation sit beneath a national document regime, a national screening procedure and national funding and visa decisions that operate independently of them, so a visitor can be simultaneously protected against private discrimination and exposed at the federal touchpoints of entry, screening, care funding and, for athletes, visa issuance.

SYN-MNP.name: Northern Mariana Islands
SYN-MNP.summary:
The Northern Mariana Islands is a US commonwealth and stands under the national framework of the United States for travel documents, immigration and airport screening. United States passports and entry documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker option was eliminated by the January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents presents a gender marker that may not match presentation at the port of entry.

Screening at the airport follows federal procedure, and the order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to such care during a visit cannot be assumed. In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

There is no criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct or of gender expression under Commonwealth law. Commonwealth Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, amends the Commonwealth Code to set criteria for enhanced sentencing in hate-motivated crimes, and the statute covers offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity; this is the principal local protection a visitor would be able to invoke after an identity-based assault, though the sources do not document how it has been applied.

Legal gender recognition exists in the territory, but only on condition that the applicant has undergone the specified medical process. A visitor relying on locally issued documents rather than a United States passport should expect that medical requirement to apply.

There is no comprehensive local nondiscrimination ordinance covering gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations. Beyond federal law, protection extends only to government employees, leaving private-sector and service-access discrimination to be pursued through federal EEOC recourse.
